questions.q: Which of the following rivers flows into the Arabian Sea?
questions.solution: The Ganga, Godavari, and Krishna flow into the Bay of Bengal (East). The Narmada is a major exception among peninsular rivers as it flows westwards into the Arabian Sea.

questions.q: What is the primary season for Rabi crops?
questions.solution: Rabi crops are sown in winter (October-November) and harvested in spring. They rely on residual soil moisture or canal irrigation rather than direct monsoon rain.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which mountain range is the oldest in India?
questions.solution: The Aravalli Range is the oldest fold mountain system in India, dating back to the Precambrian era. The Himalayas are geologically young fold mountains.

questions.q: In which state is the highest peak of India, Kanchenjunga, located?
questions.solution: Kanchenjunga (8,598 m) is located in the state of Sikkim. It stands on the border between India and Nepal.

questions.q: Which crop is primarily grown during the Kharif season?
questions.solution: Rice is a classic Kharif crop requiring heavy water from monsoon rains. Wheat, Mustard, and Gram are Rabi crops grown in winter.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the hydrological regime distinction between Himalayan and Peninsular rivers as per the National Perspective Plan?
questions.a: Himalayan rivers are perennial due to snowmelt and monsoon rain, while Peninsular rivers are rain-fed with sharp seasonal pulse.
opts: Himalayan rivers are rain-fed with 70-80% runoff in June-September, while Peninsular rivers are perennial due to glacier melt.
Himalayan rivers are perennial due to snowmelt and monsoon rain, while Peninsular rivers are rain-fed with sharp seasonal pulse.
Both Himalayan and Peninsular rivers are perennial, but Himalayan rivers have higher discharge due to larger catchment area.
Peninsular rivers receive meltwater from permanent snowfields, making them perennial unlike rain-fed Himalayan rivers.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: Himalayan rivers (Ganga, Brahmaputra, Indus) are perennial because they receive meltwater from permanent snowfields and glaciers in addition to monsoon rain. Peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, etc.) are rain-fed, showing a sharp seasonal pulse where 70-80% of annual runoff occurs between June and September, and many reaches become dry in the lean season. Option B matches this description exactly. Option A reverses the regimes. Option C incorrectly claims both are perennial. Option D incorrectly attributes snowmelt to Peninsular rivers.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Match the mineral belt with its flagship mineral(s) as per the National Mineral Policy 2019 and geological provinces described:
opts: Chotanagpur Plateau - Gold and Iron ore
Singhbhum Shear Zone - Lead-Zinc and Wollastonite
questions.solution: The lesson provides explicit belt-mineral mappings: (i) Chotanagpur Plateau - iron ore (hematite) and coal; (ii) Dharwar Craton - gold (Kolar) and iron ore (Bababudan); (iii) Singhbhum Shear Zone - copper and uranium (Jaduguda); (iv) Aravalli Range - lead-zinc (Rampura-Agucha), wollastonite, gypsum; (v) Himalayan belt - limestone and dolomite; (vi) Kerala coast - rare earths (monazite sands). Option D correctly matches Aravalli Range with lead-zinc (Rampura-Agucha). Option A incorrectly assigns gold to Chotanagpur (gold is in Dharwar). Option B assigns copper-uranium to Dharwar (they are in Singhbhum). Option C assigns lead-zinc to Singhbhum (they are in Aravalli).
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: According to the Central Ground Water Board, a stage of groundwater development exceeding what percentage indicates over‑exploitation of an assessment unit?
questions.solution: The stage of groundwater development is defined as the ratio of annual groundwater extraction to annual recharge, expressed as a percentage. The CGWB classifies units as over‑exploited when this ratio surpasses 100 %, meaning extraction exceeds the renewable recharge. The lesson explicitly states that a stage >100 % signals over‑exploitation, making 100 % the threshold.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which statement about the 2019 Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) notification is correct?
questions.a: It retained the 500 m HTL buffer and added a hazard line.
opts: It retained the 500 m HTL buffer and added a hazard line.
It removed the 500 m HTL buffer.
It reduced the buffer to 200 m.
questions.solution: The lesson notes a common misconception that the 2019 CRZ notification removed the 500 m High Tide Line buffer; in fact, it retained that buffer and introduced an additional hazard line for better risk mapping. Therefore, the only accurate description among the options is that the 500 m HTL buffer was kept and a hazard line was added.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct use of the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) fund?

questions.q: Night‑time Urban Heat Island intensity is often stronger than daytime intensity and is more relevant for heat‑health impacts.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that treating UHI intensity as a daytime phenomenon only is a misconception; night‑time UHI is often stronger and more relevant for heat‑health impacts. Hence the statement is true.

questions.q: Which soil order in India is characterized by a cation exchange capacity (CEC) of approximately 40‑60 cmol kg⁻¹ due to smectite dominance?
questions.solution: The lesson states that Black soils of the Deccan trap have a CEC of 40‑60 cmol kg⁻¹ because of high smectite clay content, whereas Alluvial soils have CEC 20‑30, Red soils are lower, and Laterite soils are heavily leached. Therefore the correct choice is Black (Regur) soil.

questions.q: As of 2022, what is the approximate national gap between irrigation potential created (IPC) and irrigation potential utilised (IPU) in India?

questions.q: What is the maximum installed capacity for a project to be classified as "small hydro" under Indian policy?

questions.q: What percentage of the summer flow in the Indus basin is contributed by glacier melt?

questions.q: Which battle marked the beginning of British political power in India?

questions.q: If the radius of a circle is doubled, how does its area change?
questions.solution: The area of a circle is proportional to the square of the radius (A = πr²). If the radius (r) is multiplied by 2, the new area becomes π(2r)² = 4πr². Thus, the area increases by a factor of 4.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: What is the formula for the Curved Surface Area (CSA) of a cylinder?
questions.solution: The Curved Surface Area refers to the lateral surface excluding the top and bottom bases. The formula is 2 × π × radius × height, written as 2πrh.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A cube has a side length of 5 cm. What is its volume?
questions.solution: The volume of a cube is calculated by cubing the side length (Side × Side × Side). For a side of 5, Volume = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Which shape has a volume formula involving '4/3'?
questions.solution: The volume of a sphere is given by the unique formula (4/3)πr³. Cones involve 1/3, while cuboids and cylinders do not use this fraction.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: If the diameter of a circle is 14 cm, what is its circumference?
questions.solution: The circumference formula is πd (pi times diameter). With d=14 and π=22/7, the calculation is (22/7) × 14 = 22 × 2 = 44 cm.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A right circular cylinder has a fixed total surface area of 924 cm². For maximum volume, what should be its radius? (Use π = 22/7)
questions.solution: For a cylinder with given total surface area S, volume is maximum when height h = 2r. Total surface area S = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 2πr(2r) = 6πr². Given S = 924 cm² and π = 22/7, we have 6 × (22/7) × r² = 924 → (132/7) r² = 924 → r² = 924 × 7 / 132 = 49 → r = 7 cm.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Two frustums of cones are similar. The ratio of their corresponding radii is 2 : 5. What is the ratio of their volumes?
questions.solution: For similar solids, linear dimensions scale by factor k. Here k = 2/5. Volume scales by k³. So volume ratio = (2³) : (5³) = 8 : 125.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A closed right circular cylinder is to be made from a fixed surface area of 150π cm². For maximum volume, what is the volume of the cylinder? (Use π = 22/7)
questions.solution: For maximum volume with fixed surface area, h = 2r. Surface area S = 2πr(r+h) = 2πr(3r) = 6πr² = 150π ⇒ r² = 25 ⇒ r = 5 cm, h = 10 cm. Volume = πr²h = π×25×10 = 250π = 250×(22/7) = 5500/7 ≈ 785.7 cm³.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A right circular cylinder of maximum possible volume is inscribed in a sphere of radius 9 cm. What is the volume of this cylinder? (Use π = 22/7, √3 ≈ 1.732)
questions.solution: For a cylinder inscribed in a sphere, maximum volume = (4π/3√3)R³. With R = 9 cm, R³ = 729. Volume = (4×22/7)/(3×1.732) × 729 = (88/7)/(5.196) × 729 ≈ 12.571/5.196 × 729 ≈ 2.419 × 729 ≈ 1763 cm³.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: How many trailing zeros does 250! have?
questions.solution: Trailing zeros equal the exponent of 5 in 250! (Legendre's formula). Compute floor(250/5) = 50, floor(250/25) = 10, floor(250/125) = 2, floor(250/625) = 0. Sum = 50 + 10 + 2 = 62. Thus 250! ends with 62 zeros.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: What is the least positive integer x such that 3^x ≡ 1 (mod 16)?
questions.solution: For modulus 16=2^4, Carmichael function λ(16)=2^{4-2}=4. Since gcd(3,16)=1, the order of 3 divides λ(16)=4. Check 3^2=9≠1, 3^4=81≡1 (mod 16). Thus smallest exponent is 4.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Simplify √(11+√120).
questions.solution: For √(a+√b) to denest, a^2−b must be a perfect square. Here a=11, b=120, a^2−b=121−120=1=1^2. Then c=1. The denested form is √((a+c)/2)+√((a−c)/2) = √((11+1)/2)+√((11−1)/2) = √6+√5.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: What is the digital root of the product 12345 × 6789?
questions.solution: Digital root of 12345: 1+2+3+4+5=15→1+5=6. Digital root of 6789: 6+7+8+9=30→3+0=3. Digital root of product = digital root of (6×3=18) = 1+8=9. Hence the product's digital root is 9.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: The decimal number 156 is written in base 5. What is the sum of its digits in that base?
questions.solution: Convert 156 to base 5: 5^3=125 fits once, remainder 31. 5^2=25 fits once, remainder 6. 5^1=5 fits once, remainder 1. 5^0=1 fits once. The base‑5 representation is 1111₅. The sum of its digits is 1+1+1+1 = 4.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: If (121)_b = (100)_10, what is the value of base b?
questions.solution: Write the polynomial expansion: 1*b^2 + 2*b + 1 = 100. This simplifies to b^2 + 2b + 1 = 100, or (b+1)^2 = 100. Taking the positive square root gives b+1 = 10, so b = 9. The digits 1, 2, 1 are all less than 9, satisfying the base condition. Therefore the base is 9.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: How many litres of a 30% alcohol solution must be added to 20 litres of a 50% alcohol solution to obtain a 40% alcohol solution?
questions.solution: Let the required quantity of 30% solution be x litres. Using alligation: concentrations are 50% (C1) and 30% (C2), desired 40% (Cm). Ratio (Cm - C2) : (C1 - Cm) = (40-30) : (50-40) = 10 : 10 = 1 : 1. Hence the two solutions must be mixed in equal quantities. Since 20 litres of 50% solution is used, x = 20 litres of 30% solution is needed. Check: total alcohol = 20×0.5 + 20×0.3 = 10+6 = 16 litres; total volume = 40 litres; concentration = 16/40 = 40%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: An asset worth ₹50,000 depreciates at 15% per annum. What will be its value after 2 years?
questions.solution: Depreciation is a successive percentage decrease. Multiplier per year = (1 - 15/100) = 0.85. After 2 years, value = Initial × (0.85)^2 = 50000 × 0.7225 = ₹36,125. The overall percentage decrease = [1 - (0.85)^2] × 100 = (1 - 0.7225) × 100 = 27.75%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: The true discount on a sum due of Rs 1100 at 10% per annum for 1 year is?
questions.solution: True discount TD = S*r*t/(100+r*t). Here S=1100, r=10, t=1. TD = 1100*10*1/(100+10) = 11000/110 = 100. So true discount is Rs 100.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: For the cubic equation 2x³ − 5x² + 3x − 1 = 0, what is the product of its three roots?
questions.solution: For a polynomial aₙxⁿ + … + a₀, the product of roots = (−1)ⁿ a₀ / aₙ. Here n = 3, aₙ = 2, a₀ = −1. Product = (−1)³ × (−1) / 2 = (−1) × (−1) / 2 = 1/2 = 0.5.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: If 2^x = 3^y = 6^z, then which of the following relations is true?
questions.solution: Let the common value be k. Then 2 = k^{1/x}, 3 = k^{1/y}, 6 = k^{1/z}. Since 2 × 3 = 6, we have k^{1/x} × k^{1/y} = k^{1/z} ⇒ k^{1/x+1/y} = k^{1/z}. Equating exponents gives 1/x + 1/y = 1/z.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A bank offers a nominal interest rate of 12% per annum compounded quarterly. What is the effective annual rate (EAR)?
questions.solution: The quarterly periodic rate is 12%/4 = 3% = 0.03. The effective annual rate is (1 + 0.03)^4 - 1. Compute (1.03)^2 = 1.0609, then (1.0609)^2 = 1.12550881. Subtract 1 gives 0.12550881, i.e. 12.550881%. Rounded to two decimals, EAR = 12.55%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A sum of ₹50,000 grows to ₹66,550 in 3 years with interest compounded annually. What is the annual nominal rate of interest?
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: At 8% per annum, after how many whole years will the compound interest exceed the simple interest by at least 50%? (i.e., CI ≥ 1.5 × SI)
questions.solution: We need smallest integer T such that [(1.08)^T - 1] / (0.08 T) ≥ 1.5. Test T=10: (1.08)^10 ≈ 2.1589, CI factor = 1.1589, SI factor = 0.8, ratio = 1.449 < 1.5. T=11: (1.08)^11 ≈ 2.3316, CI factor = 1.3316, SI factor = 0.88, ratio = 1.513 ≥ 1.5. Thus T = 11 years.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A bank quotes a nominal rate of 12% per annum compounded monthly. What is the force of interest (δ) for this rate?
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A machine costing ₹10,00,000 must be replaced after 8 years. A sinking fund earning 8% per annum is set up with annual deposits at the end of each year. What is the required annual deposit?
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: In how many whole years will ₹5,000 grow to at least ₹8,000 at 9% per annum compounded annually?
questions.solution: Solve 5000(1.09)^n ≥ 8000 → (1.09)^n ≥ 1.6. Take natural logs: n ln(1.09) ≥ ln(1.6). ln(1.6) ≈ 0.4700, ln(1.09) ≈ 0.08618. n ≥ 0.4700/0.08618 ≈ 5.45. Since n must be an integer number of compounding periods and the amount must reach or exceed the target, round up to the next whole year: 6 years.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: The present value of a machine is ₹2,00,000. It depreciates at 15% per annum on written‑down value. What was its value 2 years ago?
questions.solution: Reverse depreciation: Past value = Present / (1 - r/100)ⁿ. Here r = 15, n = 2. Factor = (0.85)² = 0.7225. Past value = 200000 / 0.7225 = 276816 (approximately). Hence the value 2 years ago was ₹2,76,816.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A 5‑year bond with face value ₹1,000 pays an annual coupon of 8 %. If the prevailing market yield is 9 % per annum, what is the bond’s price (rounded to nearest rupee)?
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A loan of ₹10,00,000 is taken at 10 % annual interest, to be repaid in equal annual installments over 5 years, but with a balloon payment of ₹2,00,000 due at the end of year 5 in addition to the regular installment. What is the annual installment amount (rounded to nearest rupee)?
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Spot USD/INR = 83.00. 1‑year USD risk‑free rate = 4 %, 1‑year INR risk‑free rate = 7 %. According to covered interest rate parity, what is the 1‑year forward rate? If the market quotes a forward of 81.20, what is the arbitrage profit per USD 100,000 borrowed?
questions.solution: CIRP forward = Spot × (1+USD rate)/(1+INR rate) = 83 × 1.04/1.07 = 83 × 0.9719626 = 80.672 ≈ 80.68. Market forward 81.20 > 80.68, so INR is expensive forward. Arbitrage: borrow USD 100,000 at 4% → owe 104,000. Convert at spot: 100,000 × 83 = 83,00,000 INR. Invest at 7% → 83,00,000 × 1.07 = 88,81,000 INR. Sell INR forward at 81.20 → receive 88,81,000 / 81.20 = 1,09,370 USD. Repay loan 1,04,000 USD. Profit = 1,09,370 – 1,04,000 = USD 5,370.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A bond with face value Rs. 1,000 pays 8% coupon semi‑annually. The clean price is quoted at Rs. 980. Settlement occurs 45 days after the last coupon date; the coupon period is 182 days (actual/actual). What is the dirty price?
questions.solution: Semi‑annual coupon = 1,000 × 8% / 2 = Rs. 40. Accrued interest = 40 × (45/182) = 40 × 0.2472527 = Rs. 9.8901. Dirty price = clean price + accrued interest = 980 + 9.8901 = Rs. 989.8901 ≈ Rs. 989.89.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs. 20,000. Expected cash inflows are: Year 1: Rs. 5,000; Year 2: Rs. 7,000; Year 3: Rs. 9,000; Year 4: Rs. 4,000. Using a discount rate of 10% p.a., what is the Net Present Value (NPV)?
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A deferred perpetuity pays Rs. 1,000 per year with the first payment at the end of year 4. If the discount rate is 8% p.a., what is its present value?

questions.q: A person walks on an escalator at a constant rate of 2 steps per second. Walking with the escalator he counts 40 steps to reach the end. Walking against the escalator he counts 60 steps to reach the other end. The escalator moves at a constant speed. How many steps are visible on the escalator when it is stationary?
questions.solution: Let escalator speed be e steps/s and total visible steps N. With escalator: effective speed = 2+e, time t1 = 40/2 = 20 s, so N = (2+e)×20. Against escalator: effective speed = 2−e, time t2 = 60/2 = 30 s, so N = (2−e)×30. Equate: 20(2+e)=30(2−e) → 40+20e=60−30e → 50e=20 → e=0.4 steps/s. Then N = 20×(2+0.4)=20×2.4=48 steps.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A boat can row at 5 km/h in still water. The river flows at 3 km/h. The boat heads directly across a 1 km wide river (perpendicular to the banks). How far downstream (in metres) will the boat drift by the time it reaches the opposite bank?
questions.solution: Crossing speed across the river = boat speed in still water = 5 km/h (since heading is perpendicular). Time to cross = width / across speed = 1 km / 5 km/h = 0.2 h. During this time the river current carries the boat downstream at 3 km/h. Drift distance = current speed × time = 3 km/h × 0.2 h = 0.6 km = 600 m.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A journey consists of two parts. The first half of the total distance is covered at 40 km/h. The second half of the total time is covered at 60 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey (in km/h)?
questions.solution: Let total distance = 2D. First half distance D at 40 km/h takes time t₁ = D/40. Remaining distance D is covered at 60 km/h during the second half of total time. Let total time = 2T, then second half time = T. Distance in second half = 60×T = D → T = D/60. Total time = 2T = D/30. But total time also = t₁ + T = D/40 + D/60 = 5D/120 = D/24. Equating D/30 = D/24 is inconsistent; correct approach: total time = t₁ + t₂ where t₂ = D/60. So total time = D/40 + D/60 = 5D/120 = D/24. Average speed = total distance / total time = 2D / (D/24) = 48 km/h.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A vehicle must cover 300 km. The speed limit is 60 km/h. A mandatory rest of 30 minutes is required after every 2 hours of driving. What is the minimum total time to complete the journey?
questions.solution: Driving time at maximum speed = 300/60 = 5 h. Driving is split into 2 h, 2 h, 1 h segments. Rests occur after the first two 2‑hour segments: 2 rests × 0.5 h = 1 h. Total time = 5 + 1 = 6 h.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A person walks up a moving escalator in 30 seconds. When the escalator is stationary, he walks up in 50 seconds. How long would he take if he stands still on the moving escalator?
questions.solution: Use the harmonic relation for escalators: 1/t_e = 1/t_w - 1/t_s, where t_w = 30 s (walking on moving), t_s = 50 s (walking on stationary). 1/t_e = 1/30 - 1/50 = (5-3)/150 = 2/150 = 1/75. Hence t_e = 75 seconds.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s, cruises at 20 m/s for 30 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. It then rests for 15 s. What is the average speed for the whole journey?
questions.solution: Distance during acceleration = ½ × 20 × 10 = 100 m. Cruise distance = 20 × 30 = 600 m. Deceleration distance = ½ × 20 × 5 = 50 m. Total distance = 750 m. Total time = 10 + 30 + 5 + 15 = 60 s. Average speed = 750 / 60 = 12.5 m/s.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A train 180 m long runs at 72 km/h. A man walks on the platform at 6 km/h in the same direction as the train. The train enters the platform from the end where the man starts. What is the time taken for the train to completely cross the man?
questions.solution: Convert speeds to m/s: train = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s; man = 6 × 5/18 = 1.666... m/s. Relative speed (same direction) = 20 - 1.666... = 18.333... m/s. The train must cover its own length relative to the man, i.e., 180 m. Time = distance / relative speed = 180 / 18.333... = 9.818... seconds ≈ 9.8 seconds.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: An escalator of length 60 m moves at 0.5 m/s. A person walks on it at 1.5 m/s relative to ground in the direction of the belt. How long does he take to cross the escalator?
questions.solution: Effective speed = walking speed + belt speed = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m/s. Time = length / effective speed = 60 / 2 = 30 seconds.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A person travels 120 km by car at 60 km/h, rests for 30 minutes, then travels 80 km by train at 80 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire journey?
questions.solution: Car time = 120/60 = 2 h. Rest = 0.5 h. Train time = 80/80 = 1 h. Total distance = 200 km. Total time = 2 + 0.5 + 1 = 3.5 h. Average speed = 200 / 3.5 = 57.14 km/h.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A tank of capacity 1200 litres is filled by an inlet pipe at 150 L/hr. A leak initially drains 30 L/hr. After 4 hours the leak is partially closed, reducing its rate by 50%. How long will it take to fill the tank?
questions.solution: Phase 1 (first 4 hours): net inflow = 150 - 30 = 120 L/hr. Volume filled = 120 × 4 = 480 L. Remaining volume = 1200 - 480 = 720 L. Phase 2: leak reduced by 50% → new leak = 15 L/hr. Net inflow = 150 - 15 = 135 L/hr. Time for remaining = 720 / 135 = 5.333... hr = 5 hr 20 min. Total time = 4 hr + 5 hr 20 min = 9 hr 20 min.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A worker produces 10 units per day for the first 10 days. From day 11 onward his efficiency increases by 20%. He rests on every 7th day (day 7, 14, 21, ...). How many units does he produce in 25 calendar days?
questions.solution: Rest days in 25 days: days 7, 14, 21 → 3 rest days. Working days = 22. Days 1‑10 contain day 7 rest, so 9 working days at 10 units = 90 units. Days 11‑25 are 15 calendar days; rest days 14 and 21 fall here, leaving 13 working days. Efficiency from day 11 = 10 × 1.2 = 12 units/day. Production = 13 × 12 = 156 units. Total = 90 + 156 = 246 units.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Three grades of workers: Grade 1 efficiency 1.0 (baseline 20 units/day), Grade 2 = 0.75, Grade 3 = 0.5. A project requires at least 2 Grade 1 workers each day. The pool has 3 Grade 1, 4 Grade 2, 2 Grade 3. If the daily target is 100 units, what is the minimum number of workers needed on a day when one Grade 1 is absent?
questions.solution: Baseline Grade 1 = 20 units/day. Grade 2 = 15, Grade 3 = 10. With one Grade 1 absent, only 2 Grade 1 are available; both must be used to satisfy the “at least 2 Grade 1” rule. Their contribution = 2 × 20 = 40 units. Remaining target = 60 units. Use highest‑efficiency substitutes: Grade 2 gives 15 each. 60 ÷ 15 = 4 Grade 2 workers. Pool has exactly 4 Grade 2. Total workers = 2 + 4 = 6. Using any Grade 3 would increase the count.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Pipe A fills a tank at 30 L/min. Pipe B fills at 20 L/min. After 5 minutes, Pipe A is partially closed reducing its flow by 40%. Both pipes continue until the 500 L tank is full. What is the total time taken to fill the tank?
questions.solution: First 5 min: combined rate = 30 + 20 = 50 L/min → 250 L filled. Remaining = 250 L. After closure, Pipe A flow = 30 × (1‑0.4) = 18 L/min. Combined rate = 18 + 20 = 38 L/min. Time for remainder = 250 ÷ 38 = 125/19 min. Total time = 5 + 125/19 = (95 + 125)/19 = 220/19 min ≈ 11.58 min.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Contractor A has contract value ₹5,00,000, deadline 30 days, actual finish 38 days. Penalty: ₹2,000 per day for first 5 days delay, ₹4,000 per day thereafter. Bonus: ₹1,000 per day saved up to max ₹15,000. What is Contractor A's net earning?
questions.solution: Delay = 38‑30 = 8 days. Penalty: first 5 days × ₹2,000 = ₹10,000. Remaining 3 days × ₹4,000 = ₹12,000. Total penalty = ₹22,000. No bonus because finish is late. Net earning = ₹5,00,000 – ₹22,000 = ₹4,78,000.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A worker takes 10 hours to produce the first unit. After every 10 units his speed increases by 10% (time per unit reduces by 10%). How many total hours are required to produce 30 units?
questions.solution: First 10 units at 10 h each = 100 h. Next 10 units at 10 × 0.9 = 9 h each = 90 h. Last 10 units at 9 × 0.9 = 8.1 h each = 81 h. Total = 100 + 90 + 81 = 271 h.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Worker A follows a 5‑work‑2‑rest cycle. Worker B follows a 4‑work‑1‑rest cycle. Both start on Day 1. In the first 20 calendar days, what is the total number of working days for both workers combined?
questions.solution: Worker A: cycle 7 days. 20 = 2×7 + 6. Full cycles give 2×5 = 10 work days. Remainder days 1‑6 of cycle are work,work,work,work,work,rest → 5 work days. Total A = 15. Worker B: cycle 5 days. 20 = 4×5 exactly. Each cycle 4 work days → 4×4 = 16 work days. Combined = 15 + 16 = 31.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A worker produces 20 units per day. After completing 500 units his daily output rises to 25 units. How many days are needed to produce 800 units?
questions.solution: First 500 units at 20 units/day = 25 days. Remaining 300 units at 25 units/day = 12 days. Total days = 25 + 12 = 37 days.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A contract worth Rs 5,00,000 assigns 60% of the total work to a contractor. He completes 80% of his assigned portion. The contract retains 10% of the payable amount. What is the amount released to the contractor?
questions.solution: Contractor's share of total work = 0.60 × 0.80 = 0.48. Pro‑rata payment = 5,00,000 × 0.48 = 2,40,000. Retention = 10% of 2,40,000 = 24,000. Released amount = 2,40,000 − 24,000 = 2,16,000.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A pump fills a tank in 10 hours at full capacity. After the tank is half full, the pump's efficiency drops to 60% of the original. What is the total time taken to fill the tank completely?
questions.solution: Total work = 1 tank. First half at rate 1/10 tank per hour → time = (1/2) ÷ (1/10) = 5 hours. Remaining half at 60% rate = 0.6 × (1/10) = 0.06 tank per hour → time = (1/2) ÷ 0.06 = 8.333… hours = 8 hours 20 minutes. Total = 5 + 8 hr 20 min = 13 hr 20 min.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A worker can complete a job in 20 days at constant efficiency. After working for 5 days, his efficiency falls to 75% of the original. In how many total days will the job be finished?
questions.solution: Total work = 1 unit. Initial rate = 1/20 per day. Work done in first 5 days = 5 × (1/20) = 1/4. Remaining work = 3/4. New rate = 0.75 × (1/20) = 3/80 per day. Time for remaining = (3/4) ÷ (3/80) = 20 days. Total days = 5 + 20 = 25 days.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A worker produces 100 units on the first day. His daily output increases by 20% each subsequent day. After how many days will the cumulative production reach at least 1000 units?
questions.solution: First term a = 100, ratio r = 1.2. Sum after n days = a(rⁿ–1)/(r–1) = 100(1.2ⁿ–1)/0.2 = 500(1.2ⁿ–1). Need 500(1.2ⁿ–1) ≥ 1000 → 1.2ⁿ ≥ 3. Taking logs: n ≥ log(3)/log(1.2) ≈ 6.02 → smallest integer n = 7. Check: n=6 gives 500(1.2⁶–1) ≈ 993 < 1000; n=7 gives ≈1292 ≥ 1000.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A project requires 400 worker‑days. A team of 10 workers earns Rs. 500 per worker per day. The deadline is 30 days; each day of delay incurs a penalty of Rs. 2000. Extra workers can be hired at the same wage. What is the minimum number of extra workers needed to minimize the total cost (wages + penalty)?
questions.solution: Total work = 400 worker‑days. Wage cost = 400 × 500 = Rs. 200,000 (constant regardless of crew size). With k extra workers, crew = 10+k, days = 400/(10+k). Penalty = max(0, days–30) × 2000. To avoid penalty, need 400/(10+k) ≤ 30 → 10+k ≥ 13.33 → k ≥ 4. For k=3, days≈30.77, penalty≈Rs.1,538, total≈Rs.201,538. For k=4, days≈28.57, penalty=0, total=Rs.200,000. Any k≥4 gives same minimum cost, so minimum extra workers = 4.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Find the missing term: Book : Chapter :: Tree : ?
questions.solution: A book is divided into chapters. Similarly, a tree is divided into branches. This is a part-whole relationship.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the missing term: 5 : 35 :: 8 : ?
questions.solution: 5 × 7 = 35. Similarly, 8 × 10 = 80. The multiplier increases by 3 each time (5→7→10). Actually, the pattern is: n × (n+2): 5×7=35, 8×10=80.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the missing term: Odometer : Distance :: Compass : ?
questions.solution: An odometer measures distance. A compass measures direction. This is an instrument-function relationship.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the missing term: 16 : 64 :: 25 : ?
questions.solution: 16 = 4² → 4³ = 64. 25 = 5² → 5³ = 125. The pattern is square to cube of the same base.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Five friends A,B,C,D,E sit in a row facing north. A at left end. B immediate right of A. C two places right of B. D left of E. Who is at right end?
questions.solution: A B _ C _. D left of E, so D then E at end. A B D C E. E at right end.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a queue, Ram is 8th from front and 12th from back. Total people?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Six people sit in a circle facing center. P between Q and R. S left of Q. T opposite S. Who opposite P?
questions.solution: Order clockwise: S-Q-P-R-?-T. U fills remaining. Opposite P is U.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A older than B. C older than A. D younger than B but older than E. Who is second youngest?
questions.solution: C > A > B > D > E. Second youngest = D.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In class of 40, Ravi ranks 5th from top. Rank from bottom?
questions.solution: Rank from bottom = 40+1-5 = 36.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Four people on floors 1-4. A on even floor. B above C. D on floor 1. Who on floor 3?
questions.solution: D=1, C=2, B=3, A=4. B on floor 3.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a line, every 3rd person gets prize. First prize at person 3. 10th prize at which position?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Five books: Math left of Science. English right of Science. History left of Math. Geography between Math and Science. Middle book?
questions.solution: History, Math, Geography, Science, English. Geography in middle.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A taller than B, shorter than C. D shorter than E, taller than C. Second tallest?
questions.solution: E > D > C > A > B. D is second tallest.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Seema 10th from left, 15th from right. Total girls?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Rohan walks 10 km N, turns right 15 km, right 20 km, left 10 km. Distance from start?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A man faces north, turns 135° clockwise, then 90° anticlockwise. Which direction now?
questions.solution: N to 135°CW=SE, then 90°ACW=NE.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Walking 50 m south, right 30 m, right 50 m, left 20 m. How far from start?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A faces east, turns 45° anticlockwise, then 135° clockwise, then 90° anticlockwise. Direction now?
questions.solution: E→45°ACW=NE→135°CW=S→90°ACW=E. East.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A is the brother of B. B is the sister of C. C is the father of D. How is A related to D?
questions.solution: A and B are siblings. B is sister of C, so A and C are also siblings (brothers). C is father of D. So A is the brother of D's father → A is D's uncle.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A is the mother of B. C is the brother of A. D is the daughter of C. E is the sister of D. How is E related to B?
questions.solution: A is B's mother. C is A's brother (so C is B's maternal uncle). D is C's daughter (so D is B's cousin). E is D's sister (also C's daughter). So E is also B's cousin.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Sita is the daughter of the only son of my mother's husband.' How is Sita related to Ravi?
questions.solution: My mother's husband = my father. The only son of my father = me (Ravi), assuming Ravi is male and the only son. So Sita is the daughter of Ravi → Ravi is Sita's father → Sita is Ravi's daughter.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A is father of B. C is sister of A. D is mother of C. How is D related to B?
questions.solution: A and C siblings. D mother of C and A. D is grandmother of B.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: P brother of Q. R sister of Q. S father of R. How is S related to P?
questions.solution: P,Q,R siblings. S father of R, so father of P too.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: X mother of Y. Y sister of Z. Z brother of W. W daughter of V. How is V related to X?
questions.solution: X mother of Y,Z,W. W daughter of V, so V is father. V is husband of X.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A father of B,C. D daughter of B. E son of C. How is E related to A?
questions.solution: E is child of C who is child of A. E is grandson of A.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Ramesh to Suresh: "Your mother is sister of my father." How is Suresh related to Ramesh?
questions.solution: Their parents are siblings. Ramesh and Suresh are cousins.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A brother of B. B wife of C. C father of D. How is A related to D?
questions.solution: A is B's brother, B is D's mother. A is maternal uncle of D.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Woman: "He is son of my mother's only daughter." How is man related to woman?
questions.solution: Woman's mother's only daughter = the woman. Son of woman = her son.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: M father of N. N mother of O. O sister of P. How is M related to P?
questions.solution: M father of N, N mother of P. M is grandfather of P.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A husband of B. C brother of A. D son of C. E wife of A. How is E related to D?
questions.solution: E wife of A, A is brother of C, D son of C. E is aunt of D.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Man: "She is daughter of the mother of my sister's only brother." Relation?
questions.solution: Man's sister's only brother = man. Daughter of man's mother = his sister.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: X,Y brothers. Z daughter of Y. W wife of X. How is W related to Z?
questions.solution: W is wife of X (Y's brother). Z is Y's daughter. W is Z's aunt.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Pointing to girl, Raj: "Her mother's husband's daughter is my sister." Relation?
questions.solution: Girl's mother's husband = girl's father. His daughter = girl. Girl is Raj's sister.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A mother of B. B sister of C. D son of C. E brother of D. How is E related to B?
questions.solution: B and C siblings. C parent of E. E is B's nephew.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A is husband of B. B mother of C. C sister of D. E father of D. Relation of E to A?
questions.solution: If D is child of B and A, then E=A. Self-referential. Cannot determine distinct relationship.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: X is daughter of Y. Y is husband of Z. Z is sister of W. How is X related to W?
questions.solution: X daughter of Y and Z. Z sister of W. X is niece of W.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "APPLE" is coded as "BQQMF", how is "MANGO" coded?
questions.solution: Each letter +1: M→N, A→B, N→O, G→H, O→P = NBOHP.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "DELHI" is coded as "EFMIJ", find "MUMBAI".
questions.solution: All +1: M→N, U→V, M→N, B→C, A→B, I→J = NVNCBJ.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "STUDENT" is coded as "TVWFOSV", find "CLASS".
questions.solution: Each letter +1: C→D, L→M, A→B, S→T, S→T = DMBTT.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "INDIA" is coded as "JOEJB", find "CHINA".
questions.solution: All +1: C→D, H→I, I→J, N→O, A→B = DIJOB.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "WORLD" is coded as "YQTNF", find "PEACE".
questions.solution: All +2: P→R, E→G, A→C, C→E, E→G = RGCEG.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "GOOD" is coded as "HPPE", find "WORK".
questions.solution: All +1: W→X, O→P, R→S, K→L = XPSL.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "BOMBAY" is coded as "CPNCBZ", find "DELHI".
questions.solution: All +1: D→E, E→F, L→M, H→I, I→J = EFMIJ.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "RIVERS" is coded as "SKWFST", find "WATER".
questions.solution: All +1: W→X, A→B, T→U, E→F, R→S = XBUFS.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "HONESTY" is coded as "IPNFTUZ", find "BEAUTY".
questions.solution: Each letter +1: B→C, E→F, A→B, U→V, T→U, Y→Z = CFBVUZ.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "NIGHT" is coded as "OKHIW", find "BRIGHT".
questions.solution: Pattern: +1,+2,+2,... B→C, R→S, I→K, G→H, H→I, T→W = CSKHIW.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "ABROAD" is coded as "BCSPBE", find "FOREIGN".
questions.solution: All +1: F→G, O→P, R→S, E→F, I→J, G→H, N→O = GPSFJHO.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "GOODNESS" is coded as "HPPOFTT", find "PROJECT".
questions.solution: All +1: P→Q, R→S, O→P, J→K, E→F, C→D, T→U = QSPKDFU.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "LAPTOP" is coded as "MBQUPQ", find "MOBILE".
questions.solution: All +1: M→N, O→P, B→C, I→J, L→M, E→F = NPCJMF.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If "WINDOW" is coded as "XJOEPX", find "DOOR".
questions.solution: All +1: D→E, O→P, O→P, R→S = EPPS.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A man walks 5 km towards North, turns right and walks 3 km, then turns left and walks 2 km, then turns left and walks 3 km. How far is he from the starting point?
questions.solution: North: 5+2 = 7 km (first 5N, then after detours 2N). East-West: 3E - 3W = 0. Net displacement = 7 km North.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Raju walked 30 m towards North, then 20 m towards East, then 30 m towards South. How far and in which direction is he from the starting point?
questions.solution: North-South: 30N - 30S = 0. East-West: 20E. So net displacement = 20 m East.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a linear seating arrangement, the concepts of leftmost and rightmost are described as absolute references. What does this imply about the ends of the row?
questions.a: The leftmost and rightmost positions are fixed and do not change regardless of perspective.
opts: The leftmost position changes depending on the perspective of the seated persons.
The leftmost and rightmost positions are fixed and do not change regardless of perspective.
Only the rightmost position is absolute; the leftmost is relative.
Neither end is fixed; both are relative to the observer.
questions.solution: The lesson states that because the row has two distinct ends, the concepts of leftmost and rightmost are absolute references that never change regardless of the perspective of the individuals seated. This absolute frame of reference makes linear puzzles straightforward. Therefore, the ends are fixed and do not vary with viewpoint.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Which category of clue does the statement "A sits third to the left of B" belong to in a linear arrangement puzzle?
questions.solution: The lesson classifies clues into definite, relative, and negative. A definite clue pins an entity to a specific slot (e.g., "D sits at the left end"). A relative clue describes the positional relationship between two entities without fixing either absolutely; typical forms include "A is second to the left of B". The given statement matches this definition, so it is a relative clue.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: What is the primary function of negative clues in linear seating arrangement puzzles?
questions.a: They eliminate impossible slots and prune the search space.
opts: They directly assign a person to a specific seat.
They create a set of possible pairs of slots for two persons.
They eliminate impossible slots and prune the search space.
They link two separate arrangement models together.
questions.solution: According to the lesson, negative clues state where an entity cannot be (e.g., "H is not at either end"). Although they do not place anyone directly, negative clues are powerful because they prune the search space and often resolve ambiguities left by relative clues. Thus, their main role is elimination of impossible slots.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a circular seating arrangement where all persons face the centre, the direction "clockwise" corresponds to which relative side for each person?
questions.solution: The lesson explains that facing inside versus facing outside changes the mapping of clockwise/anticlockwise to left/right. When persons face the centre, their right side points in the clockwise direction and their left side points anticlockwise. Hence, clockwise is equivalent to the right side for each individual.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a sequencing puzzle, the clue "Event C occurs immediately after Event D" translates into which constraints in the directed graph representation?
questions.a: An edge D → C and a restriction that no other event can be placed between D and C.
opts: An edge D → C and a restriction that no other event can be placed between D and C.
No edge is added; it only fixes the rank of C.
questions.solution: The lesson states that a clue like "C immediately after D" adds edges D → C and also forbids any other event between D and C. This is stricter than simple precedence (which would only add D → C). Therefore, the correct representation includes both the precedence edge and the immediate‑precedence restriction.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a multi‑attribute matrix puzzle, a relational clue states: "The engineer likes cricket." How should this clue be processed during constraint propagation?
questions.a: Intersect the candidate sets of the two linked attributes for that entity; if the intersection becomes a singleton, fix the value and cascade eliminations
opts: Assign both attributes directly to the engineer without checking other entities
Intersect the candidate sets of the two linked attributes for that entity; if the intersection becomes a singleton, fix the value and cascade eliminations
Eliminate all other values for those attributes across all entities immediately
Treat the clue as a negative clue and remove the engineer‑cricket pair from all entities
questions.solution: The multi‑attribute matrix method uses cross‑attribute propagation. For a clue linking two attributes of the same entity, the solver intersects the candidate sets of those attributes for that entity. If the intersection reduces to a single value, that value is fixed for the entity, and the elimination cascades to other entities sharing the same attribute value. Direct assignment without intersection, blanket elimination, or treating it as a negative clue would ignore the constraint‑propagation mechanism described.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A hybrid puzzle includes an arithmetic constraint: the sum of the floor numbers of three persons equals 12. Each person occupies a distinct floor from 1 to 5. What must the solver ensure when applying this constraint?
questions.a: Combine the arithmetic constraint with the permutation of distinct values to prune domains
opts: Treat the sum constraint as independent of the distinctness requirement
Combine the arithmetic constraint with the permutation of distinct values to prune domains
Ignore distinctness because the sum already limits possibilities
Assume floors can repeat to satisfy the sum
questions.solution: Hybrid puzzles with quantitative constraints require integrating arithmetic restrictions with the permutation of distinct values. The solver must consider the sum together with the fact that floors are distinct and drawn from 1‑5, which prunes the domain of each person’s floor. Ignoring distinctness or treating the sum in isolation would miss deductions and could allow invalid repetitions, while assuming repeats contradicts the puzzle’s distinct‑value rule.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a circular table with 8 equally spaced seats, A sits opposite B. If A is anchored at seat 1, which seat must B occupy?
questions.solution: Opposite seats on an even‑sized circle are separated by half the total seats. With 8 seats, half is 4 steps. Starting from seat 1 and moving clockwise 4 positions lands on seat 5 (1→2→3→4→5). The 180° rotational flip would map seat 1 to itself and seat 5 to itself, so the opposite relation uniquely fixes B at seat 5. Therefore the correct seat is 5.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A multi‑attribute puzzle assigns each person a profession and a floor. The clue "The engineer lives on the third floor" is processed by arc consistency (AC‑3). How are the domains pruned?
questions.a: Removes all floors except third from engineer's floor domain and removes engineer from other persons' profession domains
opts: Removes all floors except third from engineer's floor domain and removes engineer from other persons' profession domains
Removes only the third floor from engineer's floor domain
Adds engineer to all persons' profession domains
questions.solution: AC‑3 enforces binary constraints. The clue gives a unary restriction on the engineer's floor domain (only floor 3 remains) and a binary all‑different constraint on professions: since each profession is unique, "engineer" is eliminated from the profession domain of every other person. This simultaneous pruning of the floor and profession domains is exactly what arc consistency achieves for such a direct clue.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A conditional clue states: "If P sits at position 2 then Q sits at position 4." In an implication graph used for conditional clause chains, how is this clue represented?
questions.a: As a directed edge from node (P=2) to node (Q=4)
opts: As a directed edge from node (P=2) to node (Q=4)
As an undirected edge between P and Q
As a bidirectional edge between (P=2) and (Q=4)
questions.solution: Implication graphs treat each possible assignment as a node. A conditional "If antecedent then consequent" becomes a directed edge from the antecedent node (P=2) to the consequent node (Q=4). The edge is activated only when the antecedent becomes true during search; it does not create a permanent binary constraint nor a bidirectional link. This representation allows unit propagation to fire Q=4 automatically once P=2 is assigned.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a linear row of 6 seats, A is to the left of B with at least one person sitting between them. What is the minimum possible number of seats separating A and B?
questions.solution: "At least one person between" means the positional difference must be ≥2 seats (e.g., A at seat 1, one person at seat 2, B at seat 3). The distance measured as the number of seats from A to B exclusive of A but inclusive of B is 2. Any smaller gap would place B immediately next to A, violating the condition. Hence the minimum separation is 2 seats.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Floors are numbered 1 to 4. The clue "The engineer's floor number is the square of the teacher's floor number" appears. Which teacher–engineer floor pair is forced by this arithmetic constraint?
questions.solution: We need integer floors t (teacher) and e (engineer) with e = t² and both in {1,2,3,4}. Testing t=1 gives e=1 (valid but does not use the square relation uniquely). t=2 gives e=4 (both within range). t=3 gives e=9 (out of range). t=4 gives e=16 (out of range). Only the pair (2,4) satisfies the square relation while keeping both floors inside the allowed domain, so the clue deterministically fixes teacher=2 and engineer=4.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a circular seating puzzle, fixing one person breaks rotational symmetry. What additional clue is needed to eliminate the remaining reflection symmetry?
questions.a: A clue stating the person faces north
opts: A clue stating the person faces north
A clue stating two persons are adjacent
A clue stating the number of persons is even
A clue stating the table has a diameter
questions.solution: A circular arrangement has dihedral symmetry Dn. Fixing one person removes the rotational part, but a reflection (180° flip) may still map the arrangement onto itself. An asymmetric clue such as "A faces north" distinguishes the two mirror images because facing direction changes under reflection. Adjacency, even count, or table diameter do not break the reflection symmetry. Therefore, a facing clue is required.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Which propagation method is necessary to enforce a global cardinality constraint like "exactly three doctors" in a seating puzzle?
questions.a: Flow-based filtering on a bipartite graph
opts: Flow-based filtering on a bipartite graph
questions.solution: Global cardinality constraints couple many variables simultaneously. Pairwise arc consistency only checks binary relations and cannot guarantee that the overall count of a value (e.g., doctors) can be satisfied. The standard algorithm builds a flow network: source to variable nodes (capacity 1), variable to value nodes (capacity 1), value nodes to sink with capacity equal to the allowed maximum (and lower bound for minimum). A feasible flow proves GCC consistency, and edges carrying zero flow in all maximum flows are pruned. This flow-based filtering is stronger than AC-3.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: When multiple step-size clues are given on a circular arrangement, which invariant must be checked to avoid inconsistency?
questions.a: The parity (even/odd) of the distance between any two persons must be consistent across all clues
opts: The sum of all step sizes must equal the number of persons
The parity (even/odd) of the distance between any two persons must be consistent across all clues
The step sizes must all be prime numbers
The clockwise distance must always be less than the anticlockwise distance
questions.solution: Step-size clues on a circle fix distances modulo the number of persons. If several clues relate the same pair of persons through different paths, the parity (mod 2) of the resulting distances must agree; otherwise the clues contradict. For example, if one clue says A is 3 steps clockwise from B (odd distance) and another implies an even distance between them, the puzzle is inconsistent. Checking parity consistency is a quick necessary condition before deeper search. The other options are not general invariants.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a puzzle where each profession allows only a subset of colours, what propagation technique removes a profession value when none of its allowed colours remain?
questions.a: Support-count propagation from child to parent
opts: Support-count propagation from child to parent
questions.solution: The hierarchy has parent attributes (profession) and child attributes (colour). Each profession value maintains a counter of currently supported colour values. When a colour is eliminated from a person's domain, the counters for professions that allowed that colour are decremented. If a profession's counter drops to zero, that profession value has no remaining support and is deleted from the domain. This bottom-up support-checking is analogous to arc consistency on the hierarchy edges and is more efficient than treating all profession-colour pairs as independent flat domains.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How should the conditional clue "If A sits at position 3 then B is a Doctor" be encoded in a SAT/SMT model?
opts: As a permanent binary constraint between A's position and B's profession
As a global cardinality constraint on the number of doctors
As a parity constraint on the positions
questions.solution: In SAT/SMT encoding, each possible assignment becomes a Boolean variable (e.g., x_A,3 for "A at position 3", y_B,Doctor for "B is Doctor"). A conditional clue is an implication that activates only when the antecedent holds. It is encoded as the clause (¬x_A,3 ∨ y_B,Doctor), which is logically equivalent to x_A,3 → y_B,Doctor. A permanent binary constraint would force the relation even when A is not at position 3, which is incorrect. Global cardinality and parity constraints address different aspects.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a multi-stage puzzle, three conditionals form a cycle: if A then B, if B then C, and if C then A. What does this cycle force about the truth values of the antecedents?
questions.a: Either all three are true or all three are false
opts: All three antecedents must be true
All three antecedents must be false
Either all three are true or all three are false
No definite conclusion can be drawn
questions.solution: The three conditionals create a directed cycle in the implication graph. In Boolean logic, a cycle of implications (A→B, B→C, C→A) means A, B, and C are logically equivalent: each implies the others. Therefore they must share the same truth value. The only consistent assignments are all true or all false. Recognising this hidden equivalence lets the solver collapse the chain into a single binary choice, drastically reducing the search space.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A scheduling puzzle includes the clue "A and B cannot overlap". Before branching on the disjunction, which propagation technique can tighten the earliest and latest start bounds of the tasks?
questions.solution: The non-overlap clue creates a disjunctive constraint: either A finishes before B starts or B finishes before A starts. Before case splitting, the solver applies edge-finding rules, which examine the cumulative resource profile and the relative ordering of tasks to deduce tighter bounds on start times. Edge-finding can prove that one of the two orders is impossible, thereby narrowing the temporal windows without explicit branching.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A double-row puzzle states "the two rows are mirror images". Which single anchoring constraint is sufficient to break the row-wise reflection symmetry?
questions.a: Fix the leftmost person of the first row
opts: Fix the rightmost person of the second row
Fix the leftmost person of the first row
Fix the middle person of both rows
questions.solution: A mirror-image clue introduces a reflection symmetry that swaps the two rows while reversing left-right order. This symmetry has order 2. To break it, we must fix a variable that is not mapped onto itself by the reflection. Fixing the leftmost person of the first row selects a unique representative from each orbit of the group action, eliminating the duplicate solution branches caused by the row-swap symmetry.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a hybrid seating-resource puzzle, after listing all feasible seat-person pairs from the seating sub-problem, what is the correct next step to verify resource feasibility?
questions.a: Build a bipartite graph between persons and resource units and compute a maximum matching
opts: Assign resources greedily to the highest-ranked persons
Build a bipartite graph between persons and resource units and compute a maximum matching
Ignore resource constraints and solve seating completely first
Randomly pair persons with resources until all capacities are filled
questions.solution: The coupling clues link seats to resources, so resource assignment depends on which person occupies which seat. After obtaining the support matrix of feasible seat-person pairs, we construct a bipartite graph where persons are connected to resource units they are eligible for. Running a maximum-matching algorithm (e.g., Hopcroft-Karp) determines whether a perfect matching exists. If not, any seat-person pair that participates in no perfect matching is pruned, and the process iterates to a fixed point.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: What is the direct consequence of failing to propagate the contrapositive of a conditional clue during puzzle solving?
questions.a: Antecedents that should be false remain active
opts: Antecedents that should be false remain active
questions.solution: A conditional "if X then Y" yields the contrapositive "if not Y then not X". When Y is proven false, the contrapositive forces X to be false. If this propagation is omitted, X stays marked as active (possible) even though it must be false. This leaves spurious antecedents in the implication graph, potentially triggering incorrect consequents later and expanding the search space with invalid branches.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a temporal evolution puzzle, a clue states 'the arrangement repeats every three steps'. What does this imply for the solving process?
questions.a: The puzzle has only three distinct layers that need to be solved.
opts: The puzzle has only three distinct layers that need to be solved.
The puzzle has no solution because of periodicity.
The puzzle requires exactly three time steps to complete.
The puzzle becomes static after three steps.
questions.solution: The clue 'the arrangement repeats every three steps' introduces a modulo‑3 periodicity. This means the configuration at step t is identical to step t+3. Therefore, only three distinct time layers (e.g., steps 1, 2, 3) need to be solved; all other steps are determined by this cycle. The solver can reduce the problem to three linked layers, propagate constraints forward and backward within this cycle, and then extend the solution to any number of steps. This avoids solving each step independently and exploits the hidden transition rule.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: For a conflict‑free seating assignment around a circular table with an odd number of seats, what is the chromatic number of the seat‑proximity graph for adjacency conflicts?
questions.solution: In graph coloring terms, the seat‑proximity graph for adjacency on a circle has vertices for seats and edges between adjacent seats. For an even cycle, the graph is bipartite and its chromatic number χ = 2 (alternating colors). For an odd cycle, bipartiteness fails and χ = 3 because three colors are needed to avoid adjacent seats sharing a color. The lesson explicitly states: 'a circle of even size also has χ = 2, but an odd circle requires χ = 3.' Hence the correct answer is 3.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: When a disjunctive clue in a puzzle uses wording that permits both disjuncts to be true, what error occurs if the solver treats it as an exclusive‑or?
questions.a: The solver may miss valid solutions where both disjuncts hold.
opts: The solver may miss valid solutions where both disjuncts hold.
The solver will always find a unique solution.
The solver must add an extra constraint.
questions.solution: A disjunctive clue such as 'A sits next to B or C' may allow both possibilities simultaneously (A next to B and also next to C if B and C are on either side). If the solver incorrectly assumes exclusive‑or (XOR), they would forbid the case where both disjuncts are true, potentially eliminating valid arrangements. The lesson warns: 'Assuming a disjunctive clue is exclusive‑or when the wording permits both disjuncts to be true, leading to missed solutions.' Therefore, the error is missing solutions where both hold.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the integer linear programming formulation for hybrid seating‑resource puzzles, why does solving the linear relaxation often yield an integral solution for the seating variables?
questions.a: Because the seating constraints form a totally unimodular matrix (assignment polytope).
opts: Because the seating constraints form a totally unimodular matrix (assignment polytope).
Because the resource variables are continuous.
Because the big‑M formulation forces integrality.
Because the conflict graph is bipartite.
questions.solution: The seating constraints (each person exactly one seat, each seat at most one person) form an assignment problem. The constraint matrix of an assignment problem is totally unimodular, meaning the linear programming relaxation (allowing variables between 0 and 1) has extreme points that are integral. Thus solving the LP relaxation yields binary values for the seating variables without needing integer programming. The lesson states: 'the linear relaxation often yields integral extreme points because the seating constraints form a totally unimodular matrix (assignment polytope).'
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: What is a common mistake when a clue states that a group of persons 'sit together' without specifying their internal order?
questions.a: Treating the group as a rigid block with fixed internal order, over‑constraining the puzzle.
opts: Treating the group as a rigid block with fixed internal order, over‑constraining the puzzle.
Assuming the group must be split across rows.
Applying graph coloring to the group.
questions.solution: When a clue says a group 'sit together' it only imposes that the members occupy consecutive seats (or adjacent positions), but does not fix their internal order. A common mistake is to treat the group as a single rigid block with a predetermined internal sequence, which adds false constraints and may make the puzzle appear unsolvable or hide valid arrangements. The lesson lists this pitfall: 'Treating a hierarchical group as a rigid block when a clue only says “sit together” without fixing internal order, causing over‑constraining.'
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the next term: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ?
questions.solution: Pattern: 1×3=3, 2×4=8, 3×5=15, 4×6=24, 5×7=35, 6×8=48. Or alternatively: differences are 5,7,9,11,13 (increasing by 2 each time), so next difference = 13, next term = 35+13 = 48.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the next term: A, D, I, P, ?
questions.solution: A=1, D=4, I=9, P=16. These are squares: 1², 2², 3², 4². Next is 5²=25 → Y.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the missing term: 2, 6, 12, ?, 30, 42
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the next term: Z, X, V, T, R, ?
questions.solution: Z=26, X=24, V=22, T=20, R=18. Each term decreases by 2. Next: 18-2=16 → P.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the missing term: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ?
questions.solution: This is the Fibonacci series: each term is the sum of the two preceding terms. 5+8 = 13.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: 1. All birds are animals. 2. No animal is a fish. Conclusions: I. No bird is a fish. II. Some animals are birds.
questions.solution: All birds are inside animals. No animal is fish, so birds cannot be fish either → I follows. Since all birds are animals, there is definitely at least some overlap → some animals are birds (the same set of birds) → II follows. Both conclusions follow.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: 1. Some books are pens. 2. All pens are tables. Conclusions: I. Some books are tables. II. Some tables are pens.
questions.solution: Some books are pens, and all pens are tables → those books which are pens are also tables → Some books are tables (I follows). All pens are tables → there exists at least one pen that is a table → Some tables are pens (II follows). Both follow.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: 1. No apple is a mango. 2. All mangoes are fruits. Conclusions: I. No apple is a fruit. II. Some fruits are mangoes.
questions.solution: No direct relation between apple and fruit is given. Apples could be fruits or not → I does not follow. All mangoes are fruits → there exist mangoes that are fruits → some fruits are mangoes (II follows). Only II follows.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: 1. Some cups are plates. 2. No plate is a bowl. Conclusions: I. Some cups are not bowls. II. No cup is a bowl.
questions.solution: Some cups are plates. No plate is a bowl. So those cups which are plates cannot be bowls → some cups are definitely not bowls → I follows. However, there could be other cups (not plates) that are bowls, so we cannot say 'no cup is a bowl' → II does not follow. Only I follows.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: 1. All dogs are cats. 2. All cats are animals. Conclusions: I. All dogs are animals. II. Some animals are dogs.
questions.solution: All dogs are cats, all cats are animals → by transitive property, all dogs are animals → I follows. Since all dogs are animals, there exists at least one dog that is an animal → some animals are dogs → II follows. Both follow.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: All pens are pencils. No pencil is an eraser. Conclusions: I. No pen is an eraser. II. Some pencils are pens.
questions.solution: All pens inside pencils. No pencil is eraser, so pens cannot be erasers (I). All pens are pencils means some pencils are pens (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: Some apples are bananas. All bananas are cherries. Conclusions: I. Some apples are cherries. II. All cherries are bananas.
questions.solution: Apples that are bananas are also cherries (I). But all cherries need not be bananas - there could be cherries that are not bananas.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: No cat is dog. All dogs are animals. Conclusions: I. No cat is animal. II. Some animals are dogs.
questions.solution: Cats and dogs no overlap. Dogs inside animals, but cats and animals may overlap. Cannot conclude I. All dogs are animals means some animals are dogs (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: All books are pages. No page is a cover. Conclusions: I. No book is a cover. II. Some pages are books.
questions.solution: Books inside pages. Pages no overlap with covers, so books no overlap with covers (I). All books are pages means some pages are books (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: Some doctors are engineers. All engineers are scientists. Conclusions: I. Some doctors are scientists. II. All scientists are engineers.
questions.solution: Doctors that are engineers are also scientists since all engineers are scientists (I). But all scientists need not be engineers.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: All birds are animals. All animals are living beings. Conclusions: I. All birds are living beings. II. Some living beings are birds.
questions.solution: Birds inside animals inside living beings (I). All birds are living beings means some living beings are birds (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: Some professors are researchers. No researcher is a student. Conclusions: I. Some professors are not students. II. Some students are professors.
questions.solution: Some professors are researchers. Since no researcher is a student, those professors who are researchers are not students (I).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: All tigers are mammals. No mammal is a reptile. Conclusions: I. No tiger is a reptile. II. Some mammals are tigers.
questions.solution: Tigers are mammals. No mammal is reptile, so tigers cannot be reptiles (I). All tigers are mammals means some mammals are tigers (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: Some vegetables are fruits. No fruit is a grain. Conclusions: I. Some vegetables are not grains. II. Some fruits are not grains.
questions.solution: Some vegetables are fruits. No fruit is grain, so those vegetables which are fruits are not grains (I). "No fruit is grain" means all fruits are not grains (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: All balls are round. Some round objects are red. Conclusions: I. Some balls are red. II. Some red objects are round.
questions.solution: Balls inside round objects. Some round are red - those may not be balls. "Some round are red" = "some red are round" (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: Some chairs are tables. No table is a stool. Conclusions: I. Some chairs are not stools. II. All stools are chairs.
questions.solution: Some chairs are tables. No table is stool, so those chairs which are tables are not stools (I).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statements: All students are hardworking. Some hardworking people are successful. Conclusions: I. Some students are successful. II. Some successful people are hardworking.
questions.solution: Students are inside hardworking people. Some hardworking are successful - may not be students. "Some hardworking are successful" = "some successful are hardworking" (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Which organelle is known as the 'control centre' of the cell?
questions.solution: b) The nucleus contains DNA and controls all cellular activities, making it the control centre.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which vitamin is produced when the skin is exposed to sunlight?
questions.solution: c) Vitamin D is synthesized in the skin upon exposure to UV rays from sunlight. It helps in calcium absorption.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the largest organ in the human body?
questions.solution: c) The skin is the largest organ, covering about 1.5-2 m² in an average adult. The liver is the largest internal organ.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a communicable disease?
questions.solution: b) Diabetes is a non-communicable (lifestyle) disease. TB, influenza, and chickenpox are caused by pathogens and can spread.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Photosynthesis occurs in which organelle of plant cells?
questions.solution: b) Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll which captures sunlight for photosynthesis. Mitochondria is for energy production.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the chemical formula of water?
questions.solution: b) H₂O (two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is a strong acid?
questions.solution: c) Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is a strong acid that fully dissociates in water. Acetic, citric, and carbonic acids are weak acids.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the pH range of bases?
questions.solution: b) Bases have pH values greater than 7 (7-14). Acids have pH 0-7, and pure water is exactly 7 (neutral).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which gas is produced when an acid reacts with a metal?
questions.solution: c) Hydrogen gas (H₂) is produced when an acid reacts with a metal. Example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing:
questions.solution: b) Atomic number. Mendeleev arranged by atomic mass, but the modern periodic table is based on increasing atomic number.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Newton's First Law of Motion is also known as the law of:
questions.solution: b) Inertia. Newton's first law states that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by an external force.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.solution: c) Ampere (A). Volt is the unit of potential difference, Ohm is resistance, Watt is power.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the speed of sound in air at 20°C approximately?
questions.solution: a) 343 m/s. The speed of sound in air at 20°C is approximately 343 m/s.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which type of mirror is used in rearview mirrors of vehicles?
questions.solution: b) Convex mirror provides a wider field of view and forms smaller, erect images, making it ideal for rearview mirrors.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In a series circuit, if three resistors of 2Ω, 3Ω, and 5Ω are connected, what is the total resistance?
questions.solution: b) 10Ω. In series, R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10Ω.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following words derived from the root "act" functions as an adjective?
questions.solution: The lesson explains that the root "act" can become a noun ("action" with -ion), a verb ("activate" with -ate), and an adjective ("active" with -ive). Recognising these morphological patterns helps identify the grammatical category of each form. Among the options, only "active" carries the adjectival suffix -ive, making it the adjective. The other choices are a noun (action), a verb (activate), and a noun (actor). Therefore, the correct answer is option C (index 2).
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Identify the sentence type of the following: "Although the committee has decided, the members have disagreed."
questions.solution: The lesson defines a complex sentence as one independent clause combined with one or more dependent clauses introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as "although". In the given sentence, "Although the committee has decided" is a dependent clause (it cannot stand alone) and "the members have disagreed" is an independent clause. There is only one independent clause, so the sentence is not compound or compound‑complex. Hence it is a complex sentence, corresponding to option C (index 2).
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In the sentence "The committee's decision was ______ by the chairperson," which word form fits the syntactic slot?
questions.solution: The lesson notes that errors often arise when a word form does not match its syntactic slot. After the passive construction "was" a past participle is required. "Activated" is the past participle of the verb "activate" and correctly completes the passive voice. "Activate" is the base form, "activation" is a noun, and "active" is an adjective; none of these can follow "was" in a passive structure. Therefore the appropriate form is "activated" (index 2).
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Which of the following sentences correctly applies the punctuation rule for a subordinate clause that precedes the main clause?
questions.a: Although the data were incomplete, the analysis proceeded.
opts: Although the data were incomplete the analysis proceeded.
Although the data were incomplete, the analysis proceeded.
The analysis proceeded although the data were incomplete.
The analysis proceeded, although the data were incomplete.
questions.solution: The lesson states that subordinate clauses preceding the main clause are usually followed by a comma. Option B places the subordinate clause “Although the data were incomplete” before the main clause and inserts the required comma. Option A omits the comma, violating the rule. Options C and D place the subordinate clause after the main clause; in that position the comma is omitted unless the clause is non‑restrictive, so they do not illustrate the rule being tested.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Which sentence illustrates object control in a non‑finite clause?
questions.a: She persuaded him to submit the draft.
opts: She promised to submit the draft.
She persuaded him to submit the draft.
When ready, the document will be forwarded.
questions.solution: Object control occurs when the matrix object controls the understood subject of the infinitive. In “She persuaded him to submit the draft,” the matrix object “him” is the understood subject of “to submit,” matching the lesson’s example of object control. Option A shows subject control (the matrix subject “She” controls the infinitive). Option C exemplifies a raising verb (“seems”) where the subordinate subject raises to matrix subject position. Option D is a verbless clause, not a non‑finite infinitive with control.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Which of the following extractions violates the Coordinate Structure Constraint?
questions.a: Which report did you read and the summary?
opts: Which report did you read and summarise?
Which report did you read and the summary?
Which report did you read and which summary did you write?
Which report did you read and which report did you summarise?
questions.solution: The Coordinate Structure Constraint prohibits extraction from a single conjunct. Option B attempts to extract “which report” from the first conjunct (“read”) while leaving the second conjunct (“the summary”) untouched, which is illicit. Option A is an Across‑the‑Board extraction, permitted because the same element is extracted from both conjuncts (“read” and “summarise”). Options C and D involve separate wh‑phrases for each conjunct, not a single extraction targeting one conjunct, so they do not violate the constraint.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Identify the logical fallacy in the argument: “Either we adopt the full plan or we do nothing.”
opts: False cause (post hoc ergo propter hoc)
questions.solution: The lesson defines a false dilemma as presenting only two extremes, e.g., “Either we adopt the full plan or we do nothing.” This argument excludes any middle‑ground alternatives, fitting the false dilemma pattern exactly. Hasty generalisation involves drawing a broad conclusion from insufficient evidence. False cause asserts a causal link based solely on temporal succession. Slippery slope claims a chain reaction leading to an extreme outcome without justification. None of these match the structure of the given statement.
questions.subject: English
