questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A standard die shows 1 on top, 3 in front. What is the right face?
questions.solution: a) 2. Top=1(bottom=6). Front=3(back=4). The remaining faces are 2 and 5. Standard orientation: right face = 2.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A cube of side n has 8 corner cubes with 3 faces painted. For what n does this hold?
questions.solution: b) n ≥ 2. For n=1, there are no separate corner cubes (the single cube has all 6 faces). For n ≥ 2, there are always 8 distinct corner cubes.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a dice net, four squares are in a row and the other two are attached above the 2nd square and below the 3rd. Which pairs are opposite?
opts: Top square and the square 3 positions away
Squares separated by 1 in the net
questions.solution: d) Many pairs possible depending on folding. The net described is a valid one; opposite pairs depend on which squares are selected as base.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Total number of small cubes in a 9×9×9 cube cut into 1×1×1 cubes?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Two faces of a die sum to 7 always. If one face is 1, the sum of the other 5 faces is?
questions.solution: c) 20. Total sum = 21. If 1 is one face, sum of remaining 5 = 21-1 = 20.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A 3×3×3 cube is painted and cut. Number of cubes with exactly 1 face painted?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: View 1 of a die: Top=F, Front=G, Right=H. View 2: Top=I, Front=G, Right=J. If F, G, H, I, J are distinct numbers from 1-6, find opposite of G.
questions.solution: c) The number not shown. G is adjacent to F, H, I, J. The remaining number (not in {F,G,H,I,J}) is opposite to G.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If a mirror is placed on the right, find the mirror image of 'HELLO'.
questions.solution: b) O⅂⅂ƐH. H→H(symmetric), E→Ɛ, L→⅂, L→⅂, O→O. Sequence reversed: O⅂⅂ƐH.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Find the water image of 'P6b'.
questions.solution: c) q9d. P→q(flipped), 6→9(flipped), b→d(flipped). Sequence order stays the same.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many holes appear when a paper folded vertically twice is punched once at the folded corner?
questions.solution: b) 4. Two vertical folds = 2² = 4 layers. One punch = 4 holes.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many triangles are in a pentagon with all its diagonals?
questions.solution: b) 35. A pentagon with all diagonals forms 35 triangles (5 small at centre + 10 medium + 10 larger + 10 largest around edges).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A clock shows 2:30. What is its mirror image time?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many squares are in a 2×3 grid?
questions.solution: b) 8. 1×1 squares: 6, 2×2 squares: 2 (rows 1-2, columns 1-2 and 2-3). Total = 8.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If mirror is on the left, find the mirror image of 'BAT'.
questions.solution: b) TⱯᗺ. Mirror on left: reverse sequence and invert each. B→ᗺ, A→Ɐ, T→T. Sequence reversed: TⱯᗺ.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many rectangles (including squares) in a 3×4 grid?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A paper is folded in half vertically, then diagonally. A hole is punched. How many holes after unfolding?
questions.solution: b) 4. Two folds = 2² = 4 holes.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Water image of 'SSC CGL'?
questions.solution: d) SSƆ ⅂⅂Ɔ. S→S(vertical symmetry), C→Ɔ(flipped), G→⅂(flipped). Sequence order preserved.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many triangles in a triangle with 2 lines from each vertex?
questions.solution: c) 12. With 2 lines from each vertex of a triangle, the total triangles formed is 12.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Mirror image of '2025' with mirror on right?
questions.solution: b) 5202. Reverse sequence: 5202. Digits 0,2,5 are mirror-symmetric.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many squares in a 6×6 grid?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A clock shows 4:40. What is its water image?
questions.solution: a) 7:20. Water image time = 12:00 - given time = 12:00 - 4:40 = 7:20.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many triangles in a regular hexagon with all its diagonals?
questions.solution: c) 110. A regular hexagon with all diagonals has 110 triangles (including overlapping regions).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Which figure contains a star shape?
opts: A hexagon with all sides equal
questions.solution: a) A pentagon with intersecting diagonals forms a pentagram (star) shape.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Paper folded horizontally twice, then a hole punched at top-right of folded paper. How many holes?
questions.solution: b) 4. Two horizontal folds = 4 layers. 1 punch → 4 holes.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Water image of '9PM'?
questions.solution: b) 6qW. 9→6, P→q, M→W. Sequence: 6qW.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many rectangles (non-square) in a 3×3 grid?
questions.solution: a) 22. Total rectangles = 36. Squares = 14. Non-square rectangles = 36-14 = 22.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Mirror image of an arrow pointing North-East with mirror on right?
questions.solution: b) North-West. Mirror swaps East↔West. North stays North. So North-East → North-West.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many triangles in a star-shaped figure (pentagram)?
questions.solution: b) 35. A pentagram (5-pointed star) contains 35 triangles: 5 small, 5 medium, 5 large, plus 20 others formed by overlapping lines.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: What is the mirror image of 'MADAM' with mirror on right?
questions.solution: a) MADAM. M→M(symmetric), A→A(symmetric), D→D(vertical symmetry), A→A, M→M. The word is a palindrome and all letters are mirror-symmetric.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Water image of '8:15' on a clock?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: How many squares in a figure with a 4×4 grid?
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A folded paper (folded twice vertically) is punched at the centre of the folded edge. How many holes?
questions.solution: b) 4. Two folds = 4 layers. The centre of folded edge corresponds to mid-line after unfolding.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should the government ban the use of mobile phones while driving? Argument I: Yes, because it distracts drivers and causes accidents. Argument II: No, because people need phones for emergencies.
questions.solution: I is strong — distraction is a proven cause of accidents. II is weak — emergencies are rare exceptions, not a justification against a general safety rule.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should college admissions be based solely on entrance exam scores? Argument I: Yes, because exams provide an objective assessment. Argument II: No, because exams cause stress and anxiety.
questions.solution: I is strong — objective assessment is a valid criterion. II is weak — stress is subjective and not specific enough to reject the entire exam system.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The company has decided to give a 10% bonus to all employees this year.' Assumption I: The company had a profitable year. Assumption II: Employees will be motivated by the bonus.
questions.solution: I is implicit — a bonus usually follows good financial performance. II is not necessarily implicit — the company may give bonuses for other reasons (retention, goodwill) without assuming motivation.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The school has introduced a dress code for teachers.' Assumption I: Teachers were not dressing appropriately before. Assumption II: A dress code will improve the school's image.
questions.solution: I is implicit — a dress code is introduced when current attire is deemed unsuitable. II is not implicit — the school's image may not be the primary concern; the code could be for discipline or professionalism.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: All mammals are warm-blooded. Whales are mammals. Conclusion: Whales are warm-blooded.
questions.solution: Definitely true. All mammals are warm-blooded. Whales are a subset of mammals, so they must be warm-blooded.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: No fish can fly. Some aquatic animals can fly. Conclusion: Some aquatic animals are not fish.
questions.solution: Definitely true. Those aquatic animals that can fly are definitely not fish (since no fish can fly). So there exist aquatic animals that are not fish.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Situation: 'Instances of cyberbullying among teenagers have increased significantly.' Course I: Schools should conduct awareness programs on cyber safety. Course II: The government should ban social media for teenagers.
questions.solution: I follows — awareness addresses the root cause. II is extreme and impractical — banning social media is disproportionate and hard to enforce.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should smoking be banned in public places? Argument I: Yes, because second-hand smoke harms non-smokers. Argument II: No, because it infringes on personal freedom.
questions.solution: I is strong — public health is a valid concern. II is weak — personal freedom does not extend to harming others in shared spaces.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The government plans to build more airports in Tier-2 cities.' Assumption I: There is sufficient passenger demand in Tier-2 cities. Assumption II: Tier-2 cities currently have no air connectivity.
questions.solution: I is implicit — airports are built where demand exists. II is not implicit — 'more airports' implies some exist already.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Some apples are red. All red fruits are sweet. Conclusion: Some apples are sweet.
questions.solution: Possibly true. Some apples are red, and all red fruits are sweet, so those red apples are sweet. But not all apples are necessarily red, so the conclusion is true for red apples only.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should there be a uniform civil code in India? Argument I: Yes, because it will ensure gender equality in personal laws. Argument II: No, because it will hurt religious sentiments.
questions.solution: I is strong — gender equality is a constitutional value. II is weak — religious sentiment is subjective and not a sound argument against legal reform.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Situation: 'Many patients in rural areas travel over 50 km to reach the nearest hospital.' Course I: The government should build primary health centres in every village cluster. Course II: The government should provide free ambulances for all rural patients.
questions.solution: I follows — building local health centres addresses the root cause. II is a partial solution (transport, not care) and may be logistically challenging.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The municipal corporation has decided to plant 10,000 trees in the city.' Assumption I: The city currently lacks adequate green cover. Assumption II: Trees will help reduce air pollution.
questions.solution: Both are implicit. I: Planting trees implies a need for more greenery. II: One of the main purposes of urban trees is pollution reduction.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: All politicians are public speakers. Some public speakers are not honest. Conclusion: Some politicians are not honest.
questions.solution: Does not follow. All politicians are in the 'public speaker' set. But the dishonest public speakers may be different from the politician subset. We cannot conclude anything about politicians.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Situation: 'A spike in road accidents has been linked to drunk driving.' Course I: Police should conduct random breathalyzer checks. Course II: The government should increase the legal drinking age.
questions.solution: I follows — enforcement directly addresses drunk driving. II is indirect — increasing drinking age may not affect those who already drink and drive illegally.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should animal testing for cosmetics be banned? Argument I: Yes, because it causes unnecessary suffering to animals. Argument II: No, because alternatives are not yet widely available.
questions.solution: Both are strong. I raises an ethical concern. II raises a practical limitation. Both are directly relevant and based on substantive considerations.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The HR department has launched a skill development program for employees.' Assumption I: Employees currently lack some required skills. Assumption II: The program will improve employee productivity.
questions.solution: Both are implicit. A skill program exists because there is a skill gap (I) and with the expectation it will improve performance (II).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Every square is a rectangle. Some rectangles are coloured. Conclusion: Some squares are coloured.
questions.solution: Possibly true. All squares are rectangles, and some rectangles are coloured. Those coloured rectangles could be squares, but not necessarily. The colour could be in non-square rectangles.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Situation: 'Villagers near a forest are frequently attacked by wild animals venturing into human settlements.' Course I: The forest department should strengthen fencing around the forest boundary. Course II: Villagers should be relocated to safer areas.
questions.solution: I follows — fencing directly prevents animals from entering settlements. II is extreme and impractical — relocation is costly and disrupts lives unnecessarily.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should the retirement age be increased to 65? Argument I: Yes, because people are living longer and healthier lives. Argument II: No, because it will reduce job opportunities for the youth.
questions.solution: Both are strong. I cites demographic reality. II cites economic impact on employment. Both are directly relevant and evidence-based.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The airline has reduced baggage allowance for economy class passengers.' Assumption I: The airline wants to save fuel costs. Assumption II: Passengers will accept this change without complaint.
questions.solution: I is implicit — reducing weight saves fuel, a common airline practice. II is not implicit — the airline does not assume acceptance; it may anticipate complaints but proceed anyway.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: No cloud is a stone. Some clouds are rain-bearing. Conclusion: Some rain-bearing things are not stones.
questions.solution: Definitely true. Rain-bearing clouds exist (from statement 2). No cloud is a stone (statement 1). So those rain-bearing clouds are not stones.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Situation: 'Exams have been postponed due to a natural calamity.' Course I: The education board should announce revised dates immediately. Course II: The board should reduce the syllabus to reduce student burden.
questions.solution: I follows — announcing revised dates is necessary and within the board's authority. II is not directly related to the postponement; syllabus reduction is a separate policy decision.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: Should genetically modified (GM) crops be allowed in India? Argument I: Yes, because they can increase agricultural yield. Argument II: No, because their long-term health effects are unknown.
questions.solution: Both are strong. I cites a concrete benefit (yield). II cites a legitimate concern (unknown health effects). Both are directly relevant to the policy decision.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Statement: 'The police department has installed CCTV cameras in all public parks.' Assumption I: CCTV cameras deter criminal activity. Assumption II: Parks previously had security concerns.
questions.solution: Both are implicit. I: Cameras are installed assuming they will reduce crime. II: The decision implies there were security issues that warranted surveillance.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A candidate encounters an inference question where one option is factually true in the real world but not supported by the passage. According to the Principle of Passage‑Only Reasoning, how should this option be treated?
questions.a: Eliminate it because answers must be grounded exclusively in the passage
opts: Select it because it is factually correct
Eliminate it because answers must be grounded exclusively in the passage
Select it if it aligns with the candidate's domain knowledge
Mark it as correct only if the passage does not contradict it
questions.solution: Section 1.3 states: 'A fundamental rule governing all questions is that answers must be grounded exclusively in the information presented in the passage. Options that introduce outside knowledge, even if factually correct in the real world, are considered incorrect because the examination measures reading comprehension, not general awareness.' This directly supports option B.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: According to the passage, which of the following best describes an implicit assumption in an argument?
questions.a: An unstated belief necessary for the argument to hold.
opts: A stated reason supporting the claim.
An unstated belief necessary for the argument to hold.
A statistical evidence cited by the author.
questions.solution: The passage defines implicit assumptions as "unstated beliefs or propositions that must be true for the argument to hold" and gives examples such as the government's capacity to implement a stimulus. Option B matches this definition exactly. Option A describes a premise, option C describes a counterargument, and option D describes evidence. Therefore, B is the correct answer.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In a passage where the author writes, "Some argue that the policy will increase inflation; however, this view overlooks the stabilizing effect of monetary controls," what is the function of the clause beginning with "Some argue that"?
questions.a: It introduces a counterargument that the author refutes.
opts: It presents the author's main claim.
It introduces a counterargument that the author refutes.
It provides evidence for the author's premise.
questions.solution: The passage lists signal phrases for counterarguments such as "some argue that" and for refutations such as "however" and "this view overlooks." The clause "Some argue that" introduces an opposing viewpoint, and the following "however" signals its refutation. Thus, the clause functions as a counterargument presented for refutation, making option B correct.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Which signal phrase most reliably indicates a refutation of a counterargument, according to the passage?
questions.solution: The passage explicitly provides a list of signal words for refutations, including "however," "but," "nevertheless," "this view overlooks," "such arguments fail to consider," and "this objection is flawed because." Among the options, only "this objection is flawed because" appears in that list. The other options are signals for evidence ("for example," "according to") or counterarguments ("some argue that"). Hence, option C is correct.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: When a passage presents multiple perspectives and integrates statistical information, expert opinions, and case studies, the passage suggests that the reader should primarily do which of the following?
questions.a: Determine which perspective each piece of data supports.
opts: Determine which perspective each piece of data supports.
Ignore the author's stance and focus only on the data.
Treat all perspectives as equally valid.
questions.solution: The section "Managing Passages with Divergent Perspectives and Data Integration" states that the key is to "understand how each piece of data relates to the different perspectives" and asks "Does a statistic support one theory over another? Does an expert opinion align with the author's view or a counterargument?" This directly supports option B. The passage does not advise memorization (A), ignoring the author's stance (C), or treating all perspectives as equally valid (D).
questions.subject: English

questions.q: The passage lists several common traps in advanced reading comprehension. Which of the following is explicitly identified as a trap?
opts: Confusing the author's tone with the tone of a cited expert.
Failing to identify the main idea of each paragraph.
questions.solution: The "Common Traps" section includes the bullet point: "Over-Inferring from Limited Evidence: Drawing conclusions that are plausible but not strictly necessitated by the information provided in the passage." This matches option B exactly. The other options, while plausible reading errors, are not listed among the explicit traps in the passage.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: According to the passage, which piece of evidence would be considered most reliable for supporting a conclusion?
questions.a: A peer‑reviewed meta‑analysis with methodology disclosed
opts: A newspaper op‑ed citing a scholar's opinion
A peer‑reviewed meta‑analysis with methodology disclosed
An anecdotal illustration from a single chronicler
A secondary summary that omits original conditions
questions.solution: The passage states that a reliable primary datum such as a laboratory measurement reported with methodology carries more weight than a secondary summary, and that passages juxtaposing a peer‑reviewed meta‑analysis with a newspaper op‑ed test the ability to rank evidentiary hierarchy. A peer‑reviewed meta‑analysis with disclosed methodology represents the highest level of methodological transparency and peer scrutiny, making it the strongest support for a conclusion.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In the three‑layer annotation system described for long passages, what is the purpose of Layer 1 tags?
questions.a: To mark the thesis, major supporting paragraphs, counter‑arguments, and conclusion
opts: To label each piece of evidence with its type and credibility
To mark the thesis, major supporting paragraphs, counter‑arguments, and conclusion
To note shifts in tone and qualifying language
To convert visual elements into bullet lists of numeric facts
questions.solution: Layer 1 is defined as structural tags: marking the thesis statement (T), each major supporting paragraph (S1, S2…), counter‑argument sections (C), and the concluding synthesis (Z). This creates a quick outline for main‑idea and organization questions. The other options describe Layer 2 (evidential tags), Layer 3 (rhetorical tags), and the treatment of visual elements, respectively.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: When reading comparative passages, the passage recommends constructing a comparative matrix. What common error does this matrix help avoid?
questions.a: Attributing a counter‑argument’s evidence to the main author
opts: Attributing a counter‑argument’s evidence to the main author
Overlooking modal qualifiers in abstract texts
Confusing statistical significance with practical relevance
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly lists "Attributing a counter‑argument’s evidence to the main author in comparative passages" as a common error. The comparative matrix aligns each text’s thesis, evidence, and stance side by side, preventing the test‑taker from mistakenly assigning evidence from a counter‑argument to the primary author. The other errors relate to abstract passages, quantitative integration, and evidence evaluation, not comparative passages.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: The passage suggests that in abstract texts, modal qualifiers such as ‘necessarily’ and ‘contingently’ are important because they:
questions.a: Delimit the strength of the claim
opts: Delimit the strength of the claim
Identify the provenance of each claim
Signal the degree of peer scrutiny
questions.solution: The text states: "pay attention to modal qualifiers (‘necessarily’, ‘possibly’, ‘contingently’) because they delimit the strength of the claim." This directly matches option B. Tone shifts are covered by rhetorical tags, provenance by evidential tags, and peer scrutiny by source credibility markers, not by modal qualifiers.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: If a table shows overlapping confidence intervals for two groups but the prose claims ‘a clear advantage’, what inference does the passage support?
questions.a: The author’s claim overstates the evidence
opts: The data confirms the author’s claim
The author’s claim overstates the evidence
The confidence intervals are irrelevant to the claim
The prose correctly interprets statistical significance
questions.solution: The passage gives this exact example: "a table may show overlapping confidence intervals for two groups, yet the text claims ‘a clear advantage’. The correct inference is that the author’s claim overstates the evidence." Overlapping confidence intervals indicate no statistically significant difference, so the author’s qualitative claim exceeds what the quantitative data supports.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In a passage, the author opens with a Nobel laureate’s endorsement before presenting statistical data. This rhetorical move primarily serves to:
questions.a: Establish the author’s credibility through ethos.
opts: Establish the author’s credibility through ethos.
Appeal to the reader’s emotions through pathos.
Summarize the main argument of the passage.
questions.solution: The classical appeals are ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), and logos (logic). Citing a Nobel laureate leverages the authority and prestige of the laureate to pre‑empt scepticism and lend weight to the subsequent data. This is a textbook ethos strategy. The passage does not primarily evoke emotion, present a logical syllogism, or summarize the argument at that point. Therefore, the correct function is establishing credibility.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Paragraph 1 cites a single study showing a 12% rise in test scores after a policy change. Paragraph 3 reveals the study had a small sample and short duration. The author concludes the policy is universally effective. This conclusion is:
questions.a: Weakened by the omitted limitations noted later.
opts: Weakened by the omitted limitations noted later.
Strengthened by the later paragraph’s details.
questions.solution: The argument commits a hasty generalisation by extrapolating universal effectiveness from one limited study. The later paragraph supplies the omitted methodological limitations (small sample, short duration), which directly undermine the generalisation. The conclusion is therefore weakened, not supported, by the full evidence. Option B captures this logical gap; the other options misrepresent the relationship between the evidence and the conclusion.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: A direct quote in a passage reads: “We must act now,” said the activist. The author later reports it indirectly as: “He argued that they must act now.” The primary effect of this shift is:
questions.a: The pronoun shift reduces the immediacy of the call.
opts: The modal verb changes from obligation to recommendation.
The pronoun shift reduces the immediacy of the call.
The tense shift alters the time reference of the claim.
The reporting verb ‘argued’ adds skepticism to the claim.
questions.solution: The lesson highlights that embedded dialogue often involves pronoun adjustments and modal verb tracking. In the example, the modal “must” (obligation) remains unchanged, so the force of obligation is preserved. However, the shift from first‑person plural “We” to third‑person “they” distances the reader from the original collective urgency, reducing immediacy. The tense does not change, and “argued” is a neutral reporting verb. Thus, the key alteration is the pronoun shift.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: A passage describes policy supporters as “advocates” and opponents as “detractors.” Supporting data is labeled “robust evidence” while contrary data is called “anecdotal reports.” This framing reveals:
questions.a: The author’s bias against the opponents.
opts: A neutral presentation of both sides.
The author’s bias against the opponents.
A balanced analysis of the policy.
questions.solution: Framing bias appears in lexical choices that assign positive connotations to one side and negative connotations to the other. “Advocates” and “robust evidence” carry favorable tones, whereas “detractors” and “anecdotal reports” are pejorative. This systematic asymmetry indicates the author’s slant against the opponents. The passage is therefore not neutral, balanced, or objective. Option B correctly identifies the bias revealed by the framing ledger.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: According to the passage, which distinction is specifically identified as critical when evaluating a study's Methods paragraph?
questions.a: Identifying the study design and its hierarchy of evidence
opts: Distinguishing a hypothesis from a prediction
Distinguishing a control variable from a confounding variable
Identifying the study design and its hierarchy of evidence
Distinguishing statistical significance from practical significance
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states under 'Decoding the Methods Paragraph' that one must 'Identify the study design: randomized controlled trial (RCT), cohort study, case-control, cross-sectional, or qualitative. Each design carries a hierarchy of evidence'. While the introduction lists other distinctions (hypothesis/prediction, control/confounding, statistical/practical), the hierarchy of study designs is specifically located in the Methods paragraph section.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: What is the primary risk described in the passage when a test-taker confuses obiter dicta with ratio decidendi in case-law passages?
questions.a: Selecting the broader, non-binding principle as binding precedent
opts: Misidentifying the legislative intent behind the statute
Selecting the broader, non-binding principle as binding precedent
Misapplying the rule of lenity to a civil regulatory provision
Overlooking the purposive construction of the legal text
questions.solution: The passage lists 'Confusing obiter dicta for ratio decidendi in case-law passages and selecting the broader, non-binding principle' as a key error in the final summary. Ratio decidendi is the binding legal reasoning, while obiter dicta are non-binding judicial remarks; confusing them leads to treating persuasive commentary as mandatory authority.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: The passage argues that treating a primary source's account as unmediated truth is an error primarily because:
questions.a: Primary sources require OPVL analysis to assess purpose and limitations
opts: Primary sources are inherently unreliable due to author bias
Primary sources require OPVL analysis to assess purpose and limitations
Primary sources lack corroboration from secondary historical literature
Primary sources are written from a presentist perspective
questions.solution: Under 'Interrogating Historical Narratives', the passage states 'Primary Sources as Evidence, Not Truth' and identifies the error: 'Accepting a primary source's account at face value without applying OPVL to assess its purpose and limitations.' OPVL (Origin, Purpose, Value, Limitation) is the mandated framework for evaluating primary sources.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In the context of literary and critical theory passages, what key error does the passage identify regarding the interpretation of ambiguity?
questions.a: Forcing a single definitive interpretation on a passage that sustains ambiguity
opts: Failing to identify the specific theoretical lens employed by the author
Forcing a single definitive interpretation on a passage that sustains ambiguity
Overlooking intertextual allusions that structure the passage's meaning
Confusing the author's intentional ambiguity with textual undecidability
questions.solution: The final summary of errors explicitly lists: 'Forcing a single definitive interpretation on a literary passage that deliberately sustains ambiguity or undecidability.' The passage emphasizes that literary passages often resist closure, and the 'Resistant Reading' protocol requires tolerating ambiguity rather than resolving it.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Which of the following best defines the 'Almost Right' trap as described in the passage's section on Diagnostic Answer-Option Forensics?
questions.a: An option that contains a verifiably true statement from the passage but fails the question's specific demand
opts: An option that uses high-frequency passage vocabulary to exploit familiarity heuristic
An option that contains a verifiably true statement from the passage but fails the question's specific demand
An option that applies a statutory interpretation canon outside its proper jurisdictional domain
An option that infers causation from a historical correlation without corroborating evidence
questions.solution: The section 'The "Almost Right" Trap: Partial Truth as Bait' defines it as: 'The most dangerous distractor contains a verifiably true statement from the passage but fails the question's specific demand.' It illustrates this with an option describing a methodology (true detail) that does not answer the question about primary purpose (specific demand).
questions.subject: English

questions.q: According to the passage, what should a test‑taker do first when a reading‑comprehension passage includes a chart or table?
questions.a: Scan the graphic to note variable names, units, time spans, and any highlighted outliers.
opts: Read the passage thoroughly before looking at the graphic.
Scan the graphic to note variable names, units, time spans, and any highlighted outliers.
Memorize every data point in the visual display.
Ignore the visual unless a question explicitly refers to it.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly advises: "Begin by scanning the graphic before reading the passage; note the variable names, units, time spans, and any highlighted outliers." This step lets the reader treat the visual as a parallel text and catch discrepancies between the prose and the data. Option A contradicts the recommended order. Option C is impractical and not suggested. Option D would cause the test‑taker to miss information that the passage assumes the reader has already observed. Therefore, the correct procedure is described in option B.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: Which of the following sentences contains a Tier 2 (probability) hedging marker as defined in the passage?
questions.a: The data suggest that the new drug lowers blood pressure.
opts: The study proves that the new drug lowers blood pressure.
The results indicate that the new drug may lower blood pressure.
The data suggest that the new drug lowers blood pressure.
The author speculates that the new drug could lower blood pressure.
questions.solution: The passage maps hedging markers to confidence tiers: Tier 1 (certainty) – shows, proves, establishes; Tier 2 (probability) – indicates, suggests, points to; Tier 3 (possibility) – may, might, could; Tier 4 (speculation) – speculates, conjectures, hypothesises. Option A uses "proves" (Tier 1). Option B uses "may" (Tier 3). Option D uses "speculates" (Tier 4). Option C uses "suggest", which the passage lists under Tier 2. Hence, option C is the only sentence with a Tier 2 marker.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In evaluating an analogy within a passage, the recommended approach is to:
questions.a: Map the shared mechanism and check for critical disanalogies.
opts: Accept the analogy if the two domains share any similarity.
Map the shared mechanism and check for critical disanalogies.
Focus only on surface similarities between the domains.
Assume the analogy is valid whenever the author uses concessive clauses.
questions.solution: The passage states: "When evaluating analogies, map each separately; the question may ask which analogy the author relies on most heavily… Beware of ignoring a critical disanalogy when evaluating an analogy, leading to an over‑extension distractor." This directs the test‑taker to identify the underlying mechanism that links the two domains and then scrutinize any important differences (disanalogies). Option A and C describe superficial acceptance, which the lesson warns against. Option D confuses concessive language with analogical validity. Thus, option B reflects the prescribed method.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: For a question stem “All of the following are supported by the passage EXCEPT,” the most efficient method described in the passage is:
questions.a: Locate evidence for each option in the passage; the one lacking support is the answer.
opts: Choose the option that is false in the real world.
Locate evidence for each option in the passage; the one lacking support is the answer.
Select the option that contains the strongest hedging language.
questions.solution: The lesson outlines a systematic technique: "treat the three true options as ‘find‑the‑evidence’ tasks and the false option as a ‘find‑the‑gap’ task. Scan each option, locate the corresponding passage segment, and mark it with a check (✓) or cross (✗). The option with a cross is the answer." This directly corresponds to option B. Option A confuses real‑world truth with textual support. Option C and D are irrelevant heuristics not mentioned in the passage. Therefore, option B is the correct procedure.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: In a passage the author writes: "Had the policy been implemented earlier, the crisis would have been averted." Which hidden premise must the author assume for this counterfactual to be logically valid?
questions.a: All other variables remained constant (ceteris paribus).
opts: The policy was the only factor influencing the crisis.
All other variables remained constant (ceteris paribus).
The crisis would have occurred regardless of the policy.
The policy was implemented later than planned.
questions.solution: A genuine counterfactual requires the assumption that no other relevant factors changed between the actual and the imagined scenario. The lesson states that examiners often embed a hidden premise such as the ceteris‑paribus clause. Option B restates this necessary assumption, while the other options either over‑generalise the policy's exclusivity, contradict the counterfactual, or describe a factual timing detail not required for the logical link.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: A passage presents the chain: "Higher carbon taxes raise fuel prices; higher fuel prices may reduce vehicle kilometres travelled; reduced kilometres lower emissions." Which link does the author treat as the most uncertain?
questions.a: Higher fuel prices may reduce vehicle kilometres travelled.
opts: Higher carbon taxes raise fuel prices.
Higher fuel prices may reduce vehicle kilometres travelled.
The overall effect on emissions is negligible.
questions.solution: The lesson explains that hedging language ("may reduce", "could lower") marks the weakest link in an implicit causal chain. The second link contains the qualifier "may", indicating the author views that step as uncertain. The first and third links are stated without qualifiers, so they are treated as more certain. Option B correctly identifies the hedged link.
questions.subject: English

questions.q: The basic structure doctrine was established in:
questions.solution: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) established that Parliament cannot alter the Constitution's basic structure.

questions.solution: Habeas corpus is used to produce a detained person before the court.

questions.solution: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognized privacy under Article 21.

questions.solution: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 introduced GST.

questions.solution: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties under Article 51A (Part IVA).

questions.q: A pre‑Constitution statute regulating motor vehicle permits was inconsistent with Article 19(1)(g) when the Constitution came into force. In 1960, a constitutional amendment removed the inconsistency. The statute became enforceable again without fresh legislation. Which doctrine explains this revival?
questions.solution: The doctrine of eclipse applies to pre‑Constitutional laws that conflict with a fundamental right. Such a law is not void but becomes dormant (eclipsed) while the fundamental right exists. When the fundamental right is amended or removed, the eclipse lifts automatically and the original law revives without new legislation. This was first articulated in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), where a pre‑Constitution motor‑vehicles tax was eclipsed by Article 19(1)(g) and revived after the 1951 amendment to that article.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court refuse to apply the doctrine of severability because the invalid provision formed the "heart" of the legislation, and striking it down would defeat the legislative design?
questions.a: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
opts: K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1972)
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951)
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955)
questions.solution: The doctrine of severability allows a court to strike down only the offending part of a statute if the remainder can operate independently and reflects legislative intent. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court held that the amendment curtailing judicial review of constitutional amendments was the core purpose of the amendment; removing it would defeat the legislative design. Consequently, the entire amendment was struck down rather than severed.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A State legislature enacts a law on "public health" (a State List entry) which incidentally affects "trade and commerce" (a Union List entry). The court upholds the law, finding that its dominant purpose lies within the State's competence. Which test did the court apply?
questions.solution: Colourable legislation questions are resolved by the pith‑and‑substance test. The court examines the true nature and dominant purpose of the law; incidental encroachment on another legislature's field is permissible if the law's pith and substance falls within the enacting legislature's competence. Here, the law's dominant purpose is public health (State List), so the incidental effect on trade and commerce does not render it ultra vires.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which case established that judicial review of constitutional amendments is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution, leading to the striking down of a clause that sought to curtail such review?
questions.a: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
opts: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
questions.solution: The basic‑structure doctrine evolved from Shankari Prasad (Parliament can amend FRs) through Golaknath (Parliament cannot amend FRs) to Kesavananda Bharati (basic structure limits amending power). In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court specifically held that judicial review of constitutional amendments is an essential feature of the basic structure. The amendment clause that attempted to oust judicial review was therefore struck down as violating the basic structure.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which body acts as the adjudicatory authority for data‑privacy violations and can impose penalties up to ₹250 crore?
opts: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)
questions.solution: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 creates the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI) as an adjudicatory body for data‑privacy violations. The DPBI can impose penalties up to ₹250 crore, issue compliance directions, and hear appeals from data principals. Its chairperson and members are appointed by the Central Government. The IBBI regulates insolvency professionals, the CCI enforces competition law, and the NCLAT is an appellate tribunal for corporate matters.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Under the doctrine of eclipse, a pre‑constitutional statute inconsistent with a fundamental right becomes:
questions.a: Dormant and capable of revival if the constitutional impediment is removed by amendment
opts: Repealed and cannot be revived without fresh legislation
Void ab initio and permanently unenforceable
Dormant and capable of revival if the constitutional impediment is removed by amendment
Valid but subject to judicial modification to conform to the fundamental right
questions.solution: The lesson states that in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), the Supreme Court held that a pre‑constitutional law inconsistent with Part III is not dead but merely eclipsed — dormant — and can revive if the constitutional impediment is removed by amendment. The eclipse operates only while the fundamental right remains in force; once amended, the original statute regains full effect without fresh legislation. Option A describes repeal, which the doctrine explicitly avoids. Option B describes void ab initio, which applies to post‑constitutional laws under Article 13(2), not pre‑constitutional laws under Article 13(1). Option D is incorrect because the statute is not judicially modified; it revives in its original form.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965), the Supreme Court established which principle regarding legislative privileges?
questions.a: Judicial review extends to examining whether a claimed privilege is consistent with the Constitution
opts: The House is the sole and final judge of its own privileges
Judicial review extends to examining whether a claimed privilege is consistent with the Constitution
Legislative privileges are absolute and cannot be questioned in any court
Privileges under Article 105 are subject to the President's prior approval
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that in Keshav Singh v. Speaker (1965), the Supreme Court held that the judiciary can examine whether a claimed privilege is consistent with the Constitution and that the House cannot be the sole judge of its own privileges. This principle was reiterated in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker (2007). Option A is the exact position the Court rejected. Option C contradicts the holding that privileges are not absolute. Option D has no basis in the text or constitutional law.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) in the Fourth Judges Case (2015) primarily because:
questions.a: The inclusion of the Law Minister and two eminent persons impaired the primacy of the judiciary, violating the basic structure
opts: It violated the seniority convention for appointing the Chief Justice of India
The inclusion of the Law Minister and two eminent persons impaired the primacy of the judiciary, violating the basic structure
It failed to provide adequate representation for women and marginalized communities
The amendment procedure under Article 368 was not followed correctly
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in the Fourth Judges Case (2015) because the inclusion of the Law Minister and two eminent persons impaired the primacy of the judiciary, which the Court held to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution. The Court reaffirmed the collegium system with a Memorandum of Procedure for transparency. Option A concerns a convention, not the constitutional ground for striking down NJAC. Option C, while a policy concern, was not the ratio decidendi. Option D is factually incorrect; the 99th Constitutional Amendment followed Article 368 procedure.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which case marked the beginning of the shift in locus standi by recognizing that a letter addressed to a judge could be treated as a writ petition?
questions.a: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)
opts: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987)
Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984)
questions.solution: The lesson states that the shift in locus standi began with S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), where the Court recognised that a letter addressed to a judge could be treated as a writ petition. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) entertained a petition on behalf of undertrial prisoners but did not establish the letter‑as‑writ principle. M.C. Mehta (1987) expanded Article 21 to include a healthy environment. Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) treated a newspaper report as a PIL. The specific innovation of treating a letter as a writ petition is attributed to S.P. Gupta.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly matches the South African capital city with its governmental function?

Pretoria – Executive; Cape Town – Legislative; Bloemfontein – Judicial
Pretoria – Judicial; Cape Town – Executive; Bloemfontein – Legislative
Pretoria – Executive; Cape Town – Judicial; Bloemfontein – Legislative

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a basis for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to exercise contentious jurisdiction over a dispute between States?
questions.a: A resolution of the UN General Assembly referring the dispute to the Court
opts: A special agreement (compromis) between the parties
A compromissory clause in a treaty to which both States are parties
A unilateral declaration accepting the Court's compulsory jurisdiction under Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute
A resolution of the UN General Assembly referring the dispute to the Court
questions.solution: The lesson explains that ICJ jurisdiction is consent-based and lists three bases: (1) acceptance of compulsory jurisdiction under Article 36(2) (the "optional clause"), (2) a special agreement (compromis), or (3) a compromissory clause in a treaty. A UN General Assembly resolution can request an advisory opinion, but it does not confer contentious jurisdiction over a dispute between States. Thus, a General Assembly resolution is not a basis for contentious jurisdiction.

Automatically for all UN member states after 2018 activation.
