questions.q: Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees:
questions.a: Right to life and personal liberty
opts: Right to life and personal liberty
questions.solution: Article 21 guarantees right to life and personal liberty.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In a contract, 'consideration' means:
questions.solution: Consideration = something of value given in exchange — essential element of a valid contract.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: An employee of a courier company, while delivering a package, detours 15 kilometres to visit a friend and causes an accident. The employer argues the employee was on a "frolic of his own". Which factor is decisive for determining whether the employer remains vicariously liable?
questions.a: The degree of deviation from the assigned delivery route and duties
opts: Whether the employer exercised direct control over the manner of driving at the time of the accident
Whether the act of driving was expressly authorised by the employer
The degree of deviation from the assigned delivery route and duties
The employee's personal motive for making the detour
questions.solution: Vicarious liability hinges on whether the tort was committed "in the course of employment". The lesson states that the "frolic of his own" test focuses on the degree of deviation from assigned duties, not on the employee's motive or the employer's moment‑to‑moment control. A substantial deviation for personal purposes breaks the course of employment, while a minor or incidental deviation does not. Therefore, the decisive factor is the extent of the deviation from the assigned delivery route and duties.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract is frustrated when a supervening event makes performance impossible or unlawful. Which of the following is NOT a required element for frustration?
questions.a: The event renders performance merely more expensive or delayed
opts: The event occurs without fault of either party
The event was unforeseen and not provided for in the contract
The event renders performance merely more expensive or delayed
The event destroys the foundation of the contract or makes performance fundamentally different
questions.solution: The lesson lists three key requirements for frustration: (i) the event must be without fault of either party; (ii) it must be unforeseen and not provided for in the contract; (iii) it must destroy the foundation of the contract or make performance fundamentally different. An event that only makes performance more costly or delayed does not satisfy the third requirement, because the contract’s core purpose remains achievable. Hence, increased expense or delay alone is insufficient for frustration.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In criminal law, the presumption regarding mens rea for regulatory offences is best described by which statement?
questions.a: Courts presume mens rea unless the statute expressly excludes it, especially when imprisonment is prescribed
opts: All regulatory offences are strict liability offences by default
Courts presume mens rea unless the statute expressly excludes it, especially when imprisonment is prescribed
Specific intent must be proved for every regulatory offence
General intent is sufficient to convict for any strict liability offence
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly warns against treating all regulatory offences as strict liability. It states that courts presume mens rea unless the statute expressly excludes it, particularly when the offence carries imprisonment. This presumption protects individuals from conviction without a guilty mind unless Parliament clearly indicates otherwise. Therefore, the correct description of the presumption is that mens rea is presumed unless expressly excluded by statute.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Under Hindu law, which statement accurately reflects the position on matrimonial property division on divorce?
questions.a: There is no automatic community of property; division depends on joint ownership and judicial discretion
opts: The wife automatically receives half of the husband’s property upon divorce
There is no automatic community of property; division depends on joint ownership and judicial discretion
The Hindu Succession Act, 2005 grants the wife an equal share in all of the husband’s self‑acquired property
Section 27 of the Hindu Marriage Act allows division of all property acquired during the marriage regardless of title
questions.solution: The lesson states that India has no uniform matrimonial property regime and that under the Hindu Marriage Act there is no automatic community of property. Each spouse retains ownership of property in their name, and courts may divide only joint assets under Section 27 (property presented at or about marriage). The 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act gives daughters coparcenary rights in joint family property, not a share in the husband’s self‑acquired property. Hence, division depends on joint ownership and judicial discretion, not on an automatic half‑share.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A chemical plant licensed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 stores large quantities of toxic gas. An unprecedented earthquake — an act of God — causes a tank rupture, releasing gas that kills nearby residents. The plant management pleads the defence of act of God and statutory compliance. Under the principle of absolute liability established in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, what is the plant's liability?
questions.a: The plant is absolutely liable because hazardous industries owe a non-delegable duty to the community, and no defence of act of God, statutory authority, or due care is available.
opts: The plant is not liable because the escape was caused by an unforeseeable act of God, which is a valid defence under absolute liability.
The plant is absolutely liable because hazardous industries owe a non-delegable duty to the community, and no defence of act of God, statutory authority, or due care is available.
The plant is liable only under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher if the residents prove negligence in maintenance of the tanks.
The plant is not liable because the statutory licence under the Environment (Protection) Act expressly authorizes the activity and compliance shields the enterprise.
questions.solution: The M.C. Mehta principle establishes absolute liability for enterprises engaged in inherently dangerous activities. The Supreme Court explicitly held that no defence — including act of God, third-party act, statutory authority, or due care — can absolve such enterprises. The storage of toxic gas on a large scale qualifies as a hazardous activity under the Environment (Protection) Act. Therefore, the plant is liable irrespective of the earthquake or its licence. Option A incorrectly imports the act-of-God defence from strict liability. Option C wrongly suggests negligence must be proved. Option D misstates the law: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum confirmed that regulatory compliance does not override the polluter-pays principle under absolute liability.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A purchases poison, mixes it into a dish of food, and places the dish on the dining table where B usually eats dinner. A intends to kill B. Before B returns home, the police, acting on a tip-off, enter the house and seize the dish. A is charged with attempt to murder under Section 307 IPC read with Section 511 IPC. Applying the proximity test from Mohd. Yakub v. State, what is the correct legal position?
questions.a: A is not guilty of attempt; the acts amount only to preparation because B was not present and the chain of causation could still be broken by A's voluntary desistance or external intervention.
opts: A is guilty of attempt because he completed all preparatory steps and the act of placing the poisoned food is proximate to the commission of murder.
A is guilty of attempt because mixing poison and placing the food constitutes an act towards the commission of the offence under Section 511 IPC.
A is not guilty of attempt; the acts amount only to preparation because B was not present and the chain of causation could still be broken by A's voluntary desistance or external intervention.
A is not guilty of attempt because the poison was not actually consumed, and attempt requires the last act necessary for completion of the offence.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Mohd. Yakub distinguished preparation from attempt by the proximity test: an act is an attempt only if it is so close to the completed offence that it would have resulted in commission but for interruption. Here, B was absent; the poisoned food was merely placed on the table. A retained the opportunity to desist (e.g., remove the dish) before B's arrival. The act is not the "last step" — consumption by B is still required. Thus, the acts constitute preparation, not attempt. Option A misapplies proximity by treating placement as the final act. Option B incorrectly equates any act towards the offence with attempt under Section 511. Option D states the "last act" test, which is not the sole criterion in Indian law; proximity is the governing standard.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A State Government issues a notification announcing a new recruitment policy for Group C posts, stating that candidates who have cleared a specific skill test will be given preference. Relying on this, 500 candidates appear for and clear the test. Before appointments are made, the Government withdraws the notification without giving the candidates a hearing. The candidates challenge the withdrawal. Applying the doctrine of legitimate expectation, which conclusion follows?
questions.a: The candidates have a procedural legitimate expectation to be heard before the policy is withdrawn, as the notification created a clear representation.
opts: The candidates have a substantive legitimate expectation to appointment because they fulfilled the condition in the notification.
The candidates have a procedural legitimate expectation to be heard before the policy is withdrawn, as the notification created a clear representation.
The candidates have no legitimate expectation because recruitment is a sovereign function and promissory estoppel does not apply against the State.
The candidates can claim a substantive right to appointment under Article 14, as the withdrawal is manifestly arbitrary.
questions.solution: The notification created a clear, unambiguous representation (policy expectation), generating a legitimate expectation. Under the doctrine, this imposes a procedural fairness obligation — the authority must give an opportunity to be heard before departing from the representation. The candidates do not acquire a substantive right to appointment (substantive expectation is enforced only if conduct is "unfair" or "arbitrary" in a narrower sense), and the doctrine is distinct from promissory estoppel, which requires detriment and has stricter limits against sovereign functions. The correct remedy is a hearing, not automatic appointment.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In a claim for medical negligence against a surgeon, the plaintiff argues that a newer surgical technique with better outcomes was available but not used. The surgeon's practice conformed to a method accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion at the time. Applying the principle in Kusum Sharma v Batra Hospital (2010), how should the court rule on breach of duty?
questions.a: Hold the surgeon not liable because the Bolam test is satisfied if the practice is accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion
opts: Hold the surgeon liable because a better alternative existed and the standard of care requires the best available practice
Hold the surgeon not liable because the Bolam test is satisfied if the practice is accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion
Remand for expert testimony on whether the newer technique was standard practice in that specialty
Apply the reasonable person test instead of Bolam because the newer technique was widely known
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Kusum Sharma v Batra Hospital (2010) clarified that a doctor is not negligent merely because a better alternative existed. The Bolam test governs medical negligence in India: the standard is whether the practice is accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion. The existence of a superior technique does not, by itself, establish breach if the chosen method meets this threshold. Option A misstates the law by imposing a 'best practice' standard. Option C is unnecessary because the principle is settled. Option D incorrectly substitutes the general reasonable person test for the professional Bolam standard.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A supplies necessaries to B, a minor, for B's maintenance. B's property is insufficient to reimburse A. A then supplies further necessaries to B's wife, C, who is an adult of sound mind, for her maintenance. C has independent means but refuses to pay. Under Sections 68 and 69 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which claim(s) can A successfully maintain?
questions.a: Claim against B's property under Section 68 only
opts: Claim against B's property under Section 68 only
Claim against C personally under Section 69 only
Claims against both B's property under Section 68 and C personally under Section 69
Neither claim, because Section 68 requires the recipient to be incapable of contracting and Section 69 requires payment of another's legal obligation
questions.solution: Section 68 allows reimbursement from the property of a person incapable of contracting (e.g., a minor) for necessaries supplied to them or to someone they are legally bound to support. B is a minor, so A can claim against B's property for necessaries supplied to B. Section 69 applies when a person pays money due by another in which they have a legal interest. Here, A supplied goods to C, not paid C's debt. C is an adult of sound mind, not incapable of contracting, and A did not discharge a legal obligation of C's. Thus, no Section 69 claim arises. Option B and C incorrectly extend Section 69. Option D misreads Section 68, which precisely covers minors.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: X, a foreign national, is charged under the Indian Penal Code for an act committed in India. X pleads ignorance of Indian law as a defence under Section 76 IPC (mistake of fact). The prosecution argues that Section 76 does not apply. Which statement correctly states the law?
questions.a: Section 76 excuses only mistake of fact, not mistake of law, and ignorance of law is no excuse
opts: Mistake of law is a valid defence under Section 76 if the mistake is reasonable and in good faith
Section 76 excuses only mistake of fact, not mistake of law, and ignorance of law is no excuse
Section 76 applies to both mistake of fact and mistake of law if the accused believed they were legally bound
The defence is available because X, as a foreign national, cannot be presumed to know Indian law
questions.solution: Section 76 IPC expressly provides that an act done by a person who is, or by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law, in good faith believes himself to be bound by law, is not an offence. The section explicitly excludes mistake of law. The maxim ignorantia juris non excusat applies universally in Indian criminal law, regardless of nationality. Option A and C incorrectly include mistake of law. Option D creates a non-existent exception for foreign nationals. The statutory text and settled interpretation limit Section 76 to mistake of fact.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, a male Hindu adopter with a living wife adopts a female child without his wife's consent. The wife had not renounced the world nor been declared of unsound mind. The adoption is challenged. What is the legal effect?
questions.a: The adoption is void because Section 7 requires the wife's consent for any adoption by a male Hindu with a living wife
opts: The adoption is valid because consent is required only for adoption of a son
The adoption is void because Section 7 requires the wife's consent for any adoption by a male Hindu with a living wife
The adoption is voidable at the instance of the wife within one year
The adoption is valid if the adopter proves the wife's consent was unreasonably withheld
questions.solution: Section 7 of HAMA states that a male Hindu who has a wife living cannot adopt except with the consent of his wife, unless she has renounced the world or is of unsound mind. The provision applies to adoption of any child, son or daughter — it is not gender-specific. The wife's consent is mandatory. Without it, the adoption is void, not merely voidable. There is no provision for curing the defect by proving unreasonable withholding. The Supreme Court has held adoption under HAMA creates an irrevocable status; a void adoption confers no rights. Option A misreads Section 7. Option C invents a voidability period not in the Act. Option D introduces a judicial exception the statute does not provide.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A statute provides: "The District Magistrate, the Superintendent of Police, the Chief Medical Officer and any other officer shall constitute the District Disaster Management Committee." A private citizen, appointed as a member of a local NGO, claims the right to sit on the Committee under the phrase "any other officer". Applying the rule of ejusdem generis, which of the following is the correct legal position?
questions.a: The phrase "any other officer" is restricted to public functionaries of the same genus as the designated officers, and does not extend to private individuals.
opts: The phrase "any other officer" includes any person appointed by the District Magistrate for disaster management purposes.
The phrase "any other officer" is restricted to public functionaries of the same genus as the designated officers, and does not extend to private individuals.
The rule of ejusdem generis does not apply because the list is not exhaustive and the legislative intent shows a broader sweep.
The phrase "any other officer" must be interpreted harmoniously with the rest of the statute to include all stakeholders, including private citizens.
questions.solution: The rule of ejusdem generis applies when a general term follows a specific enumeration. Here, the specific words — District Magistrate, Superintendent of Police, Chief Medical Officer — are all public functionaries holding statutory office. They constitute a distinct genus: "public officers". The general phrase "any other officer" must be confined to that genus. The lesson explicitly states the Supreme Court held that "any other person" in a list of designated officers could not extend to private individuals because the preceding enumeration comprised only public functionaries. Option A incorrectly expands the scope. Option C is wrong because the list does constitute a distinct genus. Option D confuses ejusdem generis with harmonious construction, which deals with reconciling conflicting provisions, not restricting general terms following specific lists.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The State Legislature enacts the "State Agricultural Produce Marketing Act" which regulates the sale and purchase of agricultural produce within the State. The Act also fixes minimum quality standards for produce that is transported across State borders for inter-State trade. The Union challenges the Act as ultra vires. Applying the doctrine of pith and substance, what is the correct outcome?
questions.a: The Act is valid because its dominant purpose is regulation of markets, a State List subject, and the impact on inter-State trade is merely incidental.
opts: The Act is wholly ultra vires because it prescribes standards for inter-State trade, a Union List subject.
The Act is valid because its dominant purpose is regulation of markets, a State List subject, and the impact on inter-State trade is merely incidental.
The Act is valid only if the State can prove that the quality standards do not actually affect inter-State trade volumes.
The Act is ultra vires because the doctrine of pith and substance does not apply when a State law expressly regulates a Union List subject.
questions.solution: The doctrine of pith and substance requires identifying the dominant purpose of the legislation. The lesson states the test involves two stages: first, identify the dominant purpose by examining the preamble, title, and operative provisions; second, match that purpose with the appropriate legislative entry. Here, the Act's title and main operative provisions concern regulation of markets (Entry 28, State List). The fixing of quality standards for produce that happens to cross State borders is an incidental encroachment on inter-State trade (Entry 42, Union List). Following State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, where a prohibition law incidentally affecting import/export was upheld because its pith and substance was public health (State List), this Act is valid. Option A ignores the doctrine entirely. Option C imposes an incorrect evidentiary burden. Option D misstates the law — the doctrine applies precisely when there is incidental encroachment.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A State Legislature, which has competence over "Public Health" (State List) but not over "Regulation of Mines" (Union List), enacts a law titled "Public Health (Protection of Mine Workers) Act". The Act imposes detailed safety standards for mining operations, including ventilation, structural support, and shift durations, applicable only to mines. The Union challenges the Act as colourable legislation. What is the correct legal position?
questions.a: The Act is colourable legislation because its dominant purpose is regulation of mines, a Union List subject, disguised under the guise of public health.
opts: The Act is valid because public health is a State subject and the law genuinely aims to protect workers' health.
The Act is colourable legislation because its dominant purpose is regulation of mines, a Union List subject, disguised under the guise of public health.
The Act is valid unless the Union proves the State Legislature had a mala fide motive in enacting it.
The Act is not colourable legislation because the State Legislature has ancillary powers to regulate safety in any workplace affecting public health.
questions.solution: The doctrine of colourable legislation strikes down a law when the legislature, lacking competence over a subject, enacts a law under a permissible entry while its real object lies in a forbidden field. The lesson cites K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa: the doctrine does not permit a legislature to "colourably" enact a law under a permissible entry while its real object lies in a forbidden field. Here, the Act's detailed regulation of mining operations — ventilation, structural support, shift durations — goes far beyond incidental public health measures and constitutes direct regulation of mines (Union List). The dominant purpose is regulation of mines, not public health. The title is a mere colourable device. Option A ignores the dominant purpose test. Option C is wrong because colourable legislation focuses on legislative competence, not subjective motive. Option D misstates the scope of ancillary powers.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In a suit for partition of joint family property, the plaintiff claimed a 1/4th share. The court decreed the suit, granting the plaintiff a 1/4th share. The plaintiff did not claim mesne profits in that suit. Two years later, the plaintiff files a second suit claiming mesne profits for the period before the decree. The defendant pleads res judicata. Which of the following correctly states the legal position?
questions.a: The second suit is barred by constructive res judicata because the plaintiff might and ought to have claimed mesne profits in the first suit.
opts: The second suit is not barred by res judicata because mesne profits is a distinct cause of action from partition.
The second suit is barred by constructive res judicata because the plaintiff might and ought to have claimed mesne profits in the first suit.
The second suit is barred by issue estoppel because the issue of the plaintiff's share was already decided in the first suit.
The second suit is not barred because the parties are not identical — the defendant in the second suit is the legal heir of the original defendant.
questions.solution: Constructive res judicata (Explanation IV to Section 11, CPC) bars a matter that "might and ought" to have been raised in the former suit. The lesson explicitly states: "Examiners test the 'might and ought' standard by presenting a plaintiff who omitted a ground of relief in the first suit and later files a second suit on that ground. The correct answer invokes constructive res judicata." Mesne profits arising from the same property and period are a relief that could and should have been claimed in the partition suit. Option A is incorrect because constructive res judicata applies even to distinct reliefs if they arise from the same cause of action. Option C confuses issue estoppel (which binds a specific issue decided) with constructive res judicata (which bars omitted claims). Option D is factually unsupported and legally irrelevant — privies are covered by res judicata.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which of the following numbers is an integer but not a whole number?
questions.solution: Integers include all positive and negative whole numbers and zero (…, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …). Whole numbers are the non‑negative integers (0, 1, 2, 3, …). Therefore a negative integer such as -3 belongs to the set of integers but is excluded from the set of whole numbers. Zero and 5 are both whole numbers, and 2.5 is not an integer at all. Hence the only number that satisfies the condition is -3.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Which of the following four‑digit numbers is divisible by 11 according to the divisibility rule?
questions.solution: For divisibility by 11, find the difference between the sum of digits in odd positions and the sum of digits in even positions (counting from the rightmost digit as position 1). For 3080: digits from right are 0(pos1),8(pos2),0(pos3),3(pos4). Odd‑position sum = 0+0 = 0; even‑position sum = 8+3 = 11; difference = 11‑0 = 11, a multiple of 11, so 3080 is divisible. Checking the other options gives differences that are not multiples of 11. Thus only 3080 satisfies the rule.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Evaluate the expression: 12 + 18 ÷ 3 × (4 - 1)² - 5.
questions.solution: Apply BODMAS: Brackets first → (4‑1)=3. Orders → 3² = 9. Division and Multiplication left to right → 18 ÷ 3 = 6; 6 × 9 = 54. Addition and Subtraction left to right → 12 + 54 = 66; 66 - 5 = 61. The correct value is 61.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: How many integers from 1 to 500 inclusive are divisible by at least one of 3, 5, or 7?
questions.solution: Use inclusion–exclusion. Multiples of 3: ⌊500/3⌋ = 166. Multiples of 5: ⌊500/5⌋ = 100. Multiples of 7: ⌊500/7⌋ = 71. Multiples of lcm(3,5)=15: ⌊500/15⌋ = 33. Multiples of lcm(3,7)=21: ⌊500/21⌋ = 23. Multiples of lcm(5,7)=35: ⌊500/35⌋ = 14. Multiples of lcm(3,5,7)=105: ⌊500/105⌋ = 4. Total = 166+100+71 − 33−23−14 + 4 = 271.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: What is the sum of all positive integers k ≤ 360 such that gcd(k, 360) = 1?
questions.solution: First compute φ(360). Since 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5, φ(360) = 360 × (1 − 1/2) × (1 − 1/3) × (1 − 1/5) = 360 × 1/2 × 2/3 × 4/5 = 96. For n > 1, the sum of integers ≤ n that are coprime to n is n φ(n) / 2. Thus the required sum = 360 × 96 / 2 = 17280.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Denest the radical √(11 − 6√2).
questions.solution: We seek √x − √y such that (√x − √y)² = x + y − 2√(xy) = 11 − 6√2. Thus x + y = 11 and 2√(xy) = 6√2 ⇒ xy = 18. The pair (x, y) = (9, 2) satisfies both. Hence √(11 − 6√2) = √9 − √2 = 3 − √2.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Let X be the face value of a fair die roll. If Var(X) = 35/12, what is Var(2X + 3)?
questions.solution: For any random variable X and constants a, b, Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). Here a = 2, b = 3, so Var(2X + 3) = 2² × Var(X) = 4 × (35/12) = 35/3.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: The probability of a defective item is 0.02. In a sample of 100 items, approximate the probability of at most 3 defectives using the Poisson distribution.
questions.solution: For the binomial with n = 100, p = 0.02, the Poisson parameter is λ = np = 2. The required probability is P(X ≤ 3) = Σ_{k=0}^{3} e^{−2} 2^k / k! = e^{−2} (1 + 2 + 2 + 8/6) = e^{−2} × 6.3333. Using e^{−2} ≈ 0.135335, the product is 0.8571, which rounds to 0.857.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Compute φ(720) using the product formula for Euler's totient function.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: Simplify the nested radical √(7+4√3).
questions.solution: We seek √(7+4√3). Assume it equals √x + √y with x,y rational. Squaring gives x+y+2√(xy) = 7+4√3, so x+y=7 and 2√(xy)=4√3 → xy=3. The pair (x,y) = (4,3) satisfies these, giving √4+√3 = 2+√3. Checking: (2+√3)^2 = 4+3+4√3 = 7+4√3.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: How many derangements (permutations with no fixed points) exist for 5 distinct objects?
questions.solution: Derangements D_n satisfy D_0=1, D_1=0, D_n = (n−1)(D_{n−1}+D_{n−2}). Computing: D_2=1, D_3=2, D_4=9, D_5=4×(9+2)=44. Alternatively D_5 = round(5!/e) = round(120/2.71828) = round(44.145) = 44.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: How many solutions does the congruence x^2 ≡ 3 (mod 13) have?
questions.solution: Compute the Legendre symbol (3/13). Since 3 ≡ 3 (mod 4) and 13 ≡ 1 (mod 4), quadratic reciprocity gives (3/13) = (13/3) because the exponent ((3−1)/2)*((13−1)/2) = 1*6 = 6 is even. Now 13 ≡ 1 (mod 3), so (13/3) = (1/3) = 1. Hence 3 is a quadratic residue modulo 13, and the congruence has exactly two distinct solutions modulo 13. The answer is 2.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: For which of the following moduli does a primitive root NOT exist?
questions.solution: A primitive root exists exactly for n = 2, 4, p^k, 2p^k where p is an odd prime. The modulus 2 and 4 are explicitly allowed. The modulus 9 = 3^2 is of the form p^k with odd prime p = 3, so a primitive root exists. The modulus 8 = 2^3 is not of any allowed form (it is a power of 2 greater than 4), therefore the multiplicative group (ℤ/8ℤ)× is not cyclic and no primitive root exists. The correct choice is 8.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: What is the number of onto functions from a 5‑element set to a 3‑element set?
questions.solution: The number of onto functions from an n‑set to a k‑set equals k!·S(n,k), where S(n,k) is a Stirling number of the second kind. Using the recurrence S(n,k) = k·S(n−1,k) + S(n−1,k−1) with S(0,0)=1, we find S(4,2)=7, S(4,3)=6, then S(5,3)=3·6+7=25. Multiplying by 3! = 6 gives 6·25 = 150 onto functions. The other options correspond to common miscalculations such as omitting the factorial factor or using an incorrect Stirling value.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A factory produces 20 000 items per day with a defect rate of 0.0005. Which approximation is most appropriate for the probability of at most 8 defects in a day?
opts: Both Poisson and normal approximations are equally accurate
questions.solution: Here n = 20 000 and p = 0.0005, so np = 10. The rule of thumb for Poisson approximation is n ≥ 50 and p ≤ 0.1 (or np ≤ 5); although np = 10 is slightly above 5, the very small p makes the Poisson distribution with λ = np = 10 a good fit. The normal approximation requires p not too close to 0 or 1; with p = 0.0005 the distribution is highly skewed, so the normal approximation would be poor even with continuity correction. Therefore the Poisson approximation is the most appropriate choice.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A spherical cap of height 3 is cut from a sphere of radius 5. What is the volume of the cap?
questions.solution: The volume of a spherical segment (cap) of height h from a sphere of radius R is V = π h^2 (R − h/3). Substituting h = 3 and R = 5 gives h^2 = 9 and R − h/3 = 5 − 1 = 4. Hence V = π × 9 × 4 = 36π. The other options arise from common errors such as using the formula for a spherical zone, forgetting the factor 1/3, or miscalculating the height term.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: When computing the last three digits of 7^1000 using Carmichael's theorem, which step correctly applies the universal exponent?
opts: Since gcd(7,1000)≠1, factor 1000 and apply the Chinese Remainder Theorem
Use Euler's theorem directly because λ(1000)=φ(1000)
questions.solution: λ(1000)=lcm(λ(8),λ(125))=lcm(2,100)=100. Because gcd(7,1000)=1, Carmichael's theorem gives 7^1000 ≡ 7^(1000 mod 100) = 7^0 ≡ 1 (mod 1000). The last three digits are 001. Reducing modulo φ(1000)=400 would also work but is not the sharpest exponent; the universal exponent λ(1000)=100 is the smallest positive integer that works for all bases coprime to 1000.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.q: A semicircle of radius 6 cm is revolved about its diameter to generate a sphere. Using Pappus's first centroid theorem, what is the volume of the sphere?
questions.solution: Area of semicircle = (1/2)πr² = 18π cm². Centroid distance from diameter = 4r/(3π) = 8/π cm. Distance traveled by centroid = 2π × (8/π) = 16 cm. Volume = Area × distance = 18π × 16 = 288π cm³. This matches the known formula (4/3)πr³ = 288π cm³ for r=6.

questions.q: A board consists of two disjoint 2×2 blocks. The rook polynomial for a single 2×2 block is R(x)=1+4x+2x². How many ways are there to place 2 non‑attacking rooks on the combined board?
questions.solution: The rook polynomial for the union of disjoint boards is the product: (1+4x+2x²)² = 1 + 8x + (16+4)x² + … = 1 + 8x + 20x² + … The coefficient of x² is 20, which equals the number of ways to place 2 non‑attacking rooks on the combined board.

questions.q: A clock gains 5 minutes per day. It is set correctly at 12:00 noon on Monday. What time will the clock show at 6:00 PM on Wednesday?
questions.solution: Real elapsed time = 2 days 6 h = 2.25 days. Gain = 5 min/day × 2.25 = 11.25 min = 11 min 15 s. Displayed time = 6:00 PM + 11 min 15 s = 6:11:15 PM.

questions.q: A tank of capacity 2000 L is filled by two pipes: Pipe A delivers 12 L/min, Pipe B delivers 8 L/min. A leak that drains 5 min/L starts only after the tank is half full. How long does it take to fill the tank completely?
questions.solution: First half (1000 L) at 20 L/min → 50 min. After half, net rate = 20−5 = 15 L/min. Remaining 1000 L → 1000/15 = 66.67 min. Total = 50 + 66.67 = 116.67 min.

questions.q: What comes next in the number series: 3, 6, 12, 24, ?
questions.solution: The pattern is multiplying by 2 at each step (x2). 3 x 2 = 6; 6 x 2 = 12; 12 x 2 = 24. Therefore, the next number is 24 x 2 = 48.

questions.q: Identify the Odd One Out from the following set: A) Apple B) Banana C) Carrot D) Grape
questions.solution: Apple, Banana, and Grape are all fruits. Carrot is a root vegetable. Therefore, Carrot is the odd one out based on botanical classification.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Complete the letter series: Z, Y, X, W, ?
questions.solution: The pattern is moving backward in the alphabet by one position at each step. Z -> Y (1 back), Y -> X (2 back? No, 1 back). Wait, Z to Y is -1. Y to X is -1. X to W is -1. The next letter after W going backwards is V.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Keyboard : Input :: Monitor : Output :: Processor : ?
questions.solution: The chain contains two distinct relations. The first pair (Keyboard : Input) and second pair (Monitor : Output) establish a device‑function pattern: an input device and an output device. The third term (Processor) asks for the component that mediates between input and output, i.e., the central processing unit. Among the options, only CPU performs that processing function. Mouse is another input device (fails the second relation), Printer is an output device (fails the first), and Motherboard is a platform, not the processing unit. Hence the correct completion is CPU.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: If a number is even it must be a multiple of 4; otherwise it must be prime. Which number violates this rule?
questions.solution: Test each option against the conditional rule. 8 is even and 8÷4=2 → satisfies. 12 is even and 12÷4=3 → satisfies. 9 is odd, so it must be prime; 9 = 3×3, not prime → violates. 11 is odd and prime → satisfies. Only 9 fails the condition, making it the odd one out.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the series 3, 6, 12, 24, ?, which time‑pressure heuristic yields the answer fastest?
questions.solution: The first two terms (3 and 6) show a clear multiplicative relation of ×2. The Two‑Term Lock heuristic advises assuming this relation holds unless a later term contradicts it. Checking the next terms: 6×2=12, 12×2=24 — the rule persists, so the next term is 24×2=48. This heuristic solves the item in seconds without scanning options or constructing concrete analogies. The other heuristics either require option inspection (Elimination), concrete mapping (Anchor‑Term), or long‑term practice (Timed Drills) and are slower for this straightforward geometric series.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the recursive analogy ‘Pseudo‑science : Science :: Pseudo‑scientific : ?’, the prefix ‘pseudo‑’ forms a noun in the first pair and an adjective in the second. Applying the same morphological operator to the base term yields which answer?
questions.solution: The first pair shows ‘pseudo‑’ attached to the noun ‘science’ producing the noun ‘pseudo‑science’. The second pair uses the same prefix on an adjective base: ‘pseudo‑scientific’ is the prefixed form of the adjective ‘scientific’. The analogy preserves the morphological operation (prefix addition) and the part‑of‑speech shift (noun→noun, adjective→adjective). Therefore the missing term is the adjective ‘scientific’, which matches option A.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: The analogy ‘Adult : Child :: Kitten : ?’ exhibits a relational reversal: the first pair orders the terms as ‘older : younger’, while the second pair requires the reverse order ‘younger : older’. Which option correctly completes the analogy?
questions.solution: The first pair ‘Adult : Child’ expresses the relation ‘older stage : younger stage’. The second pair ‘Kitten : ?’ gives the younger stage first; to maintain the same semantic relation we need the older stage of the same species. A kitten grows into a cat, so the correct completion is ‘Cat’. The other options either belong to a different species or represent the same developmental stage.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the set {Oak, Pine, Maple, Spruce, Fern}, four members belong to the taxonomic group of seed‑producing trees (gymnosperms or angiosperms), while one is a non‑seed vascular plant. At the deepest scientific classification level, which item is the odd one out?
questions.solution: Hierarchical classification prioritises the most scientifically robust level. Oak, Pine, Maple, and Spruce are all seed plants (angiosperms or gymnosperms). Fern is a pteridophyte, a non‑seed vascular plant, placing it in a different division. Superficial features like initial letter or syllable count are ignored. Therefore Fern is the outlier at the taxonomic level.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Algorithm : Subroutine :: Program : ?
questions.solution: The analogy follows a recursive containment hierarchy: an algorithm contains subroutines, and a program contains functions. Both subroutine and function occupy the same recursive tier (the next lower granularity). Module and library are larger containers, while script is a synonym for program, not a sub‑unit. Therefore the term that preserves the identical depth offset is Function.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Recipe : Ingredients :: Algorithm : ?
questions.solution: The relation is functional input: a recipe processes ingredients, just as an algorithm processes data. Steps are part of the algorithm itself, output is the result, and function is a programming construct. The cross‑domain mapping requires matching the role of the second term as the raw material consumed by the first term, which is Data.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Select the word that does not belong: Lion, Tiger, Leopard, Cheetah, Panther.
questions.solution: All listed animals are big cats, but the hidden taxonomic condition is membership in the genus Panthera. Lion, tiger, leopard, and panther belong to Panthera; cheetah belongs to Acinonyx. The property "genus Panthera" covers four of the five items, making Cheetah the outlier.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 5 and aₙ = 2·aₙ₋₁ − n for n ≥ 2. What is the 4th term?
questions.solution: Compute sequentially: a₁ = 5. a₂ = 2·5 − 2 = 8. a₃ = 2·8 − 3 = 13. a₄ = 2·13 − 4 = 22. The fourth term is 22.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the triple analogy Mammal : Dog :: Bird : Sparrow :: Reptile : ?, which option completes the third mapping while preserving the same class‑to‑prototypical‑instance relation at all three levels?
questions.solution: The governing rule is "class : typical instance". Dog is a prototypical mammal, Sparrow a prototypical bird. Among reptiles, Lizard is the most commonly cited typical example in basic taxonomy, whereas Snake, Crocodile and Turtle are more specialised or peripheral members. Therefore Lizard satisfies the same relational verb across all three pairs.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Which of the following pairs exhibits the identical relational verb phrase "instrument used by the primary practitioner of" as the stem pair Scalpel : Surgeon?
questions.solution: Write the stem as a sentence: "Scalpel is the instrument used by the primary practitioner of surgery." The verb phrase is "instrument used by the primary practitioner of". Testing each option: Brush is used by a painter (practitioner of painting) – matches but painter is not the primary practitioner of a professional domain in the same sense; Hammer is used by a carpenter (practitioner of carpentry) – also matches; Stethoscope is used by a doctor (practitioner of medicine) – matches; Pen is used by an author (practitioner of writing) – matches the exact professional‑creative domain shift described in the lesson. The lesson explicitly cites Scalpel : Surgeon :: Pen : Author as the canonical example of a domain‑shift analogy preserving the instrumental role, making Pen : Author the intended answer.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: The sequence 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … follows the triangular number formula Tₙ = n(n+1)/2. What is the 8th term of this series?
questions.solution: Compute T₈ = 8×9/2 = 72/2 = 36. The first differences are 2,3,4,5,6,7,8 and the second difference is constant at 1, confirming the quadratic nature. Hence the 8th triangular number is 36.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A modular arithmetic series is given as 5, 11, 4, 10, 3, 9, … . Assuming the rule "add a constant k modulo m" generates the series, what is the modulus m?
questions.solution: Observe the successive differences: +6, −7, +6, −7, +6. A constant addition modulo m means each step adds the same value k modulo m. Here k = 6. Starting from 5, (5+6) mod m = 11 → m > 11. Next (11+6) mod m = 4 → 17 mod m = 4 → m = 13. Verify: (4+6) mod 13 = 10, (10+6) mod 13 = 3, (3+6) mod 13 = 9. All terms fit with modulus 13.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the analogy "cell : nucleus :: computer : CPU :: organization : headquarters", which relational schema must the correct answer preserve?
questions.solution: Each stem pair exhibits the relation "system : central control unit". A cell's nucleus controls cellular activity; a computer's CPU controls processing; an organization's headquarters controls operations. The schema is not part-whole (nucleus is not the whole cell), not creator-product, and not container-contents. The solver must abstract this exact relational schema across domains.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Five items are described by four attributes (shape, colour, size, material): 1. (circle, red, small, plastic) 2. (circle, red, small, metal) 3. (circle, blue, small, plastic) 4. (square, red, small, plastic) 5. (circle, red, large, plastic) Using the majority-profile method with Hamming distance, which item is the odd one out?
questions.solution: Majority profile (mode per attribute): shape=circle (4/5), colour=red (4/5), size=small (4/5), material=plastic (4/5). Hamming distances from profile: Item1=0, Item2=1 (material), Item3=1 (colour), Item4=1 (shape), Item5=1 (size). Four items tie at distance 1. Among these four (Items 2-5), the attribute with zero variance is material (all plastic). Item2 alone differs on this invariant attribute (metal), making it the unique outlier.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A piecewise series starts at 2. Rule: if current term < 20, multiply by 3; otherwise subtract 7. What is the 8th term?
questions.solution: Simulate stepwise: a₁=2 (<20) → a₂=6. a₂=6 (<20) → a₃=18. a₃=18 (<20) → a₄=54. a₄=54 (≥20) → a₅=47. a₅=47 (≥20) → a₆=40. a₆=40 (≥20) → a₇=33. a₇=33 (≥20) → a₈=26. a₈=26 (≥20) → a₉=19. The 8th term is 26. The threshold is value-dependent, so simulation is required; the rule re-evaluates at each step using the mutated term as the new base.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In the analogy “author → writes → novel → published by → publisher”, the source graph has three nodes and two directed edges labelled “writes” then “published by”. Which of the following options preserves the same node‑type sequence and the same ordered edge labels?
questions.a: composer → composes → symphony → performed by → orchestra
opts: composer → composes → symphony → performed by → orchestra
composer → performed by → symphony → composes → orchestra
composer → composes → symphony → recorded by → label
questions.solution: The stem establishes a two‑edge path: creation (writes) followed by dissemination (published by). A label‑preserving graph isomorphism requires the target path to have the identical ordered edge labels. Option A mirrors this with “composes” (creation) then “performed by” (dissemination), keeping the node types (creator, work, distributor) in the same order. Options B and D reverse the edge order, and Option C substitutes a different terminal relation (“recorded by”) that belongs to a different semantic cluster (recording vs. publication). Hence only Option A satisfies the isomorphism.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: When applying the generating‑function method to a non‑linear recurrence, after listing the first k terms and assuming a rational form G(x)=P(x)/Q(x) with deg Q≤2, what is the immediate algebraic step that yields linear equations for the unknown coefficients of P and Q?
questions.solution: The method described in the lesson writes the known terms a₀…aₖ, assumes G(x)=P(x)/Q(x) with a low‑degree denominator, and then cross‑multiplies: Q(x)·G(x)=P(x). Substituting the series ∑aₙxⁿ for G(x) and expanding the product gives a polynomial identity. Equating coefficients of like powers of x produces a system of linear equations in the unknown coefficients of P and Q. Differentiation, partial fractions, or further iteration are later steps, not the immediate algebraic operation that creates the linear system.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Four animals are described by a three‑level taxonomy (Class, Order, Habitat). The entries are: 1) Mammalia, Carnivora, Terrestrial; 2) Mammalia, Carnivora, Terrestrial; 3) Mammalia, Cetacea, Marine; 4) Mammalia, Carnivora, Terrestrial. A binary conditional constraint requires that all members share the same Order. Which entry violates the constraint?
questions.solution: The constraint is a binary conditional on the hierarchical attribute Order: every item must have Order = Carnivora. Entries 1, 2, and 4 satisfy this (Carnivora). Entry 3 has Order = Cetacea, which differs from the required value, so it breaches the constraint. Treating the taxonomy as flat would miss the deeper mismatch at the Order level; the CSP formulation forces the solver to check the conditional at the correct hierarchical depth, making Entry 3 the unique odd‑one‑out.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: The morphological chain “construct → construction → constructive” uses the derivational affixes ‑tion (verb→noun) and ‑ive (noun→adjective) with the allomorph ‑tion after a final ‑t. Applying the same allomorphic rule to the root “comprehend” yields which correct chain?
questions.solution: The stem shows two successive derivations: verb → noun via ‑tion (allomorph ‑tion after ‑t) and noun → adjective via ‑ive. The root “comprehend” ends in ‑d, so the noun‑forming allomorph is ‑sion (comprehension), not ‑tion or ‑nsion. The adjective then adds ‑ive to the noun stem, giving “comprehensive”. Option A follows exactly this pattern. Options B and D use the incorrect allomorph ‑tion, and Option C invents an unattested ‑nsion form. Therefore only Option A respects the allomorphic rule.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Consider the series 1, 1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 16, … . The odd‑position terms follow the triangular numbers Tₙ = n(n+1)/2 and the even‑position terms follow the squares n². What is the ninth term of the series?
questions.solution: Separate the series by index parity (1‑based). Odd positions 1,3,5,7 give 1, 3, 6, 10 — the triangular numbers T₁=1, T₂=3, T₃=6, T₄=10. Even positions 2,4,6,8 give 1, 4, 9, 16 — the squares 1²,2²,3²,4². The ninth term is at odd position 5, so it equals T₅ = 5·6/2 = 15. The other options correspond to incorrect meta‑patterns (e.g., continuing squares or arithmetic progression).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: An argument claims: "Since the new policy reduces traffic congestion, it will improve air quality." Which of the following is a necessary assumption for this argument?
questions.a: Reducing traffic congestion leads to improved air quality.
opts: Reducing traffic congestion leads to improved air quality.
The new policy will be popular among commuters.
Air quality is the only factor affected by traffic congestion.
The policy will be implemented without delay.
questions.solution: A necessary assumption is a proposition that must be true for the argument to hold; if false, the conclusion cannot be drawn. The argument moves from reduced congestion to improved air quality, so it assumes that reduced congestion actually causes better air quality. The other options are irrelevant to the logical link between congestion and air quality.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: The argument: "A new teaching method improves test scores because it increases student engagement." Which option would most strengthen this argument?
questions.a: A study showing higher engagement scores in classrooms using the method.
opts: A study showing higher engagement scores in classrooms using the method.
The method is cheaper than traditional methods.
The author of the method is a well‑known educator.
The method has been adopted in several other countries.
questions.solution: A strengthen answer must supply evidence that supports the core assumption linking engagement to higher test scores. The lesson's example states that a study showing higher engagement scores in classrooms using the method would strengthen the claim. Cost, author popularity, and adoption elsewhere do not address the engagement‑score causal link and are therefore irrelevant.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: An argument observes that ice‑cream sales rise when drowning incidents rise and concludes that ice‑cream consumption causes drowning. Which logical flaw does this argument exhibit?
questions.solution: The lesson identifies 'Correlation Versus Causation' as a common flaw where a correlation between two variables is mistaken for a causal relationship. The argument confuses the simultaneous increase of ice‑cream sales and drowning incidents with a cause‑effect link, ignoring a third factor (e.g., hot weather). The other listed flaws do not describe this error.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Given the conditional statement "If it rains, then the ground gets wet," which of the following conclusions is logically valid?
questions.a: If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain.
opts: If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain.
If the ground is wet, then it rained.
If it did not rain, then the ground is not wet.
If it rained, then the ground is not wet.
questions.solution: From a conditional "If P then Q" the only valid inferences are the contrapositive ("If not Q then not P") and direct affirmation ("P, therefore Q"). Option A is the contrapositive and is therefore valid. Option B affirms the consequent, Option C denies the antecedent, and Option D contradicts the original conditional; all are fallacies.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In argument mapping, a box that has no incoming arrows and is not the main conclusion indicates which of the following?
questions.solution: Argument mapping makes inferential links explicit. A box with no incoming arrows means nothing in the diagram supports that statement; if it is not the main conclusion, the statement must be an unstated assumption the argument relies on. The lesson states that “any box that has no incoming arrows but is not the main conclusion signals a hidden premise.” Therefore the correct identification is a hidden premise.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Given the conditional chain “If A then B; if B then C; if C then D,” which inference is logically valid without assuming biconditionals?
questions.solution: From A→B, B→C, C→D we derive the transitive closure A→D. The only safe backward inference is the full contrapositive of this final implication, ¬D→¬A. Intermediate contrapositives such as ¬C→¬A or ¬B→¬D are not guaranteed unless each link is biconditional, which the passage does not assert. Hence ¬D→¬A is the sole valid inference.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: When evaluating an analogical argument, which critical question must be asked to test its strength?
questions.a: Do the shared properties bear on the inferred property?
opts: Do the shared properties bear on the inferred property?
Is the analogy presented by an authority?
Does the analogy use emotional language?
questions.solution: The lesson emphasizes that analogical reasoning must be assessed by checking whether the similarities cited are relevant to the conclusion. The critical question is whether the shared properties (the basis of the analogy) actually bear on the property being inferred. Vividness, authority, or emotional language are not logical criteria for analogical strength.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: The argument “Because the new law reduces traffic fatalities, it should be adopted nationwide” relies on a hidden premise. What is that premise?
questions.a: Local conditions (road design, enforcement culture) are replicable elsewhere
opts: The law is popular among voters
Local conditions (road design, enforcement culture) are replicable elsewhere
The law has no unintended side effects
questions.solution: The passage explicitly gives this example: the argument hides the premise that “the local conditions (road design, enforcement culture) are replicable elsewhere.” Without assuming uniformity of context, the generalization from a local effect to a nationwide recommendation is a hasty generalization. The other options are not identified as the hidden premise in the lesson.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A universal claim “All policies that increase taxes reduce economic growth” can be refuted by which of the following?
questions.a: A single historical case where a tax increase coincided with growth
opts: A statistical trend showing growth after a tax increase
A single historical case where a tax increase coincided with growth
An expert opinion that tax increases sometimes help
questions.solution: The lesson states that a universal generalisation is falsified by a single well‑documented counterexample. A statistical trend does not overturn a universal claim because the claim allows no exceptions. An expert opinion or theoretical model does not constitute a concrete counterexample. Therefore, a single historical instance where a tax increase coincided with growth suffices to refute the claim.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A policy brief argues: "Since 85% of surveyed economists support carbon pricing, the government should implement a carbon tax immediately." The brief treats the survey as conclusive proof without addressing whether the sample represents the relevant specialist sub-field or whether dissenting views exist. In Toulmin terms, which component is most directly flawed by this omission?
questions.a: The warrant, because the inferential bridge from expert survey to policy necessity assumes consensus and representativeness without backing
opts: The claim, because it asserts a policy prescription rather than a factual conclusion
The data, because the survey percentage is factually incorrect
The warrant, because the inferential bridge from expert survey to policy necessity assumes consensus and representativeness without backing
The qualifier, because the argument uses "should" instead of "probably should"
questions.solution: The argument moves from data (survey results) to claim (implement carbon tax) via a warrant that expert support entails policy necessity. The flaw is that the warrant assumes the survey constitutes sufficient consensus and representativeness to justify immediate action, but no backing is provided for this assumption. The qualifier ("should" vs "probably should") is a secondary issue; the primary structural flaw is the unwarranted warrant. Option A misidentifies the claim type; policy claims are valid in Toulmin. Option B attacks the data's accuracy, which is not the stated flaw. Option D focuses on modal strength rather than the missing justification for the inference.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: An editorial argues: "Professor Chen, a distinguished physicist, testified that the new nuclear waste storage facility poses no significant geological risk. Therefore, the facility is safe." Which critical question from Walton's expert opinion scheme most directly challenges the argument's validity?
questions.a: Is there consensus among geologists and seismologists on the facility's geological risk?
opts: Is Professor Chen's testimony biased by research funding from the nuclear industry?
Is there consensus among geologists and seismologists on the facility's geological risk?
Has Professor Chen published peer-reviewed papers on nuclear waste storage?
Does the argument acknowledge the possibility of human error in facility operation?
questions.solution: The argument uses the expert opinion scheme: Expert E (physicist) asserts P (no geological risk); therefore P is true. Walton's critical questions for this scheme are: (1) Is E an expert in the relevant domain? (2) Is there consensus among experts on P? (3) Is E biased? Professor Chen is a physicist, but the claim concerns geological risk — a domain of geologists/seismologists. Question (1) attacks domain relevance; question (2) attacks consensus in the actual relevant field. Option B directly targets the consensus among the *relevant* experts (geologists/seismologists), exposing the domain mismatch. Option A addresses bias (question 3), which is secondary to domain relevance. Option C checks credentials within physics, not the relevant domain. Option D introduces an unrelated issue (human error) not part of the expert opinion scheme's critical questions.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A study claims: "Cities with higher police funding have higher crime rates; therefore, increased police funding causes higher crime." The study aggregates data across all cities without controlling for city size, poverty rates, or pre-existing crime trends. Which statistical flaw does this argument most clearly exhibit?
questions.a: Simpson's paradox, because the aggregated trend reverses when data are disaggregated by confounding variables like city size
opts: Base-rate neglect, because the argument ignores the overall probability of crime in the population
Simpson's paradox, because the aggregated trend reverses when data are disaggregated by confounding variables like city size
Post hoc ergo propter hoc, because the argument infers causation from temporal sequence alone
Sampling bias, because the cities studied were not randomly selected from all cities
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly mentions Simpson's paradox as a risk when "aggregated data are presented as conclusive" without controlling for confounders. Here, city size, poverty, and pre-existing crime are confounding variables: larger cities tend to have both higher police funding and higher crime rates. When data are disaggregated by these variables, the positive correlation may disappear or reverse. This is the definition of Simpson's paradox. Base-rate neglect (Option A) concerns ignoring prior probabilities in diagnostic reasoning. Post hoc (Option C) requires temporal sequence, not just correlation. Sampling bias (Option D) concerns selection method, not the aggregation flaw described.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A researcher observes that the laboratory lights are off and concludes that the main power station has failed. Which of the following would most strengthen this abductive inference?
questions.a: A controlled experiment shows that power‑station failures cause building‑wide outages in 95% of cases.
opts: A controlled experiment shows that power‑station failures cause building‑wide outages in 95% of cases.
A local fuse blow is discovered that also explains the lights being off.
The researcher asserts that no other cause could possibly produce the observed effect.
The base‑rate probability of power‑station failure in the region is extremely low.
questions.solution: The argument is abductive: it infers the best explanation for the observed phenomenon. Strengthening an abductive claim requires independent evidence that raises the probability of the proposed explanation relative to rivals. Option A provides a well‑established mechanism (controlled experiment) confirming that power‑station failures reliably produce the observed effect, thereby increasing its explanatory plausibility. Option B introduces a rival explanation, which weakens the argument. Option C merely asserts exclusivity without evidence, a common pitfall. Option D lowers the prior probability of the hypothesis, also weakening the inference.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In Chisholm’s contrary‑to‑duty paradox, standard deontic logic struggles because it cannot represent which of the following?
questions.a: Conditional obligations that trigger only when a primary obligation is violated.
opts: Conditional obligations that trigger only when a primary obligation is violated.
The interdefinability of permission and obligation operators.
The consistency of multiple simultaneous obligations.
The derivation of a deontic conclusion from a factual premise.
questions.solution: The paradox shows that when Jones fails to help, a new obligation (not to tell) arises that is conditional on the violation of the first obligation. Standard deontic logic uses unconditional operators O, P, F and cannot capture obligations that are activated only upon breach of another duty. This requires a conditional deontic operator (e.g., O(φ/ψ)). The other options describe features that standard deontic logic handles adequately: interdefinability, consistency checks, and factual‑to‑deontic inference.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: According to the Prakken & Sartor dialogue‑game model, a premise counts as “granted” in a critical discussion only if:
questions.a: It belongs to the shared commitment base of the participants.
opts: It belongs to the shared commitment base of the participants.
It is asserted by the proponent without challenge.
The opponent explicitly concedes it in the current move.
It is supported by an external authority cited in the dialogue.
questions.solution: In the formal dialogue framework, a premise is granted when both parties have committed to it, i.e., it resides in the shared commitment base. Mere assertion (option B) does not grant it; the opponent must accept it. An explicit concession (option C) is one way to add it to the base, but the defining condition is membership in the shared base, not the act of concession itself. External authority (option D) is irrelevant to the internal commitment structure.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Consider an abstract argumentation framework with arguments A, B, C, D and attacks: A attacks B, B attacks C, C attacks A, and D is unattacked. Under grounded semantics, which argument(s) must be accepted (i.e., are skeptically justified)?
questions.solution: The grounded extension is the minimal complete extension, constructed by iteratively adding unattacked arguments and those defended by already accepted ones. D is unattacked, so it enters the grounded extension immediately. A, B, C form a 3‑cycle; none is unattacked, and none becomes defended because each has an attacker that is not OUT. Hence they remain UNDECIDED and are not in the grounded extension. Therefore only D is skeptically accepted.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Which of the following errors is committed when an argument treats an abductive conclusion as if it were deductively certain?
questions.a: Ignoring rival explanations that could also account for the evidence.
opts: Ignoring rival explanations that could also account for the evidence.
Applying Occam’s razor when competing explanations have unequal explanatory power.
Confusing the base‑rate probability of the hypothesis with its posterior probability.
Concluding that the explanation is true because it is the simplest.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly lists “Treating an abductive conclusion as deductively certain, ignoring rival explanations” as a common pitfall. Abductive reasoning yields the best available explanation, not a logically necessary one; its force depends on comparative plausibility. Ignoring rival explanations (option A) directly reflects this error. Option B misstates the condition for using parsimony. Option C describes the base‑rate fallacy, a different error. Option D conflates simplicity with truth, which is related but not the specific error of treating abductive inference as deductive.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A stimulus argues: "Professor Rao's critique of the new environmental policy must be dismissed because he receives research funding from a fossil-fuel consortium." The argument commits which specific sub-type of the ad hominem fallacy?
questions.solution: The argument attacks Professor Rao's circumstances (his funding source) rather than engaging with the content of his critique. This matches the definition of circumstantial ad hominem, which exploits an irrelevant attribute of the arguer's situation or interests. Abusive ad hominem would involve a direct personal insult; tu quoque would allege hypocrisy by pointing to inconsistent past actions; poisoning the well is a pre-emptive discrediting tactic. The lesson explicitly distinguishes these sub-types and notes that test items reward fine-grained discrimination among them.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Consider the argument: "Because the treaty was ratified by Parliament, the obligations are binding on domestic courts." The necessary assumption bridging the explicit premise to the conclusion is that the ratification procedure satisfies constitutional requirements for treaty incorporation. If this assumption is negated, what happens to the argument?
questions.a: The entailment between premise and conclusion is broken
opts: The conclusion becomes false while the premise remains true
The entailment between premise and conclusion is broken
The argument becomes valid but unsound
questions.solution: The lesson states: "The negation test works precisely because denying the bridge premise breaks the entailment while leaving the explicit premises intact." The assumption is a bridge premise connecting the explicit premise (ratification occurred) to the conclusion (obligations are binding). Negating it — i.e., the ratification procedure does NOT satisfy constitutional requirements — severs the logical link without falsifying the explicit premise that ratification occurred. The argument fails because the inference no longer holds, not because the premise or conclusion changes truth value independently.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A stimulus states: "A new diagnostic test for Condition Z has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Therefore, a patient who tests positive is highly likely to have Condition Z." Which answer choice would most strengthen this argument?
questions.a: Condition Z has a prevalence of 30% in the tested population
opts: The test's sensitivity increases to 99% in a follow-up study
Condition Z has a prevalence of 30% in the tested population
The test's false-positive rate drops to 2% when administered twice
Condition Z is more severe than previously thought
questions.solution: The lesson identifies base-rate neglect as the central trap: "If the disease prevalence is 0.1%, a positive result yields a posterior probability of only about 0.95% — far from 'highly likely'. A strengthen answer would supply a higher base rate." Sensitivity and specificity alone are insufficient; the posterior probability depends critically on the prior (prevalence). Option B provides a moderate/high prior (30%), which, combined with the given sensitivity/specificity, yields a high posterior probability. Option A improves sensitivity but leaves the prior unstated; Option C describes a protocol change not in evidence; Option D addresses severity, not probability.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: An argument claims: "Since most citizens support the new surveillance law, the law must be justified." A critic responds: "That reasoning is flawed because popular belief does not establish truth." The critic correctly identifies which fallacy?
questions.solution: The argument uses widespread belief as proof of the conclusion's truth, which is the definition of appeal to popularity (argumentum ad populum) given in the lesson: "The appeal to popularity (argumentum ad populum) treats widespread belief as proof of truth." The critic's response isolates the inferential link — popularity does not raise the probability of justification — matching the diagnostic pattern: "if the premise, even if true, would not raise the probability of the conclusion, the move is a relevance failure." The other fallacies involve emotion (pity), diversion (red herring), or distortion (straw man), none of which fit the structure.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Premise: All managers are leaders. Which of the following conclusions follows necessarily?
questions.solution: The premise is a universal affirmative (A) proposition: All M are L. In immediate inference, an A statement converts only to a particular affirmative (I): Some L are M. The universal converse (All L are M) illicitly distributes the predicate, which is not allowed. The negative conclusions (No L are M; Some M are not L) are not supported by an affirmative premise. Therefore only "Some leaders are managers" is a valid immediate inference.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Premises: (1) All poets are dreamers. (2) Some dreamers are writers. Which conclusion follows?
questions.solution: The first premise is an A proposition (All P are D) where the middle term D is the predicate and undistributed. The second premise is an I proposition (Some D are W) where D is the subject and also undistributed. Since the middle term is not distributed in either premise, the syllogism violates the rule that the middle term must be distributed at least once. Consequently no definite conclusion linking poets and writers can be drawn; the correct answer is that no conclusion follows.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Premises: (1) No cats are dogs. (2) Some dogs are pets. Which conclusion is valid?
questions.solution: Premise 1 is an E proposition (No C are D) separating cats and dogs completely. Premise 2 is an I proposition (Some D are P) placing at least one dog inside the pet circle. Because that dog is not a cat, there exists at least one pet that is not a cat. This makes "Some pets are not cats" necessarily true in every Venn diagram satisfying the premises. The other options either assert a relation between cats and pets that is not forced or make universal claims unsupported by the particular premise.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Premises: (1) All A are B. (2) Some B are not C. Consider the two conclusions: (i) Some A are not C. (ii) No A are C. Which statement about these conclusions is correct?
questions.solution: The middle term B is the predicate in the A premise (undistributed) and the subject in the O premise (undistributed). Because B is never distributed, the syllogism fails the distribution rule and yields no valid conclusion. Moreover, the two conclusions are not logical complements (one is particular negative, the other universal negative), so the either‑or rule does not apply. Hence neither conclusion can be deduced from the given premises.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Premises: (1) No engineers are artists. (2) Some artists are musicians. Which conclusion can be validly drawn?
questions.solution: Premise 1 is an E proposition (No E are A) distributing both terms. Premise 2 is an I proposition (Some A are M). The middle term A is distributed in the first premise, satisfying the distribution rule. A negative premise requires a negative conclusion. In every Venn diagram, the artists that are musicians lie outside the engineer circle, guaranteeing at least one musician who is not an engineer. Thus "Some musicians are not engineers" follows. The other negative options are either not forced (some engineers not musicians) or too strong (universal negatives).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Under the Boolean interpretation of categorical syllogisms, why is the mood Darapti (AAI‑3) invalid?
questions.a: The premises are both universal while the conclusion is particular, asserting existence not guaranteed.
opts: The middle term is not distributed in either premise.
The premises are both universal while the conclusion is particular, asserting existence not guaranteed.
The singular subject lacks existential import.
The conclusion illicitly distributes the minor term.
questions.solution: In the Boolean interpretation universal propositions (A and E) carry no existential import. Darapti has two A premises (All M are P; All M are S) and an I conclusion (Some S are P). Since the premises do not assert that any M, S, or P exists, the particular conclusion cannot be derived. The invalidity stems precisely from moving from universal premises to a particular conclusion without an existential premise.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: A relational syllogism states: ‘All A are related to B by R; all B are related to C by R; therefore all A are related to C by R.’ This inference is valid only when the relation R possesses which property?
questions.solution: The chain requires that whenever aRb and bRc hold, aRc must also hold. This is exactly the definition of a transitive relation. Symmetry would give bRa from aRb, not aRc. Reflexivity (aRa) and asymmetry (if aRb then not bRa) do not guarantee the needed link between A and C.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: In a disjunctive syllogism using an inclusive ‘or’, the argument ‘P or Q; P; therefore not Q’ exemplifies which formal fallacy?
questions.solution: With inclusive disjunction both disjuncts may be true simultaneously. Inferring the falsity of Q from the truth of P incorrectly treats the ‘or’ as exclusive. This mistake is named the fallacy of affirming a disjunct. The other options refer to conditional fallacies or conversion errors, which are unrelated to disjunctive reasoning.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: When a categorical syllogism is rendered into natural deduction, a particular conclusion (∃x) can be derived only if the premise set includes at least one:
questions.solution: Natural deduction introduction rules for the existential quantifier require an explicit existential premise (or an existential assumption discharged by ∃‑introduction). Universal premises alone provide only ∀‑statements, which cannot yield ∃x without an additional existential claim. This mirrors the syllogistic rule that every particular conclusion demands an existential premise.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Treating a singular statement such as ‘Socrates is mortal’ as a mere universal affirmative without acknowledging that its subject class is non‑empty commits which logical error?
questions.solution: A singular term denotes a class with exactly one member, so ‘Socrates is mortal’ carries existential import automatically. Interpreting it as a Boolean universal (which lacks existential force) and then drawing a particular conclusion from such premises commits the existential fallacy — deriving existence from premises that do not assert it.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Consider the following premises: 1. All engineers are technicians. 2. Some technicians are managers. The term "technicians" is used in the first premise to denote a professional qualification and in the second premise to denote a functional role. Which of the following correctly describes the logical status of the argument?
opts: Either some engineers are managers or no engineers are managers.
questions.solution: The argument contains four distinct terms: engineers, technicians (qualification), technicians (role), and managers. Because the middle term is not identical in both premises, the syllogism commits the fallacy of four terms (quaternio terminorum). The standard distribution rules break down — the middle term is undistributed in both premises — so no valid categorical inference can be drawn. Hence none of the offered conclusions is forced; the correct response is that no conclusion follows.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.q: Premises: 1. All scientists respect some philosophers. 2. All philosophers respect some artists. Which conclusion, if any, follows validly from these premises?
questions.solution: The first premise formalises as ∀x(Scientist(x) → ∃y(Philosopher(y) ∧ Respects(x,y))). The second is ∀z(Philosopher(z) → ∃w(Artist(w) ∧ Respects(z,w))).
