The weather, being fine, we went for a walk.
questions.solution: An absolute (nominative absolute) construction consists of a noun phrase followed by a non‑finite verb form (usually a present participle) that stands grammatically detached from the main clause, with no conjunction or preposition linking it. Option A follows the pattern Noun Phrase + Present Participle ("The weather being fine") and is separated from the main clause by a comma, satisfying the structure. Option B inverts the order, breaking the required NP‑participle sequence. Option C omits the participle, leaving a bare adjective phrase, which is not an absolute. Option D inserts a comma after the noun phrase, incorrectly splitting the absolute from its participle.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the sentence "Only she gave him a book," which constituent does the focus particle "only" modify?
questions.a: The subject "she" (no one else gave him a book).
opts: The subject "she" (no one else gave him a book).
The direct object "a book" (she gave him nothing else).
The indirect object "him" (she gave a book to no one else).
The verb "gave" (the action was limited to giving).
questions.solution: Focus particles such as "only," "even," and "just" take scope over the constituent they immediately precede (or are associated with via intonation). In "Only she gave him a book," "only" is placed directly before the subject "she," so its scope is the subject NP. The sentence therefore means that she, and no other person, gave him a book. Options B, C, and D would require "only" to appear before "a book," "him," or "gave" respectively, which is not the case here.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the standard interpretation of the sentence "All the students did not pass"?
questions.solution: The lesson notes that using "all … not" for total negation (meaning "none") is an error; the construction normally conveys partial negation, i.e., "not all." Therefore "All the students did not pass" is interpreted as "Not all the students passed," implying that at least one student passed while at least one did not. Option A reflects the erroneous total‑negation reading. Option C restates A. Option D is a weaker paraphrase but does not capture the quantificational meaning of "not all."
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following sentences correctly pied‑pipes the preposition in a relative clause with "which"?
questions.a: The reason for which he left is unknown.
opts: The reason which he left for is unknown.
The reason for which he left is unknown.
The reason that he left for is unknown.
The reason of which he left is unknown.
questions.solution: Pied‑piping is obligatory when the preposition belongs to a fixed noun‑preposition collocation such as "reason for." The relative pronoun "which" can be pied‑piped, but "that" cannot. Option B moves the preposition "for" before "which," yielding the grammatical "The reason for which he left is unknown." Option A strands the preposition, which is disallowed for this collocation. Option C uses "that," which cannot be pied‑piped. Option D uses the wrong preposition ("of") for the noun "reason."
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Select the sentence that obeys the syntactic constraints on embedded questions.
questions.a: Whether he will come is uncertain.
opts: Whether he will come is uncertain.
I asked that he would come.
questions.solution: Embedded questions block subject‑auxiliary inversion, so "where is he" is wrong (Option A). The complementizer whether is required in subject position; if cannot appear there, making Option B correct. After a preposition, whether is mandatory, so "if to proceed" (Option C) is disallowed. The complementizer that never introduces an embedded question, rendering Option D ungrammatical.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Identify the error in the following sentence: "Although he was tired, but he finished the work."
questions.a: Use of although with but in the same clause.
opts: Use of although with but in the same clause.
Missing comma after the concessive clause.
Incorrect verb form in the main clause.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly lists as a trap the treatment of although and but as compatible in the same clause. A concessive clause introduced by although (or even though) must not be followed by a coordinating but; the two convey the same contrastive relation and cannot co‑occur. The other options describe issues not present in the sentence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the sentence that conforms to standard English negation rules.
opts: Unless you don't study, you will fail.
questions.solution: Standard English prohibits negative concord; a single negative operator must be paired with a non‑assertive form. Option A uses two negatives (didn't + nothing) yielding an affirmative meaning. Option C combines unless with not, which the lesson identifies as a trap; the correct form is "Unless you study" or "If you don't study." Option D pairs hardly (a negative polarity item) with no one, creating double negation. Option B correctly uses the single negative never with the non‑assertive anything.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following sentences correctly applies heavy NP shift?
questions.a: She gave to her friend the book that she had borrowed from the library.
opts: She gave her friend the book that she had borrowed from the library.
She gave to her friend the book that she had borrowed from the library.
She gave the book that she had borrowed from the library her friend.
She gave the book that she had borrowed her friend.
questions.solution: Heavy NP shift moves a long direct object to the end of the clause, but only when the verb allows a prepositional dative (e.g., give to). Option B shows the shifted order with the prepositional phrase "to her friend" preceding the heavy NP, which is licensed. Option A leaves the NP in situ (no shift). Options C and D attempt shift without the required preposition, which the lesson states is ungrammatical for double‑object verbs.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which coordinated sentence illustrates a licensing violation of right‑node raising because the shared constituent satisfies different valency frames across the conjuncts?
questions.a: The teacher explained and the students understood the problem.
opts: John prepared and Mary reviewed the manuscript.
The committee approved and the director signed the document.
The teacher explained and the students understood the problem.
She baked and he ate the cake.
questions.solution: Right‑node raising is licensed only when the raised constituent fulfills the same valency requirements in each conjunct. In option C, "explained" typically requires a prepositional phrase (explain the problem to someone) whereas "understood" takes a direct object; the shared NP "the problem" cannot satisfy both frames simultaneously. The other pairs (prepare/review, approve/sign, bake/eat) all share a simple transitive valency, so RNR is grammatical there.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In formal English, which negative hortative construction is preferred?
questions.a: Let us not consider the evidence.
opts: Let us not consider the evidence.
Don't let us consider the evidence.
Let us to not consider the evidence.
Let not us consider the evidence.
questions.solution: The standard formal negative hortative uses "let us not" followed by the bare infinitive. The lesson states that "Don't let us consider" is colloquial, and that inserting "to" after "let" ("let us to not consider") is ungrammatical. "Let not us consider" violates the required word order for the hortative. Therefore only option A conforms to the formal rule.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the best improvement: 'He is good in English.'
questions.solution: 'Capable/good/proficient' takes 'at' + language/skill: 'good at English'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the best improvement: 'Due to the fact that it rained, the match was cancelled.'
questions.a: Because it rained, the match was cancelled.
opts: Because it rained, the match was cancelled.
Due to the fact that it rained...
In spite of the fact that it rained...
questions.solution: Replace wordy 'Due to the fact that' with concise 'Because'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the best improvement: 'I have seen him yesterday.'
questions.solution: Definite past time 'yesterday' takes Past Simple: 'I saw him yesterday'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the best improvement: 'Each of the boys have a pen.'
questions.a: Each of the boys has a pen.
opts: Each of the boys has a pen.
Each of the boys have a pen.
Each of boys has a pen.
questions.solution: 'Each of' takes a singular verb: 'has'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the best improvement: 'The box of chocolates are expensive.'
questions.a: The box of chocolates is expensive.
opts: The box of chocolates is expensive.
The boxes of chocolate is expensive.
The box of chocolates are expensive.
questions.solution: Real subject is 'box' (singular); intervening phrase doesn't change it → 'is'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The director insisted that the report ______ submitted by Friday.
questions.solution: The verb 'insisted' triggers the mandative subjunctive in the following 'that'-clause. The mandative subjunctive requires the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to') regardless of the subject or tense. 'Be submitted' is the passive base form. Options A, C, and D are indicative forms (present, past, present perfect) and are incorrect in this formal subjunctive construction.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: We appreciate ______ taking the time to review the proposal.
questions.solution: In formal English, a pronoun modifying a gerund ('taking') must be in the possessive case. The gerund phrase 'your taking the time' functions as the object of 'appreciate'. 'Your' shows possession of the action. Option A ('you') uses the objective case, which is considered a common error (fused participle) in formal writing. Options C and D incorrectly use the infinitive 'to take' after 'appreciate', which does not fit the idiom 'appreciate [possessive] [gerund]'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The cost of living in Metro City is significantly higher ______.
questions.solution: The sentence compares 'the cost of living in Metro City' (singular) with the cost of living in Small Town. To avoid an illogical comparison between a 'cost' and a 'town', a substitute word for 'cost' is needed. 'That of' correctly refers back to the singular noun 'cost'. Option A compares cost to town. Option C ('Small Town's') is a possessive noun but creates ambiguity (Small Town's what?). Option D uses 'those of', which is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent 'cost'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the sentence that correctly applies subject-auxiliary inversion after a fronted negative adverb.
questions.a: Never have I seen such dedication.
opts: Never I have seen such dedication.
Never have I seen such dedication.
Never did I saw such dedication.
questions.solution: When a sentence begins with a negative adverb (e.g., 'Never', 'Rarely', 'Seldom', 'Not only'), formal English requires inversion of the subject and the auxiliary verb. The original tense is present perfect ('have seen'), so the auxiliary 'have' must invert with the subject 'I'. Option B correctly forms 'Never have I seen'. Option A lacks inversion. Option C incorrectly uses 'did' (past tense auxiliary) with the past tense verb 'saw' (double past) instead of the base form 'see', and mismatches the original perfect aspect. Option D lacks inversion and uses simple past.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In formal writing, which version best resolves the ellipsis in the comparative clause “He ran faster than I”?
questions.a: He ran faster than I did.
opts: He ran faster than I do.
He ran faster than I did.
questions.solution: The lesson states that in comparative clauses the auxiliary “do” (in the appropriate tense) is preferred to a bare pronoun to avoid tense ambiguity. Since the main clause is past tense (“ran”), the elliptical clause must restore the past‑tense auxiliary “did”. Option C supplies “than I did”, matching the required finiteness and tense, whereas option B uses present “do” and option A leaves the pronoun bare. Option D uses the object pronoun “me”, which is not the standard formal elliptical form. Therefore, option C is the correct improvement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which revision correctly matches the complement type required by the matrix verb “avoid”?
questions.solution: The verb “avoid” licenses a gerund‑participle complement, not an infinitive. The lesson warns against “choosing an infinitive where the matrix verb requires a gerund”. Option B provides the gerund “making”, which is the grammatical complement of “avoid”. Option A uses the infinitive “to make”, option C uses the bare verb “make”, and option D mixes “to” with the gerund “making”, all of which are ungrammatical after “avoid”. Therefore, option B is the correct improvement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the principle of end‑weight, which version best positions the heavy adverbial clause?
questions.a: The committee rejected the proposal because the data were incomplete and the methodology was flawed.
opts: Because the data were incomplete and the methodology was flawed, the committee rejected the proposal.
The committee rejected the proposal because the data were incomplete and the methodology was flawed.
The committee, because the data were incomplete and the methodology was flawed, rejected the proposal.
The committee rejected because the data were incomplete and the methodology was flawed the proposal.
questions.solution: The principle of end‑weight states that longer, more complex constituents should appear later in the sentence for smoother processing. The adverbial clause “because the data were incomplete and the methodology was flawed” is heavy; placing it at the end (option B) follows this principle. Option A fronts the heavy clause, option C inserts it medially, disrupting flow, and option D scrambles word order. The lesson explicitly notes that improvement items often shift a fronted heavy adverbial to final position. Thus option B is the preferred structure.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following sentences violates the licensing conditions for gapping in a coordinate structure?
questions.a: Because the data was incomplete, the analysis was delayed, and the report too.
opts: The committee approved the proposal, and the board the amendment.
Because the data was incomplete, the analysis was delayed, and the report too.
She has visited Paris, and he Rome.
They will submit the draft by Friday, and we the final version by Monday.
questions.solution: Gapping requires a coordinate structure (conjoined by and, or, but) and cannot operate across a clause boundary introduced by a subordinating conjunction. Option B embeds the gapped clause "and the report too" inside a because-clause, making it a subordinate rather than a coordinate conjunct; the gapped verb "was delayed" is not in a main clause conjoined by and. Options A, C, and D are well-formed gapping: remnants are parallel noun phrases (the board / the amendment; he / Rome; we / the final version) and the shared verb/tense is recoverable from the first conjunct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which sentence is a strong negative polarity item (NPI) correctly licensed by an anti-additive operator?
questions.a: No candidate has in years applied for the position.
opts: Few students have ever read that manuscript.
Many researchers have in years published on this topic.
Hardly anyone has ever seen the document.
No candidate has in years applied for the position.
questions.solution: Strong NPIs such as "in years" require an anti-additive (downward-entailing and upward-entailing) licensor like "no", "not", or "never". "No candidate" is anti-additive, so "in years" is licensed in D. "Few" is downward-entailing but not anti-additive (it licenses weak NPIs like "any" but not strong ones like "in years"), so A is incorrect. "Many" is not downward-entailing, so B fails. "Hardly" is downward-entailing but not anti-additive; it licenses weak NPIs ("anyone") but not strong NPIs ("ever" in the sense of "at any time" is borderline, but "in years" would be unlicensed), making C incorrect for a strong NPI.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Select the sentence that observes the correct complementation pattern for the matrix verb.
questions.a: The witness promised to testify at the hearing.
opts: The director avoided to mention the budget shortfall.
The team enjoyed to collaborate with the consultants.
The witness promised to testify at the hearing.
The analyst suggested to revise the methodology.
questions.solution: "Promise" selects an infinitival complement (promise to VP), so C is grammatical. "Avoid" and "enjoy" require gerund-participle complements (avoid mentioning, enjoy collaborating), ruling out A and B. "Suggest" takes a finite clause (suggest that...) or a gerund (suggest revising), not an infinitive, so D is ungrammatical.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which revision correctly converts the finite concessive clause into a non-finite "despite" construction while preserving grammaticality?
questions.a: Although the budget was reduced, the project continued. → Despite the budget being reduced, the project continued.
opts: Although the budget was reduced, the project continued. → Despite the budget was reduced, the project continued.
Although the budget was reduced, the project continued. → Despite the budget being reduced, the project continued.
Although the budget was reduced, the project continued. → Despite reduced the budget, the project continued.
Although the budget was reduced, the project continued. → Despite the budget reduced, the project continued.
questions.solution: "Despite" is a preposition requiring a gerund-participle clause or a noun phrase as its complement; it cannot take a finite clause. Option B uses the gerund-participle "being reduced" (passive gerund), which is the correct non-finite form. Option A retains a finite clause ("the budget was reduced"), which is ungrammatical after "despite". Option C uses a bare verb form ("reduced") without a subject or gerund marker. Option D uses a past participle ("reduced") without an auxiliary, yielding a reduced clause that is not a licensed complement of "despite".
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which sentence does the discourse marker fail to scope properly over the elliptical remnant, creating an ill-formed structure?
questions.a: She will attend the conference; however, not he.
opts: She will attend the conference; however, he won't.
The report was thorough; moreover, it was concise.
The experiment failed; therefore, the hypothesis was rejected.
She will attend the conference; however, not he.
questions.solution: When a discourse marker precedes an elliptical clause, it must scope over a full proposition. In D, "however" attempts to contrast "She will attend" with the fragment "not he", which is not a clause and cannot serve as the second argument of the contrastive relation. The remnant "not he" lacks a verb and cannot be interpreted as "he will not attend" under the licensing conditions for stripping (which requires a particle like "too" or "either" matching the antecedent's polarity). Options A, B, and C each pair the marker with a complete clause (finite in A and C, full clause in B), so the markers scope correctly.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which revision corrects the ungrammatical wh‑cleft *What he did was left early*?
questions.a: What he did was leave early.
opts: What he did was leave early.
What he did was to leave early.
What he did was left early.
What he did was leaves early.
questions.solution: The lesson states that a wh‑cleft complement must be a gerund or a bare infinitive. *What he did was leave early* uses the bare infinitive *leave* and satisfies the selectional restriction. *What he did was to leave early* adds *to*, which the lesson does not license. *What he did was left early* retains the finite past form *left*, which is explicitly ruled out. *What he did was leaves early* mismatches tense and form. Therefore only the first option is grammatical.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In a context where several poets exist, which punctuation correctly marks the restrictive appositive in "The poet Kalidasa wrote Shakuntala"?
questions.solution: A restrictive appositive narrows the reference and takes no commas. The lesson explains that *My brother Arjun* (no commas) implies multiple brothers, whereas *My brother, Arjun,* (with commas) implies a single brother. Since the context allows multiple poets, the name *Kalidasa* must appear without commas. Options B, C, and D each insert at least one comma, incorrectly signalling a non‑restrictive reading. Only option A presents the restrictive form.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which revision eliminates the dangling absolute construction in "He being late, the meeting started without him"?
questions.a: Because he was late, the meeting started without him.
opts: He being late, the meeting started without him.
His being late, the meeting started without him.
Because he was late, the meeting started without him.
Being late, the meeting started without him.
questions.solution: An absolute construction must have a logical subject that either matches the matrix subject or is recoverable from context. In the original, *He being late* has subject *He*, but the matrix subject is *the meeting*, so the absolute dangles. Option B changes to a possessive gerund, which the lesson notes is prescribed only for gerunds, not absolutes, and still dangles. Option D omits the subject entirely, leaving a dangling participle. Option C replaces the absolute with a subordinate *because* clause, providing a clear causal link and a proper subject (*he*). This revision preserves meaning and removes the attachment error.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which revision corrects the illicit expletive construction with the control verb *try*?
opts: It is tried that he succeeds.
questions.solution: The verb *try* is a control verb: it assigns an agent role to its subject and requires an overt controller for the infinitival complement. The expletive *it* cannot serve as that controller, so *It tries that he succeeds* is ungrammatical. The grammatical form must have a real subject (*he*) controlling the infinitive, yielding *He tries to succeed*. Passive or extraposed versions (*It is tried that…*, *He is tried to…*) are also impossible because control verbs resist passivisation of their complements. Therefore option B is the only well‑formed sentence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In formal writing, which reformulation of *Every student did not pass* expresses the preferred wide‑scope negation reading?
questions.solution: The sentence *Every student did not pass* is ambiguous: it can mean *Not every student passed* (negation takes wide scope over the quantifier) or *Every student failed* (negation takes narrow scope). The lesson states that formal written English strongly prefers the wide‑scope reading, which is unambiguously rendered by placing the quantifier inside the negation: *Not every student passed*. Option B forces the narrow‑scope reading, option C changes the quantifier to *no*, and option D retains the ambiguous structure. Hence option A is the correct revision.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which version properly resolves the left‑dislocation and control‑verb mismatch in *The proposal, it is hoped that it will be accepted*?
questions.a: It is hoped that the proposal will be accepted.
opts: The proposal, it is hoped that it will be accepted.
The proposal is hoped to be accepted.
It is hoped that the proposal will be accepted.
The proposal, it is hoped will be accepted.
questions.solution: *Hope* is a control verb, not a raising verb, so it cannot passivise its infinitival complement (*The proposal is hoped to be accepted* is ungrammatical). Left‑dislocation requires a resumptive pronoun that matches the dislocated phrase, but the original also misuses *hope* in a passive frame. The grammatical alternative uses extraposition with an expletive *it* and a *that*‑clause: *It is hoped that the proposal will be accepted*. This preserves the deontic meaning, provides a proper subject for *hope*, and avoids illicit passivisation. Options A and D retain the left‑dislocation without a licit structure, and option B attempts an impossible passive. Thus option C is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which punctuation correctly joins the two independent clauses *The report is believed to be accurate* and *it was submitted yesterday*?
questions.a: The report is believed to be accurate; it was submitted yesterday.
opts: The report is believed to be accurate, it was submitted yesterday.
The report is believed to be accurate; it was submitted yesterday.
The report is believed to be accurate: it was submitted yesterday.
The report is believed to be accurate it was submitted yesterday.
questions.solution: The two clauses are both independent; joining them with only a comma creates a comma splice, which the lesson identifies as an error. A semicolon is the standard punctuation for linking independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. A colon is used for anticipation or explanation, not for simple coordination, and omitting punctuation entirely produces a run‑on sentence. Therefore the only grammatically acceptable choice is the semicolon in option B.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: For a universal scientific law, which determiner choice is appropriate with the mass noun *water*?
questions.solution: Mass nouns such as *water* take the zero article when used generically to express a universal law. The lesson explicitly states that inserting *the* forces a specific portion of water, which is inappropriate for a general truth. *A water* is ungrammatical because *water* is non‑count, and *some water* introduces an existential reading rather than a generic one. Hence the correct generic form is *Water boils at 100°C* (option B).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which revision eliminates the dangling modifier in the sentence "Walking down the street, the shop was noticed by her"?
questions.a: Walking down the street, she noticed the shop.
opts: Walking down the street, the shop was noticed by her.
Walking down the street, she noticed the shop.
Walking down the street, the shop noticed her.
Walking down the street, it was noticed the shop.
questions.solution: A present‑participle phrase at the start of a sentence must attach to the subject of the main clause. In the original, "the shop" cannot be the entity walking, creating a dangling modifier. Option B supplies "she" as the subject, so the participle "Walking down the street" correctly modifies "she." Options A and D retain the mismatched subject, and Option C absurdly makes the shop the walker. Therefore only B resolves the dangling modifier.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which sentence correctly expresses future ability without stacking two true modals?
questions.a: She will be able to finish the project.
opts: She will can finish the project.
She will be able to finish the project.
She must can finish the project.
She should can finish the project.
questions.solution: English does not allow two true modals (e.g., will, can, must, should) to appear consecutively. The lesson advises using a modal plus a semi‑modal such as "be able to" to convey future ability. Option B follows this pattern: "will" (modal) + "be able to" (semi‑modal). Options A, C, and D each stack two true modals (will can, must can, should can), which are ungrammatical in standard English.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which sentence does the placement of "only" convey that giving a book was the sole action performed?
questions.a: She only gave him a book.
opts: Only she gave him a book.
She gave only him a book.
She only gave him a book.
She gave him only a book.
questions.solution: The focus‑sensitive adverb "only" scopes over the constituent it directly precedes. To indicate that the entire action of giving a book was the only thing she did, "only" must precede the verb phrase "gave him a book." Option C places "only" immediately before the verb, yielding the intended reading. Option A restricts the subject, Option B restricts the indirect object, and Option D restricts the direct object, each altering the scope away from the intended meaning.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which pseudo‑cleft construction obeys the requirement for a bare infinitive after "do"?
questions.a: What he did was solve the problem.
opts: What he did was to solve the problem.
What he did was solve the problem.
What he did was solving the problem.
What he did was solved the problem.
questions.solution: The lesson specifies that in a pseudo‑cleft with "do," the focused verb must appear as a bare infinitive (without "to"). Option B provides the bare infinitive "solve" after "was," satisfying this rule. Option A incorrectly inserts "to," Option C uses a gerund‑participle, and Option D uses a past participle; none of these are licensed in the standard pseudo‑cleft pattern.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Select the appropriate verb for the compound subject joined by 'and': 'Ram and Shyam ____ going to the market.'
questions.solution: When two or more subjects are linked by the coordinating conjunction 'and', the resulting compound subject is plural because it denotes more than one entity. The present‑tense plural verb form for the verb 'be' is 'are'. 'Is' and 'was' are singular, while 'were' is past plural; only 'are' matches a present‑tense plural subject.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Apply the proximity principle to choose the verb: 'Either the manager or the employees ____ responsible for the delay.'
questions.solution: With disjunctive conjunctions such as 'or' or 'nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it (the proximity rule). In the sentence, the nearer subject is 'employees', which is plural. Therefore the verb must be plural. In the present tense the plural form of 'be' is 'are'. 'Is' and 'was' are singular; 'were' is past plural, so 'are' is the only correct present‑tense choice.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Identify the verb that agrees with the true subject despite an intervening phrase: 'The box of chocolates ____ expensive.'
questions.solution: The head noun of the subject phrase is 'box', which is singular. The prepositional phrase 'of chocolates' intervenes but does not change the number of the subject. Therefore the verb must agree with the singular head 'box'. In the present tense the singular form of 'be' is 'is'. 'Are' and 'were' are plural; 'have been' is a perfect construction that also requires a plural subject. Hence 'is' is the only verb that matches the singular subject.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Select the verb that correctly completes the sentence: 'A majority of the committee ____ voted in favour of the proposal.'
questions.solution: The phrase “a majority of” is a complex quantifier with a partitive “of” construction. The governing rule states that the verb agrees with the noun immediately following “of”. Here that noun is “committee”, a collective noun treated as singular in this context. Therefore the singular verb “has” is required. “Have” would be used only if the noun after “of” were plural (e.g., “a majority of the members have voted”). Options “is” and “are” are linking verbs and do not fit the perfect aspect.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the correct verb form: 'The director, along with the actors, ____ attending the premiere.'
questions.solution: Additive phrases such as “along with”, “as well as”, and “together with” do not create a compound subject. The verb must agree solely with the head subject that precedes the additive phrase. In this sentence the head subject is “director”, which is singular. Consequently the singular verb “is” is correct. The plural noun “actors” inside the additive phrase is ignored for agreement. “Are” and “were” would incorrectly match the plural noun, and “be” is not a finite verb form appropriate for this indicative clause.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Complete the comparative elliptical clause: 'No student understands the concept better than she ____.'
questions.solution: Elliptical comparative clauses introduced by “than” omit a verb that is recoverable from the main clause. The omitted verb must agree in person, number, and tense with the subject of the elliptical clause. The subject here is “she” (third‑person singular), and the main clause uses present tense (“understands”). Therefore the appropriate auxiliary is the present‑tense third‑person singular “does”. “Do” is plural, “did” is past tense, and “has” is a perfect auxiliary that does not match the simple present sense of the comparison.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which verb agrees with the subject in the sentence: 'The criteria ____ clear and measurable.'
questions.solution: “Criteria” is the plural form of the Greek‑derived noun “criterion”. Greek and Latin plurals retain their original inflections, and the verb must agree with the grammatical number of the form actually used. Because “criteria” is plural, the plural verb “are” is required. “Is” and “was” are singular, while “were” is past tense; the sentence is in present tense, so “are” is the only correct choice.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Identify the correct subjunctive form: 'It is essential that he ____ present at the meeting.'
questions.solution: The construction “It is essential that …” triggers the present mandative subjunctive. In the present subjunctive the verb takes the base form for all persons and numbers; it never adds an “‑s” ending. Hence the invariant form “be” is used regardless of the singular subject “he”. “Is” and “was” are indicative forms, and “were” is the past subjunctive (counterfactual) form, which is not appropriate for a present‑time mandate.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Each of the candidates ______ submitted the form.
questions.solution: Step 1: Identify the grammatical subject — the distributive pronoun each. Step 2: Recognise that each is singular regardless of the plural noun in the following of-phrase (of the candidates). Step 3: Apply the rule that the verb must agree with the singular subject each, not with the object of the preposition. Step 4: Select the singular present-perfect auxiliary has. The plural have, are, and were are attracted incorrectly by candidates.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: He is one of those leaders who ______ confidence.
questions.solution: Step 1: Locate the relative pronoun who. Step 2: Determine its antecedent by asking "who inspires?" The antecedent is the plural noun phrase those leaders, not the singular one. Step 3: The relative clause verb must agree with that plural antecedent. Step 4: Choose the plural present-tense form inspire. The singular inspires would mistakenly agree with one; the non-finite forms inspiring and inspired cannot function as the main verb of the relative clause.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Five kilometres ______ a long distance to walk.
questions.solution: Step 1: Recognise that measurements of distance, time, or money are treated as singular units when they express a single quantity. Step 2: The subject Five kilometres denotes one collective distance, not five separate kilometres. Step 3: Apply singular agreement with the linking verb. Step 4: Select is (present singular). Are and were are plural; have is not a linking verb for this construction.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The United States ______ a federal republic.
questions.solution: Step 1: Identify the subject as a proper noun with plural form but singular reference — a single political entity. Step 2: Recall the rule that titles, names, and proper nouns denoting one country, organisation, or work take singular verbs. Step 3: The predicate a federal republic confirms the singular conception. Step 4: Choose the singular present verb is. Are and were would imply the individual states; have is ungrammatical here.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The police ______ investigating the case.
questions.solution: Step 1: Note that the police is a collective noun that is always plural in standard English; it refers to the body of officers, not a singular unit. Step 2: Contrast with the singular police force. Step 3: The verb must be plural to agree with this invariant plural subject. Step 4: Select are (present plural). Is and was are singular; has is a singular auxiliary and cannot serve as the progressive auxiliary.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: That the proposals were rejected ______ surprising.
questions.solution: The subject is a that‑clause ("That the proposals were rejected"). Clausal subjects are syntactically singular units, so the verb must be singular regardless of any plural nouns inside the clause. "Is" is the singular present‑tense form that agrees with the clausal subject. "Are," "were," and "have been" are plural or past forms and would incorrectly treat the clause as plural.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Only the managers ______ responsible for the decision.
questions.solution: The focus particle "only" precedes the true subject "the managers" but does not carry number. The verb must agree with the head noun "managers," which is plural. Therefore the plural verb "are" is correct. "Is," "was," and "has been" are singular and would mistakenly let the particle dictate agreement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A variety of options ______ available.
questions.solution: With collective quantifiers like "a variety of," the verb agrees with the noun following "of" (the of‑complement). Here "options" is a plural countable noun, so the verb must be plural. "Are" is the plural present form; "is," "was," and "has been" are singular and would incorrectly match the quantifier head instead of the of‑noun.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The bulk of the data ______ corrupted.
questions.solution: In partitive expressions such as "the bulk of," the verb mirrors the number of the of‑noun. The lesson notes that "data" is traditionally plural in formal usage, so the verb must be plural. "Are" is the correct plural present form. "Is," "was," and "has been" are singular and would wrongly agree with the singular partitive head "bulk."
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Not only the students but also the teacher ______ responsible.
questions.solution: The correlative "not only … but also" follows the proximity rule: the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. In this sentence the nearer subject is "the teacher" (singular), so the verb must be singular. "Is" is the singular present form. "Are," "were," and "have been" are plural and would incorrectly apply a default plural agreement because two entities are mentioned.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which sentence contains a free relative clause functioning as a plural subject requiring a plural verb?
opts: Whoever arrives first gets the prize.
questions.solution: Free relative clauses take singular or plural verbs depending on whether they denote a singular or plural entity. The lesson explains that when the clause denotes a plural set, the paraphrase uses plural heads like 'the things that' or 'the people who', requiring a plural verb. Option C, 'What matter are the details', paraphrases as 'The things that matter are the details' — plural head 'things', plural verb 'matter' and 'are'. Options A, B, and D all paraphrase with singular heads ('the thing that', 'the person who') and correctly take singular verbs ('matters', 'is', 'gets'). The plural verb 'matter' in option C signals a plural interpretation of the free relative 'What'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: After a fronted negative adverbial triggering subject-auxiliary inversion, what determines the verb number?
questions.a: The logical subject following the verb.
opts: The logical subject following the verb.
The nearest noun phrase before the verb.
questions.solution: Inversion after negative/restrictive adverbials (e.g., 'Never have I seen...', 'Rarely does he complain...') does not change agreement rules. The verb must agree with the true logical subject, which appears after the verb in inverted order. The lesson states: 'The inverted order does not change the agreement rule: the verb agrees with the logical subject, not with any noun in the fronted phrase.' Options A and B are distractors: the adverbial never controls agreement, and 'there' is a dummy subject that never determines number. Option D describes the proximity principle, which applies only to 'or/nor' coordinations, not inversion structures.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which quantifier phrase is correctly paired with the noun type it modifies?
questions.solution: The lesson specifies selectional restrictions: 'a great deal of' is restricted to singular mass nouns (ungrammatical with plural countables like 'books'), and 'a large number of' is restricted to plural countables (ungrammatical with mass nouns like 'water'). 'Plenty of' is neutral and works with both mass and count nouns, so 'plenty of reasons' (plural count) is correct. Option D fails because 'a lot of equipment' takes a singular verb ('is') since 'equipment' is a mass noun; 'are' would be incorrect. The rule: verb matches the of-noun — 'equipment' is singular mass → 'is'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the sentence 'The reports each contain an executive summary', why is the plural verb 'contain' correct?
questions.a: The plural antecedent 'The reports' remains the syntactic subject.
opts: Each is the subject and is plural in this construction.
The plural antecedent 'The reports' remains the syntactic subject.
Each of the reports functions as a partitive subject.
Every can replace each here without changing the verb.
questions.solution: When 'each' follows a plural noun phrase, it acts as an appositive distributive and does not alter the subject's number. The syntactic subject remains the plural noun 'The reports', so the verb must be plural ('contain'). The lesson contrasts this with partitive 'each of' where 'each' is the head and forces singular agreement ('Each of the candidates is qualified'). Option A is false: 'each' is singular as a determiner/head. Option C describes the partitive construction, not the post-subject use. Option D is false: 'every' cannot appear post-nominally in standard English ('*The students every have...' is ungrammatical).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence: The Grapes of Wrath ___ a novel by John Steinbeck.
questions.solution: The title The Grapes of Wrath refers to a single literary work. Even though the title contains a plural noun (Grapes), titles of books, films, or artworks are treated as singular concepts. Therefore the singular verb is is required. Options are, were, and have been are plural or inappropriate tense forms.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Select the verb that agrees with the subject: The Philippines ___ an archipelago in Southeast Asia.
questions.solution: The Philippines denotes a collection of islands, not a single political unit. Geographical names ending in -s that refer to a group of islands take a plural verb. Hence are is correct. Is would treat it as a singular entity, which is inappropriate for an archipelago.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Fill in the blank with the appropriate verb: Two‑thirds of the budget ___ already been allocated.
questions.solution: In fractional expressions the verb agrees with the noun following of. Here the noun is budget, which is singular and uncountable. Consequently the singular auxiliary has is needed. Have would agree with a plural noun, had is past tense, and having is a participle, not a finite verb.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct verb form: Swimming and cycling ___ cardiovascular health.
questions.solution: When two gerund phrases are coordinated with and, the compound subject is plural. Swimming and cycling are two distinct activities, so the plural verb improve is required. Improves would be singular, improved is past tense, and improving is a participle, not a finite verb.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: She ________ in this office since 2019.
questions.solution: Since 2019 marks an action continuing to the present, so the present perfect continuous is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: By the time we reached the station, the train ________.
questions.solution: The train left before another past action, so the past perfect is required.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: He avoided ________ the question directly.
questions.solution: Avoid takes a gerund, so answering is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: If it ________ tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.
questions.solution: The first conditional uses present simple in the if-clause and will in the main clause.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence:
questions.a: He said that the earth is round.
opts: He said that the earth was round.
He said that the earth is round.
He said that the earth will be round.
He said that the earth has been round.
questions.solution: A universal truth keeps the present tense even after a past reporting verb.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the correct meaning of 'to beat around the bush':
questions.solution: To beat around the bush means to avoid coming to the main point.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The phrase 'once in a blue moon' means:
questions.solution: Once in a blue moon means something happens very rarely.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the meaning of 'to bite the bullet':
questions.a: To face a difficult situation bravely
opts: To face a difficult situation bravely
questions.solution: To bite the bullet means to endure a difficult or unpleasant situation with courage.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'To feel the pinch' means:
questions.solution: To feel the pinch means to experience financial difficulty or shortage.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the correct meaning of 'at the eleventh hour':
questions.solution: At the eleventh hour means at the last possible moment, not literally eleven o'clock.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: One who loves books is called a:
questions.solution: A bibliophile loves books. A philatelist collects stamps and a numismatist collects coins.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A place where birds are kept is an:
questions.solution: An aviary keeps birds. An apiary keeps bees and an aquarium keeps fish.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A speech delivered without preparation is called:
questions.solution: Extempore means speaking without preparation. An elegy is a mournful poem and an epitaph is a tomb inscription.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The study of weather is called:
questions.solution: Meteorology is the study of weather. Geology studies the earth's crust and etymology studies word origins.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A person who hates mankind is a:
questions.solution: A misanthrope hates mankind. A philanthropist loves mankind and an altruist lives for others.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'Give up' means:
questions.solution: 'Give up' = stop trying/quit.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'Run out of' means:
questions.solution: 'Run out of' = have no more of something.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which is correct pronoun placement?
questions.solution: Pronoun object goes between verb and particle: 'Turn it off'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'Put off' means:
questions.solution: 'Put off' = postpone/delay.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'Look after' means:
questions.solution: 'Look after' = take care of.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following sentences demonstrates the passive test correctly identifying a transitive phrasal verb as opposed to a prepositional verb?
questions.a: The meeting was called off by the manager.
opts: The meeting was called off by the manager.
The client was called on by the manager.
The noise was put up with by the residents.
The lights were turned off by the janitor.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the passive test is the most reliable separability diagnostic: only transitive phrasal verbs with a direct object can be passivised. 'Call off' is a transitive phrasal verb (The manager called off the meeting → The meeting was called off), making option A grammatical. 'Call on' is a prepositional verb (*The client was called on is ungrammatical in standard English). 'Put up with' is a three-part phrasal verb, which is uniformly inseparable and resists passivisation (*The noise was put up with). 'Turn off' is a transitive phrasal verb, so option D is also grammatical, but the question asks for the demonstration of the test *identifying* a transitive phrasal verb *as opposed to* a prepositional verb. Option A explicitly contrasts with the ungrammatical prepositional verb example given in the text ('The client was called on'), making it the clearest demonstration of the diagnostic contrast.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following sentences is ungrammatical because it extracts the particle alone from a transitive phrasal verb?
questions.a: Off what did the manager call?
opts: What did the manager call off?
Off what did the manager call?
The meeting that the manager called off was cancelled.
The manager called off the meeting.
questions.solution: Extraction facts in the lesson show that the direct object of a transitive phrasal verb can be fronted (sentence 1) or relativised (sentence 3) while the particle stays adjacent to the verb. However, moving the particle itself to the front strands the verb and violates the Complex NP Constraint, yielding the ungrammatical *Off what did the manager call?*. Sentence 4 is a simple declarative with no extraction. Therefore, sentence 2 is the only illicit extraction.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In a formal academic essay, which single‑word verb best replaces the phrasal verb "call off" without creating a register mismatch?
questions.solution: The lesson warns against ignoring register mismatch when substituting a phrasal verb with a simplex verb in formal writing tasks. "Call off" is an informal phrasal verb; its formal equivalent is the simplex verb "cancel", which matches the elevated register of academic prose. The other options either retain the phrasal verb ("call off") or use different particles ("call up", "call out") that do not convey the meaning of termination and remain informal.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which particle choice for the verb "fill" when completing a form is characteristic of American English according to the cross‑dialectal variation section?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly contrasts British and American preferences: British English commonly uses "fill in (a form)" whereas American English prefers "fill out". The other particles ("up", "over") are not mentioned as standard variants for this verb in either major variety. Hence, "fill out" is the American norm.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Why do high‑frequency idiomatic phrasal verbs such as "give up" show faster comprehension times than literal combinations like "walk up"?
questions.a: They are processed via a direct lexical route.
opts: They are processed via a direct lexical route.
They allow particle extraction in wh‑questions.
questions.solution: Psycholinguistic research cited in the lesson indicates that high‑frequency phrasal verbs are accessed through a direct lexical route, behaving like single words in lexical decision and eye‑tracking tasks. Low‑frequency or transparent combinations engage a compositional route where verb and particle are processed separately, leading to longer fixation times. The speed advantage therefore stems from direct lexical access, not from syntactic complexity, extraction properties, or transitivity.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following sentences violates the standard syntactic constraint on negation and particle placement in contemporary formal English?
questions.a: She gives never up on her dreams.
opts: She did not give up the search.
They haven't called off the meeting.
She gives never up on her dreams.
He didn't call off the event but the meeting.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'frequency adverbs occupy the pre-auxiliary position; they cannot split the verb-particle bond' and gives '*She gives never up' as an example of misplaced 'never'. Option C places 'never' between the verb 'gives' and particle 'up', splitting the verb-particle complex. Options A and B correctly attach negation to the auxiliary. Option D shows contrastive focus on the object, which the lesson describes as a valid structure ('He called off not the event but the meeting').
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: When the verb is a change-of-state verb (e.g., 'heat', 'wake'), the particle 'up' typically contributes which aspectual value?
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'Up with motion verbs (go up, climb up) retains a directional sense, but with change-of-state verbs (heat up, wake up) it shifts to inceptive or completive aspect.' Option A applies to motion verbs. Option C describes 'away'. Option D describes 'out'. The question specifies change-of-state verbs, triggering the aspectual shift to inceptive/completive.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the correctly spelt word:
questions.solution: Accommodation has double c and double m.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The head of a school is the:
questions.solution: The head of a school is the principal; a rule is a principle.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the sentence with the correct word:
questions.a: The medicine had a bad effect.
opts: The medicine had a bad affect.
The medicine had a bad effect.
The medicine had a bad efect.
The medicine had a bad affact.
questions.solution: Effect is the noun meaning result; affect is usually the verb.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the antonym of 'Frugal':
questions.solution: Frugal means careful with money; extravagant means spending excessively, the opposite. The other three are synonyms.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In 'The judge was impartial throughout the trial', 'impartial' means:
questions.solution: Impartial means not favouring one side; neutral is the correct synonym. Biased is the antonym.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Transient':
questions.solution: Transient means lasting only a short time; permanent is the opposite. Fleeting, temporary and passing are synonyms.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which pair are near-synonyms with different tone?
questions.solution: Famous and notorious both mean well known, but notorious implies disapproval. The other pairs are direct opposites.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The root 'tract' means:
questions.solution: 'tract' = pull/draw (attract = pull toward, contract = pull together, extract = pull out).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The prefix 'anti' means:
questions.solution: 'anti' = against/opposing (antibiotic, antisocial, antiseptic).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The suffix '-ment' forms a:
questions.solution: '-ment' forms abstract nouns (development, agreement, statement).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'Bene' means:
questions.solution: 'Bene' = good/well (benefit, benevolent, benediction).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which word means 'fear of water'?
questions.solution: 'hydro' = water, 'phob' = fear → hydrophobia = fear of water.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A test item requires forming a noun from the Latin root *fract-* (break) using a suffix that typically attaches to Latinate bases. Which suffix would be morphologically expected based on the diagnostic patterns for Latin noun formation?
questions.solution: The lesson states that Latin nouns favour suffixes such as -or (actor), -ura (fracture, aperture), and -men (specimen). The example *fracture* is explicitly given as a Latin noun ending in -ura. Greek nouns, by contrast, often end in -sis (analysis), -ma (schema), or -on (electron). Since the root *fract-* is Latin (from *frangere*), the expected Latinate noun suffix is -ura, yielding *fracture*.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: When the negative prefix *in-* attaches to a base beginning with a bilabial consonant, which allomorph appears, and which of the following words illustrates this phonological conditioning?
questions.solution: The lesson explains that the negative prefix *in-* assimilates to *im-* before bilabials (p, b, m), *il-* before *l*, and *ir-* before *r*. *Imbalance* begins with the bilabial *b*, so the prefix surfaces as *im-*. *Inactive* shows the default *in-* before a vowel, *illegal* shows *il-* before *l*, and *irregular* shows *ir-* before *r*.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A Spanish-speaking test-taker reads *eventually* in an English passage and interprets it as “possibly” because of Spanish *eventualmente*. Which lesson concept describes this systematic divergence, and what is the typical historical path?
questions.a: False friend; English retains the original Latin sense while Romance develops a modal nuance.
opts: False friend; English retains the original Latin sense while Romance develops a modal nuance.
Cognate trap; English narrows the meaning while Romance widens it.
Morphological interference; the prefix *e-* is misparsed as a negator.
Polysemy resolution failure; the test-taker selects the wrong sense from a shared polysemous entry.
questions.solution: The lesson’s “Systematic Cognate Divergence Patterns” section explains that many false friends arise because “the English form retains the original Latin sense, while the Romance language develops a modal or aspectual nuance.” *Eventually* (from Latin *eventualis*) keeps the sense “finally” in English, whereas Spanish *eventualmente* shifted to “possibly.” This is a predictable cognate divergence, not a morphological misparsing or polysemy confusion.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Descriptive writing practice is best done:
questions.solution: Regular timed practice builds speed, quality, and exam temperament.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In self-evaluation of an essay, which is NOT checked?
questions.solution: Handwriting should be legible but 'beauty' is not a scoring criterion.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A formal letter body paragraph rule is:
questions.solution: Purpose → details → request, one idea per paragraph.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: A précis targets approximately:
questions.solution: Précis ≈ one-third of original word count.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: If running out of time in an exam descriptive answer:
questions.a: Write structured bullet points with intro & conclusion
opts: Write structured bullet points with intro & conclusion
questions.solution: Structured partial answer earns partial credit; blank earns zero.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the recommended timed‑essay framework, what is the function of the linking sentence in each body paragraph?
questions.a: Tie the paragraph’s argument back to the central thesis
opts: Restate the thesis in fresh language
Tie the paragraph’s argument back to the central thesis
questions.solution: The lesson states that each body paragraph should follow a mini‑structure: a topic sentence that restates one dimension, evidence or reasoning, and a linking sentence that ties back to the thesis. The linking sentence’s explicit purpose is to connect the paragraph’s point to the overall claim, ensuring logical cohesion. It does not introduce a new dimension (that is the topic sentence’s role), nor does it restate the thesis in fresh language (that is the conclusion’s job), and it is not meant to present a counter‑argument. Therefore, option C correctly captures the described function.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the précis guidelines, which of the following should be retained when compressing a source text?
questions.a: Qualifying language such as “largely” or “under certain conditions”
opts: Illustrative examples that clarify the argument
Qualifying language such as “largely” or “under certain conditions”
Repetitive elaboration of the same point
questions.solution: The précis section instructs writers to discard illustrative examples, rhetorical flourishes, and repetitive elaboration, while explicitly stating: “Maintain the original’s qualifying language (“largely”, “partially”, “under certain conditions”) because examiners penalise over‑generalisation.” Qualifying language preserves nuance and the author’s intended scope, making it essential to retain. The other three items are listed as material to be removed during compression. Hence, option B is the only element that must be kept.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In a semi‑formal letter, which combination of linguistic features is recommended?
questions.a: First‑person active, modals of suggestion (“could”, “might”), shorter sentences
opts: Third‑person passive, modals of obligation (“shall”, “must”), long balanced sentences
First‑person active, modals of suggestion (“could”, “might”), shorter sentences
First‑person passive, modals of necessity (“have to”), very long sentences
Third‑person active, modals of permission (“may”), fragmented sentences
questions.solution: The tone calibration section contrasts formal and semi‑formal registers. For semi‑formal letters it specifies: “first‑person active (“I request…”), modals of suggestion (“could”, “might”), and shorter sentences for readability.” Option B mirrors this description exactly. The other options describe formal register features (third‑person passive, obligation modals, long sentences) or mismatched combinations not supported by the text. Thus, option B is the correct choice.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the recommended maximum number of quantitative data insertions per paragraph in a timed essay?
questions.solution: The evidence integration section states: “Limit quantitative insertions to one per paragraph in essays, two in reports.” This direct instruction sets the ceiling at a single quantitative figure per essay paragraph to avoid data overload. Options B, C, and D contradict this explicit guideline. Therefore, the correct answer is one insertion per paragraph, corresponding to option A.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which practice in formal correspondence is identified as a trap that undermines professional register?
opts: Using the 'you-attitude' to emphasise reader benefits
Including a clear subject line and reference
Structuring the letter with a logical opening, body, closing
questions.solution: The lesson lists "Using emotive language in formal letters, which undermines the professional register expected by evaluators" as a common trap. The other options describe recommended practices: the you‑attitude, a clear subject line, and logical structure all support persuasive yet professional framing. Hence, employing emotive language is the identified error.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In précis writing, why must quantifiers such as 'approximately' be reproduced exactly?
questions.a: Because rounding alters the evidential weight
opts: Because rounding alters the evidential weight
To match the original's colloquial tone
To allow the writer to simplify numbers
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly warns that quantifiers like "approximately", "nearly", "over" must be reproduced exactly; rounding "approximately 3.7 million" to "about 4 million" alters the evidential weight of the source. This precision preserves the author's intended degree of certainty and avoids misrepresenting data. The other options contradict the lesson's emphasis on fidelity.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the paragraph‑cohesion toolkit, which device is NOT included among the four cohesive devices that must be internalised for high‑scoring timed essays?
questions.solution: The lesson enumerates the compact toolkit of cohesive devices as (a) lexical chains, (b) referential pronouns, (c) logical connectors, and (d) parallel structure. Rhetorical questions are not mentioned anywhere in the toolkit; they are a stylistic device, not a cohesion device prescribed for timed essays. Hence option D is the correct answer.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the three‑pillar checklist for persuasive letter framing, which element is NOT a pillar?
questions.a: Include emotive language to convey urgency
opts: Include emotive language to convey urgency
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly lists the three‑pillar checklist as "quantify, align, deadline." It also notes that using emotive language (e.g., "I am deeply distressed") instead of impact data is a framing failure. Therefore, including emotive language is not a pillar; it is a mistake to avoid. Options A, B, and D correspond directly to the three pillars, making option C the correct choice.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the suggested time budget for a 300‑word essay, how many minutes are allocated for the drafting phase?
questions.solution: Section 1.2 outlines a practical schedule: five minutes for topic selection, five minutes for outline, twenty minutes for drafting, three minutes for review, and a two‑minute buffer. The drafting phase is therefore twenty minutes.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the evidence hierarchy outlined for UPSC essays, which sources are given top priority?
questions.a: Constitutional provisions, landmark judgments, and verifiable data.
opts: Constitutional provisions, landmark judgments, and verifiable data.
Unverified statistics rounded to the nearest thousand.
questions.solution: The lesson states that evidence must be prioritized as “Constitutional Provisions, Judgments, and Data”. It warns against citing data without a source, using rounded figures that cannot be verified, or over‑quoting secondary commentary. Options A, C, and D represent lower‑tier or unacceptable evidence. Therefore, the correct answer is B.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How should a candidate structure the thesis for a hybrid prompt that combines a quote with a topic?
questions.a: Fuse the quote’s thematic lens with the topic’s domain in a single thesis statement.
opts: Ignore the quote and write a thesis solely on the topic.
Fuse the quote’s thematic lens with the topic’s domain in a single thesis statement.
Write two separate theses, one for the quote and one for the topic.
Use the quote only in the conclusion, not in the thesis.
questions.solution: The lesson explains that for hybrid prompts the thesis should “fuse both”: the quote supplies the thematic lens (e.g., data as a resource) while the topic defines the domain (e.g., India’s digital economy). The example thesis merges them: “Treating data as a strategic resource can propel India’s digital economy, provided governance frameworks enforce consent…”. Options A, C, and D do not follow this fused approach. Thus, B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: When applying the SPACER framework for dimension prioritisation, what determines which dimensions receive the core word budget?
questions.a: Only dimensions directly invoked by specific claims in the thesis statement receive core allocation
opts: The six dimensions must always receive equal word allocation to ensure breadth
Dimensions are selected based on the examiner's known preferences for Social and Political lenses
Only dimensions directly invoked by specific claims in the thesis statement receive core allocation
The Economic and Constitutional dimensions are mandatory for every UPSC essay prompt
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'Begin by mapping each dimension to a specific claim in the thesis. If the thesis asserts "Inclusive digital governance requires constitutional safeguards, administrative capacity, and economic incentives", three dimensions — Constitutional, Administrative, Economic — are directly invoked. The remaining dimensions become optional enrichments.' Core allocation follows thesis claims, not fixed rules (A, D) or examiner bias (B).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How should the conclusion of a high-band essay resolve the narrative tension introduced in the thesis?
questions.a: By evaluating the conditional claim, acknowledging gaps, and articulating a concrete policy pathway
opts: By summarising each body paragraph in reverse order and ending with a rhetorical question
By evaluating the conditional claim, acknowledging gaps, and articulating a concrete policy pathway
By introducing a new dimension not previously discussed to demonstrate comprehensive thinking
By quoting a constitutional vision statement and appealing to the examiner's sense of justice
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The conclusion must resolve the narrative tension introduced in the thesis. If the thesis posed a conditional claim... the conclusion should evaluate the alignment, acknowledge gaps, and articulate a concrete pathway (e.g., "A statutory framework that empowers the NGT with suo-motu powers...")'. This forward vision transforms the essay into a policy-oriented argument. Option A is mechanical summary; Option C introduces new material; Option D relies on rhetoric over analysis.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: During the final three-to-five-minute review window, what is the correct order of the five sequential editing sweeps?
questions.a: Thesis-Echo Sweep → Connector Audit → Precision Sweep → Citation Verification → Word-Count Trim
opts: Connector Audit → Thesis-Echo Sweep → Precision Sweep → Citation Verification → Word-Count Trim
Thesis-Echo Sweep → Connector Audit → Precision Sweep → Citation Verification → Word-Count Trim
Precision Sweep → Thesis-Echo Sweep → Connector Audit → Word-Count Trim → Citation Verification
Citation Verification → Word-Count Trim → Thesis-Echo Sweep → Connector Audit → Precision Sweep
questions.solution: The lesson lists the protocol in exact sequence: 'First, the "Thesis-Echo Sweep"... Second, the "Connector Audit"... Third, the "Precision Sweep"... Fourth, the "Citation Verification Sweep"... Fifth, the "Word-Count Trim".' This order ensures structural coherence (thesis alignment, connectors) before micro-editing (precision, citations) and final length compliance. Only Option B matches this prescribed sequence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Mechanics of Sequencing, what is the correct hierarchical order of evidentiary proximity for ranking SPACER dimensions?
questions.a: Constitutional text > landmark judgment > statutory data > policy report > historical illustration
opts: Constitutional text > landmark judgment > statutory data > policy report > historical illustration
Landmark judgment > constitutional text > statutory data > policy report > historical illustration
Statutory data > constitutional text > landmark judgment > policy report > historical illustration
Policy report > statutory data > landmark judgment > constitutional text > historical illustration
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states the ranking order: constitutional text > landmark judgment > statutory data > policy report > historical illustration. This hierarchy reflects evidentiary proximity to the thesis. Option A matches this order; the other options invert the hierarchy.

questions.q: In the layered evidence hierarchy, which of the following belongs to the second tier of evidence?
opts: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
questions.solution: The lesson defines three evidence tiers. The top tier includes constitutional provisions and binding Supreme Court judgments. The second tier comprises statutory schemes and authoritative committee reports. The Right to Information Act 2005 is a statutory scheme, placing it in the second tier. Article 21 and Kesavananda Bharati belong to the top tier, while National Sample Survey Office rounds are third tier.

questions.q: What is the essential requirement for a cross‑paragraph evidence echo to demonstrate synthesis?
questions.a: It must add analytical value by contrasting interpretations or adding a later judicial gloss.
opts: It must add analytical value by contrasting interpretations or adding a later judicial gloss.
It must repeat the primary source verbatim to reinforce memory.
It must introduce a new primary source not cited earlier.
It must appear in the immediate next paragraph to maintain continuity.
questions.solution: The lesson states that a cross‑paragraph echo must add analytical value, such as contrasting the original interpretation with a later judicial gloss, rather than merely restating the source. This demonstrates synthesis. Option A captures this requirement; verbatim repetition, introducing a new primary source, or immediate placement are not required.

questions.q: Where should a concession‑refutation cycle be embedded to preserve paragraph unity and word economy?
questions.a: Inside the Explanation (E) segment of the PEEL paragraph.
opts: Inside the Explanation (E) segment of the PEEL paragraph.
In a standalone rebuttal paragraph after the primary dimensions.
In the Link (L) segment to transition to the next paragraph.
In the Point (P) segment to preempt the counter‑argument.
questions.solution: The lesson advises against a separate rebuttal paragraph and instead recommends embedding the concession‑refutation cycle within the Explanation (E) segment of the PEEL structure. This preserves paragraph unity and word economy. Option A reflects this; a standalone paragraph, the Link segment, or the Point segment are incorrect.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: During Sweep 3 of the Final Polish Checklist, what specific action is prescribed for vague quantifiers such as “many” or “significant”?
questions.a: Replace them with qualified ranges or sourced figures.
opts: Replace them with qualified ranges or sourced figures.
Delete them entirely to reduce word count.
Retain them but add a hedging phrase for nuance.
Move them to the counter‑argument paragraph for balance.
questions.solution: Sweep 3 of the Final Polish Checklist explicitly instructs replacing vague quantifiers such as many or significant with qualified ranges or sourced figures, for example billions of monthly UPI transactions. Deleting them, retaining them with hedging, or moving them to a counter‑argument paragraph are not prescribed. Option A matches the directive.

questions.q: In the post‑writing self‑assessment rubric, what does a total score of 8‑10 indicate about the essay?
questions.solution: The rubric assigns 2 points for fully met, 1 for partially met, and 0 for absent across five criteria, yielding a maximum of 10. questions.q: In a formal letter layout described in section 2.1, what is the correct sequence of components immediately following the sender's address?

opts: Date, receiver's address, subject line, salutation
Receiver's address, date, subject line, salutation
Subject line, date, receiver's address, salutation
Date, subject line, receiver's address, salutation

Below the date, the receiver's designation and complete address are placed... A concise subject line... The salutation... opens the body'. This establishes the sequence: sender's address → date → receiver's address → subject line → salutation. Option B reverses date and receiver's address. Option C places subject line before date and receiver's address. Option D places subject line before receiver's address.

questions.q: According to section 5.2, what three questions must the introduction of a report answer to set the context?
questions.a: Why it was commissioned, what it covers, how information was gathered

Why it was commissioned, what it covers, how information was gathered

Who the audience is, what the tone should be, what the format requires

Option A introduces irrelevant elements (cost, due date). Option C describes body/content elements (findings, recommendations, methodology) that belong in later sections, not the introduction's contextual questions. questions.q: According to the Central Information Commission template, which element is NOT mandatory in an RTI reply?
questions.a: A complimentary close such as "Yours faithfully"
opts: Reference number and date of receipt

Citation of the relevant exemption clause if information is denied
A complimentary close such as "Yours faithfully"
