questions.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, enacted under Lord Lytton, was a targeted measure against Indian-language newspapers. Which of the following publications would NOT have been subject to its penalties?
opts: Kesari (Marathi) edited by Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengali edition) edited by Sisir Kumar Ghosh
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Believing the Vernacular Press Act 1878 applied to English-language newspapers; it targeted only Indian-language publications." The Hindu was an English-language newspaper (though published in Madras). Kesari (Marathi), Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengali), and Zamindar (Urdu) were all vernacular/Indian-language publications explicitly mentioned in the lesson as part of the vernacular press landscape, making them liable under the Act. The Act was repealed in 1881 by Lord Ripon.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Communal Award of 1932 provided for separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with 71 reserved seats. The Poona Pact, signed between Gandhi and Ambedkar, replaced this with a system of reserved seats filled by joint electorates. What was the total number of reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures under the Poona Pact?
questions.solution: The Communal Award allocated 71 seats for Depressed Classes through separate electorates. The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) replaced separate electorates with reserved seats filled by joint electorates and increased the number of reserved seats in provincial legislatures to 148. Additionally, 18 seats were reserved in the Central Legislative Assembly. Option B (148) correctly states the provincial legislature figure.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Cripps Mission (March 1942) proposed dominion status after the war, a constituent assembly, and a specific clause regarding provinces. Which clause in the Cripps Offer was viewed by the Congress as a blueprint for partition and led to its rejection?
questions.a: Right of any province to opt out of the future union
opts: Retention of the Viceroy's veto power
Absence of immediate transfer of power
Right of any province to opt out of the future union
No explicit concession of a sovereign Pakistan
questions.solution: The Cripps Offer included the right of any province to opt out of the future Indian union, a concession aimed at the Muslim League's Pakistan demand. The Congress Working Committee rejected the offer on 7 April 1942, citing this opt-out clause as a blueprint for partition, along with the absence of immediate power transfer and retention of the Viceroy's veto. Option C identifies the specific clause viewed as a partition blueprint.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Regarding the Indian National Army (INA) and the Azad Hind Government (1942-1945), which statement accurately reflects their political status and command structure?
questions.a: The INA maintained an independent command structure and the Azad Hind Government was recognised by multiple Axis powers
opts: The INA operated as a purely Japanese puppet force with no independent command
The Azad Hind Government was recognised only by Japan as a legitimate provisional government
The INA maintained an independent command structure and the Azad Hind Government was recognised by multiple Axis powers
Subhas Chandra Bose served as a ceremonial head while Japanese generals controlled military operations
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that the INA "maintained an independent command structure and a provisional government recognised by multiple Axis powers." This distinguishes it from being a mere Japanese puppet force. The Azad Hind Government, proclaimed in October 1943, received recognition from Japan, Germany, Italy, and other Axis-aligned states. Option C correctly captures this dual aspect of independent command and multi-power recognition.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Great Depression (1929-1939) halved the export value of Indian cotton, wheat, and jute while land revenue demands remained fixed in rupees. This economic distress directly influenced nationalist strategy in which of the following ways?
questions.a: It radicalised the Congress left wing, leading to the formation of the All-India Kisan Sabha in 1936 and a platform combining civil liberties with agrarian relief in the 1937 elections
opts: It led to the immediate launch of the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930
It caused the Congress to abandon constitutional agitation entirely in favour of armed revolution
It radicalised the Congress left wing, leading to the formation of the All-India Kisan Sabha in 1936 and a platform combining civil liberties with agrarian relief in the 1937 elections
It prompted the British to permanently reduce land revenue demands across all provinces through the Government of India Act 1935
questions.solution: The lesson states the Depression "radicalised the Congress left wing; at the 1936 Faizpur session the All-India Kisan Sabha was formed under Sahajanand Saraswati, demanding debt relief, tenancy reform and a moratorium on revenue collection." The 1937 provincial elections were fought on a platform combining civil liberties with agrarian relief, bringing Congress ministries to power in seven provinces where they enacted tenancy legislation. Option C accurately traces this causal chain from economic distress to organisational and electoral strategy shifts.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Montagu Declaration of August 1917 promised "progressive realisation of responsible government" in India. What was a key strategic driver for this British announcement besides Indian nationalist pressure?
questions.a: British imperial strategic needs during the First World War
opts: The need to secure Indian merchant capital for post-war reconstruction
British imperial strategic needs during the First World War
Pressure from the American President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points
The 1916 Lucknow Pact between Congress and Muslim League
questions.solution: The Montagu Declaration was driven not only by Indian pressure (including the 1916 Lucknow Pact) but also by British imperial strategic needs during the First World War. India had contributed over a million soldiers and a war loan of £100 million in 1917 alone. The British sought to sustain Indian war effort and loyalty by holding out the prospect of gradual constitutional advance. Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918) came later.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Regarding the Communist Party of India's (CPI) stance during the Quit India Movement (1942), which statement is accurate?
questions.a: The CPI opposed the movement in 1942 but shifted to support by 1944 following the "People's War" line
opts: The CPI consistently supported the movement from its inception in August 1942
The CPI opposed the movement in 1942 but shifted to support by 1944 following the "People's War" line
The CPI led the movement after the arrest of Congress leaders in 1942
The CPI boycotted the movement due to its alliance with the Muslim League
questions.solution: The CPI initially opposed the Quit India Movement (1942) because the Soviet Union had entered the war against fascism in 1941, leading the CPI to adopt a "People's War" line supporting the Allied war effort. By 1944, the party shifted to support the nationalist upsurge. This tactical turn is a well-documented shift in CPI's wartime strategy.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Why did the All-India Federation envisaged under the Government of India Act 1935 never come into existence?
questions.a: Princely states did not accede to the federation in sufficient numbers
opts: The British Parliament repealed the federal provisions before implementation
The Indian National Congress refused to participate in the federal legislature
Princely states did not accede to the federation in sufficient numbers
The Federal Court declared the federation scheme unconstitutional
questions.solution: The Government of India Act 1935 provided for an All-India Federation comprising British Indian provinces and princely states. However, the federation required accession by rulers of states representing at least half the total population of the states. The princely states, wary of losing autonomy and under no compulsion to join, did not accede in sufficient numbers. Consequently, only the provincial autonomy provisions (Part III) were implemented in 1937; the federal scheme (Part II) remained inoperative.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence and nature of the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947)?
questions.a: A unilateral British decision announced after the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan
opts: A negotiated settlement between Congress and Muslim League brokered by the Cabinet Mission
A unilateral British decision announced after the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan
An agreement reached in the Interim Government before the Constituent Assembly convened
A plan formulated by the Constituent Assembly's Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights
questions.solution: The Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) was a unilateral British decision imposed after the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) to secure agreement between Congress and the Muslim League on a united India. Lord Mountbatten, appointed Viceroy in March 1947 with a mandate for swift transfer, announced partition into two dominions based on Muslim-majority contiguous areas. The Indian Independence Act 1947 gave it legal effect. It was not a negotiated Congress-League settlement.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly of India held its first meeting on 9 December 1946. Which of the following statements accurately describes its composition as per the provided text?
questions.a: Members were elected by the provincial legislatures
opts: Members were directly elected by universal adult franchise
Members were nominated by the British Crown and the Princely States
Members were elected by the provincial legislatures
Members were selected by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League jointly
questions.solution: The text explicitly states: "The Constituent Assembly, composed of representatives elected by provincial legislatures, met for the first time on 9 December 1946." This rules out direct election (A), nomination by the British Crown (B), or selection by political parties (D). The Assembly derived its legitimacy from the provincial legislatures elected under the 1935 Act, making option C the only factually correct description based on the lesson.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a salient feature of the Indian Constitution in the provided text?
questions.a: A parliamentary system at both Centre and States with a ceremonial President and real executive headed by the Prime Minister
opts: A presidential system of government at the Centre and a parliamentary system in the States
A unicameral legislature at the Centre with a fixed term of five years
A parliamentary system at both Centre and States with a ceremonial President and real executive headed by the Prime Minister
Complete separation of powers between the judiciary and the legislature with no judicial review
questions.solution: The text under "Salient Features" states: "The document establishes a parliamentary system of government at both the centre and the states, with a ceremonial President and a real executive headed by the Prime Minister." Option C matches this verbatim. Option A is incorrect because the system is parliamentary at both levels. Option B is wrong as Parliament is bicameral. Option D is false because the text mentions "an independent judiciary with the power of judicial review."
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which Supreme Court case first adopted a proportionality analysis for reviewing executive action that affects fundamental rights, moving beyond the Wednesbury unreasonableness test?
questions.a: Om Kumar v. Union of India (2000)
opts: State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2002)
Om Kumar v. Union of India (2000)
K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997)
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Supreme Court in Om Kumar v. Union of India (2000) held the Wednesbury standard insufficient for decisions affecting fundamental rights and adopted a proportionality analysis requiring suitability, necessity and balance. The three‑limbed test was later refined in Puttaswamy (2017), but the initial adoption occurred in Om Kumar (2000). The other cases either applied Wednesbury or dealt with legitimate expectation and service matters, not the first introduction of proportionality for fundamental rights review.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: What parliamentary majority is required to approve a proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352?
questions.a: Special majority of total membership and two‑thirds of members present and voting
opts: Simple majority of members present and voting
Special majority of total membership and two‑thirds of members present and voting
Two‑thirds majority of total membership only
questions.solution: According to the lesson, a National Emergency proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority, defined as a majority of the total membership of each House and a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting. This distinguishes it from the simple majority required for President’s Rule under Article 356. The other options describe lesser majorities that do not satisfy the constitutional requirement for Article 352.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: What majority does the Constitution mandate for decisions of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly corrects the misconception that GST Council decisions require unanimity, stating that the Constitution mandates a three‑fourths weighted majority for its decisions. This weighted majority reflects the federal structure, giving the Centre one‑third weight and the states two‑thirds weight. The other options represent lower thresholds or unanimity, which are not the constitutionally prescribed voting rule for the GST Council.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the removal procedure for the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) versus other Election Commissioners?
questions.a: CEC can be removed only by a special majority address of Parliament, while other Commissioners are removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC.
opts: Both CEC and other Commissioners are removed by the President on the recommendation of the Prime Minister.
CEC can be removed only by a special majority address of Parliament, while other Commissioners are removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC.
CEC and other Commissioners are removed by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
CEC is removed by the President on the recommendation of the Supreme Court, while other Commissioners are removed by the CEC.
questions.solution: The lesson highlights a common error: treating the Election Commission’s removal procedure as identical to that of the CAG. It clarifies that the CEC requires a special‑majority address by Parliament for removal (similar to a Supreme Court judge), whereas the other Election Commissioners can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC. This distinction ensures the CEC’s greater independence. The other options either conflate the procedures or introduce incorrect authorities such as the Prime Minister or Supreme Court.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: What is the extent of judicial review over parliamentary privileges as established by the Supreme Court?
questions.a: Courts can examine whether a claimed privilege exists under the Constitution but cannot review the merits of internal disciplinary decisions.
opts: Courts can review both the existence and the merits of disciplinary decisions of the House.
Courts can examine whether a claimed privilege exists under the Constitution but cannot review the merits of internal disciplinary decisions.
Courts have no jurisdiction to examine any aspect of parliamentary privileges.
Courts can review parliamentary privileges only if a fundamental right is violated, but not the existence of the privilege.
questions.solution: The lesson cites Keshav Singh v. Speaker (1965), where the Supreme Court held that the judiciary may determine whether a privilege claimed by the House exists under Article 105, but it cannot review the House’s internal disciplinary decisions. Later, in Raja Ram Pal v. Speaker (2007), the Court added that parliamentary privilege is subject to fundamental rights, yet the core principle remains: courts adjudicate the existence of a privilege, not the merits of its exercise. Option B captures this precise scope, while the others either overextend or unduly restrict judicial review.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the effect of the 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) on the Tenth Schedule?
questions.a: A merger of a legislature party with another party is recognised only if at least two‑thirds of its members agree to the merger.
opts: The one‑third split defence for a legislature party was retained, while the merger exception was removed.
A merger of a legislature party with another party is recognised only if at least two‑thirds of its members agree to the merger.
The Speaker’s decision on disqualification petitions became final and non‑reviewable by any court.
The amendment introduced a new ground of disqualification for voting against a party whip without prior permission.
questions.solution: The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the "split" exception that previously protected a group of one‑third members of a legislature party from disqualification. It retained only the "merger" exception, stipulating that a merger is recognised only when at least two‑thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge with another party. The amendment did not alter the Speaker’s adjudicatory role; the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan (1992) had already held that the Speaker’s decision is subject to judicial review for jurisdictional error, mala fide, perversity or breach of natural justice.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Regarding the special provisions for States under Articles 371 to 371J, which of the following is accurate?
questions.a: They require a special majority of Parliament and, where specified, ratification by the concerned State legislature(s).
opts: These articles can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament.
They require a special majority of Parliament and, where specified, ratification by the concerned State legislature(s).
They apply exclusively to the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir.
They are not part of the Constitution but are statutory provisions enacted by Parliament.
questions.solution: Articles 371 to 371J constitute special provisions for certain States (e.g., Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka). As part of the Constitution, any amendment to these articles follows the procedure under Article 368: a special majority of Parliament and, where the provision explicitly requires it, ratification by the legislature(s) of the affected State(s). They are not ordinary statutes and cannot be altered by a simple majority.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments devolve functions to Panchayats and Municipalities through the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules. Which statement correctly describes the operational requirement for this devolution?
questions.a: State conformity legislation is mandatory to actualise the devolution of functions, finances and functionaries to local bodies.
opts: The functions listed in the Schedules are automatically transferred to local bodies without any State legislation.
State conformity legislation is mandatory to actualise the devolution of functions, finances and functionaries to local bodies.
Only Panchayats receive devolved functions; Municipalities are governed solely by State municipal acts.
Fiscal devolution to local bodies is optional and left entirely to the discretion of the State Finance Commission.
questions.solution: The 73rd and 74th Amendments inserted Part IX and Part IXA and the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules, listing 29 and 18 functions respectively. However, the Constitution requires States to enact conformity legislation to devolve these functions, along with finances and functionaries, to Panchayats and Municipalities. The Schedules merely enumerate the subjects; they do not automatically transfer powers. State laws must provide for the composition, powers, and fiscal resources of local bodies, and the State Finance Commission recommends the distribution of finances, but the devolution itself is not optional.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: A State legislature enacts a law that incidentally encroaches upon a Union List subject. To determine whether the law is within the State’s legislative competence, the Supreme Court will primarily apply which doctrine?
questions.solution: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance is used to ascertain the true nature and character of a legislation. If the pith and substance of a State law falls within a State List entry, incidental encroachment on a Union List subject does not render the law ultra vires. This doctrine was illustrated in K. C. Gajapati v. State of Orissa (1954) and State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977). The Doctrine of Eclipse applies only to pre‑Constitution laws inconsistent with fundamental rights; Severability deals with separating invalid portions of a statute; Colourable Legislation examines whether a legislature is indirectly doing what it cannot do directly, which is a secondary test after establishing the pith and substance.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: According to the Supreme Court's test for repugnancy under Article 254, which of the following is a required condition?
questions.a: Both laws must operate on the same field and contain directly contradictory provisions
opts: The Union law must have been enacted under an exclusive Union power
The State law must have received Presidential assent under Article 254(2)
Both laws must operate on the same field and contain directly contradictory provisions
The State law must be on a subject enumerated in the Union List
questions.solution: The Court's repugnancy test (M. Karunanidhi, Hoechst Pharmaceuticals) requires three elements: (1) both laws operate on the same field; (2) their provisions are directly contradictory so that obedience to one entails disobedience to the other; and (3) the Union law was not enacted under a power that excludes State legislation altogether (the "occupied field" doctrine). Presidential assent under Article 254(2) is a saving mechanism, not a prerequisite for repugnancy. Repugnancy arises only on Concurrent List subjects, not Union List subjects. Therefore, option C correctly states a required condition.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Under Article 239AA of the Constitution, the Lieutenant Governor of the National Capital Territory of Delhi exercises discretionary powers only in matters relating to:
opts: All legislative and executive matters of the NCT
questions.solution: Article 239AA(3)(a) provides that the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi shall act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers except in so far as he is required by or under any law to act in his discretion. The Constitution (Sixty‑ninth Amendment) Act, 1991 and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 limit this discretion to three specific subjects: public order, police and land. The LG does not have general discretion over finance, education or other transferred subjects. Hence, option B is correct.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution to:
opts: Both Fifth and Sixth Schedule Areas
questions.solution: PESA was enacted under Article 243M(4)(b) to extend the Panchayati Raj provisions (Part IX) to the "Scheduled Areas" referred to in Article 244(1), i.e., the Fifth Schedule Areas. The Sixth Schedule Areas (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) have their own autonomous district and regional councils under Articles 244(2) and 275(1) and are expressly excluded from PESA's application. Therefore, PESA applies only to Fifth Schedule Areas, making option B the correct answer.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Article 345 of the Constitution empowers a State Legislature to adopt as the official language of the State:
questions.a: Any language in use in the State
opts: Only languages included in the Eighth Schedule
Any language in use in the State
Only the language spoken by the majority of the State's population
questions.solution: Article 345 states that the Legislature of a State may by law adopt any one or more of the languages in use in the State or Hindi as the official language(s) of that State. The provision does not restrict the choice to the Eighth Schedule languages; several States have adopted languages not listed in the Eighth Schedule (e.g., Khasi in Meghalaya, Mizo in Mizoram). The Eighth Schedule merely lists languages for the Union's official purposes and for certain constitutional guarantees. Hence, option B correctly reflects the constitutional position.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In the three‑step judicial analysis for a State measure challenged under Article 301, the second step requires the Court to examine whether the measure:
questions.a: Is a compensatory tax or a regulatory measure saved by Article 304(b) with Presidential assent
opts: Directly restricts the inter‑State movement of goods
Is a compensatory tax or a regulatory measure saved by Article 304(b) with Presidential assent
Falls within the exemption provided by the Goods and Services Tax regime
Has been enacted under a Union List entry
questions.solution: The Supreme Court's framework (Atiabari, Automobile Transport, Hansa Corporation, Jindal Stainless) involves: (1) determining if the measure restricts inter‑State trade; (2) if it does, checking whether it qualifies as a compensatory tax for services rendered or a regulatory measure under Article 304(b) that has received Presidential assent; and (3) assessing whether the goods are covered by the GST regime, which subsumes most indirect taxes but leaves Article 301 operative for non‑GST goods like petroleum and alcohol. The second step is precisely the compensatory tax/Article 304(b) inquiry, making option B correct.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court invoked the doctrine of constitutional morality to:
questions.a: Decriminalise consensual same‑sex relations by prioritising constitutional morality over majoritarian moral disapproval
opts: Uphold Section 377 IPC on the ground of prevailing public morality
Decriminalise consensual same‑sex relations by prioritising constitutional morality over majoritarian moral disapproval
Refer the matter to Parliament for legislative amendment
Hold that constitutional morality is subordinate to essential religious practices protected under Article 25
questions.solution: The lesson states that in Navtej Singh Johar the five‑judge Bench decriminalised consensual same‑sex relations, holding that constitutional morality requires protection of dignity and autonomy of LGBTQ+ individuals, overriding majoritarian moral disapproval. The Court emphasised that Articles 14 and 15 cannot be subordinated to societal notions of morality. Therefore, option B correctly reflects the judicial application described.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: The tenure and removal of the Attorney General of India are governed by which constitutional provision?
questions.a: Holds office during the pleasure of the President
opts: Fixed term of five years as per Article 76
Holds office during the pleasure of the President
Removable only by impeachment by Parliament
Appointed by the Chief Justice of India for a renewable term
questions.solution: Article 76 provides that the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President, with no fixed term and no impeachment process. The lesson explicitly states this and contrasts it with the CAG's fixed tenure. Therefore option B is correct.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Attorney General from the Solicitor General of India?
questions.a: The Solicitor General is appointed by statute and lacks constitutional status
opts: The Solicitor General is a constitutional authority under Article 76
The Attorney General can vote in Parliament proceedings
The Solicitor General is appointed by statute and lacks constitutional status
The Attorney General enjoys a fixed tenure like the Comptroller and Auditor General
questions.solution: The lesson notes that the Attorney General is a constitutional authority under Article 76, while the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are appointed on a contractual basis and do not enjoy constitutional status. It also clarifies that the Attorney General cannot vote in Parliament and has no fixed tenure. Hence option C is the only accurate distinction.
questions.subject: General Awareness

questions.q: Which principle best captures the 'one idea per sentence' rule for UPSC essays?
questions.a: Each sentence should advance exactly one claim
opts: Each sentence should contain multiple claims for density
Each sentence should advance exactly one claim
Long sentences with many clauses show sophistication
Sentence length does not matter if vocabulary is advanced
questions.solution: One idea per sentence ensures clarity; examiners penalise sentences that force re-reading.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The constitutional register in UPSC essays requires all EXCEPT:
questions.solution: Partisan language violates the non-partisan, administrative tone expected of future civil servants.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: 'Mitigate' and 'alleviate' are often confused. Which is correct for poverty?
questions.solution: Mitigate = reduce severity of risk/harm; Alleviate = relieve suffering/burden. Poverty is alleviated.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which sentence structure is best for a thesis statement?
questions.a: Simple or compound — clear, emphatic, one claim
opts: Simple or compound — clear, emphatic, one claim
questions.solution: Thesis statements need maximum clarity and punch; simple/compound sentences deliver this.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The '20% Cut' economy drill aims to:
questions.a: Cut filler and compress phrasing without losing arguments
opts: Reduce word count by removing arguments
Cut filler and compress phrasing without losing arguments
questions.solution: Economy = maximum meaning per word. The drill removes noise, not signal.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the SPACER framework, the 'R' dimension stands for:
questions.solution: R = Religious/Environmental/International — covers ecology, climate, global order, India's role, spirituality, science & technology. Source: UPSC evaluation rubrics emphasising multidimensional analysis.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the ideal word count for each UPSC Mains essay?
questions.solution: UPSC expects approximately 1000–1200 words per essay (about 10–12 pages). Under 900 words signals insufficient development; over 1300 risks rambling and time loss on the second essay.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which conclusion type is explicitly rewarded by UPSC evaluation guidelines?
questions.solution: UPSC Annual Report 2022 states evaluation rewards 'synthesis' — a new insight derived from the discussion, not a mechanical summary. Visionary, policy-action, or dialectical synthesis are the three archetypes.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In PEEL paragraph structure, the 'Link' element serves to:
questions.a: Connect back to thesis and transition to next paragraph
opts: Connect back to thesis and transition to next paragraph
questions.solution: Link = connect the paragraph's argument back to the essay's central thesis AND provide a semantic bridge to the next dimension. This creates macro coherence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: During the 3-hour Essay paper, how much time should be allocated to brainstorming and outlining BOTH essays combined?
questions.solution: Standard protocol: 10 minutes per essay (20 total) for brainstorming and outlining on rough sheet. This prevents mid-essay structural confusion and saves ~20 minutes of rewriting time. Selection: 12 min. Writing: ~60 min/essay. Review: 15 min combined.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the CLAIM deconstruction framework, what does 'L' stand for?
questions.solution: L = Locate Tension — find the paradox, trade-off, or 'vs' in the topic (e.g., leveller vs inequality). This is the central argument axis.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which theme has appeared in Section A (philosophical) every year from 2013-2024?
questions.solution: Philosophy/Ethics is the core Section A theme — appears every year (2013-2024) in quote-based topics. Other themes rotate in Section B.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the maximum recommended number of quotations per UPSC essay?
questions.solution: Maximum 2-3 quotations per essay. More signals padding. Each must be verified, attributed, and explained — never dropped in without analysis.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Supreme Court judgment established that 'Constitutional morality > Social morality'?
questions.solution: Navtej Johar v. Union of India (2018) — SC held constitutional morality (individual dignity, equality) prevails over social morality (majoritarian norms). Essential for governance/gender essays.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes a key feature of Mesolithic adaptations in the Indian subcontinent as evidenced by the Bhimbetka rock shelters?
questions.a: The rock art includes hunting scenes, dancing figures, and possible ritual motifs, marking the first clear expression of symbolic behaviour.
opts: The rock art exclusively depicts agricultural activities and domesticated animals, reflecting a fully Neolithic economy.
Microlithic tools were absent at Bhimbetka, which instead yielded only large Acheulean handaxes and cleavers.
The rock art includes hunting scenes, dancing figures, and possible ritual motifs, marking the first clear expression of symbolic behaviour.
Mesolithic groups at Bhimbetka practiced intensive wet-rice cultivation and lived in permanent mud-brick settlements.
questions.solution: The lesson text explicitly states: 'The appearance of rock art at Bhimbetka, depicting hunting scenes, dancing figures and possible ritual motifs, marks the first clear expression of symbolic behaviour in the subcontinent.' Option A is incorrect because the art depicts hunting, not agriculture, and the economy was a broad-spectrum hunting-gathering-fishing one. Option B is false because Bhimbetka is noted for dense concentrations of microliths, not Acheulean tools. Option D describes Neolithic features (wet-rice cultivation, mud-brick settlements) which appear later at sites like Mehrgarh, not at Mesolithic Bhimbetka.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) dates obtained from sediment covering painted surfaces at Pachmarhi indicate:
questions.a: A minimum age of 9,500 ± 800 years for the overlying deposits, providing a terminus ante quem for the art.
opts: A maximum age of 9,500 years for the paintings themselves.
A minimum age of 9,500 ± 800 years for the overlying deposits, providing a terminus ante quem for the art.
A direct date of 9,500 BP for the pigment used in the paintings.
The exact age of the Mesolithic phase at Bhimbetka.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) on sediment covering painted surfaces at Pachmarhi yields minimum ages of 9,500 ± 800 years for the overlying deposits.' Since the sediment covers the paintings, the deposit is younger than the art, giving a minimum age (terminus ante quem) for the art. Option A incorrectly states 'maximum age'. Option C is wrong because OSL dates the sediment, not the pigment directly. Option D incorrectly extrapolates Pachmarhi dates to Bhimbetka.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the water management system at Dholavira as detailed in the archaeological record?
questions.a: A series of 16 rock-cut reservoirs with a combined capacity of approximately 250,000 m³ were linked by stone-lined channels and check-dams to regulate seasonal runoff.
opts: The site relied exclusively on groundwater extraction through wedge-shaped brick-lined wells similar to those at Mohenjo-daro.
A series of 16 rock-cut reservoirs with a combined capacity of approximately 250,000 m³ were linked by stone-lined channels and check-dams to regulate seasonal runoff.
The Great Bath at Dholavira measured 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m and was waterproofed using gypsum mortar, identical to the Mohenjo-daro structure.
Irrigation canals traced via satellite imagery at Dholavira follow the paleochannel of the Indus River, confirming direct Harappan control over the Indus drainage.
questions.solution: The text explicitly states that Dholavira had 'a series of 16 rock-cut reservoirs, together capable of storing an estimated 250,000 m³ of rainwater, are linked by a network of stone-lined channels and check-dams that regulate seasonal runoff from the surrounding catchment.' Option A describes Mohenjo-daro's wells, not Dholavira's system. Option C incorrectly attributes the Great Bath (which is at Mohenjo-daro) to Dholavira. Option D misidentifies the river system; the canals follow the Ghaggar-Hakra paleochannel, not the Indus.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the development of Sanskrit prosody, which statement correctly distinguishes the Rigvedic practice from the later Chandas-shastra of Pingala?
questions.a: The Rigvedic hymns exhibit a developed metrical practice, but the systematic codification of meters and the binary combinatorial matrix (prastara) are attributed to Pingala's later Chandas-shastra.
opts: The Rigveda hymns employ the binary matrix (laghu/guru) combinatorics formally codified by Pingala in the 3rd century BCE.
The term 'chandas' in the Rigveda refers exclusively to the Gayatri meter, while Pingala expanded it to include Tristubh and Jagati.
The Rigvedic hymns exhibit a developed metrical practice, but the systematic codification of meters and the binary combinatorial matrix (prastara) are attributed to Pingala's later Chandas-shastra.
Pingala's Chandas-shastra (c. 3rd century BCE) is a direct commentary on the Rigveda Samhita, preserving the original accentuation rules lost in later recensions.
questions.solution: The text states: 'The Rigveda preserves the earliest systematic reflection on poetic meter... the Chandas-shastra attributed to Pingala (c. 3rd century BCE) later codifies these rules, but the Rigvedic hymns themselves already exhibit a co[ntinuity]...' This confirms that the Rigveda shows developed practice, while Pingala's work is the later codification including the binary matrix (prastara). Option A incorrectly attributes Pingala's binary matrix to the Rigveda itself (a listed trap). Option B misrepresents the scope of 'chandas' in the Rigveda. Option D falsely claims Pingala's work is a direct commentary on the Rigveda Samhita.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Naneghat inscription (c. 70 CE) is a primary source for understanding which aspect of Satavahana administration?
questions.a: The fiscal policy regarding tolls (sulka) levied on specific commodities passing through the Naneghat pass.
opts: The administrative division of the empire into ahara and vishaya governed by amatya and mahamatra.
The fiscal policy regarding tolls (sulka) levied on specific commodities passing through the Naneghat pass.
The land grant procedure to Buddhist monasteries recorded in the donative portion of the inscription.
The genealogy and regnal years of the Satavahana kings from Simuka to Yajna Sri Satakarni.
questions.solution: The text states: 'Satavahana inscriptions at Naneghat (c. 70 CE) record the donation of a cave by Queen Naganika and list tolls (sulka) levied on merchandise passing the pass: 1 karshapana per cartload of textiles, 2 karshapana per load of iron, and a variable rate for spices.' It also lists as a trap: 'Overlooking the role of the Naneghat pass toll records as primary evidence for Satavahana fiscal policy.' This confirms the inscription's primary value for fiscal policy (tolls). Option A describes Mauryan administrative terms not linked to this inscription. Option C mentions the cave donation but the fiscal data is the highlighted primary evidence. Option D is not supported by the text regarding this specific inscription.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Arthashastra (2.12), the basic monetary measure for state revenue was the kārṣāpaṇa. What was its approximate weight and metal content as evidenced by punch‑marked coin hoards?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the weight standard most frequently encountered for punch‑marked coins is the kārṣāpaṇa of approximately 3.4 grams of silver, and the Arthashastra (2.12) describes this unit as the basic monetary measure for state revenue. The Mauryan rūpya (≈3.2 g silver) and Gupta dīnāra (≈8 g gold) are later, distinct standards. Copper punch‑marked pieces existed but were lighter, less standardized small change, not the primary kārṣāpaṇa standard.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī is the foundation of Classical Sanskrit. Which statement correctly characterizes its methodological nature?
questions.a: A prescriptive, generative system for the sacred language (chandas)
opts: A descriptive grammar of the spoken Sanskrit of his time
A prescriptive, generative system for the sacred language (chandas)
A lexicon of Vedic roots with accent markings
A comparative grammar of Prākrit and Sanskrit dialects
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly warns against "Equating Pāṇini’s sūtras with a descriptive grammar of spoken Sanskrit; they are a prescriptive, generative system for the sacred language." It notes the Aṣṭādhyāyī distinguishes between the spoken bhāṣā and the sacred chandas through the chandas‑sūtra (6.1.1) and employs a meta‑language to derive all valid forms from a finite set of roots and affixes.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts, which official was instructed to tour the country every five years to verify the practice of Dhamma?
questions.solution: The edicts explicitly state that the Mahāmātras were ordered to “tour the country every five years” to ensure Dhamma was being followed. The Kumāra was the provincial governor, the Pradeśika administered the district, and the Grāmika headed the village; none of them are described as undertaking this quinquennial inspection.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The earliest Gupta religious monuments, dated to the reign of Chandragupta II, are the rock‑cut caves at which site?
questions.solution: The lesson identifies the rock‑cut caves at Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh) as the earliest Gupta monuments, dated to Chandragupta II (c. 380‑415 CE). The Dashavatara temple is a later structural temple, Sanchi is primarily Mauryan/early Buddhist, and Ellora belongs to a later period.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Statistical analysis of the Indus Valley sign inventory and entropy values suggests that the script is of which type?
questions.solution: The lesson notes that the sign inventory and statistical entropy point to a logo‑syllabic system, ruling out a purely alphabetic, purely logographic, or purely syllabic classification.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement accurately reflects the survival and regional distribution of Vedic śākhās?
questions.a: Only a handful of śākhās survive, and their regional distribution is highly uneven.
opts: All śākhās survive in equal numbers across India.
Only a handful of śākhās survive, and their regional distribution is highly uneven.
Śākhās were uniformly transmitted and written down during the Mauryan period.
Every region preserves a complete set of the four Saṃhitās.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that only a few Vedic śākhās have survived and that their regional distribution is highly uneven, making the second option the correct description.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Saka era used for dating Western Kṣatrapa coins begins in which year?
questions.solution: The lesson specifies that the Saka era (epoch 78 CE) appears consistently on Kṣatrapa coins, allowing precise absolute dating (e.g., year 150 = 228 CE). The Vikrama era starts in 58 BCE, while 320 CE and 3102 BCE are unrelated epochs.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement about the regional variation in Ashokan edicts is correct?
questions.a: The Kandahar bilingual inscription translates "Dhamma" as "Eusebeia" and "Dikaiosyne".
opts: Kharosthi versions include additional passages on animal welfare not found in Brahmi texts.
The Kandahar bilingual inscription translates "Dhamma" as "Eusebeia" and "Dikaiosyne".
Southern edicts at Sannati are written entirely in early Kannada using Brahmi script.
Pillar Edicts use exclusively Magadhi Prakrit without any Sanskritisms.
questions.solution: The Kandahar bilingual inscription is explicitly mentioned in the lesson as translating "Dhamma" into Greek "Eusebeia" (piety) and "Dikaiosyne" (justice), showing diplomatic adaptation for Hellenistic audiences. Option A is incorrect because Kharosthi versions omit animal welfare passages, not add them. Option C is wrong because southern edicts retain Magadhi text with only a postscript in early Kannada, not entirely in Kannada. Option D is false because Pillar Edicts show higher Sanskritisms, not pure Magadhi. Thus B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Arthashastra, who was responsible for the maintenance of road segments passing through villages?
opts: Royal engineers appointed by the central government
Merchant guilds using the trade routes
questions.solution: The Arthashastra stipulates that the village headman (gramika) is accountable for the upkeep of the road segment passing through his jurisdiction, with fines levied for potholes or obstructions. Option A is not mentioned; maintenance was decentralized. Option B is incorrect; merchant guilds are not assigned this duty. Option D is wrong; the courier corps used the roads but did not maintain them. Therefore C is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which scholar first explicitly defined zero as a number and prescribed rules for arithmetic operations involving it?
questions.solution: Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta explicitly defined zero (shunya) as a number and gave rules for its arithmetic operations. Aryabhata used a place-value alphabetic numeral system without a zero symbol. Varahamihira's Panchasiddhantika summarized five astronomical treatises but did not introduce zero. The concept of zero as a number appears first in Brahmagupta, not Aryabhata. Hence B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What evidence directly corroborates Roman trade at the port of Muziris mentioned in Sangam literature?
questions.a: Excavation of Mediterranean amphorae at Pattanam (identified as Muziris)
opts: Discovery of punch-marked coins with Roman legends
Excavation of Mediterranean amphorae at Pattanam (identified as Muziris)
References to Roman embassies in the Pattuppattu
Inscriptions detailing trade treaties with Roman emperors
questions.solution: Sangam texts mention Yavana (Roman) ships at Muziris exchanging gold for pepper, and archaeology at Pattanam (identified as Muziris), Arikamedu, and Korkai has uncovered Mediterranean amphorae, corroborating this trade. Option A is unsupported; no Roman-legend punch-marked coins are mentioned. Option C is incorrect; the Pattuppattu contains poems but not references to Roman embassies. Option D is not mentioned; no inscriptions detailing trade treaties with Roman emperors are cited. Thus C is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which feature of Satavahana urbanization is directly attested by an inscription at Nashik?
questions.a: Donation of a water tank by Queen Naganika
opts: Construction of a grid-planned city layout
Donation of a water tank by Queen Naganika
Issuance of uniform gold coinage across the empire
Establishment of a centralized bureaucratic administration
questions.solution: The Nashik Cave 3 inscription records Queen Naganika's donation of a tank, directly evidencing royal involvement in hydraulic infrastructure. Option A is false: Satavahana cities grew organically around citadels and markets, unlike the Indus grid plan. Option B is contradicted by the documented debasement of lead coinage from high-lead to low-lead alloys. Option D is incorrect because the Amaravati stupa complex included monastic quarters, pilgrim rest-houses, and artisan workshops, forming a service economy, not a centralized bureaucracy. Therefore C is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Baudhayana Sulba Sutra approximates the value of √2 as:
questions.solution: The Baudhayana Sulba Sutra provides an explicit fractional approximation for √2: 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3×4) − 1/(3×4×34). Evaluating this expression yields approximately 1.4142156, accurate to five decimal places. This demonstrates the advanced computational geometry embedded in Vedic altar construction.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which directive word requires presenting both merits and demerits before arriving at a conclusion?
questions.solution: Critically examine means break down the topic, assess strengths and weaknesses, and give a reasoned judgment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the MCLMPBOL framework for movement-based history questions, what does 'P' stand for?
questions.solution: P = Participants: class/caste/region/gender breakdown of who joined the movement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: For a 10-mark GS I question, the approximate word limit and time allocation are:
questions.solution: UPSC expects approximately 150 words for a 10-mark question, to be written in ~7 minutes.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following adds precision to an Indian culture answer?
questions.solution: Geographical Indication (GI) tag and named examples (e.g., Madhubani, Pashmina, Channapatna) make culture answers precise and verifiable.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In a geography answer, linking 'process → pattern' means:
questions.a: How a physical process creates an observed pattern
opts: How a physical process creates an observed pattern
questions.solution: Process → pattern means explaining the mechanism (e.g., plate collision creates fold mountains) before describing the observed distribution.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Harappan civilization employed a standardized brick ratio of 4:2:1 (length:width:height) based on an Indus unit of approximately 5.5 cm. Which construction technique was used for laying walls to ensure structural stability without high-tensile mortar?
questions.a: English bond with alternating headers and stretchers
opts: Flemish bond with alternating headers and stretchers in each course
English bond with alternating headers and stretchers
Stack bond with vertical joints aligned
Header bond using only header courses
questions.solution: The lesson text explicitly states: 'Walls were laid in English bond, alternating headers and stretchers, providing structural stability without the need for mortar of high tensile strength.' English bond alternates courses of headers and stretchers, unlike Flemish bond which alternates within each course. This standardization facilitated large-scale construction and durability of Harappan structures.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The earliest surviving rock-cut chambers in the subcontinent are located at Barabar and Nagarjuni hills near Gaya. To which religious sect were these Mauryan-period caves donated by Ashoka and Dasharatha?
questions.solution: The lesson text clearly states: 'These caves, donated by Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha to the Ajivika sect, feature highly polished interior surfaces and simple rectangular chambers with barrel-vaulted roofs.' The Barabar and Nagarjuni caves (3rd century BCE) represent the earliest rock-cut architecture in India and were patronized for the Ajivikas, a heterodox sect contemporary with Buddhism and Jainism.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which architectural style represents a synthesis of Nagara and Dravida elements in the Deccan region, characterized by a stellate plan and a tower that combines curvilinear and tiered features?
questions.a: Vesara style of Chalukya and Hoysala temples
opts: Vesara style of Chalukya and Hoysala temples
questions.solution: The lesson identifies 'Vesara Synthesis in the Deccan' as a distinct third style (section 3.3). Vesara architecture, developed under the Chalukyas and later Hoysalas in the Deccan, combines the curvilinear shikhara of the Nagara style with the tiered vimana of the Dravida style, often on a stellate (star-shaped) plan. The other options represent pure regional variants of Nagara (Khajuraho, Maru-Gurjara) or Dravida (Chola) styles.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The design of New Delhi (1912-1931) by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker embodied the Beaux-Arts vision of imperial order. Which ceremonial axis, dominated by the Rashtrapati Bhavan and India Gate, forms the central spine of this plan?
questions.solution: The lesson text states: 'a grand axial plan dominated by the Rashtrapati Bhavan, the Secretariat buildings and the India Gate, arranged along the Rajpath with generous roundabouts and extensive lawns, embodying the Beaux-Arts vision of imperial order.' Rajpath (formerly Kingsway) is the specific ceremonial boulevard forming the central east-west axis of Lutyens' Delhi, connecting the Viceroy's House (now Rashtrapati Bhavan) to the India Gate.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How do the rock‑cut caves of the eastern Deccan differ from those of the western Deccan in terms of roofing systems?
questions.a: Geological constraints in the eastern Deccan led to fundamentally different roofing systems, favouring pillared halls.
opts: Eastern caves employ the same vaulted chaitya roofs as the western ghats.
Geological constraints in the eastern Deccan led to fundamentally different roofing systems, favouring pillared halls.
Eastern caves lack any Buddhist chaitya halls altogether.
Western caves use pillared halls while eastern caves use vaulted roofs.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly warns against conflating western Deccan chaitya vaults with eastern Deccan pillared halls, stating that geological constraints produce fundamentally different roofing systems. It describes the earliest eastern caves (e.g., Guntupalli) as having a simple chaitya hall flanked by a single row of plain pillars, and later sites like Ramatheertham and Undavalli continue the pillared‑hall tradition. Thus, the eastern Deccan caves are characterised by pillared halls rather than the vaulted chaitya roofs typical of the western ghats.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What distinctive feature marks the Sharqi style of mosque architecture in Jaunpur?
opts: Presence of towering minarets at each corner.
Extensive use of marble inlay work.
Adoption of the Persian double‑dome system.
questions.solution: The lesson lists a specific trap: overlooking the absence of minarets in Jaunpur mosques, and states that the Sharqi style deliberately omits them, making this a distinctive regional marker. The other options describe features not mentioned for Jaunpur in the lesson. Hence, the correct answer is the deliberate omission of minarets.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How did colonial hill‑station architecture adapt the European "Swiss chalet" motif?
questions.a: By using local timber (sal, teak) and simplified joinery, not imported Swiss craft.
opts: By importing Swiss craftsmen and authentic Alpine timber for exact replication.
By using local timber (sal, teak) and simplified joinery, not imported Swiss craft.
By replacing timber framing with brick nogging entirely.
By adopting the motif only for decorative façades while retaining traditional Indian roof forms.
questions.solution: The lesson explains that the "Swiss chalet" motif appears in buildings like the Viceregal Lodge at Simla and the Raj Bhavan at Ootacamund, but cautions that colonial versions use local timber and simplified joinery, not imported Swiss craft. This indicates a hybrid adaptation where the aesthetic repertoire came from Europe, but material and construction realities forced structural modifications. The other options either claim exact replication or complete replacement, both contradicted by the lesson.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between the Harappan binary weight unit and later Mauryan metrological units?
questions.a: The Mauryan masha (≈0.97 g) and karshapana (≈13.7 g) preserve the 1 : 14 ratio of the Harappan grain unit to its larger counterpart.
opts: The Harappan unit of 13.7 g is identical to the Mauryan masha.
The Mauryan karshapana of 13.7 g is exactly twice the Harappan grain unit.
The Mauryan masha (≈0.97 g) and karshapana (≈13.7 g) preserve the 1 : 14 ratio of the Harappan grain unit to its larger counterpart.
The Mauryan system abandoned the binary progression and adopted only a decimal series.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Harappan grain averages 13.7 g and that the Mauryan masha is about 0.97 g while the karshapana is about 13.7 g, retaining the same 1 : 14 ratio (0.97 g × 14 ≈ 13.7 g). Hence option C correctly captures this continuity. Option A is wrong because the masha is not 13.7 g. Option B misstates the relationship as a factor of two. Option D ignores the explicit mention of the retained ratio.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the rock‑cut monastic complexes of the Western Deccan, the spatial sequence that guides a devotee from the communal area to the stupa‑focused worship space is best described as:
questions.a: Courtyard → Cells on three sides → Chaitya hall on the fourth side → Central stupa
opts: Cell → Courtyard → Chaitya hall → Pillared verandah
Courtyard → Cells on three sides → Chaitya hall on the fourth side → Central stupa
Chaitya hall → Courtyard → Cells → Stupa at the entrance
Pillared verandah → Courtyard → Cells → Chaitya hall with stupa at the apse
questions.solution: The lesson explains that each vihara has a rectangular courtyard flanked by cells on three sides and a chaitya hall on the fourth. The entrance to the chaitya aligns with the courtyard’s central axis, creating a processional route that moves the devotee from the communal courtyard into the chaitya where the stupa is placed at the apse. Therefore the correct sequence is courtyard → cells → chaitya hall → stupa, matching option B. The other options misplace elements or reverse the order.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which material source was identified by compositional analyses as the exclusive origin of Harappan chert weights?
questions.solution: The passage notes that XRF and LA‑ICP‑MS analyses reveal a restricted raw‑material source in the Rohri Hills for the chert weights. This indicates a specialized production likely overseen by the state. Hence option B is correct. The other locations are not mentioned in connection with the weights.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In Mughal garden hydraulics, the seasonal operation of the canal network is achieved by:
questions.a: Closing sluice gates during the monsoon to prevent overflow
opts: Adjusting the gradient of the main canal each season
Closing sluice gates during the monsoon to prevent overflow
Replacing water with rain‑water harvested in step‑wells
Reorienting the garden’s axial pathways to follow prevailing winds
questions.solution: The lesson specifically mentions that Mughal garden canals have sluice gates that close the system during the monsoon, a detail often missed in answers. This seasonal closure regulates water flow and prevents damage. Therefore option B is correct. Changing canal gradients, substituting water sources, or reorienting pathways are not described as mechanisms for seasonal control.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The structural system that enables the great hall of the Madras High Court to span 30 m without intermediate columns combines which of the following features?
questions.a: Riveted wrought‑iron trusses imported from Glasgow concealed behind load‑bearing basalt walls
opts: Riveted wrought‑iron trusses imported from Glasgow and a timber post‑and‑beam roof
A series of pointed arches clad in Mangalore tiles supported by stone arches
Riveted wrought‑iron trusses imported from Glasgow concealed behind load‑bearing basalt walls
A double‑shell dome with an inner brick vault and outer stone skin
questions.solution: According to the text, the great hall’s 30 m span is achieved by riveted wrought‑iron trusses imported from Glasgow, which are concealed behind load‑bearing basalt walls. This combination provides the required strength while preserving the aesthetic of basalt masonry. Option C accurately reflects this description. Option A adds a timber roof not mentioned; option B describes the roof of a different building; option D refers to the dome of the Victoria Terminus, not the High Court hall.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the metrological system evidenced at Harappan sites Chanhudaro, Lothal, and Dholavira?
questions.a: Both a binary series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 units) and a decimal series coexisted, the latter reserved for bulk commodities such as grain.
opts: A single decimal weight series was used uniformly for all commodities including carnelian beads and grain.
A binary weight series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) was used for bulk commodities while a decimal series served precision crafts.
Both a binary series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 units) and a decimal series coexisted, the latter reserved for bulk commodities such as grain.
Weight standardization was absent; each workshop produced its own weights leading to inter-site variation in bead-drill bit sizes.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "Standardized weights — binary series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 units) and a decimal series for bulk commodities — appear in all three sites." This confirms two distinct, coexisting series. Option A is incorrect because it claims a single decimal series for all commodities. Option B reverses the usage: the binary series is the one listed with specific units, while the decimal series is noted for bulk commodities. Option D contradicts the evidence of standardized weights and identical bead-drill bits across sites, which implies a shared technological repertoire.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the structural evolution of the chaitya arch, which site marks the first appearance of fully monolithic stone ribs forming a true masonry barrel vault, eliminating tensile stresses at the crown?
questions.solution: The lesson outlines a clear sequence: Bhaja and early Karla use wooden ribs on stone capitals (timber prototype). The later Karla (c. 50 CE) replicates timber joints in stone but retains mortise-and-tenon logic (stone imitation). At Ajanta (5th century CE), "the ribs are fully monolithic stone arches, the vault becomes a true masonry barrel, and the apse is crowned with a stone stupa-shaped finial." This stage eliminates tensile stresses in the vault crown, transferring thrust directly to side walls and allowing wider spans (14 m at Ajanta vs 9 m at Karla). Ellora Cave 10 (7th century CE) adopts a hybrid system using timber false-work, which is a later development, not the first fully lithic vault.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the planning of New Delhi's Central Vista, the selection of *Ficus religiosa* and *Dalbergia sissoo* for the avenue's double rows primarily reflects:
questions.a: A deliberate climatic adaptation using indigenous species to mitigate summer heat, while adopting the Garden City 'green belt' concept.
opts: A colonial ornamental preference for exotic species to symbolize imperial grandeur.
A direct replication of Ebenezer Howard's specific planting lists from Letchworth Garden City.
A deliberate climatic adaptation using indigenous species to mitigate summer heat, while adopting the Garden City 'green belt' concept.
A symbolic alignment with Mughal charbagh geometry where these two species represent the four rivers of paradise.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "The avenue's cross‑section incorporates a 30 m wide carriageway flanked by double rows of *Ficus religiosa* and *Dalbergia sissoo*, a planting scheme derived from Ebenezer Howard's 'green belt' concept but executed with indigenous species to mitigate the summer heat." This directly supports option C. Option A is contradicted by the phrase "indigenous species" and the explicit note that selection was "not a colonial ornamental preference." Option B is wrong because Howard's concept was adopted, not his specific species lists. Option D conflates the later Mughal-style gardens of the presidential estate (charbagh geometry) with the Central Vista avenue planting, which serves a climatic and Garden City function.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Archaeometric analyses of Harappan bronze artefacts from sites such as Mohenjo-Daro and Dholavira reveal a consistent tin concentration in the range of:
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that archaeometric analyses of artefacts from Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa and Dholavira reveal a consistent bronze composition of 8–12 % tin, indicating deliberate alloy control. This distinguishes Harappan bronze from later South Indian bronzes which often have higher tin content. Options A, C, and D represent incorrect ranges not supported by the textual evidence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the narrative art arrangement on the stupa railings (vedika) of the Amaravati/Nagarjunakonda phase from that of the Sanchi stupa?
questions.a: Amaravati uses continuous friezes; Sanchi uses discrete gateway panels
opts: Sanchi uses continuous friezes; Amaravati uses discrete gateway panels
Amaravati uses continuous friezes; Sanchi uses discrete gateway panels
Both use identical continuous frieze arrangements
Neither site employs narrative panels on railings
questions.solution: The text states that at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, "the railings (vedika) are adorned with narrative panels arranged in continuous friezes, a departure from the discrete gateway scenes of Sanchi." This makes option B the accurate distinction. Option A reverses the correct attribution, while C and D contradict the explicit description of both sites having narrative art, albeit arranged differently.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Royal Enclosure at Vijayanagara is best described as:
questions.a: A fortified precinct containing multiple ceremonial platforms, stables, and water tanks
opts: A single walled palace complex housing the king's residence
A fortified precinct containing multiple ceremonial platforms, stables, and water tanks
An open market street aligned with the sacred centre
A purely religious zone with temples and ritual tanks
questions.solution: The lesson directly addresses a common misconception: "Assuming Vijayanagara's royal enclosure is a single walled palace — it contains multiple ceremonial platforms, stables, and water tanks within a fortified precinct." This matches option B exactly. Option A describes the misconception itself. Options C and D confuse the Royal Enclosure with the market streets and sacred centre, which are distinct spatial zones in the Vijayanagara urban form described in the lesson.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Deccan hill forts adapted to artillery warfare by incorporating which of the following features?
questions.a: Trace italienne bastions, gun ports, and acoustic signalling
opts: Trace italienne bastions, gun ports, and acoustic signalling
Underground tunnel networks for surprise attacks
questions.solution: The text lists a key misconception: "Treating Deccan hill forts as static medieval castles — they incorporate trace italienne bastions, gun ports, and acoustic signalling designed for artillery." Option B reproduces these three specific artillery-era adaptations. Option A describes pre-artillery fortification. Option C describes earlier or simpler defences. Option D is not mentioned in the lesson as a systematic artillery adaptation in Deccan forts.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The structural system of Bombay's Victoria Terminus (1878–1888) employed a train shed spanning 30 m using:
questions.a: Riveted wrought-iron Fink trusses fabricated at the Parel foundry
opts: Riveted wrought-iron Fink trusses fabricated at the Parel foundry
Steel girders with reinforced concrete decking
Laminated timber arches sheathed in corrugated iron
questions.solution: The lesson states: "The train shed spans 30 m using riveted wrought-iron trusses of the Fink type, a technology imported from Britain but fabricated in Indian workshops at the Parel foundry." Option B matches this description precisely. Option A incorrectly cites cast-iron arches. Option C describes later stations (Delhi Junction, 1920s) that used reinforced concrete. Option D describes Madras Central's roof system, not Victoria Terminus.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The interpretation of the large rectangular basin at Lothal as a tidal dockyard is primarily contested on the basis of which palaeogeographic factor?
questions.a: The basin's elevation above estimated mid-Holocene palaeo-sea levels
opts: The discovery of Mesopotamian-style cylinder seals at Ur and Kish
The basin's elevation above estimated mid-Holocene palaeo-sea levels
The presence of a 12-metre-wide inlet channel on the northern side
The use of English bond in the baked-brick wall construction
questions.solution: The lesson states that critics of the dockyard hypothesis note the basin's elevation above estimated palaeo-sea levels as a key argument. The debate hinges on palaeogeographic reconstruction: sediment cores indicate a mid-Holocene highstand around 4000 BCE followed by regression. If the Bhogavo river was not navigable to Lothal during the Mature Harappan phase due to lower sea levels, the basin functioned as a freshwater reservoir. Options A, C, and D are cited by proponents (Rao) or are neutral structural features.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following temples represents the earliest surviving structural temple with a flat roof over a square garbhagriha and a shallow pillared porch, marking the prototype stage before the curvilinear Nagara shikhara?
questions.solution: The lesson identifies Temple 17 at Sanchi (c. 400 CE) and the Tigawa temple (c. 415 CE) as the earliest surviving structural temples retaining a flat roof over a square garbhagriha with a shallow pillared porch, constructed via corbelling. The Dasavatara Temple at Deogarh (c. 500 CE) introduces the curvilinear shikhara and panchayatana plan. Bhitargaon is the earliest brick temple with a shikhara. Kailasanatha is a later Pallava monument.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of Chola bronze casting using the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique, which statement accurately describes the casting method for large processional images (utsava murtis) compared to smaller icons?
questions.a: Large processional images are hollow-cast to reduce weight, while small icons are typically solid-cast.
opts: Both large processional images and small icons are solid-cast to ensure ritual purity.
Large processional images are hollow-cast to reduce weight, while small icons are typically solid-cast.
Large processional images are solid-cast for durability, while small icons are hollow-cast.
The lost-wax technique was exclusively used for solid casting; hollow casting was introduced later by the Vijayanagara rulers.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that large processional images (utsava murtis) are hollow-cast using the lost-wax technique to manage weight, while solid casting is reserved for small icons only. This technical distinction is a specific canon of Chola bronze technology. Options A, C, and D contradict this stated fact regarding the differentiation based on size and function.
