opts: Jammu and Kashmir had no Legislative Assembly at the time.
The State was under President's Rule under Article 356, allowing the President to dispense with the referral requirement.
Article 3 does not require State consultation for the creation of Union Territories.
The Bill was introduced as a Constitutional Amendment requiring a special majority.
questions.solution: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 bifurcated the State into two Union Territories. At that time, Jammu and Kashmir was under President's Rule imposed under Article 356. The Constitution permits the President to dispense with the mandatory referral of an Article 3 Bill to the State Legislature when the State is under Central rule. Accordingly, a Presidential order waived the consultation requirement, and the Bill was introduced after the President's recommendation, passed by simple majority, and received Presidential assent. This episode underscores that the procedural safeguard of State consultation under Article 3 can be overridden during President's Rule. The other options are incorrect: the State did have a Legislature (though dissolved), Article 3 does require consultation for UT creation unless dispensed, and the Bill was not a constitutional amendment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Supreme Court case laid down the "instrumentality test" to determine whether a body qualifies as "State" under Article 12 of the Constitution?
questions.a: R. D. Shetty v. Airport Authority of India
opts: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
R. D. Shetty v. Airport Authority of India
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
questions.solution: The lesson states that in R. D. Shetty v. Airport Authority of India (1979) the Supreme Court formulated the "instrumentality test"—examining functional, financial and administrative control—to decide if an entity falls within the definition of "State" under Article 12. Kesavananda Bharati dealt with the basic structure doctrine, Maneka Gandhi expanded Article 21, and Olga Tellis concerned the right to livelihood under Article 21. Therefore, the correct case is R. D. Shetty v. Airport Authority of India.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are classified in the constitutional scheme into which three categories?
questions.solution: According to the lesson, the Directive Principles are grouped into three ideological strands: Socialistic principles (e.g., Articles 38, 39), Gandhian principles (e.g., Articles 40, 43, 47) and Liberal‑Intellectual principles (e.g., Articles 44, 45, 50). The other options describe classifications of Fundamental Rights or generic legal categories, not the specific threefold classification of DPSP given in the text.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which constitutional amendment inserted the Fundamental Duties and which later amendment added the duty to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years?
questions.a: 42nd Amendment inserted duties; 86th Amendment added education duty
opts: 42nd Amendment inserted duties; 86th Amendment added education duty
44th Amendment inserted duties; 86th Amendment added education duty
42nd Amendment inserted duties; 91st Amendment added education duty
44th Amendment inserted duties; 91st Amendment added education duty
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly mentions that Part IVA containing Fundamental Duties was introduced by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 and later expanded by the 86th Amendment in 2002, which added the duty regarding education for children aged 6‑14. The 44th and 91st Amendments are unrelated to the insertion or expansion of Fundamental Duties. Hence, the correct combination is the 42nd and 86th Amendments.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The doctrine of harmonious construction, holding that the amending power under Article 368 cannot destroy the basic structure including the balance between Parts III and IV, was notably affirmed in which landmark case?
questions.a: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
opts: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy
questions.solution: The lesson states that in Kesavananda Bharati the Supreme Court held that the amending power under Article 368 cannot be used to destroy the basic structure, which includes the balance between Parts III and IV. Minerva Mills later applied the basic structure doctrine to strike down clauses of the 42nd Amendment, Golak Nath dealt with the amendability of Fundamental Rights, and State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy concerned land ceiling laws under Article 31C. Therefore, Kesavananda Bharati is the case that articulated the harmonious construction principle in this context.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The shift from the "procedure established by law" doctrine in A.K. Gopalan to the "due process" interpretation in Maneka Gandhi primarily expanded the scope of which Fundamental Right?
questions.solution: The lesson describes the landmark expansion from Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi as a development concerning Article 21. In Gopalan, the Court read "procedure established by law" narrowly, while Maneka Gandhi interpreted Article 21 to require a fair, just and reasonable procedure, effectively importing due process into the right to life and personal liberty. Articles 14, 19 and 22 were not the primary focus of this doctrinal shift. Hence, the correct answer is Article 21.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to the Doctrine of Eclipse under Article 13, consider the following statements: 1. A pre-constitutional law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights becomes void ab initio. 2. Such a law revives automatically if the conflicting constitutional provision is amended. 3. The doctrine applies equally to post-constitutional laws. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution: Statement 1 is incorrect: The doctrine of eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, 1955) holds that pre-constitutional laws are not dead or void ab initio; they are merely eclipsed and remain dormant. Statement 2 is correct: When the constitutional provision causing the eclipse is amended or repealed (e.g., 44th Amendment removing restriction on Article 19(1)(g) in Ambica Mills, 1974), the pre-constitutional law revives automatically. Statement 3 is incorrect: The doctrine does not apply to post-constitutional laws; a statute enacted after 26 January 1950 violating a Fundamental Right is void ab initio and cannot be revived by a later constitutional amendment — a fresh law is required.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court transformed Article 21 by interpreting 'procedure established by law' as requiring the procedure to be:
opts: Enacted by a competent legislature only
questions.solution: Prior to Maneka Gandhi, Article 21 was read as a procedural guarantee (A.K. Gopalan). In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Court held that 'procedure established by law' must be 'fair, just and reasonable', not merely enacted by a competent legislature. This imported the American substantive due process standard into Article 21, requiring the law itself to be non-arbitrary, reasonable, and proportionate (legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity, balancing). The judgment also established the inter-linkage between Articles 14, 19, and 21.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Article 31C, as originally enacted by the 25th Amendment (1971), protected laws giving effect to which Directive Principles from challenge under Articles 14 and 19?
opts: All Directive Principles in Part IV
questions.solution: The 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C to protect laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) (distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth) from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31. The 42nd Amendment (1976) expanded this protection to all Directive Principles, but this expansion was struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) as violating the basic structure (judicial review and balance between Parts III and IV). Thus, the valid scope of Article 31C remains limited to Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the 'dual test' laid down in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a law placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 is:
questions.a: Subject to judicial review if it violates the basic structure
opts: Subject to judicial review only if it violates Article 21
Subject to judicial review if it violates the basic structure
Valid only if ratified by half the State Legislatures
questions.solution: I.R. Coelho (2007) established a dual test for Ninth Schedule laws: (a) Temporal test: Laws inserted after 24 April 1973 (date of Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are subject to judicial review on the touchstone of the basic structure doctrine. (b) Substantive test: Even pre-1973 laws can be challenged if they abrogate fundamental rights that form part of the basic structure (e.g., equality, rule of law). The judgment ended absolute immunity for post-1973 insertions, preventing the Ninth Schedule from becoming a 'constitutional dustbin'.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the current legal status of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A?
questions.a: They are non-justiciable but have acquired legal traction through statutes and judicial interpretation
opts: They are justiciable and directly enforceable by courts
They are purely moral exhortations with no legal effect
They are non-justiciable but have acquired legal traction through statutes and judicial interpretation
They are enforceable only through constitutional writs under Article 32
questions.solution: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) were introduced by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and expanded by the 86th Amendment (2002). They are non-justiciable (not directly enforceable by courts). However, they have acquired legal traction: (1) Statutes like the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (Article 51A(a)), Environment Protection Act (Article 51A(g)) give them enforceable dimensions. (2) In Rangnath Mishra (2021), the Supreme Court held duties can be used as interpretive aids to expand Fundamental Rights (e.g., Article 51A(g) informs Article 21). (3) The State may enact laws to enforce duties; failure to do so may be challenged. They remain aspirational but increasingly legislatively anchored.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the "reasonable classification" test and the "manifest arbitrariness" test under Article 14 as per the Supreme Court?
questions.a: Manifest arbitrariness supplements the reasonable classification test; a law may pass classification but still fail manifest arbitrariness.
opts: Manifest arbitrariness replaces the reasonable classification test entirely.
The reasonable classification test is applied only when manifest arbitrariness fails.
Manifest arbitrariness supplements the reasonable classification test; a law may pass classification but still fail manifest arbitrariness.
Both tests are mutually exclusive and cannot be applied together.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court has held that the manifest arbitrariness doctrine does not replace the traditional Anwar Ali Sarkar classification test but supplements it. A statute may satisfy the two‑pronged classification test (intelligible differentia and rational nexus) yet be struck down if its underlying rationale is irrational, capricious or disproportionate — i.e., manifestly arbitrary. This was affirmed in the Sabarimala judgment where the majority observed that a law surviving classification can still fall foul of manifest arbitrariness. Hence, the two tests operate at different analytical levels and are applied cumulatively.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: On what primary ground did the Supreme Court declare Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 unconstitutional in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)?
questions.a: Being vague and overbroad, thereby violating freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).
opts: Violation of the right to equality under Article 14.
Violation of the right to privacy under Article 21.
Being vague and overbroad, thereby violating freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).
Exceeding the legislative competence of Parliament.
questions.solution: In Shreya Singhal, the Court struck down Section 66A IT Act because its terms — "grossly offensive", "menacing", "annoyance" — were undefined, making the provision vague and overbroad. Such indeterminacy chills legitimate expression and fails the test of reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). The judgment rested squarely on Article 19(1)(a), holding that the provision’s lack of precise standards rendered it unconstitutional on the ground of violating free speech, not on equality, privacy or legislative competence grounds.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following accurately reflects the scope of the right guaranteed under Article 21A of the Constitution?
questions.a: It guarantees free and compulsory access to education for children aged 6‑14 years, not outcomes.
opts: It guarantees quality education outcomes for every child aged 6‑14 years.
It guarantees free and compulsory access to education for children aged 6‑14 years, not outcomes.
It applies only to private unaided schools receiving no state aid.
It is enforceable only through executive orders and not subject to judicial review.
questions.solution: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment, provides that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years. The lesson clarifies that the right is to free and compulsory *access* to schooling, not a guarantee of qualitative outcomes. The RTE Act, 2009 operationalises this access‑oriented entitlement, and courts have enforced it as a justiciable right concerning admission, infrastructure and non‑discrimination, not learning outcomes.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of Public Interest Litigation and the doctrine of prospective overruling, which statement is correct?
questions.a: The Supreme Court in S.P. Gupta laid down that a PIL petitioner must act bona fide, involve substantial public interest, and show no alternative remedy.
opts: A PIL can be filed without demonstrating the absence of an alternative remedy.
Prospective overruling automatically shields all past actions from a declaration of unconstitutionality.
The Supreme Court in S.P. Gupta laid down that a PIL petitioner must act bona fide, involve substantial public interest, and show no alternative remedy.
Prospective overruling is a substantive right available to any litigant.
questions.solution: The S.P. Gupta judgment established the gatekeeping criteria for PIL: the petitioner must act bona fide, the matter must involve a substantial public interest, and the court must be satisfied that no alternative remedy exists. Prospective overruling, articulated in Golak Nath and refined in Keshavananda Bharati, is a remedial tool — not a substantive right — and applies only when the Court expressly limits the retrospective effect of its declaration, as seen in the NJAC case. It does not automatically protect all past actions, nor can a PIL bypass the alternative‑remedy requirement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the 103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019) and the Supreme Court's ruling in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022)?
questions.a: It provides 10% reservation for EWS without creamy layer and the 50% ceiling does not apply to economic criteria.
opts: It provides 10% reservation for EWS subject to the creamy layer and the 50% ceiling applies.
It provides 10% reservation for EWS without creamy layer but the 50% ceiling applies.
It provides 10% reservation for EWS without creamy layer and the 50% ceiling does not apply to economic criteria.
It provides 10% reservation for EWS only in State‑aided institutions and the creamy layer test applies.
questions.solution: The 103rd Amendment inserted Article 15(6) allowing up to 10% reservation for economically weaker sections (EWS) not covered by existing quotas. The amendment explicitly exempts the EWS quota from the creamy layer requirement. In Janhit Abhiyan (2022) the Supreme Court upheld the amendment and held that the 50% ceiling laid down in Indra Sawhney applies only to caste‑based reservations, not to economic criteria. Therefore, the EWS quota is neither subject to creamy layer nor to the 50% cap.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Article 16(4B) of the Constitution, inserted by the 81st Amendment (2000), permits the State to:
questions.a: Carry forward unfilled reserved vacancies to subsequent years without breaching the 50% ceiling.
opts: Provide reservation in promotions for SCs and STs with consequential seniority.
Carry forward unfilled reserved vacancies to subsequent years without breaching the 50% ceiling.
Extend reservation to economically weaker sections in public employment.
Remove the creamy layer exclusion for OBCs in promotions.
questions.solution: Article 16(4B) was introduced by the 81st Constitutional Amendment (2000). It allows the State to treat unfilled reserved vacancies of a year as a separate class of vacancies to be filled in succeeding years, and such carry‑forward vacancies are not counted towards the 50% ceiling on reservations. This provision addresses the problem of lapsing reserved posts while maintaining the overall cap established in Indra Sawhney.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding Article 300A (Right to Property), which statement is accurate?
questions.a: It is a constitutional right but not a fundamental right; remedies lie under Article 226.
opts: It is a fundamental right enforceable directly under Article 32 of the Constitution.
It is a constitutional right but not a fundamental right; remedies lie under Article 226.
It was inserted by the 44th Amendment and restores the pre‑1978 fundamental right to property.
It grants an absolute, non‑derogable right to acquire, hold and dispose of property.
questions.solution: Article 300A, inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978), declares that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law. It is a constitutional/legal right, not a fundamental right; therefore it cannot be enforced directly under Article 32 (Supreme Court writ jurisdiction). Aggrieved persons may approach High Courts under Article 226 for judicial review of property deprivation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court apply the doctrine of proportionality to uphold a ban on gutkha under Article 19(1)(g) read with Article 19(6)?
questions.a: Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
opts: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
questions.solution: The doctrine of proportionality requires that a restriction on a fundamental freedom must pursue a legitimate aim, be suitable, necessary (least restrictive), and proportionate stricto sensu. In Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Court examined a statutory ban on gutkha and found that the measure satisfied all four steps of the proportionality test, thereby upholding the restriction on the freedom of trade under Article 19(1)(g).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What was the principal holding of the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) concerning the 42nd Amendment?
questions.a: It struck down the provisions that sought to make Directive Principles immune from judicial scrutiny.
opts: It upheld the amendment giving Directive Principles primacy over Fundamental Rights.
It struck down the provisions that sought to make Directive Principles immune from judicial scrutiny.
It declared all Directive Principles justiciable and enforceable by courts.
It expanded the protective scope of Article 31C to all socio‑economic legislation.
questions.solution: The 42nd Amendment attempted to elevate Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights by amending Article 31C and curtailing judicial review. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court struck down those portions of the 42nd Amendment that sought to make Directive Principles immune from judicial scrutiny, reaffirming that the basic structure of the Constitution includes the balance between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles). The Court held that Article 31C protects only laws genuinely implementing Articles 39(b) and (c), not any law vaguely linked to socio‑economic goals.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the evolution of the right to privacy under Article 21, which of the following statements accurately describes the contribution of the Govind v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1975) judgment?
questions.a: It accepted that privacy could be inferred from Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(d) and 21, but subjected it to 'reasonable restrictions' on grounds of public order.
opts: It unanimously declared privacy a fundamental right intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
It held that 'personal liberty' did not include a right to privacy, upholding police surveillance regulations.
It accepted that privacy could be inferred from Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(d) and 21, but subjected it to 'reasonable restrictions' on grounds of public order.
It identified three core aspects of privacy: bodily integrity, informational self-determination, and decisional autonomy.
questions.solution: The lesson states that in Govind v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1975), a three-judge bench accepted that privacy could be inferred from Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(d) and 21, but subjected it to 'reasonable restrictions' on grounds of public order. Option A describes the Puttaswamy (2017) judgment. Option B describes the majority opinion in Kharak Singh (1962). Option D describes the Puttaswamy (2017) judgment's identification of three core aspects.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding judicial interpretation of Article 19(1)(g), which of the following distinctions has the Supreme Court consistently maintained while evaluating state restrictions?
questions.a: The distinction between 'regulation' (which preserves the essence of the right) and 'prohibition' (which extinguishes it).
opts: The distinction between 'regulation' (which preserves the essence of the right) and 'prohibition' (which extinguishes it).
The distinction between 'reasonable restrictions' under Article 19(6) and 'procedure established by law' under Article 21.
The distinction between 'economic liberty' as a fundamental right and 'Directive Principles' as non-justiciable guidelines.
The distinction between 'professional autonomy' to set fees and 'statutory conditions' under the Industrial Disputes Act.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'The Court has also distinguished between "regulation" (which preserves the essence of the right) and "prohibition" (which extinguishes it).' This is a key doctrinal distinction in Article 19(1)(g) jurisprudence. Option B confuses Article 19(6) with Article 21 terminology. Option C misstates the relationship - Directive Principles can inform reasonableness of restrictions (as in Mirzapur Moti Kureshi). Option D describes a specific application (Excel Wear) but not the overarching distinction maintained by the Court.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the TMA Pai framework for Article 30(1), which of the following is a necessary condition for an institution to claim minority status and administrative autonomy?
questions.a: The institution must be established by the minority community and serve its interests.
opts: The institution must be affiliated to a state university and receive state aid.
The institution must be established by the minority community and serve its interests.
The institution must reserve 25% seats for economically weaker sections under the RTE Act.
The institution must be administered by a religious denomination registered under the Societies Registration Act.
questions.solution: The lesson lists as a common error: 'Neglecting the requirement that a minority institution must be established by the minority community and serve its interests to claim Article 30 protection.' This is a core requirement from the TMA Pai framework. Option A is incorrect - minority institutions can be unaided (TMA Pai dealt with unaided institutions). Option C refers to the 93rd Amendment/RTE Act which applies to non-minority unaided schools; Society for Unaided Private Schools (2012) upheld it but preserved minority autonomy. Option D adds a registration requirement not mentioned in the lesson.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The requirement that the "procedure established by law" under Article 21 must be "fair, just and reasonable" was introduced in which case?
questions.a: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
opts: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)
Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
questions.solution: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) a seven‑judge bench overruled the narrow A.K. Gopalan interpretation and held that the procedure depriving a person of life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable, thereby importing due‑process standards into Article 21.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: After the Minerva Mills judgment, Article 31C protects only which Directive Principles?
opts: All Directive Principles of State Policy
Only the Directive Principles inserted by the 42nd Amendment
questions.solution: The 42nd Amendment expanded Article 31C to cover all Directive Principles, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) struck down that expansion as violating the basic structure. The Court limited the protective umbrella of Article 31C to Article 39(b) and (c) only.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How have Indian courts used Fundamental Duties in judicial reasoning?
questions.a: As interpretive aids to construe statutes and Fundamental Rights and as guides for legislation
opts: As directly enforceable rights through writ petitions
As mere moral exhortations with no legal relevance
As interpretive aids to construe statutes and Fundamental Rights and as guides for legislation
As provisions that override Fundamental Rights in case of conflict
questions.solution: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are not directly enforceable by writs. However, the Supreme Court has repeatedly employed them as interpretive tools — to resolve ambiguities in statutes, to expand the scope of Fundamental Rights, and to guide legislative policy — thereby giving them practical legal significance beyond moral exhortation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The "triple test" mandated by the Supreme Court for any state intrusion into personal data or restriction of internet access consists of:
questions.solution: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) the Court recognised informational privacy as a facet of Article 21 and laid down that any state action affecting privacy must satisfy the triple test of legality (existence of law), necessity (legitimate aim), and proportionality (least restrictive means). This test has been applied in subsequent data‑protection and internet‑shutdown cases.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which case first articulated the principle of colourable legislation in Indian constitutional law?
questions.a: K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953)
opts: K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953)
State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952)
R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970)
K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
questions.solution: The doctrine of colourable legislation was first articulated by the Supreme Court in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), where the Court held that a law which in form falls within legislative competence but in substance encroaches upon a prohibited field is colourable and invalid. State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) applied the doctrine but did not originate it. R. C. Cooper (1970) and Puttaswamy (2017) are later applications. Therefore option A is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which case was the doctrine of pith and substance crystallised for resolving overlaps between Union and State legislative entries?
questions.a: State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951)
opts: State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951)
K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
S. P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)
questions.solution: The doctrine of pith and substance, used to resolve apparent overlaps between Union and State legislative entries, was crystallised in State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951). In that case, a State law prohibiting sale of liquor was upheld despite incidental encroachment on the Union's power over industries because its dominant purpose fell within the State List. The other cases deal with colourable legislation, basic structure, and PIL respectively. Hence option A is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the legal status of recommendations made by the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)?
questions.a: They are persuasive but not enforceable by writ.
opts: They are binding on the government and enforceable by writ.
They are persuasive but not enforceable by writ.
They have the force of law under Article 32.
They are automatically incorporated into judicial orders.
questions.solution: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) are statutory bodies whose recommendations are persuasive and advisory in nature. They do not have the force of law and cannot be enforced directly through a writ petition under Article 32 or 226. Courts may consider them but are not bound. Therefore, the correct description is that they are persuasive but not enforceable by writ, which corresponds to option B.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the constitutional basis of the Right to Information in India as established by the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975)?
questions.a: The Court held that the right to know is an intrinsic facet of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
opts: The Court declared Right to Information as an independent fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution.
The Court held that the right to know is an intrinsic facet of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
The Court ruled that the Official Secrets Act, 1923, was unconstitutional as it violated the citizens' right to information.
The Court mandated the immediate enactment of a comprehensive Right to Information legislation within six months.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975) held that the people's right to know about the functioning of government is essential for the effective exercise of democratic rights, and read this right to know as an intrinsic facet of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a). It further notes that any law restricting access to information must satisfy the test of reasonable restriction under Article 19(2). Option A is incorrect because the Court did not declare it an independent right under Article 21. Option C is incorrect because the Official Secrets Act was not struck down in this judgment. Option D is incorrect because the 2002 PUCL v. Union of India case, not the 1975 Raj Narain case, compelled the government to frame a comprehensive law within a stipulated time frame.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the role of the CPGRAMS portal in India's multi-tier grievance redress architecture?
questions.a: It integrates the three tiers of grievance redress by allowing citizens to file complaints, track escalation, and receive final orders.
opts: It serves as the exclusive platform for filing complaints under the Right to Information Act, 2005.
It integrates the three tiers of grievance redress by allowing citizens to file complaints, track escalation, and receive final orders.
It functions as the primary interface for the Lokpal to receive complaints against the Prime Minister and other public servants.
It replaces the departmental-level grievance officers and directly connects citizens to the Central Vigilance Commission.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "The CPGRAMS portal, launched in 2007 and revamped in 2020, integrates these tiers by allowing citizens to file a complaint, track its escalation, and receive a final order." This directly matches option B. Option A is incorrect because CPGRAMS is for grievance redress, not RTI applications (which have a separate mechanism). Option C is incorrect because while the Lokpal receives complaints, CPGRAMS is not described as its primary interface. Option D is incorrect because CPGRAMS integrates the departmental level (first-tier) rather than replacing it, and connects to multiple oversight bodies, not just the CVC.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following reforms was introduced by the "Mission Karmayogi" programme launched in 2019?
questions.a: Institutionalisation of continuous capacity building through a competency framework for civil servants.
opts: Mandatory cooling-off period of two years for civil servants moving to regulatory bodies after retirement.
Lateral entry of private sector professionals at the level of Joint Secretary in central ministries.
Institutionalisation of continuous capacity building through a competency framework for civil servants.
Redesign of the Performance Appraisal Report to include 360-degree feedback and key result areas.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "the 2019 'Mission Karmayogi' programme institutionalised continuous capacity building through a competency framework." This matches option C. Option A (cooling-off period) and Option D (PAR redesign) are mentioned as recommendations of the 2nd ARC (2008) that were accepted by the government, but they are not attributed to Mission Karmayogi specifically. Option B (lateral entry) is mentioned as a separate 2021 drive that inducted nine professionals, not as part of Mission Karmayogi. The lesson presents these as distinct reform initiatives.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under Section 8(2) of the RTI Act, 2005, the public‑interest override operates as:
questions.a: A mandatory requirement to disclose information once the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interest.
opts: A discretionary power of the Public Information Officer to decide whether to disclose exempted information.
A mandatory requirement to disclose information once the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interest.
A provision that applies only to intelligence and security organisations listed in the Second Schedule.
A rule that allows the Central Information Commission to override exemptions on its own motion.
questions.solution: The lesson states that Section 8(2) introduces a public‑interest override: "even if an exemption applies, the information must be disclosed if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interest." The Supreme Court has clarified that the override is mandatory once the balancing test favours disclosure, and the burden of proof lies with the public authority. Therefore, the override is not discretionary, nor limited to security organisations, nor exercisable solely by the CIC. Option B correctly captures this mandatory nature.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Supreme Court judgment held that evaluated answer scripts constitute "information" under the RTI Act and cannot be withheld under the fiduciary‑relationship exemption (Section 8(1)(e))?
questions.a: Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011)
opts: Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013)
Reserve Bank of India v. Jayantilal Mistry (2016)
Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011)
Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2019)
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly mentions: "In Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), the Court held that evaluated answer scripts are ‘information’ under the Act and cannot be withheld under the fiduciary‑relationship exemption (Section 8(1)(e)) because the public interest in transparency of examination processes prevails." The other cases dealt with file notings, bank inspection reports, and Information Commission appointments respectively. Hence, option C is the correct judgment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the 2019 CIC audit of 2,500 central ministries and departments, which of the following was NOT identified as a common compliance gap in proactive disclosure under Section 4(1)(b)?
questions.a: Absence of organisational structure and powers of officers
opts: Absence of organisational structure and powers of officers
questions.solution: The lesson lists the most common gaps found in the 2019 CIC audit as: "absence of updated decision‑making flowcharts, non‑publication of subsidy beneficiary lists, and lack of machine‑readable datasets." Organisational structure and powers of officers are among the seventeen mandatory categories under Section 4(1)(b), but the audit did not highlight their absence as a prevalent gap. Therefore, option D describes a gap not mentioned in the audit findings.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the redesigned Performance Appraisal Report (PAR) under Mission Karmayogi, what is the weightage assigned to Behavioural Competencies?
questions.solution: The lesson provides the exact weightage distribution for the new PAR: "Weightages are: KRAs (50 %), Behavioural Competencies (30 %), and Learning & Development (20 %)." Therefore, Behavioural Competencies carry a 30% weightage. Options A, C, and D correspond to the other two components or incorrect values. Option B is the correct answer.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following changes were introduced by the Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Act, 2015?
questions.a: Narrowed the definition of victimisation and added a broad exemption for disclosures affecting national security, public order, or friendly relations with foreign states.
opts: Expanded the definition of victimisation to include routine transfers and denial of promotion.
Narrowed the definition of victimisation and added a broad exemption for disclosures affecting national security, public order, or friendly relations with foreign states.
Removed the confidentiality requirement for the complainant's identity.
Extended statutory protection to private‑sector employees in public‑private partnerships.
questions.solution: The 2015 amendment made two key changes: it narrowed "victimisation" so that administrative actions such as transfer or denial of promotion are excluded unless proved mala fide, and it inserted a provision that disclosures affecting national security, public order, or friendly relations with foreign states shall not be entertained, creating a broad exemption. The amendment also introduced a prescribed filing period. It did not expand victimisation, remove confidentiality, or extend protection to private‑sector workers.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under State Public Service Guarantee Acts, what is the consequence if the designated authority fails to deliver the notified service within the stipulated timeline?
questions.a: The service is deemed approved automatically on expiry of the notified timeline.
opts: The applicant must submit a fresh application after the timeline expires.
The service is deemed approved automatically on expiry of the notified timeline.
The authority may extend the timeline at its discretion without any legal consequence.
The applicant can directly approach the Lokpal for redressal.
questions.solution: Public Service Guarantee Acts provide for "deemed approval" as a legal consequence: if the designated authority does not deliver the service within the notified period, the service is automatically deemed approved. This is not a discretionary benefit, nor does it require a fresh application or automatic recourse to the Lokpal; the deemed approval operates by law once the timeline lapses.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement accurately reflects the licensing status of datasets published on the Open Government Data Platform (data.gov.in)?
questions.a: Many State datasets still carry restrictive copyright notices unless they have been migrated to the OGL‑India badge.
opts: All datasets on the platform are released under the Open Government Licence (OGL) by default.
Only central government datasets carry the OGL; State datasets are excluded.
Many State datasets still carry restrictive copyright notices unless they have been migrated to the OGL‑India badge.
Datasets are released exclusively under the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) dedication.
questions.solution: The National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) mandates the Open Government Licence‑India for central datasets, but migration of State datasets is ongoing. Consequently, numerous State‑level datasets on data.gov.in retain restrictive copyright notices until they are formally migrated to the OGL‑India badge. The platform does not universally apply OGL or CC0 to all datasets.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the scope of the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) in public procurement?
questions.a: GeM is limited to common‑use goods and services; high‑value specialised procurements remain on the Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP).
opts: GeM covers all government procurements, including high‑value specialised tenders.
GeM is limited to common‑use goods and services; high‑value specialised procurements remain on the Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP).
GeM replaces CPPP entirely for contracts above ₹50 crore.
GeM is exclusively used for defence procurement.
questions.solution: GeM was designed as a dedicated portal for common‑use goods and services (e.g., office stationery, IT hardware). High‑value and specialised procurements continue to be processed through the Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP). The 2023 Unified Procurement Framework envisions routing standard items via GeM and specialised tenders via CPPP, confirming that GeM does not cover all procurements nor replace CPPP.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the Supreme Court judgment Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), which provision was held to give the RTI Act primacy over the Official Secrets Act when the information sought does not fall within the OSA's narrowly defined "secret" categories?
opts: Section 6 of the Official Secrets (Amendment) Act, 2021
questions.solution: The judgment emphasized the overriding clause of the RTI Act, namely Section 22, which states that the RTI Act shall have primacy over any other law. The Court held that where the information does not squarely fall within the OSA's definition of a secret, Section 22 makes the RTI Act prevail. Hence option C (Section 22 of the RTI Act) is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which two‑step test have Information Commissions adopted to adjudicate RTI requests that invoke the Official Secrets Act?
questions.a: First, determine whether the requested information falls within the OSA's definition of a secret; second, evaluate whether the public interest in disclosure outweighs the potential injury.
opts: First, check if the document is classified under the DPDP Act; second, assess the public interest under the Harm Test.
First, determine whether the requested information falls within the OSA's definition of a secret; second, evaluate whether the public interest in disclosure outweighs the potential injury.
First, verify the existence of a government‑issued certificate; second, apply the proportionality principle to decide on partial disclosure.
First, examine if the request pertains to defence procurement; second, consult the Central Information Commission’s directive of 2021.
questions.solution: The lesson describes that Information Commissions use a two‑step test: (i) does the requested information fall within the OSA’s statutory definition of a secret? (ii) if yes, does the public interest in disclosure – assessed through the “harm test” from Union of India v. R. K. Jain – outweigh the potential injury? This matches option B.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which ARC recommendation has been fully implemented across ministries, as indicated in the implementation tracker?
opts: Establishment of a Civil Service Board at the Centre and in each State
Statutory backing for the Central Vigilance Commission’s supervisory role
Mandatory cooling‑off period of two years for retired civil servants before private‑sector employment
questions.solution: The implementation tracker shows that the Sevottam service‑delivery assessment framework (Report 12) is among the fully implemented recommendations, with 60% of recommendations fully implemented overall. The Civil Service Board, CVC supervisory role, and cooling‑off period remain pending. Hence option C is the correct answer.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Supreme Court's judgment in Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013), the penalty provision under Section 20 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 is:
questions.a: Mandatory once a violation is established
opts: Discretionary and dependent on the Public Information Officer's intent
Mandatory once a violation is established
Applicable only if the information sought relates to corruption
Subject to prior approval by the High Court
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013) held that once the Central Information Commission finds a violation of the RTI Act, the penalty under Section 20(1) is mandatory and not discretionary. The Court rejected the argument that bona fide difficulty excuses the PIO, emphasizing that the statutory language "shall impose a penalty" leaves no room for discretion. This ruling strengthened the adjudicatory teeth of the Commission and clarified that the penalty regime is triggered automatically upon establishment of a contravention, subject only to the prescribed ceiling of ₹25,000.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Open API Policy, 2020 issued by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology explicitly extends to:
questions.a: All government digital services including those provided or consumed by state and local bodies
opts: Only central government ministries and departments
Central ministries and state government departments but excludes local bodies
All government digital services including those provided or consumed by state and local bodies
Only services developed under the National e-Governance Plan
questions.solution: The Open API Policy, 2020 mandates that every government digital service expose a documented, versioned API. The policy text explicitly states that it applies to all government digital services, including those provided or consumed by state and local bodies. This interoperability requirement is a core pillar of the India Enterprise Architecture (IndEA) framework, which seeks to ensure seamless data exchange across all levels of government. Therefore, the policy is not limited to central ministries or NeGP services alone.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the current Indian framework for algorithmic transparency in public decision-making, which requirement is mandated?
questions.a: Documentation of the system's logic and conduct of bias audits
opts: Mandatory publication of the source code of all automated decision systems
Documentation of the system's logic and conduct of bias audits
Real-time public access to algorithmic decision logs
Prior legislative approval for each automated decision system
questions.solution: The lesson notes that the current algorithmic transparency framework in India requires documentation of the logic behind automated decision-making systems and the conduct of bias audits. It does not mandate the release of source code, real-time decision logs, or prior legislative approval for each system. This approach balances accountability with operational security, focusing on explainability and auditability rather than full open-source disclosure.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the 2021 Memorandum of Understanding between the Lokpal Secretariat and the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, grievances on CPGRAMS alleging corruption against officials within the Lokpal's jurisdiction are:
questions.a: Automatically referred to the Lokpal's Investigation Wing after preliminary screening by a CPGRAMS Level-2 officer
opts: Automatically referred to the Lokpal's Investigation Wing after preliminary screening by a CPGRAMS Level-1 officer
Automatically referred to the Lokpal's Investigation Wing after preliminary screening by a CPGRAMS Level-2 officer
Referred only after the citizen files a separate complaint directly with the Lokpal
Referred only if the grievance remains unresolved for 90 days
questions.solution: The 2021 MoU between the Lokpal Secretariat and DARPG establishes an automated referral mechanism. Grievances received on CPGRAMS that allege corruption against officials falling within the Lokpal's jurisdiction are screened by a CPGRAMS Level-2 officer. After this preliminary screening, they are automatically forwarded to the Lokpal's Investigation Wing. This design avoids parallel proceedings and leverages CPGRAMS' analytics dashboard for trend analysis, while Level-1 officers do not have unilateral closure authority.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019), what was the scope of RTI applicability to the office of the Chief Justice of India?
questions.a: Only administrative functions such as appointments, transfers, and case allocation are subject to disclosure; judicial decision‑making remains protected.
opts: All judicial decisions and deliberative minutes are subject to disclosure.
Only administrative functions such as appointments, transfers, and case allocation are subject to disclosure; judicial decision‑making remains protected.
The CJI office is exempt from the RTI Act entirely.
The CJI office must disclose all records including collegium minutes without any override.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court held that the office of the CJI is a "public authority" under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act, but clarified that only its administrative functions — appointments, transfers, allocation of cases — are subject to disclosure. Judicial decision‑making per se remains protected by the doctrine of judicial independence. Therefore, option B correctly captures the limited scope, while A, C, and D overstate or misstate the ruling.

questions.q: As of 2023, how many states have mandated the Integrity Pact for all tenders exceeding the ₹10 crore threshold?
questions.solution: The passage states: "As of 2023, 18 states have mandated the Integrity Pact for all tenders exceeding the threshold, while the remaining states apply it selectively to high‑value infrastructure projects." Therefore, the correct figure is 18 states. Options A, C, and D do not match the given data.

questions.q: What did the 2023 CAG compliance audits reveal regarding the integration of the CVC's debarment database with state e‑procurement systems?
questions.a: Only 9 of the 18 states had fully automated the debarment feed; the rest relied on manual uploads causing up to 45‑day lag.
opts: All 18 states had fully automated the debarment feed.
Only 9 of the 18 states had fully automated the debarment feed; the rest relied on manual uploads causing up to 45‑day lag.
No state had integrated the debarment database.
The debarment database is not accessible to state portals.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that CAG audits in 2023 found only 9 of the 18 states had fully automated the debarment feed; the remaining states used manual uploads, creating a lag of up to 45 days during which debarred vendors could still bid. This directly supports option B. Options A, C, and D contradict the audit findings.

questions.q: Which statement correctly reflects the Supreme Court's position on the applicability of the RTI Act to statutory regulatory bodies?
questions.a: Statutory regulators are public authorities under the RTI Act unless a specific exemption under Section 8 applies.
opts: Statutory regulators are automatically exempt from RTI because they perform quasi‑judicial functions.
Statutory regulators are public authorities under the RTI Act unless a specific exemption under Section 8 applies.
Only regulatory bodies receiving more than 50% government funding are covered by the RTI Act.
The Central Information Commission has ruled that regulatory bodies are not public authorities.
questions.solution: The RTI Act defines "public authority" to include bodies established by law made by Parliament. The Supreme Court has held that statutory regulators such as SEBI, TRAI, CERC and IRDAI fall within this definition and are not automatically exempt merely because they exercise quasi‑judicial functions. Exemptions are available only under the specific clauses of Section 8(1), and the public‑interest override in Section 8(2) can compel disclosure. The CIC’s two‑step test first checks statutory coverage and then applies the exemption/harm test. Therefore, option B accurately captures the Court’s stance.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the key distinction between Outcome Budget targets and Citizen Charter commitments?
questions.a: Outcome Budget targets are fiscal‑physical milestones, while Citizen Charter commitments are service‑delivery timelines enforceable through Sevottam.
opts: Outcome Budget targets are service‑delivery timelines enforceable through Sevottam, while Citizen Charter commitments are fiscal‑physical milestones.
Outcome Budget targets are fiscal‑physical milestones, while Citizen Charter commitments are service‑delivery timelines enforceable through Sevottam.
Both are identical and used interchangeably in government budgeting.
Outcome Budget targets are set by the Central Information Commission, while Citizen Charter commitments are set by the Finance Ministry.
questions.solution: The Outcome Budget, introduced in 2005‑06, maps financial outlays to measurable outputs (e.g., kilometres of road built) and outcomes (e.g., reduced travel time) — these are fiscal‑physical milestones. Citizen Charters, mandated under the Sevottam framework, translate those outcomes into concrete service‑delivery standards such as timelines, quality benchmarks and grievance‑redress commitments, which are enforceable through Sevottam. The lesson explicitly warns against confusing the two, stating the former are fiscal‑physical milestones and the latter are service‑delivery timelines enforceable through Sevottam. Hence option B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court order in the Electoral Bonds case regarding disclosure of political donations?
questions.a: Retrospective publication of encashed bonds and left prospective legislation to Parliament.
opts: Real‑time disclosure of all political donations.
Retrospective publication of encashed bonds and left prospective legislation to Parliament.
Immediate ban on electoral bonds and mandatory disclosure of donor identities.
No disclosure required; the scheme was upheld as constitutional.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that the Supreme Court’s judgment on electoral bonds ordered the retrospective publication of details of encashed bonds (i.e., bonds already redeemed) and left the task of framing prospective legislation to Parliament. It did not mandate real‑time disclosure of all donations, nor did it ban the scheme outright or uphold it without disclosure. This distinction directly addresses the common misconception that the Court required real‑time transparency. Hence option B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank of civil servants?
questions.solution: Article 311 provides safeguards to civil servants — dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank only after an inquiry, with limited exceptions (criminal conviction, security of State, impracticability). (Source: Constitution, Art. 311)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is an All India Service?
questions.solution: IAS is an All India Service under Article 312. IFS, IRS, and IAAS are Central Services (Group A). (Source: Constitution, Art. 312; AIS Act, 1951)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the RTI Act, 2005, information concerning life or liberty must be provided within how many hours?
questions.solution: Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires information concerning life and liberty to be provided within 48 hours. Normal timeline is 30 days. (Source: RTI Act, 2005, Sec. 7(1))
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Sevottam model is associated with which of the following?
questions.solution: Sevottam is a service delivery excellence model developed by DARPG, built around citizen-centricity, information dissemination, and grievance redress — closely linked to Citizen's Charter implementation. (Source: DARPG, Sevottam Framework)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a method used by pressure groups?
questions.solution: Pressure groups seek to influence policy without contesting elections. Contesting elections is the role of political parties. Methods include lobbying, PIL, strikes, demonstrations, memoranda. (Source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; 2nd ARC 13th Report)

questions.q: Mission Karmayogi (NPCSCB) shifts civil service capacity building from:
questions.a: Rule-based to role-based; training to continuous learning
opts: Rule-based to role-based; training to continuous learning
Role-based to rule-based; learning to training
questions.solution: Mission Karmayogi (launched Sept 2020) introduces FRACs (Framework for Roles, Activities, Competencies), iGOT platform for lifelong learning, and competency-linked career progression — a shift from rule-based, one-time training to role-based, continuous learning. (Source: Cabinet Approval, 2 Sept 2020; NPCSCB Guidelines)

questions.q: The Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) directed:
questions.a: Fixed tenure (min. 2 years), Civil Services Boards for transfers, protection from oral directives
opts: Fixed tenure (min. 2 years), Civil Services Boards for transfers, protection from oral directives
Mandatory lateral entry at all levels
questions.solution: The 2013 judgment directed: (i) minimum 2-year tenure for civil servants, (ii) Civil Services Boards in each State/Centre for transfer/posting decisions, (iii) written records for oral directives to protect neutrality. (Source: Writ Petition (Civil) No. 82 of 2011, decided 31 Oct 2013)

questions.q: Which 2nd ARC report deals with 'Refurbishing of Personnel Administration'?

questions.q: Which agreement signed in 2008 marked a major turning point in India-US civil nuclear cooperation?

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between the Panchsheel principles and India's contemporary foreign policy approach?
questions.a: Panchsheel remains foundational, particularly for neighbourhood engagements, while strategic autonomy allows independent decision-making across diverse partnerships.
opts: Panchsheel has been formally replaced by the doctrine of strategic autonomy in all bilateral engagements.
Panchsheel remains foundational, particularly for neighbourhood engagements, while strategic autonomy allows independent decision-making across diverse partnerships.
Strategic autonomy requires India to abandon Panchsheel's non-interference principle when engaging with major powers.
Panchsheel applies only to India's relations with China, while strategic autonomy governs relations with all other states.
questions.solution: The lesson states that Panchsheel (1954) 'remains foundational, emphasizing mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference... These principles have informed India's diplomatic engagements, particularly with its neighbours.' Simultaneously, 'Strategic autonomy is another crucial pillar, allowing India to pursue its national interests without being constrained by alliances or external pressures,' evidenced by maintaining ties with both Russia and the US. Option B correctly captures this coexistence: Panchsheel as a continuing foundational framework (especially for neighbours) and strategic autonomy as a modern operational principle for diverse partnerships. Option A is incorrect because Panchsheel is not replaced. Option C is wrong as strategic autonomy does not require abandoning non-interference. Option D incorrectly limits Panchsheel to China only.

questions.q: In the context of India's 'Neighbourhood First' policy, why has BIMSTEC been emphasized as a platform for regional cooperation?
questions.a: Challenges faced by SAARC have led India to prioritize BIMSTEC for multi-sectoral technical and economic cooperation in the Bay of Bengal region.
opts: SAARC has been formally dissolved, making BIMSTEC the only available regional forum.
BIMSTEC includes all South Asian nations plus Southeast Asian members, replacing SAARC's mandate entirely.
Challenges faced by SAARC have led India to prioritize BIMSTEC for multi-sectoral technical and economic cooperation in the Bay of Bengal region.
BIMSTEC was created specifically to implement the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'Under Neighbourhood First, India has emphasized initiatives like the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) as a platform for regional cooperation, especially given the challenges faced by the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).' This directly supports Option C. Option A is factually incorrect as SAARC has not been formally dissolved. Option B is incorrect because BIMSTEC does not include all South Asian nations (e.g., Pakistan, Afghanistan are not members) and does not replace SAARC's mandate entirely. Option D is incorrect because BIMSTEC is a broader regional grouping, not created solely for the Kaladan project, which is a specific connectivity initiative.

questions.q: Which confidence‑building measure between India and Pakistan has never been missed, even after the 2008 Mumbai attacks and the 2019 Pulwama‑Balakot escalation?
questions.a: Annual exchange of nuclear installation lists
opts: Annual exchange of nuclear installation lists
Pre‑notification of ballistic missile flight tests
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that "the annual exchange of nuclear installation lists has never been missed, underscoring the resilience of this CBM architecture" despite periodic suspensions of political dialogue. The DGMO hotline was revived only in 2021, the missile‑test pre‑notification agreement dates from 2005, and the NRRC hotline, while continuous, is not highlighted as never‑missed. questions.q: What does the 2023 Border Defence Cooperation Agreement (BDCA) between India and China formalise?
questions.a: Exchange of information on military exercises, aircraft movements, and infrastructure construction within 10 km of the LAC
opts: Disengagement at Pangong Tso and Gogra‑Hot Springs
Direct hotline between the two foreign ministries
Exchange of information on military exercises, aircraft movements, and infrastructure construction within 10 km of the LAC
Five‑Point Consensus on disengagement and de‑escalation

The disengagement at Pangong Tso occurred in 2021‑22, the direct foreign‑ministry hotline was established in 2022, and the Five‑Point Consensus was reached in 2021. They are parallel but distinct initiatives
They are two names for the same programme

opts: Conclusion of the Broad‑Based Trade and Investment Agreement (BTIA)
EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) adequacy assessment for India
Completion of the joint Hydrogen Valley pilot in Gujarat
Resolution of the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) impact on Indian steel exports

India withdrew all military personnel after the 2022 "India Out" campaign and has not renewed defence pacts.
India's defence cooperation with the Maldives is limited to annual joint exercises without any hardware transfers.

It is operated solely by Iran with no Indian involvement.
It forms part of a trilateral India‑Pakistan‑Afghanistan trade corridor.

questions.a: ECTA is a goods‑focused free trade agreement, whereas CEPA covers services, investment and IPR more comprehensively.
opts: ECTA covers services, investment and intellectual property rights as comprehensively as CEPA.
ECTA is a goods‑focused free trade agreement, whereas CEPA covers services, investment and IPR more comprehensively.
ECTA includes a mutual defence obligation clause absent in CEPA.
ECTA is a strategic alliance treaty, while CEPA is merely a trade agreement.

France has signed a formal alliance treaty with India that guarantees NSG entry.

Equity investments in Indian renewable projects

Replaced by a new bilateral trade framework

opts: Both are land‑only highways connecting Northeast India to Southeast Asia

questions.q: With reference to the UPI-PayNow linkage between India and Singapore launched in February 2023, which of the following statements is correct?

opts: It enables full capital account convertibility between India and Singapore, allowing unrestricted movement of investment capital.
It operates under current-account remittance limits set by the RBI and MAS, processing over ₹12,000 crore in its first year.
It is a blockchain-based settlement system that bypasses the SWIFT network entirely for all cross-border transactions.
It allows Singaporean residents to directly purchase Indian government securities without any regulatory limits.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "UPI-PayNow (Singapore) – launched February 2023, enabling real-time, low-cost remittances between Indian and Singaporean bank accounts; processed >₹12,000 crore in the first year." It also lists as a common misconception: "Treating UPI-PayNow as a full capital-account convertibility mechanism; it operates under current-account remittance limits set by RBI and MAS." Option A is incorrect as it is not full capital account convertibility. Option C is incorrect as it is not described as blockchain-based. Option D is incorrect as it does not mention government securities purchase.

questions.q: The ASEAN-India Maritime Transport Agreement signed at the 2022 Phnom Penh Summit is best characterized as:
questions.a: A framework agreement establishing principles for direct shipping services, port-call liberalisation, and joint development of maritime logistics hubs, requiring subsequent protocol negotiations.
opts: A binding treaty that immediately enforces direct shipping services and port-call liberalisation across all ASEAN member states and India.
A framework agreement establishing principles for direct shipping services, port-call liberalisation, and joint development of maritime logistics hubs, requiring subsequent protocol negotiations.
An agreement that merges the ASEAN-India Free Trade Area with maritime transport regulations, creating a single customs territory for sea-borne cargo.
A security pact mandating joint EEZ patrols and naval exercises between the Indian Navy and all ASEAN navies.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "ASEAN-India Maritime Transport Agreement – signed at the 2022 Phnom Penh Summit, it establishes a framework for direct shipping services, port-call liberalisation, and joint development of maritime logistics hubs in Chennai, Visakhapatnam, and Da Nang." It also lists as a common misconception: "Overstating the ASEAN-India Maritime Transport Agreement as a binding treaty; it is a framework agreement requiring subsequent protocol negotiations." Option B accurately reflects this characterization. Option A is incorrect as it is not a binding treaty with immediate enforcement. Option C is incorrect as it does not merge with AIFTA or create a single customs territory. questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a pillar of the India‑Brazil Strategic Partnership elevated in 2006?

questions.q: The India‑Denmark Green Strategic Partnership focuses on which set of sectors?

questions.q: Which agreement between India and Israel marks a shift from a buyer‑seller relationship to co‑development of defence systems?

opts: 2021 $2 billion deal for 12 Heron TP drones
2023 agreement for joint production of the Medium Range Surface‑to‑Air Missile (MRSAM)
Launch of the India‑Israel Industrial R&D and Technological Innovation Fund (I4F) in 2017
Establishment of the Joint Working Group on Counter‑Terrorism in 2000

Create a free‑trade zone linking the Andaman Sea and Strait of Malacca
Lay a submarine communication cable across the Andaman Sea

Functional working groups continue to meet

Diaspora engagement programmes have been halted

questions.q: The current crisis in the WTO Dispute Settlement Mechanism (DSM) primarily stems from:
questions.a: The United States blocking the appointment of new Appellate Body members, rendering the Appellate Body non-functional since late 2019.
opts: The inability of the Dispute Settlement Body to establish panels due to consensus requirements.
The United States blocking the appointment of new Appellate Body members, rendering the Appellate Body non-functional since late 2019.
A majority of WTO members refusing to comply with Appellate Body rulings on fisheries subsidies.
The expiration of the Doha Development Agenda mandate, which removed the legal basis for the Appellate Body.
questions.solution: The lesson text states under section 2.2: "The Dispute Settlement Mechanism and Its Current Crisis" and later in section 6.2: "institutional paralysis — exemplified by the WTO Appellate Body crisis". While the text does not explicitly name the United States, it is a well-established fact in the context of the WTO DSM crisis (and consistent with UPSC syllabus expectations) that the US blocked appointments, causing the Appellate Body to cease functioning in December 2019. Option A is incorrect because panel establishment is automatic (reverse consensus). Option C is incorrect; compliance issues exist but are not the primary cause of the Appellate Body paralysis. questions.q: Regarding the governance structure of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, which statement is correct?
questions.a: Voting power in both institutions is determined primarily by quota subscriptions, which are based on relative economic size, giving advanced economies dominant control.
opts: Both institutions operate on a one-country-one-vote principle, ensuring equal representation for all member states.
Voting power in both institutions is determined primarily by quota subscriptions, which are based on relative economic size, giving advanced economies dominant control.
The World Bank uses a weighted voting system, while the IMF uses a double-majority voting system requiring both a majority of votes and a majority of member countries.
Quota reforms agreed in 2010 have been fully implemented, resulting in a significant shift of voting power to emerging market and developing economies.
questions.solution: Section 3.2 states: "Governance, Quota, and Voting Power" for the IFIs. The IMF and World Bank both use a weighted voting system where voting power is linked to financial contributions (quotas in the IMF, shareholdings in the World Bank). Quotas are based on economic size (GDP, openness, variability, reserves). This gives advanced economies (especially the US and European countries) dominant voting shares. Option A is false; they do not use one-country-one-vote (that is the UN General Assembly). Option C is false; the IMF does not use a double-majority system for routine decisions (though some major decisions require 85% supermajority). Option D is false; the 2010 quota and governance reforms were delayed for years and only partially implemented later; the text mentions "IMF quota stalemate" in section 6.2, indicating reforms are not fully realized.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the assessed contribution scale for UN peacekeeping (2024‑2026) is correct?

China contributes 20% of the peacekeeping budget.
Japan contributes 10% of the peacekeeping budget.
Germany contributes 8% of the peacekeeping budget.

Arbitrators are selected ad hoc for each appeal.
Its awards create binding precedent for all WTO members.

questions.q: Regarding IMF Article IV surveillance and programme conditionality, which statement is accurate?
questions.a: Surveillance advice is non‑binding but often shapes later conditionality.
opts: Surveillance advice is legally binding on member states.
Conditionality under lending programmes is non‑binding.
Surveillance advice is non‑binding but often shapes later conditionality.
Article IV consultations require IMF Board approval for policy changes.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the FSB’s 2024 peer review of margin requirements for non‑centrally cleared derivatives?

questions.q: Regarding the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) mechanism of the UN Human Rights Council, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: As of the 4th UPR cycle (2022-2027), over 90% of recommendations have been either supported or noted, providing a quantitative baseline for compliance assessment.
opts: The UPR examines the human rights records of all UN member states every five years through a two-stage cycle involving only state submissions.
As of the 4th UPR cycle (2022-2027), over 90% of recommendations have been either supported or noted, providing a quantitative baseline for compliance assessment.
The 2023 HRC-UPR Trust Fund was established to fund country visits by Special Procedures mandate holders for least-developed countries.
The UPR's outcome reports contain only accepted recommendations, as noted recommendations are excluded from the final adopted report.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'As of the 4th cycle (2022-2027), over 90% of recommendations have been either supported or noted, providing a quantitative baseline for assessing compliance.' Option A is incorrect because the cycle is four and a half years, not five, and it is a three-stage cycle involving national reports, UN compilations, and stakeholder summaries. Option C is incorrect because the Trust Fund assists least-developed countries in preparing national reports, not funding Special Procedures visits. Option D is incorrect because the outcome report contains both accepted and noted recommendations.

questions.q: Concerning the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005 and their amendment process, which statement is correct?
questions.a: The 2022 amendments to the IHR introduced an opt-out clause allowing States Parties to reject amendments within a defined period, unlike the standard treaty ratification process.
opts: Amendments to the IHR enter into force for all States Parties automatically after adoption by the World Health Assembly, with no opt-out provision.
A Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) declaration by the WHO Director-General is a legally binding order enforceable under international law.
The 2022 amendments to the IHR introduced an opt-out clause allowing States Parties to reject amendments within a defined period, unlike the standard treaty ratification process.
The IHR 2005 grants the WHO secretariat the authority to impose mandatory travel restrictions and trade measures on States Parties during a PHEIC.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly mentions: 'Neglecting the opt-out clause in IHR amendments, which allows states to reject amendments within a defined period, unlike treaty ratification.' This confirms Option C. Option A is incorrect because the opt-out clause exists. questions.q: Regarding the Loss and Damage Fund established at COP27 and operationalized at COP28, which statement is correct?
questions.a: The Fund's governing instrument adopted at COP28 designates the World Bank as the interim trustee for four years, with a board comprising equal representation from developed and developing countries.
opts: The Loss and Damage Fund replaces the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and operates under the same governing board with identical eligibility criteria for all developing countries.
The Fund's governing instrument adopted at COP28 designates the World Bank as the interim trustee for four years, with a board comprising equal representation from developed and developing countries.
The Fund operates exclusively on a loan-based modality for all recipient countries, with a 'rapid response window' only for small island developing states.
Initial pledges to the Fund exceeded US$7 billion, fully meeting the estimated annual need of US$290-580 billion by 2030 as assessed by the Transitional Committee.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The Fund's governing instrument was adopted at COP28, designating the World Bank as interim trustee for four years, with a board comprising equal representation from developed and developing countries.' Option B matches this exactly. Option A is incorrect because the lesson warns: 'Equating the Loss and Damage Fund with the Green Climate Fund — they have distinct governance, funding windows, and eligibility criteria.'
