questions.q: Which of the following accurately describes the effect of UN General Assembly resolution 76/262 adopted in April 2022?
questions.a: It mandates that the General Assembly convene a formal debate within ten working days after a veto is cast.
opts: It legally overrides a Security Council veto.
It mandates that the General Assembly convene a formal debate within ten working days after a veto is cast.
It requires the five permanent members to sign a binding pledge not to use the veto in atrocity situations.
It amends Article 27 of the UN Charter to remove the veto power.
questions.solution: Resolution 76/262, moved by Liechtenstein and adopted by the General Assembly, does not override or amend the veto. Its operative paragraph obliges the President of the General Assembly to convene a formal meeting within ten working days of any veto in the Security Council so that members can debate the situation. This creates political accountability but leaves the veto itself intact under Article 27 of the Charter.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of WTO Joint Statement Initiatives (JSIs), what does the "critical mass" approach entail?
questions.a: Participants aim to cover a substantial share of world trade (typically ≥90 % of the relevant sector) before seeking multilateralisation.
opts: Negotiations require consensus of all 164 WTO members.
Outcomes automatically become multilateral obligations for the entire membership.
Participants aim to cover a substantial share of world trade (typically ≥90 % of the relevant sector) before seeking multilateralisation.
JSIs are limited to negotiations on services and exclude goods‑related issues.
questions.solution: JSIs are open‑ended plurilateral tracks that proceed on a "critical mass" basis: the participating members seek to represent a very large portion of global trade in the sector (the lesson cites ≥90 %). Only after achieving that coverage do they aim to multilateralise the outcome through a Ministerial Decision or an Annex 4 agreement; the results are not automatically binding on all WTO members.

questions.q: Which statement correctly characterises the IMF’s Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)?
questions.a: It offers affordable long‑term financing to vulnerable middle‑income and low‑income members, with conditionality linked to climate resilience.
opts: It is financed from the IMF’s quota resources and replaces the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust.
It provides concessional financing exclusively to low‑income countries with no climate‑related conditionality.
It offers affordable long‑term financing to vulnerable middle‑income and low‑income members, with conditionality linked to climate resilience.
Its resources are drawn from the General Resources Account and are subject to the same conditionality as Stand‑By Arrangements.
questions.solution: The RST is a new trust funded by voluntary contributions (not quota resources) and is distinct from the PRGT. It targets vulnerable middle‑income countries and low‑income members, providing long‑term affordable financing. Its conditionality includes climate‑resilience and pandemic‑preparedness reforms, differentiating it from traditional IMF lending facilities.

questions.q: Regarding the G20 Anti‑Corruption Working Group’s 2023 High‑Level Principles on Beneficial Ownership Transparency, which of the following is true?
questions.a: The principles are political commitments without enforcement mechanisms, and the StAR initiative serves as the main multilateral coordination platform.
opts: They create legally binding obligations for all G20 members.
Beneficial‑ownership transparency is a remedial measure, while asset recovery is preventive.
The principles are political commitments without enforcement mechanisms, and the StAR initiative serves as the main multilateral coordination platform.
The principles require each member to establish a national beneficial‑ownership registry within six months.
questions.solution: The G20 ACWG’s high‑level principles are political commitments, not legally binding treaties. Beneficial‑ownership transparency is a preventive tool, whereas asset recovery is remedial. The Stolen Asset Recovery (StAR) initiative, a joint World Bank‑UNODC programme, is identified as the primary multilateral coordination platform for asset recovery, not a national agency.

questions.q: What is a key operational constraint of the SCO Regional Anti‑Terrorist Structure (RATS)?
questions.a: Decision‑making requires consensus, which can be blocked by bilateral disputes, and its budget relies on modest voluntary contributions.
opts: Decisions are taken by a two‑thirds majority vote of member states.
Its terrorist‑list database is fully integrated with INTERPOL’s I‑24/7 system for real‑time global alerts.
Decision‑making requires consensus, which can be blocked by bilateral disputes, and its budget relies on modest voluntary contributions.
The Executive Committee is headed by a permanent Director appointed for life by the SCO Secretary‑General.
questions.solution: RATS operates on a consensus basis, meaning any member can block decisions — illustrated by India‑Pakistan tensions over listings. Its budget (US$4.2 million in 2023) depends on voluntary contributions and is far smaller than the UN Office of Counter‑Terrorism’s programme. The database is not linked to INTERPOL’s I‑24/7 system, and the Director rotates every three years, not serving for life.

questions.q: Under the UN Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System (PCRS), what is the maximum deployment readiness timeline for Level 2 pledges compared to Level 3 pledges?
questions.solution: The PCRS classifies pledges into three tiers. Level 2 comprises trained and equipped units ready for deployment within 60 days. Level 3 comprises rapid-deployment units capable of moving within 30 days. The question tests the distinction between these two operational tiers; confusing the 60-day and 30-day timelines is a noted common error. Option B correctly states Level 2 at 60 days and Level 3 at 30 days.

questions.q: Regarding the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA), which statement accurately describes the funding mechanism for Category C commitments?
questions.a: Donors must approve each capacity-building project through the TFAF governance board before funding is released.
opts: Category C commitments are automatically funded by the WTO Secretariat upon notification.
Donors must approve each capacity-building project through the TFAF governance board before funding is released.
Category C commitments receive mandatory funding from the Trade Facilitation Committee's dedicated budget.
Least-developed countries' Category C commitments are funded through assessed contributions from developed members.
questions.solution: Section II of the TFA allows developing and LDC members to self-designate Category C commitments (requiring capacity-building support). The lesson explicitly states a common confusion: "Assuming all TFA Category C commitments automatically receive funding; donors must approve each project through the TFAF governance board." Therefore, funding is not automatic; each project requires donor approval via the TFA Facility governance board. Option B reflects this procedural requirement.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the IMF's 15th General Review of Quotas concluded in 2020?
questions.a: It concluded with no change in quotas and launched a separate quota formula review.
opts: It approved a 50% quota increase and a new formula reducing advanced economies' share.
It concluded with no change in quotas and launched a separate quota formula review.
It increased quotas for emerging markets by 10% while maintaining the existing formula.
It deferred quota changes pending the 16th Review but adjusted basic votes.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Treating the IMF's 15th General Review as a quota increase; it concluded with no change and launched a separate formula review." The 15th Review (completed in 2020) did not result in a quota increase; instead, it maintained the status quo and initiated a separate process to review the quota formula. Option B accurately captures this outcome.

questions.q: Under the BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA), what is a mandatory requirement for a member to access the conditional credit window?
questions.a: The member must have an IMF-supported programme or a CRA-designed adjustment plan.
opts: The member must have an IMF-supported programme or a CRA-designed adjustment plan.
The member must obtain unanimous consent from all five BRICS central bank governors.
The member must contribute additional capital equal to 20% of the drawing amount.
The member must have exhausted its unconditional drawing limit of 30% of its contribution.
questions.solution: The lesson notes a common confusion: "Believing the BRICS CRA conditional window can be accessed without any IMF-linked programme; the Treaty explicitly requires an IMF-supported or CRA-designed adjustment plan." The conditional window (beyond the unconditional 30% limit) is accessible only when the requesting member has an IMF-supported programme or a CRA-designed adjustment plan in place. Option A states this treaty requirement correctly.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Glasgow Decision on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, when does a Corresponding Adjustment (CA) apply to Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs)?
questions.a: CA applies only to ITMOs generated from within the host country's NDC scope and must be reported in the BTR under the ETF.
opts: CA applies to all ITMOs transferred under Article 6.2 regardless of their relation to the host's NDC.
CA applies only to ITMOs generated from within the host country's NDC scope and must be reported in the BTR under the ETF.
CA applies only to ITMOs generated outside the host's NDC scope as a condition for voluntary cooperation.
CA is a voluntary accounting entry that host countries may apply at their discretion for any ITMO transfer.
questions.solution: The Glasgow Decision established that ITMOs under Article 6.2 can be generated from both within and outside the host's NDC scope. However, only those inside the NDC require a Corresponding Adjustment to avoid double counting; those outside are treated as "voluntary cooperation" and do not trigger adjustment. The CA must be reflected in the host's NDC accounting and reported in the Biennial Transparency Report (BTR) under the Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF). Option B correctly states this operational nuance.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the status and function of 'soft law' instruments, such as UN General Assembly resolutions, in the international legal system?
questions.a: They are not legally binding per se but can shape state practice and evolve into binding hard law.
opts: They are legally binding on all UN member states under Article 25 of the UN Charter.
They lack any legal effect and cannot influence the development of customary international law.
They are not legally binding per se but can shape state practice and evolve into binding hard law.
They require ratification by state parties to acquire the status of international treaties.
questions.solution: The lesson clarifies that soft law instruments, such as UN General Assembly resolutions and declarations, are not legally binding in the same manner as treaties or customary international law. However, they are not devoid of legal significance. They influence state behaviour, shape normative expectations, and frequently serve as precursors to the crystallization of hard law. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is cited as a prime example of a non-binding resolution that subsequently inspired binding treaties and attained customary law status. Therefore, option C accurately captures this nuanced role.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What mechanism does the 2023 Peacekeeping Performance and Accountability Framework introduce to link mission conduct to financial incentives?
questions.a: Conduct conditionality that may reduce reimbursement rates for contingent‑owned equipment
opts: Mandatory prosecution of peacekeepers by the UN
Conduct conditionality that may reduce reimbursement rates for contingent‑owned equipment
A binding treaty on sexual exploitation and abuse
questions.solution: The 2023 Peacekeeping Performance and Accountability Framework adds a "conduct conditionality" clause. Missions that fail to meet minimum thresholds for SEA prevention training, victim‑support services, and timely investigations can face reductions in reimbursement rates for contingent‑owned equipment. This links financial incentives to conduct performance rather than imposing automatic prosecutions, dismissals, or a new treaty.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following accurately describes the nature of the Osaka Track launched at the 2019 G20 Osaka Summit?
questions.a: It is a voluntary, non‑binding framework that relies on peer review and mutual assessment
opts: It creates a legally binding treaty on cross‑border data flows
It is a voluntary, non‑binding framework that relies on peer review and mutual assessment
It mandates uniform data localisation laws for all G20 members
It establishes a formal compliance committee with judicial enforcement powers
questions.solution: The Osaka Track is a voluntary, non‑binding framework for "Data Free Flow with Trust (DFFT)". It encourages participating economies to adopt domestic regimes that allow cross‑border data flows while safeguarding privacy, security, and intellectual property. Implementation is monitored through peer review and the G20’s mutual assessment process, not through a treaty, mandatory localisation, or a judicial compliance body.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the legal status of advisory opinions issued by the International Court of Justice?
questions.a: They are authoritative interpretations but lack compulsory force
opts: They are legally binding on all UN member states
They are authoritative interpretations but lack compulsory force
They automatically become part of customary international law
They require Security Council enforcement to take effect
questions.solution: ICJ advisory opinions are authoritative legal interpretations requested by UN organs or specialized agencies. They carry significant persuasive weight and guide state practice, but they do not create binding obligations on states and lack compulsory enforcement mechanisms. They are distinct from contentious judgments, which are binding on the parties to a case.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under Pillar One of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework, Amount A applies to multinational enterprises meeting which thresholds?
questions.a: Global turnover above €20 billion and profitability above 10%
opts: Global turnover above €10 billion and profitability above 5%
Global turnover above €20 billion and profitability above 10%
Only digital service companies regardless of size
Global turnover above €5 billion and profitability above 15%
questions.solution: Amount A of Pillar One targets the largest and most profitable MNEs. It applies to groups with global turnover exceeding €20 billion and profitability above 10 % (profit above 10 % of revenue). A portion (25 %) of residual profit is then allocated to market jurisdictions via a formulaic key. The rule does not cover all MNEs, only those meeting these specific thresholds.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following constitutional provisions correctly matches the establishment of the respective court with its corresponding Article?
questions.a: Supreme Court – Article 124; High Courts – Article 214
opts: Supreme Court – Article 214; High Courts – Article 124
Supreme Court – Article 124; High Courts – Article 214
Supreme Court – Article 131; High Courts – Article 226
Supreme Court – Article 143; High Courts – Article 227
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'Article 124 provides for the establishment of the Supreme Court, while Article 214 creates a High Court for each state.' Article 131 deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, Article 143 with its advisory jurisdiction, Article 226 with the writ jurisdiction of High Courts, and Article 227 with the power of superintendence of High Courts. Therefore, only the pairing in option B is factually correct as per the constitutional framework described in the text.

questions.q: In the evolution of the judicial appointment mechanism, what was the specific composition of the collegium mandated by the Third Judges Case (1998) for appointments to the Supreme Court?
questions.a: Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges
opts: Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most judges
Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges
Chief Justice of India, the Law Minister, and two eminent persons
Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most judges of the concerned High Court
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The Third Judges Case (1998) expanded the collegium to the Chief Justice and the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court for Supreme Court appointments, and to the Chief Justice and two senior-most judges for High Court appointments.' Option A reflects the Second Judges Case (1993) composition. Option C describes the NJAC composition proposed in the 99th Amendment (2014), which was struck down. Option D incorrectly applies the High Court collegium composition to the Supreme Court.

questions.q: The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the NJAC Act, 2014 primarily on the ground that they:
questions.a: Compromised judicial independence, violating the basic structure doctrine
opts: Violated the principle of separation of powers by giving the executive a veto over appointments
Were passed without the requisite special majority under Article 368
Compromised judicial independence, violating the basic structure doctrine
Excluded the Chief Justice of India from the appointment process entirely
questions.solution: The text states: 'The Supreme Court struck down both the Amendment and the Act in 2015, holding that they violated the basic structure doctrine by compromising judicial independence. The Court reiterated that the primacy of the judiciary in appointments is an essential feature of the Constitution.' The NJAC did not give the executive a veto (it included the Law Minister and two eminent persons alongside the CJI and two senior judges), it was passed with the requisite majority, and the CJI remained the head of the NJAC. The core constitutional objection was the violation of the basic structure doctrine regarding judicial independence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately distinguishes the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 from the writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226?
questions.a: Article 131 confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court for federal disputes; Article 226 confers writ jurisdiction on High Courts for enforcement of fundamental rights and other purposes.
opts: Article 131 allows the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights; Article 226 allows High Courts to hear disputes between the Centre and States.
Article 131 confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court for federal disputes; Article 226 confers writ jurisdiction on High Courts for enforcement of fundamental rights and other purposes.
Both Articles confer concurrent original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court and High Courts for disputes involving substantial questions of law.
Article 131 is an appellate jurisdiction; Article 226 is an advisory jurisdiction.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'Article 131 confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court' (specifically for disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between States). Regarding High Courts, the text mentions 'Article 226 (writ jurisdiction)' in the context of High Court powers. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and 'for any other purpose'. Option A reverses the jurisdictions. Option C is incorrect as Article 131 is exclusive original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, not concurrent. Option D mischaracterizes both jurisdictions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Referring to the Supreme Court's observation in Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008), which principle of judicial conduct was emphasised to counter the risks of judicial activism?
questions.a: The doctrine of judicial restraint, cautioning courts against becoming 'super-administrators'
opts: The doctrine of prospective overruling to limit the retrospective effect of judgments
The doctrine of judicial restraint, cautioning courts against becoming 'super-administrators'
The principle of stare decisis, requiring strict adherence to precedent in administrative matters
The principle of separation of powers, directing the executive to frame guidelines for judicial appointments
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly mentions: 'The Supreme Court itself has acknowledged the need for restraint; in the case of Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008), it cautioned that courts should not become “super-administrators”. The doctrine of judicial restraint advocates that courts should defer to the elected branches unless a clear constitutional violation is demonstrated.' This directly supports option B. Prospective overruling (A) is a technique for applying precedent, not a restraint principle cited in this case. Stare decisis (C) relates to precedent bindingness. Separation of powers (D) is a broader concept, but the specific judicial principle articulated in the cited case is judicial restraint.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which case first articulated the Basic Structure Doctrine, holding that certain constitutional features cannot be amended by Parliament under Article 368?
questions.a: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
opts: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981)
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
questions.solution: The Basic Structure Doctrine was first articulated by a 13‑judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). The Court held that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 does not extend to destroying the Constitution’s basic structure, listing features such as supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism and rule of law. Later cases — Minerva Mills, Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho — refined, limited or extended the doctrine, but the origin remains Kesavananda Bharati.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which judicial test provides that constitutional amendments made before 24 April 1973 are immune from challenge under the Basic Structure Doctrine?
questions.solution: In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) the Supreme Court ruled that the Basic Structure Doctrine would apply prospectively. Consequently, any constitutional amendment enacted before the Kesavananda Bharati judgment date — 24 April 1973 — cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates the basic structure. The Essential Features Test and Width Test concern the content of the doctrine, while the Prospective Application test specifically addresses the temporal limitation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under which constitutional articles do the Supreme Court and the High Courts derive their inherent power to punish contempt of themselves?
questions.solution: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a court of record and empowers it to punish for contempt of itself. Article 215 confers the same power on every High Court. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 merely codifies the procedure and categories of contempt; the fountainhead of the power remains these two constitutional provisions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the in‑house procedure for judicial accountability from the statutory impeachment process under the Judges Inquiry Act?
questions.a: The in‑house procedure is an internal administrative mechanism, while impeachment is a statutory process under the Judges Inquiry Act.
opts: The in‑house procedure is a statutory mechanism, while impeachment is constitutional.
The in‑house procedure is an internal administrative mechanism, while impeachment is a statutory process under the Judges Inquiry Act.
Both the in‑house procedure and impeachment are statutory processes enacted by Parliament.
Both the in‑house procedure and impeachment derive directly from the Constitution.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly warns against confusing the two: the in‑house procedure is an internal, non‑statutory mechanism evolved by the judiciary for dealing with judicial misconduct, whereas impeachment of a Supreme Court or High Court judge is governed by the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968, a statutory framework that involves a parliamentary inquiry and removal by the President on Parliament’s address. They differ in source (judicial self‑regulation vs. legislative statute), scope (minor misconduct vs. proved misbehaviour/incapacity) and outcome (advisory/action vs. removal).
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Judicial Service Commission (JSC) with a 23‑member composition including the Chief Justice, Ministers, MPs, legal practitioners and civil‑society representatives is a feature of which country’s judicial appointment model?
questions.solution: The South African model, established by the 1996 Constitution, creates a Judicial Service Commission of 23 members comprising the Chief Justice, Ministers, Members of Parliament, legal practitioners and civil‑society representatives. The JSC conducts public interviews and recommends candidates to the President, who must appoint them. The UK uses a Judicial Appointments Commission with judicial, legal and lay members; the US follows a presidential nomination with Senate confirmation; India currently follows the collegium system.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India (1991), the Supreme Court refused to increase the compensation awarded under the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985, while exercising its power under Article 142. Which principle did this decision reinforce?
questions.a: Article 142 cannot be used to override substantive statutory provisions or create new rights.
opts: Article 142 empowers the Court to modify statutory compensation amounts when justice so requires.
Article 142 cannot be used to override substantive statutory provisions or create new rights.
The Court may invoke Article 142 to fill legislative gaps even if a specific statute governs the matter.
Orders under Article 142 are not binding on the legislature, only on the executive.
questions.solution: The Union Carbide judgment explicitly held that Article 142 cannot be used to enhance statutory compensation, reinforcing the principle from Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) that Article 142 is a curative, supplementary jurisdiction, not a legislative one. The Court may fill procedural gaps or direct executive action to enforce its judgments, but it cannot amend a statute or ignore a clear legislative mandate. Option A contradicts the ruling. Option C misstates the law: Article 142 is invoked only when existing law provides no adequate remedy, not to override a specific governing statute. Option D is incorrect because Article 142 orders are binding on all authorities, including the legislature, though they remain subject to constitutional review.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is a mandatory procedural requirement for a curative petition to be entertained by the Supreme Court, as laid down in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)?
questions.a: The petition must be certified by a senior advocate of the Supreme Court attesting that it meets the Hurra criteria.
opts: The petition must be filed within 30 days of the dismissal of the review petition.
The petitioner must have exhausted all remedies under Article 226 before approaching the Supreme Court.
The petition must be certified by a senior advocate of the Supreme Court attesting that it meets the Hurra criteria.
The petition must demonstrate that the earlier judgment violated a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution.
questions.solution: In Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), the Constitution Bench prescribed four cumulative conditions for a curative petition: (1) genuine violation of natural justice, (2) manifest error apparent on the face of the record, (3) certification by a senior advocate of the Supreme Court that the petition meets these criteria, and (4) circulation to the same Bench that decided the review petition (or the three senior-most judges). Option C correctly identifies the senior-advocate certification as a mandatory procedural prerequisite. Option A is incorrect; no fixed limitation period is prescribed. Option B is irrelevant; curative petitions arise after review under Article 137, not after High Court remedies. Option D is wrong; the grounds are violation of natural justice or palpable error, not necessarily a fundamental rights violation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the hierarchy of standards for judicial review of administrative action in India, which statement accurately reflects the Supreme Court's position?
questions.a: Wednesbury is the baseline for non-fundamental-right cases; proportionality applies when fundamental rights are engaged; legitimate expectation adds a procedural fairness layer.
opts: Wednesbury unreasonableness is the highest standard and applies exclusively to cases involving fundamental rights.
Proportionality applies only to administrative discretion involving economic policy, while Wednesbury applies to all other cases.
Legitimate expectation creates a substantive enforceable right that binds the administration to its prior representation.
Wednesbury is the baseline for non-fundamental-right cases; proportionality applies when fundamental rights are engaged; legitimate expectation adds a procedural fairness layer.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that the three standards operate hierarchically: Wednesbury unreasonableness is the baseline for non-fundamental-right cases; proportionality applies when fundamental rights are engaged; and legitimate expectation adds a procedural fairness layer. This was clarified in Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997), which held that legitimate expectation does not create a substantive right but entitles the claimant to a hearing before the expectation is frustrated. Option A reverses the hierarchy. Option B misstates the domain of proportionality. Option C incorrectly converts legitimate expectation into a substantive vested right, contrary to Ganayutham.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of inter-state water disputes, what is the relationship between the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction under Article 131 and the tribunals constituted under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956?
questions.a: The tribunals under the 1956 Act are the primary adjudicators, while the Supreme Court retains appellate and supervisory jurisdiction, including enforcement of awards.
opts: The Supreme Court has no jurisdiction once a tribunal is constituted under the 1956 Act; its award is final and non-appealable.
The tribunals under the 1956 Act are the primary adjudicators, while the Supreme Court retains appellate and supervisory jurisdiction, including enforcement of awards.
Article 131 allows the Supreme Court to adjudicate water disputes only if both states consent to bypass the tribunal mechanism.
The Supreme Court can only issue interim directions under Article 131; final adjudication rests exclusively with the tribunal.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the most prominent water disputes arise under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which provides for tribunal adjudication, but the Supreme Court retains the power to hear appeals and to issue directions for compliance. The Cauvery judgment (2018) illustrates this: the Court modified the tribunal's final award and established a supervisory mechanism. Thus, tribunals are primary adjudicators; the Supreme Court acts in an appellate and supervisory capacity. Option A is incorrect because the Supreme Court does have jurisdiction (appeal/supervision). Option C is wrong; consent is not required for Article 131 jurisdiction, though the dispute must be justiciable. Option D is false; the Court can modify final awards, not just issue interim directions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Supreme Court in Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997) clarified the scope of the doctrine of legitimate expectation. Which of the following correctly states the Court's holding?
questions.a: Legitimate expectation does not create a substantive right but entitles the claimant to a fair hearing before the expectation is frustrated.
opts: Legitimate expectation creates a substantive right enforceable against the government, akin to a fundamental right.
Legitimate expectation arises only from a statutory provision, not from executive representations or consistent practice.
Legitimate expectation does not create a substantive right but entitles the claimant to a fair hearing before the expectation is frustrated.
The doctrine of legitimate expectation applies only to contractual obligations of the state, not to policy decisions.
questions.solution: In Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997), the Supreme Court held that legitimate expectation does not create a substantive right but entitles the claimant to a hearing before the expectation is defeated. The lesson further notes that legitimate expectations must be reasonable, arise from a representation or consistent practice, and not conflict with statutory provisions. Option A is the exact misconception the Court rejected. Option B is incorrect because legitimate expectation can arise from representations or consistent practice, not only statutes. Option D wrongly limits the doctrine to contractual obligations; it applies to administrative decisions broadly, including policy, provided the criteria are met.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding post-retirement appointments of Supreme Court judges, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: The 230th Law Commission Report recommended a mandatory two-year cooling-off period before taking up government positions.
opts: Article 124(7) imposes a complete ban on accepting any government office after retirement.
The 230th Law Commission Report recommended a mandatory two-year cooling-off period before taking up government positions.
A constitutional amendment enacted in 2009 mandates a cooling-off period for all High Court judges.
The 14th Law Commission Report endorsed such appointments to utilize judicial expertise for the nation.
questions.solution: Article 124(7) only prohibits practicing law before any authority in India, not accepting government posts. The 14th Law Commission (1958) recommended a ban, not endorsement. No constitutional amendment has been enacted for a cooling-off period. The 230th Law Commission Report (2009) specifically suggested a two-year cooling-off period, but this remains a recommendation without legislative backing.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as a measure to address judicial delays through Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)?
questions.a: Establishing Lok Adalats and promoting mediation to divert disputes from the formal court system.
opts: Making arbitration awards appealable in High Courts as a matter of right to ensure fairness.
Establishing Lok Adalats and promoting mediation to divert disputes from the formal court system.
Mandating that all commercial disputes above a specified value must undergo compulsory adjudication.
Restricting the jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas to only criminal compoundable offences.
questions.solution: The lesson highlights Lok Adalats, mediation, and arbitration as key ADR mechanisms to reduce the burden on courts by diverting disputes. Making arbitration awards easily appealable would increase judicial load, not reduce it. Compulsory adjudication adds to the formal court burden. The jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas is not discussed in the provided text as an ADR measure.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the current status of Judicial Impact Assessment (JIA) in India's legislative process?
questions.a: It remains a recommended reform that is largely absent in practice and not a formal part of the process.
opts: It is a mandatory constitutional requirement for all Bills introduced in Parliament under Article 117.
It has been fully institutionalised through the Judicial Impact Assessment Act, 2017.
It remains a recommended reform that is largely absent in practice and not a formal part of the process.
It is conducted exclusively by the Law Commission of India for every subordinate legislation.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that Judicial Impact Assessment is a recommended reform which is largely absent in practice and is not a formal, institutionalised part of India's legislative process. There is no Constitutional mandate under Article 117 (which deals with financial bills), no specific Act of 2017, and it is not an exclusive function of the Law Commission for subordinate legislation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the 'Restatement of Values of Judicial Life' (1997), which statement is correct?
questions.a: It serves as a guiding resolution adopted by the Supreme Court outlining ethical principles for judges.
opts: It is a legally enforceable statute enacted by Parliament to regulate judicial conduct.
It mandates the public disclosure of assets and liabilities of all Supreme Court and High Court judges.
It serves as a guiding resolution adopted by the Supreme Court outlining ethical principles for judges.
It establishes an independent Judicial Complaints Commission to investigate allegations of misconduct.
questions.solution: The Restatement of Values of Judicial Life was adopted by the Supreme Court as a guiding document for judicial ethics; it is not a statute enacted by Parliament. While it addresses asset declarations, the 1997 resolution only mandated declaration to the Chief Justice, not public disclosure. It does not establish any independent complaints commission.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of the doctrine of prospective overruling in Indian constitutional jurisprudence, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: The Supreme Court must expressly state that its ruling shall have prospective effect; silence implies retrospective application.
opts: It was first articulated by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).
It allows a court to validate an unconstitutional law retroactively to maintain legal stability.
The Supreme Court must expressly state that its ruling shall have prospective effect; silence implies retrospective application.
It was applied in Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) to defer the enforcement of the right to equality.
questions.solution: The lesson states that Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) reiterated prospective overruling is an exception to the general retrospective rule and can be invoked only when the Court expressly states prospective effect; silence is presumed to mean retrospective application. The doctrine emerged in Golaknath (1967), not Kesavananda. It cannot validate an unconstitutional law retroactively — it only postpones the operative effect of a declaration of invalidity. In the Sabarimala case (2018), the majority declined prospective overruling, holding the right to equality cannot be deferred.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes 'constitutional morality' from 'popular morality' as interpreted by the Supreme Court?
questions.a: Constitutional morality is anchored in the constitutional text and transformative vision, whereas popular morality shifts with social majorities.
opts: Constitutional morality is derived from prevailing social norms, while popular morality is anchored in the constitutional text.
Constitutional morality is anchored in the constitutional text and transformative vision, whereas popular morality shifts with social majorities.
Constitutional morality applies only to fundamental rights adjudication, while popular morality governs directive principles.
Constitutional morality is determined by parliamentary legislation, while popular morality is determined by judicial precedent.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "Unlike popular morality, which may shift with social majorities, constitutional morality is anchored in the text and the transformative vision of the Constitution." This distinction is central to the Court's use of constitutional morality as a guiding standard for state action and judicial review, particularly in contentious social issues where it may conflict with majoritarian views.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding judicial review of ordinances under Article 123 and Article 213, what is the correct position as per Supreme Court jurisprudence?
questions.a: The Supreme Court has held the satisfaction subject to judicial review for mala fides, irrelevance, or non-application of mind.
opts: The President's or Governor's satisfaction for promulgating an ordinance is entirely non-justiciable and immune from judicial scrutiny.
The satisfaction is justiciable only on the ground of mala fides, but not on grounds of irrelevance or non-application of mind.
The Supreme Court has held the satisfaction subject to judicial review for mala fides, irrelevance, or non-application of mind.
Ordinances cannot be challenged in court until they are replaced by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature.
questions.solution: The lesson lists as a common misconception: "Assuming the President's or Governor's satisfaction for ordinance promulgation is non-justiciable; the Supreme Court has held it subject to judicial review for mala fides or irrelevance." This confirms the satisfaction is justiciable on grounds including mala fides and irrelevance (which encompasses non-application of mind). Ordinances can be challenged immediately upon promulgation; they need not wait for legislative replacement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the Representation of the People Act and judicial oversight, which statement accurately reflects the Supreme Court's role in election disputes?
questions.a: The Supreme Court exercises appellate and supervisory jurisdiction under Articles 136 and 32 over Election Commission decisions.
opts: The Election Commission's decisions on election disputes are final and immune from any judicial scrutiny under Article 329.
The Supreme Court exercises only original jurisdiction under Article 32 in election matters, not appellate jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court exercises appellate and supervisory jurisdiction under Articles 136 and 32 over Election Commission decisions.
Election petitions can be filed only in High Courts, and the Supreme Court has no jurisdiction until a High Court decision is appealed.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states as a misconception: "Believing the Election Commission's decisions are immune from judicial scrutiny; the Supreme Court exercises appellate and supervisory jurisdiction under Articles 136 and 32." Article 136 grants special leave to appeal, and Article 32 provides writ jurisdiction. The Election Commission's decisions are not immune; the Supreme Court has both appellate (Article 136) and supervisory (Article 32) roles. Election petitions are filed in High Courts under the RPA, but Supreme Court jurisdiction is not limited to appeals from High Courts.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the principle of natural justice as applied to quasi-judicial proceedings, which of the following is a settled requirement?
questions.a: The requirement of a speaking order (reasoned decision) is a settled facet of procedural fairness in quasi-judicial proceedings.
opts: The rule against bias requires proof of actual bias; mere appearance of bias is insufficient to vitiate a decision.
A quasi-judicial tribunal's order without reasons does not violate natural justice if the decision is otherwise correct on merits.
The requirement of a speaking order (reasoned decision) is a settled facet of procedural fairness in quasi-judicial proceedings.
Post-decisional hearings are never permitted, even in urgent matters like preventive detention under Article 22.
questions.solution: The lesson states: "In quasi-judicial tribunals, the Court has insisted on reasoned orders. In Union of India v. T.R. Verma (1971), the Court held that a tribunal's order without reasons violates natural justice because it denies the aggrieved party the opportunity to challenge the decision effectively. The requirement of a speaking order is now a settled facet of procedural fairness." The rule against bias requires only appearance of bias (State of Orissa v. Dr. Binapani Dei). Post-decisional hearings are permitted in urgent matters like preventive detention, with the earliest opportunity to be heard.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding Article 254(2) of the Constitution, what is the effect of the President's assent to a State law that is repugnant to a Union law on a Concurrent List subject?
questions.a: The State law prevails in that State, but Parliament retains the power to enact further legislation overriding it.
opts: The State law becomes immune from any future Parliamentary legislation on that subject.
The State law prevails in that State, but Parliament retains the power to enact further legislation overriding it.
The State law prevails only until the Union law is amended or repealed.
The State law operates only in areas not expressly covered by the Union law.
questions.solution: Article 254(2) provides that if a State law on a Concurrent subject, repugnant to an existing Union law, receives the President's assent, it prevails in that State. However, the proviso to Article 254(2) explicitly states that Parliament retains the power to enact, at any time, any law adding to, amending, varying, or repealing the State law. Therefore, Presidential assent does not grant immunity from future Parliamentary override. This distinction is a specific 'common trap' highlighted in the lesson.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement accurately reflects the judicial approach to methods of constitutional interpretation in India?
questions.a: Purposive and progressive interpretation is prioritized for Fundamental Rights, while textualism may be preferred for procedural provisions.
opts: Textualism is the sole method used for interpreting Fundamental Rights.
Purposive and progressive interpretation is prioritized for Fundamental Rights, while textualism may be preferred for procedural provisions.
The doctrine of Basic Structure applies only to the interpretation of Directive Principles of State Policy.
Harmonious construction is used exclusively for resolving Centre-State legislative conflicts.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that courts do not treat all interpretation methods as equally weighted in every case. For Fundamental Rights, the judiciary prioritizes purposive and progressive (living tree) interpretation to expand the scope of rights in line with evolving societal needs. Conversely, for procedural or technical provisions, a more textualist or literal approach may be preferred. Harmonious construction is a general principle used to avoid conflicts between statutes or provisions, not limited to Centre-State issues. The Basic Structure doctrine limits constitutional amendment power, it is not merely an interpretive tool for Directive Principles.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to the evolution of locus standi and Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India, which statement is correct?
questions.a: Epistolary jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to treat letters or newspaper reports as writ petitions, as demonstrated in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar.
opts: The relaxation of locus standi has completely abolished the requirement of being an 'aggrieved person' in all types of litigation.
Epistolary jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to treat letters or newspaper reports as writ petitions, as demonstrated in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar.
PILs are now routinely entertained in purely private disputes and service matters without restrictions.
The judiciary has not imposed any safeguards against frivolous PILs or vexatious litigation.
questions.solution: The Hussainara Khatoon case (1979) is the landmark instance where the Supreme Court treated a newspaper report on the plight of undertrials as a writ petition, inaugurating 'epistolary jurisdiction'. The relaxation of locus standi applies specifically to PILs addressing public wrongs or collective rights; it has not abolished the 'aggrieved person' rule for private disputes or service matters, where strict locus standi still applies. The judiciary has developed self-imposed restraints, including imposing costs on vexatious petitioners and requiring bona fides and 'sufficient interest', to prevent misuse of the PIL mechanism.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the primary distinction between the 'doctrine of repugnancy' and the 'doctrine of colourable legislation'?
questions.a: Repugnancy deals with conflict between Union and State laws on Concurrent subjects, while colourable legislation questions legislative competence based on the true nature of the law.
opts: Repugnancy deals with conflict between Union and State laws on Concurrent subjects, while colourable legislation questions legislative competence based on the true nature of the law.
Repugnancy applies only to Union List subjects, while colourable legislation applies to State List subjects.
Colourable legislation resolves conflicts between two State laws, while repugnancy resolves conflicts between Union and State laws.
Both doctrines operate exclusively under Article 254 of the Constitution.
questions.solution: The doctrine of repugnancy (Article 254) addresses a direct conflict between a valid Union law and a valid State law on a subject in the Concurrent List, stipulating that the Union law prevails (unless the State law has Presidential assent). The doctrine of colourable legislation, derived from the maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly', questions whether a legislature has transgressed its constitutional competence by enacting a law that, in its true nature and substance (pith and substance), falls outside its assigned legislative field. They operate in distinct spheres: repugnancy resolves inter-governmental conflict; colourable legislation tests legislative competence.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the doctrine of harmonious construction in Centre‑State legislative conflicts?
questions.a: It is an interpretive tool used to reconcile Central and State laws on Concurrent subjects before applying the repugnancy clause of Article 254.
opts: It is an interpretive tool used to reconcile Central and State laws on Concurrent subjects before applying the repugnancy clause of Article 254.
It empowers courts to rewrite legislation so that both Union and State laws can operate simultaneously.
It automatically gives precedence to Union law over State law on all subjects in the Seventh Schedule.
It applies only when the conflict arises between laws on the Union List.
questions.solution: The doctrine of harmonious construction is a rule of interpretation, not a substantive power to rewrite statutes. As held in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) and M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979), courts first try to read the Central and State laws on a Concurrent subject together so that both can operate. Only if reconciliation is impossible does the repugnancy test under Article 254 come into play. Therefore, the doctrine serves as an interpretive safeguard for federal balance before the constitutional repugnancy clause is invoked.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) guidelines, which procedural safeguard is mandatory for the appointment of an amicus curiae?
questions.a: Reasons for appointment must be recorded, the amicus’s qualifications disclosed, and the parties notified.
opts: Reasons for appointment must be recorded, the amicus’s qualifications disclosed, and the parties notified.
The amicus may introduce new factual evidence to supplement the record.
The amicus represents the party that is inadequately represented in the proceedings.
Appointment of an amicus is compulsory in every constitutional matter before the Court.
questions.solution: In Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) the Court laid down that appointment of an amicus curiae must be judicious, transparent and not a substitute for proper party representation. The judgment mandates that the Court record reasons for the appointment, disclose the amicus’s qualifications, and notify the parties. The amicus is limited to legal assistance and cannot introduce new factual evidence, nor does the amicus represent any party. The mechanism is reserved for complex constitutional or public‑interest cases, not for routine matters.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the protection of tenure for elected representatives under the 73rd Amendment, which of the following statements is accurate?
questions.a: The Governor can dissolve a Panchayat before the expiry of its term only on grounds specified in the Constitution.
opts: A Panchayat can be dissolved by the State Government at any time on grounds of administrative inefficiency.
The Governor can dissolve a Panchayat before the expiry of its term only on grounds specified in the Constitution.
The State Election Commission has the authority to dissolve a Panchayat if elections are not held on time.
A Panchayat dissolved before its term expires must be reconstituted within three months, failing which the State Government assumes its functions.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The Governor is empowered to dissolve a panchayat before the expiry of its term only on the grounds specified in the Constitution, thereby protecting the tenure of elected representatives.' This makes option B the correct statement. Option A is incorrect because dissolution power lies with the Governor on constitutional grounds, not the State Government on administrative grounds. Option C incorrectly assigns dissolution power to the State Election Commission. Option D describes a provision (reconstitution within six months) that exists in the Constitution (Article 243E) but is not mentioned in the provided lesson text, so it cannot be verified from the given material.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The 74th Amendment mandates the constitution of Ward Committees in municipalities. What is the population threshold specified in the Constitution for this requirement?
questions.solution: The lesson clearly states in two places: 'Additionally, it provides for the constitution of Ward Committees in municipalities with a population of three lakh or more' (Section 1.3) and 'In municipalities with a population of three lakh or more, the Constitution requires the constitution of Ward Committees' (Section 5.2). This makes 'Three lakh or more' the correct threshold. The other options (one lakh, two lakh, five lakh) are not mentioned in the text.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to the State Finance Commission (SFC) mandated by the 73rd and 74th Amendments, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: The SFC recommends the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the State and local bodies, and determines the grants-in-aid to local bodies from the Consolidated Fund of the State.
opts: The SFC is constituted by the President of India every five years to review the financial position of Panchayats and Municipalities.
The SFC recommends the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the State and local bodies, and determines the grants-in-aid to local bodies from the Consolidated Fund of the State.
The SFC's recommendations are binding on the State Government and do not require legislative approval.
The SFC replaces the Central Finance Commission in matters relating to local body finances.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'It also establishes a State Finance Commission to review the financial position of panchayats every five years' (73rd Amendment) and 'the State Finance Commission reviews the financial position and recommends devolution of funds' (74th Amendment). Article 243-I and 243-Y of the Constitution (implied by the lesson's description) mandate the SFC to review the financial position and make recommendations to the Governor regarding (a) the distribution of net proceeds of taxes, duties, tolls and fees between the State and Panchayats/Municipalities, (b) determination of taxes, duties, tolls and fees that may be assigned to them, and (c) grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of the State. Option A is incorrect because the SFC is constituted by the Governor, not the President. Option C is incorrect because recommendations are advisory, not binding. Option D is incorrect because the SFC operates at the state level and does not replace the Central Finance Commission.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the constitution of a Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC)?
questions.solution: Article 243ZE provides for the constitution of a Metropolitan Planning Committee in every metropolitan area (population of 10 lakh or more). Article 243ZD, in contrast, provides for a District Planning Committee (DPC) at the district level. A common error in examinations is confusing these two articles and misstating the population threshold for metropolitan areas. The constitutional design envisages a distinct planning hierarchy for metropolitan areas separate from the district-level hierarchy.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the share of local bodies in the divisible pool of taxes as recommended by the Fifteenth Finance Commission?
questions.a: 4.31% of the divisible pool of taxes
opts: 4.31% of the divisible pool of taxes
3.5% of the divisible pool of taxes
5% of the net proceeds of shareable taxes
questions.solution: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended a grant of 4.31% of the divisible pool of taxes for local bodies (both rural and urban) for the period 2021-26. A frequent misrepresentation is to cite this as a fixed percentage of GDP. The Commission also maintained the distinction between basic grants (untied) and performance grants (conditional), which is crucial for understanding the nature of devolved funds. The share is calculated on the divisible pool, not on GDP or net proceeds alone.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the constitutional and legal status of parastatal agencies such as Development Authorities and Smart City SPVs?
questions.a: They are created by state statutes and lack direct electoral accountability.
opts: They are constitutionally mandated bodies under Article 243ZE.
They are created by state statutes and lack direct electoral accountability.
They are established by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act.
They derive their statutory authority from the District Planning Committee.
questions.solution: Parastatal agencies (e.g., Development Authorities, Water Boards, Smart City SPVs) are created by state statutes, not by the Constitution. They are accountable to the state executive rather than the local electorate, creating a parallel hierarchy that overlaps with the constitutionally mandated local planning bodies (DPCs/MPCs). The 15th Finance Commission recommended a "Local Government Coordination Act" to mandate their inclusion in DPCs/MPCs and align their plans with the consolidated local plan. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs has also directed that Smart City SPV boards include the Mayor and Municipal Commissioner for democratic accountability.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which category of municipalities is the constitution of Ward Committees mandatory under the Constitution?
questions.a: Municipalities with a population of three lakh or more.
opts: All municipalities irrespective of population size.
Municipalities with a population of one lakh or more.
Municipalities with a population of three lakh or more.
questions.solution: Article 243S of the Constitution mandates the constitution of Ward Committees only in municipalities with a population of three lakh or more. It is a common misconception that Ward Committees exist in all urban local bodies. In municipalities below this threshold, the constitutional provision does not apply. This distinction is important for understanding the structure of democratic decentralisation in smaller urban centres versus larger cities.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution mandates the establishment of a State Election Commission for the conduct of elections to Panchayats?
questions.solution: Article 243K explicitly provides for a State Election Commission in every State to supervise, direct and control the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to Panchayats. Article 243ZA extends a parallel mandate to Municipalities, while Articles 243A and 243B deal with Gram Sabha and constitution of Panchayats respectively. The constitutional source of the SEC’s authority is therefore Article 243K for Panchayats.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The E‑Panchayat initiative is a digital transformation project for Panchayati Raj Institutions. Under which framework is it implemented?
questions.a: As a Centrally Sponsored Mission Mode Project under the National e‑Governance Plan (NeGP)
opts: As a State‑level scheme funded by the State government
As a Centrally Sponsored Mission Mode Project under the National e‑Governance Plan (NeGP)
As a private‑public partnership managed by NIC
Exclusively under the Ministry of Rural Development without NeGP linkage
questions.solution: E‑Panchayat is one of the Mission Mode Projects (MMPs) under the National e‑Governance Plan (NeGP), making it a centrally sponsored initiative aimed at providing online service delivery, GIS mapping and transparency across all Panchayats. It is not merely a State‑level scheme nor a standalone private partnership.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Social audit under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) is distinct from statutory audit. Which feature best characterises social audit?
questions.a: A community‑led process with a statutory basis under MGNREGA
opts: Conducted by professional chartered accountants appointed by the State
A community‑led process with a statutory basis under MGNREGA
Optional for Gram Panchayats and conducted only on demand
Performed by the State Audit Department as part of regular financial audit
questions.solution: Social audit under MGNREGA is a statutory, community‑led mechanism where beneficiaries and Gram Sabha members verify works, expenditures and entitlements. It differs from statutory audit, which is performed by professional auditors; social audit is mandatory, not optional, and is not carried out by the State Audit Department.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the powers of the Gram Sabha under the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) from the Gram Sabha in non-Scheduled Areas?
questions.a: Under PESA, the Gram Sabha enjoys substantive legislative-type powers over minor forest produce and land acquisition, unlike the advisory role in non-Scheduled Areas.
opts: Under PESA, the Gram Sabha has only advisory powers over minor forest produce, while in non-Scheduled Areas it has ownership rights.
Under PESA, the Gram Sabha enjoys substantive legislative-type powers over minor forest produce and land acquisition, unlike the advisory role in non-Scheduled Areas.
The Gram Sabha under PESA requires State Government approval for all resolutions, whereas in non-Scheduled Areas it functions autonomously.
PESA grants the Gram Sabha judicial powers to adjudicate criminal cases, a power absent in non-Scheduled Areas.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'PESA is a statutory extension of Part IX, not a constitutional amendment; (ii) the Gram Sabha under PESA enjoys substantive legislative-type powers, unlike the advisory role in non-scheduled areas.' It further lists ownership of minor forest produce and mandatory consultation before land acquisition as key statutory mandates. Option A reverses the positions. Option C is incorrect as PESA does not mandate State approval for all resolutions. Option D is incorrect as PESA deals with local dispute resolution, not criminal adjudication.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the Model Municipal Law (MML) 2003, which of the following statements is accurate?
questions.a: It provides for a directly elected Mayor with a five-year term and executive powers, but State adaptations vary widely in mayoral powers and ward committee effectiveness.
opts: It is a binding Central statute that all States must adopt without modification under Article 243Q of the Constitution.
It provides for a directly elected Mayor with a five-year term and executive powers, but State adaptations vary widely in mayoral powers and ward committee effectiveness.
It mandates the constitution of Ward Committees only in municipalities with a population exceeding 10 lakhs.
It abolishes the post of Municipal Commissioner and transfers all executive authority to the Mayor.
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The Model Municipal Law (MML) 2003... was intended as a template for states to rewrite their municipal statutes... Its salient features include: (a) a directly elected Mayor with a five-year term and executive powers; (b) mandatory Ward Committees for every ward with a population above 3 lakhs.' It further clarifies in the 'common misconceptions' section: 'Assuming the Model Municipal Law is a binding central statute; it is only a template, and state adaptations vary widely in mayoral powers and ward committee effectiveness.' Option A incorrectly calls it binding. Option C misstates the population threshold (3 lakhs, not 10 lakhs). Option D is not mentioned in the text.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly identifies a specific recommendation of the L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) regarding Panchayati Raj Institutions?
questions.a: It suggested the establishment of Nyaya Panchayats for speedy justice at the local level.
opts: It recommended a two-tier system of Panchayati Raj with Zilla Parishad at the district level.
It recommended direct elections for all three tiers of Panchayati Raj Institutions.
It suggested the establishment of Nyaya Panchayats for speedy justice at the local level.
It described PRIs as "grass without roots" and recommended the Zilla Parishad as the principal body for development programmes.
questions.solution: The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) specifically recommended the establishment of Nyaya Panchayats for speedy justice, alongside constitutional recognition for PRIs and emphasis on the Gram Sabha. The two-tier system was recommended by the Ashok Mehta Committee (1977). The description of PRIs as "grass without roots" and the recommendation to make the Zilla Parishad the principal body for development programmes were made by the G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985). The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended direct elections only for the Gram Panchayat, with indirect elections for the higher tiers.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to the composition of District Planning Committees (DPCs) as mandated by the Constitution, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: Four-fifths of the members are elected by the elected members of the Panchayats and Municipalities in the district from amongst themselves.
opts: All members of the DPC are nominated by the State Government.
Four-fifths of the members are elected by the elected members of the Panchayats and Municipalities in the district from amongst themselves.
The Chairperson of the DPC is mandatorily the District Collector in all states.
DPCs are constituted under Article 243ZE of the Constitution.
questions.solution: Article 243ZD of the Constitution provides for the constitution of District Planning Committees (DPCs). It mandates that four-fifths of the total number of members shall be elected by, and from amongst, the elected members of the Panchayats at the district level and of the Municipalities in the district, in proportion to the ratio between the population of the rural areas and of the urban areas in the district. The Chairperson is usually the District Collector or the Chairperson of the Zilla Parishad as per state legislation, not uniformly the Collector. Metropolitan Planning Committees (MPCs) are constituted under Article 243ZE.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of fiscal autonomy of local bodies in India, which one of the following sources of funds is classified as 'untied funds' allowing discretion in expenditure?
opts: Funds released under specific State Government Schemes with strict guidelines
Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) funds
questions.solution: The lesson distinguishes between 'tied' and 'untied' funds. Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) provide 'tied' funds with strict sectoral and scheme-specific guidelines, limiting the discretion of Panchayats and Municipalities. In contrast, Finance Commission Grants (both Union and State Finance Commissions) and Own Revenues are classified as 'untied' funds, granting local bodies the autonomy to prioritize and spend according to local needs. MPLADS funds are not discussed in the provided text as a revenue source for local bodies, and specific State Government Schemes are typically tied.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the legal basis and governance structure of Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) in urban development?
questions.a: SPVs are typically registered under the Companies Act, 2013, and their boards are usually chaired by senior bureaucrats.
opts: SPVs are statutory bodies constituted directly under Article 243Q of the Constitution.
SPVs are typically registered under the Companies Act, 2013, and their boards are usually chaired by senior bureaucrats.
The Mayor of the Municipal Corporation holds executive control over the SPV board as its Chairperson.
SPVs derive their legal mandate from the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act.
questions.solution: The text explicitly states that SPVs are not constituted under the 74th Amendment or Article 243Q. They are typically registered under the Companies Act, 2013 (or earlier Companies Acts). Regarding governance, the board of an SPV is usually chaired by a senior bureaucrat such as the Chief Secretary, Principal Secretary, or Municipal Commissioner. Elected representatives may be members but often lack executive control, leading to democratic accountability concerns. The Mayor does not hold executive control, and SPVs are corporate entities, not constitutional or statutory bodies under the Amendment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the mandate and process of Social Audit in India, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, explicitly mandates social audits of its works.
opts: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment explicitly mandates social audits for all rural development schemes.
The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, explicitly mandates social audits of its works.
The Gram Sabha plays only an advisory role in the social audit process under MGNREGA.
Social Audit units function under the direct administrative control of the District Collector.
questions.solution: The lesson identifies MGNREGA, 2005, as a pioneering legislation that explicitly mandates social audits of its works. The 73rd Amendment does not mandate social audits universally; their application to other schemes depends on state-specific laws. The Gram Sabha is the forum for the Public Hearing (Jan Sunwai) and approves the Gram Panchayat Development Plan (GPDP), playing a direct decision-making role rather than a merely advisory one. The text emphasizes the need for independence of social audit units, implying they should not be under the direct administrative control of the District Collector or implementing agencies to ensure impartiality.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the horizontal fiscal equalisation formula typically adopted by State Finance Commissions for Panchayats and Municipalities?
questions.a: The formula weights population (50-60%), geographical area (10-15%), a deprivation index (20-30%), and revenue effort (5-10%).
opts: Population is assigned the lowest weight (10-15%) while geographical area receives the highest weight (50-60%).
The formula weights population (50-60%), geographical area (10-15%), a deprivation index (20-30%), and revenue effort (5-10%).
Revenue effort is given the highest weight (40-50%) to incentivise own-source revenue mobilisation, while population receives only 10-15%.
Deprivation index based on SC/ST population and literacy is excluded from the formula, which relies solely on population and area.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that State Finance Commissions typically adopt a formula weighting population (50-60%), geographical area (10-15%), a deprivation index including SC/ST population, literacy, and infrastructure gaps (20-30%), and revenue effort (5-10%). Option B matches this description exactly. Option A reverses the weights for population and area. Option C incorrectly assigns the highest weight to revenue effort. Option D falsely claims the deprivation index is excluded.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in Panchayats and Municipalities, which statement is constitutionally accurate?
questions.a: Articles 243-D(6) and 243-T(6) empower State Legislatures to make provision for OBC reservation by law, but do not prescribe a constitutional quota.
opts: Articles 243-D and 243-T mandate a fixed 27% reservation for OBCs in all States, similar to SC/ST reservation.
The Constitution requires States to provide OBC reservation up to 50% of total seats, subject to the triple test laid down by the Supreme Court.
Articles 243-D(6) and 243-T(6) empower State Legislatures to make provision for OBC reservation by law, but do not prescribe a constitutional quota.
OBC reservation in local bodies is a Union subject under Article 246, and Parliament has enacted a uniform law for all States.
questions.solution: The lesson clarifies that Articles 243-D(6) and 243-T(6) allow States to make provision for reservation of seats for "backward classes" by law, but the Constitution does not prescribe a quota for OBCs (unlike SCs/STs). This has led to varying quotas across States (27% in Bihar/UP, 50% in Tamil Nadu). The Supreme Court's triple test applies to the exercise of this discretionary power. Option A is incorrect because no fixed percentage is mandated. Option B misstates the constitutional requirement. Option D is wrong as local government is a State subject.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Supreme Court's judicial interpretation of Articles 243-G (Panchayats) and 243-W (Municipalities) has established which of the following principles regarding functional devolution?
questions.a: The Articles impose a positive legislative duty on States to devolve functions, and the absence of activity mapping renders the constitutional mandate unfulfilled.
opts: These Articles are merely enabling provisions; State Legislatures have complete discretion whether to devolve any functions to local bodies.
The Articles impose a positive legislative duty on States to devolve functions, and the absence of activity mapping renders the constitutional mandate unfulfilled.
Functional devolution under these Articles is limited to the 29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule and 18 subjects in the Twelfth Schedule, with no scope for additional functions.
The Courts have held that financial devolution is a prerequisite for functional devolution, making Article 243-H/243-X justiciable before Articles 243-G/243-W.
questions.solution: The lesson states that Articles 243-G and 243-W impose a "positive legislative duty, not a mere enabling provision" and that "activity mapping is justiciable." This means States are constitutionally obligated to devolve functions, and the failure to conduct activity mapping (specifying which functions are transferred) can be challenged in court. Option A contradicts this by calling them merely enabling. Option C incorrectly limits devolution to only the scheduled subjects. Option D reverses the relationship between functional and financial devolution.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to the impact of Goods and Services Tax (GST) on Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: ULBs lost significant own-source revenue from taxes subsumed under GST (octroi, entry tax, advertisement tax), and GST compensation cess flows to States, not directly to ULBs.
opts: The GST compensation cess is directly devolved to ULBs by the Union Government as a replacement for octroi and entry tax.
ULBs lost significant own-source revenue from taxes subsumed under GST (octroi, entry tax, advertisement tax), and GST compensation cess flows to States, not directly to ULBs.
Property tax and municipal bonds were subsumed under GST, forcing ULBs to rely entirely on State grants for revenue.
The Fifteenth Finance Commission has recommended that 50% of the GST compensation cess be earmarked exclusively for ULBs as untied grants.
