questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that GST subsumed key ULB taxes (octroi, entry tax, advertisement tax, luxury tax) and that "GST compensation cess directly flows to ULBs; it is a State-level grant and varies across States" is a trap to avoid. The correct position is that the compensation cess goes to States, not directly to ULBs. Property tax was NOT subsumed under GST (it remains a major own-source revenue), and municipal bonds are a post-GST mobilisation avenue. The Finance Commission's untied grants are separate from GST compensation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The integration of Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs) with District Planning Committees (DPCs) as a convergence mechanism requires which of the following operational links?
questions.a: GPDP data integration into DPC planning software, resource pooling of CSS funds tagged to GPDP activities, and quarterly monitoring with corrective directives by the DPC.
opts: GPDP data integration into DPC planning software, resource pooling of CSS funds tagged to GPDP activities, and quarterly monitoring with corrective directives by the DPC.
Mandatory merger of all Panchayat bank accounts into a single district-level fund controlled by the DPC, with the District Collector as the sole signatory.
Annual submission of GPDPs to the State Finance Commission, which then reallocates funds based on a uniform per-capita formula across all districts.
The DPC functions solely as a consultative forum; final approval of consolidated district plans rests with the State Planning Board.
questions.solution: The lesson details three operational links for effective convergence: (i) data integration — GPDP data flowing into DPC planning software (e.g., PlanPlus); (ii) resource pooling — CSS funds (MGNREGA, NRLM, Jal Jeevan Mission) tagged to GPDP activities, with DPC ensuring district allocations match aggregated demand; (iii) monitoring and feedback — DPC reviewing quarterly physical/financial progress reports and issuing corrective directives. Option A captures all three. Option B describes an incorrect fund merger mechanism. Option C misattributes the role to the State Finance Commission. Option D contradicts the constitutional mandate (Article 243-ZD) and the lesson's emphasis that DPC must consolidate and approve plans, not merely consult.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which State's Panchayat Raj Act transferred all 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule along with matching functionaries and finances, and established a robust District Planning Committee?
questions.solution: The lesson states that Kerala's Panchayat Raj Act, 1994, transferred all 29 subjects with matching functionaries and finances and created a robust District Planning Committee that approves a consolidated district plan. Maharashtra devolved only 18 subjects, Karnataka adopted a phased approach that stalled, and Tamil Nadu kept land revenue and minor irrigation under State control. Therefore, Kerala is the correct answer.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the Model Concession Agreement (MCA) 2017 for municipal PPPs, which category of risk is retained by the Urban Local Body (ULB)?
questions.solution: The MCA allocates risk on the principle "who can best manage the risk". Construction risk stays with the concessionaire, demand risk is shared through a minimum revenue guarantee, and regulatory risk — such as tariff revisions — remains with the ULB. Technology risk is borne by the concessionaire in the Indore waste‑to‑energy example. Hence, regulatory risk is the risk retained by the ULB.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is a prerequisite for integrating District Disaster Management Plans (DDMPs) with Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs) and Municipal plans?
opts: Automatic integration under the Disaster Management Act
Central monitoring by the Ministry of Home Affairs
Uniform State legislation on disaster management
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly notes that the Disaster Management Act does not automatically integrate DDMPs with GPDPs; integration requires a deliberate joint‑planning mechanism, which many districts lack. There is no mention of automatic integration, central monitoring, or uniform State legislation as prerequisites. Thus, a deliberate joint‑planning mechanism is the necessary condition.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: According to the Model Municipal Law, 2003, what composition and tenure does it propose for the State Election Commission (SEC)?
questions.a: Three‑member SEC with a fixed term
opts: Single‑member SEC with a five‑year term
Three‑member SEC with a fixed term
SEC appointed by the Governor for six years
SEC with the same tenure and removal process as the Election Commission of India
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Model Municipal Law, 2003, proposes a State Election Commission with a three‑member composition and a fixed term. It does not mention a single‑member body, Governor‑appointed six‑year term, or parity with the Election Commission of India. Therefore, the three‑member composition with a fixed term is the correct description.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which indicator is included in the Fifteenth Finance Commission's performance‑based grant for Panchayats to promote gender‑responsive budgeting?
questions.a: Gender‑disaggregated data reporting for all Centrally Sponsored Schemes
opts: Presence of a Women's Component Plan
Earmarking of at least 10 % of plan outlay for women
Gender‑disaggregated data reporting for all Centrally Sponsored Schemes
Establishment of a Gender Budget Cell in the Panchayat
questions.solution: The lesson specifies that the 15th Finance Commission's performance‑based grant for Panchayats includes a "gender‑disaggregated data" indicator; Panchayats must report sex‑wise beneficiary counts for all Centrally Sponsored Schemes to qualify for the untied grant. While Kerala's Women's Component Plan and the 10 % earmarking are examples of GRB practices, they are not the Finance Commission indicator. The Gender Budget Cell is an urban initiative under AMRUT 2.0. Hence, gender‑disaggregated data reporting is the correct indicator.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the quorum requirement for Gram Sabha meetings?
questions.a: Quorum is prescribed by State Panchayat Raj Acts and can be as low as 50 members.
opts: The Constitution prescribes a uniform quorum of one‑tenth of registered voters for all Gram Sabhas.
Quorum is uniform across States at 100 members as mandated by the 73rd Amendment.
Quorum is prescribed by State Panchayat Raj Acts and can be as low as 50 members.
Quorum is determined by a Central Government notification applicable to all States.
questions.solution: The lesson states that most State Panchayat Raj Acts prescribe a quorum of one‑tenth of total registered voters or 100 members, whichever is lower, and the misconception list explicitly notes that the quorum varies by State legislation and can be as low as 50 members. The Constitution (Article 243A) does not fix a uniform quorum, nor does the 73rd Amendment set a national figure. Therefore, only option C reflects the correct legal position.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly states the procedural requirement for moving an Adjournment Motion in the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: Support of at least 50 members and the Speaker's consent
opts: Support of at least 30 members and the Speaker's consent
Support of at least 50 members and the Speaker's consent
Support of at least 50 members only
Support of at least 100 members and the Speaker's consent
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that an Adjournment Motion "requires the support of at least 50 members and the Speaker's consent to discuss a matter of urgent public importance." This distinguishes it from other motions such as the No‑Confidence Motion, which also needs 50 members but has a different procedural timeline. The requirement of both a minimum number of members and the Speaker's gatekeeping role is a key procedural nuance that shapes opposition strategy. Options A, C and D either understate the member threshold or omit the Speaker's consent, making them incorrect.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the Speaker's certification of a Money Bill under Article 110, which statement is accurate?
questions.a: The certification is subject to judicial review and cannot be a colourable exercise of power
opts: The certification is final and cannot be challenged in any court
The certification can be challenged only through a parliamentary resolution
The certification is subject to judicial review and cannot be a colourable exercise of power
The certification requires prior concurrence of the Rajya Sabha
questions.solution: The lesson warns against the misconception that the Speaker's Money Bill certification is immune from judicial scrutiny. It notes: "Assuming the Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is immune from any judicial scrutiny; the Supreme Court has held it cannot be a colourable exercise of power." This means the certification is justiciable and must be a genuine exercise of the power under Article 110. Options A and B incorrectly suggest finality or a purely parliamentary remedy, while D confuses the certification process with the Rajya Sabha's role, which is limited to recommendations on Money Bills.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the correct status of Department‑Related Standing Committee (DRSC) reports in relation to the executive?
questions.a: They are recommendatory, but the government must present an Action Taken Report
opts: They are binding on the government and must be implemented
They are recommendatory, but the government must present an Action Taken Report
They are advisory only to the Speaker and have no executive relevance
They automatically become law once adopted by the House
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly lists as a common error: "Treating DRSC reports as binding on the government; they are recommendatory, though the government must present an Action Taken Report." This indicates that while the committees' findings carry weight and the executive is obliged to respond formally through an Action Taken Report, the recommendations themselves do not have the force of law. Options A, C and D misrepresent the legal effect of DRSC reports.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Policy Cut Motion from a Token Cut Motion?
questions.a: Policy Cut reduces the demand to Re 1; Token Cut reduces the demand by Rs 100
opts: Policy Cut reduces the demand to Re 1; Token Cut reduces the demand by Rs 100
Policy Cut reduces the demand by Rs 100; Token Cut reduces the demand to Re 1
Both reduce the demand to Re 1
Both reduce the demand by Rs 100
questions.solution: The lesson highlights a frequent confusion: "Failing to distinguish between a Policy Cut Motion (reduces demand to Re 1) and a Token Cut Motion (reduces by Rs 100) — the former rejects policy, the latter ventilates grievance." A Policy Cut Motion signals total disagreement with the policy underlying the demand by nominally reducing it to one rupee, whereas a Token Cut Motion merely reduces the amount by a symbolic hundred rupees to allow discussion of a specific grievance. Options B, C and D reverse or conflate these definitions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes the Rajya Sabha's powers in financial legislation?
questions.a: It can only discuss and make recommendations on the Finance Bill and cannot vote on Demands for Grants
opts: It can amend or reject the Appropriation Bill
It can introduce Money Bills under Article 110
It can only discuss and make recommendations on the Finance Bill and cannot vote on Demands for Grants
It possesses a veto over the Appropriation Bill
questions.solution: The lesson states: "The Rajya Sabha cannot introduce or amend Money Bills (Article 110) and has only recommendatory powers over the Finance Bill. Its inability to vote on Demands for Grants limits its direct control over the purse." This makes clear that the Upper House's role in financial matters is confined to discussion and non‑binding recommendations on the Finance Bill, with no voting rights on the Appropriation Bill or Demands for Grants. Options A, B and D attribute powers that the Constitution explicitly denies to the Rajya Sabha.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What are the prescribed notice periods for a Starred Question and a Short‑Notice Question in the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: 15 clear days for Starred; 3 days for Short‑Notice
opts: 15 clear days for Starred; 3 days for Short‑Notice
10 clear days for Starred; 5 days for Short‑Notice
20 clear days for Starred; 7 days for Short‑Notice
15 clear days for both Starred and Short‑Notice
questions.solution: The lesson states that the notice period for a Starred or Unstarred Question is fifteen clear days, while a Short‑Notice Question requires only three days' notice. This distinction is explicitly given in the rules (Lok Sabha Rules 32‑34). Therefore, option A correctly reflects the prescribed periods.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How much maximum debate time is allotted to each Private Member's Bill in the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: Thirty minutes on Fridays (or the last sitting day of the week)
opts: Thirty minutes on Fridays (or the last sitting day of the week)
One hour on any sitting day
No fixed limit; the Speaker decides case by case
questions.solution: According to the lesson, the House allocates a maximum of two and a half hours on each Friday for Private Members' Bills, and each bill receives a maximum of thirty minutes for debate. This time limit is a procedural feature distinguishing Private Members' Bills from Government Bills. Hence option A is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the nature of the recommendations made by the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) and what follow‑up is required from the government?
questions.a: Advisory, but the government must submit an Action Taken Report
opts: Binding on the government; no further report needed
Advisory, but the government must submit an Action Taken Report
Purely advisory with no obligation for an Action Taken Report
Enforceable by Parliament through a separate resolution
questions.solution: The lesson clarifies that COPU's reports are advisory in nature; however, the government is required to submit an Action Taken Report on the recommendations. This distinguishes COPU from bodies with binding authority and underscores the accountability mechanism. Option B captures this accurately.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which category of international treaties must be enacted by Parliament before they become domestically enforceable?
questions.a: Only treaties that require domestic legislation for implementation
opts: All treaties signed by the executive
Only treaties that require domestic legislation for implementation
Only treaties ratified by the President
questions.solution: The lesson explains the distinction between "treaties requiring legislation" and "executive agreements." Only those treaties that need domestic legislation must be enacted by Parliament; executive agreements do not require parliamentary ratification. This is a frequent examiner trap. Therefore, option B is the correct statement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In which House can a Motion of No‑Confidence be moved, and what is the minimum number of members whose written support is required?
questions.a: Lok Sabha; at least fifty members
opts: Lok Sabha; at least fifty members
Rajya Sabha; at least fifty members
Lok Sabha; at least one hundred members
Either House; at least fifty members
questions.solution: Article 75(3) and Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules provide that a No‑Confidence Motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha and must be supported in writing by at least fifty members. The Rajya Sabha has no role in such motions. Thus, option A correctly states both the House and the required support.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the chairmanship of the Ethics Committee and the Committee on Privileges in the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: The Ethics Committee elects its own chairperson, while the Privileges Committee is chaired by the Deputy Speaker by convention.
opts: Both committees are chaired by the Speaker.
The Ethics Committee is chaired by the Deputy Speaker, while the Privileges Committee elects its own chairperson.
The Ethics Committee elects its own chairperson, while the Privileges Committee is chaired by the Deputy Speaker by convention.
The chairpersons of both committees are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Ethics Committee elects its own chairperson, whereas the Committee on Privileges is chaired by the Deputy Speaker by convention. Option 3 matches this description exactly. Options 1, 2, and 4 contradict the given facts: the Speaker does not chair either committee, the Deputy Speaker does not chair the Ethics Committee, and the President has no role in these appointments.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the primary limitation of the Committee on Government Assurances in ensuring executive accountability?
questions.a: It only reports on the implementation of assurances and relies on political pressure for compliance.
opts: It can impose penalties on ministers who fail to fulfil assurances.
It has the power to initiate judicial proceedings against defaulting ministries.
It only reports on the implementation of assurances and relies on political pressure for compliance.
It can amend the Rules of Procedure to make assurances legally binding.
questions.solution: According to the lesson, the Committee on Government Assurances scrutinises assurances given by ministers but its role is limited to reporting; it cannot enforce compliance and depends on political pressure. Option 3 reflects this limitation. Options 1, 2, and 4 attribute enforcement, judicial, or rule‑making powers that the committee does not possess.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement is true regarding the constitutional scope of an ordinance promulgated by the President?
questions.a: An ordinance cannot amend the Constitution; constitutional amendments require the Article 368 procedure.
opts: An ordinance can amend the Constitution if ratified by a simple majority in Parliament.
An ordinance cannot amend the Constitution; constitutional amendments require the Article 368 procedure.
An ordinance can override a Supreme Court judgment on a constitutional matter.
An ordinance remains in force indefinitely unless disapproved by both Houses.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that an ordinance cannot amend the Constitution and that constitutional amendments must follow the Article 368 procedure. Option 2 reproduces this rule. Option 1 incorrectly suggests a simple majority can amend the Constitution via ordinance, option 3 confuses ordinance power with judicial review, and option 4 misstates the lifespan of an ordinance, which lapses after six weeks from reassembly of Parliament unless approved.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How does a Calling Attention Motion differ from a Short Duration Discussion in terms of ministerial response?
questions.a: A Calling Attention Motion mandates a ministerial reply, whereas a Short Duration Discussion involves a ministerial reply but no formal motion.
opts: Both require a formal motion and a mandatory ministerial reply.
A Calling Attention Motion mandates a ministerial reply, whereas a Short Duration Discussion involves a ministerial reply but no formal motion.
A Short Duration Discussion requires a ministerial reply, while a Calling Attention Motion does not.
Neither device obliges the minister to reply; both are purely deliberative.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that a Calling Attention Motion compels a mandatory ministerial reply, while a Short Duration Discussion also entails a ministerial reply but is conducted without a formal motion. Option 2 captures this distinction. Options 1, 3, and 4 either conflate the two devices or deny the mandatory reply requirement that exists for Calling Attention Motions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Business Advisory Committee (BAC) of Parliament is correct?
questions.a: It allocates time for government bills, private members' bills, and discussions, and its recommendations are usually followed by the presiding officer.
opts: Its recommendations are legally binding on the House.
It is chaired by the Leader of the Opposition.
It allocates time for government bills, private members' bills, and discussions, and its recommendations are usually followed by the presiding officer.
It decides on the passage of constitutional amendment bills.
questions.solution: The Business Advisory Committee is constituted under Rule 331 of Lok Sabha and Rule 236 of Rajya Sabha. Its chairperson is the Speaker or Chairman ex‑officio, and its members include the Leader of the House, the Leader of the Opposition, and other members nominated to reflect party strength. The BAC's primary function is to allocate time for government bills, private members' bills, discussions, short‑duration discussions, calling‑attention motions and Zero Hour mentions. Although its recommendations are advisory and not legally binding, the presiding officer almost always follows them, making the BAC a de facto agenda‑setting body. Hence, option C is the correct description.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the constitutional amendment procedure under Article 368?
questions.a: An amendment affecting federal provisions listed in Article 368(2) requires ratification by at least half of the state legislatures, and the President's assent is obligatory.
opts: A constitutional amendment bill requires a simple majority in each House.
The President may withhold assent to a constitutional amendment bill.
State ratification is required for all constitutional amendments.
An amendment affecting federal provisions listed in Article 368(2) requires ratification by at least half of the state legislatures, and the President's assent is obligatory.
questions.solution: Article 368 prescribes a special majority for constitutional amendments: a majority of the total membership of each House and a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting. State ratification by at least half of the state legislatures is required only for amendments that affect the federal provisions enumerated in Article 368(2) (e.g., election of the President, extent of executive power, judiciary, distribution of legislative powers, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself). The 24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent obligatory, removing any pocket‑veto power. There is no provision for a joint sitting to resolve deadlocks on amendment bills. Therefore, option D correctly states the requirements.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes India's engagement with the Inter‑Parliamentary Union (IPU) and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA)?
questions.a: The Indian Parliamentary Group serves as the national group for both the IPU and the CPA.
opts: The IPU is a Commonwealth‑specific association while the CPA is a global inter‑parliamentary organisation.
The Indian Parliamentary Group serves as the national group for both the IPU and the CPA.
Resolutions adopted at the IPU automatically become part of Indian domestic law.
India has never hosted an IPU Assembly.
questions.solution: The Indian Parliamentary Group (IPG), constituted under the Speaker's chairmanship, acts as the national group for both the Inter‑Parliamentary Union (IPU) and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA). The IPU is a global organisation of parliaments, whereas the CPA is limited to Commonwealth legislatures. Resolutions adopted at the IPU or CPA do not automatically become domestic law; they require separate legislative action. India has hosted the IPU Assembly twice — in New Delhi (1997) and Hyderabad (2023). Consequently, option B is the only accurate statement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the Speaker's decisions in the Lok Sabha, which one of the following is subject to judicial review?
questions.a: Decisions on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law).
opts: Certification of a Bill as a Money Bill under Article 110.
Rulings on points of order raised during Question Hour.
Decisions on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law).
Allocation of time for discussion by the Business Advisory Committee.
questions.solution: The 'Common Traps' section clarifies: 'Assuming the Speaker's decision on all matters is beyond judicial review; while the Money Bill certification is constitutionally final, other decisions (e.g., anti-defection) are subject to review.' This refers to the Supreme Court's ruling in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) which held that the Speaker's decision under the Tenth Schedule is subject to judicial review. Money Bill certification under Article 110 is explicitly declared 'final' by the Constitution.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the primary nature of recommendations made by Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) to the Executive?
questions.a: Advisory in nature, which the Executive may accept or reject.
opts: Binding on the Ministry concerned, requiring mandatory implementation.
Advisory in nature, which the Executive may accept or reject.
Legally enforceable through a writ of mandamus by the High Courts.
Automatically incorporated into the final legislation without Parliamentary vote.
questions.solution: The lesson states in the 'Common Traps' section: 'Overlooking the advisory nature of parliamentary committee recommendations; they are not binding on the executive, which can choose to accept or reject them.' This is a fundamental principle of parliamentary oversight — committees scrutinize and recommend, but the executive retains the discretion to accept or reject recommendations. They are not legally binding or enforceable by courts.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The 'Guillotine' is a parliamentary procedural device used for which specific purpose?
questions.a: To put outstanding Demands for Grants to vote without discussion due to time constraints.
opts: To censure the Council of Ministers for a specific policy failure.
To put outstanding Demands for Grants to vote without discussion due to time constraints.
To terminate a No-Confidence Motion before it is put to vote.
To suspend a member for grossly disorderly conduct in the House.
questions.solution: The lesson defines the guillotine clearly: 'a procedural device to put outstanding demands for grants to vote without discussion due to time constraints.' It also warns in 'Common Traps': 'Mistaking the 'guillotine' for a form of censure; it is a procedural device to expedite the passage of financial business by cutting short debate.' It is applied during the Budget session when time is insufficient for detailed discussion of all Demands for Grants.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five indicia identified by the Supreme Court in Pradyut Bordoloi v. Swapan Roy (2001) for determining an "office of profit"?
questions.a: Government ownership of the office premises
opts: Government ownership of the office premises
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Pradyut Bordoloi v. Swapan Roy listed five indicia: (i) government appointment, (ii) government power to remove, (iii) government remuneration, (iv) governmental functions, and (v) patronage or influence. Ownership of the office premises is not among these factors. The test relies on the totality of circumstances, not on property ownership. Therefore, option D is the correct answer.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the parliamentary control mechanisms for delegated legislation, which procedure requires a resolution of the House to annul a rule or regulation?
questions.solution: Delegated legislation is subject to three parliamentary controls: the laying requirement, the negative resolution (where either House may pass a resolution disapproving the legislation, which annuls it), and scrutiny by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation. The Committee can only recommend; annulment requires a House resolution. Judicial review is a separate constitutional check. Hence, the negative resolution is the mechanism that directly annuls delegated legislation through a House resolution.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement accurately reflects the parliamentary scrutiny of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) reports?
questions.a: The Public Accounts Committee selects only a fraction of CAG reports for examination
opts: All CAG reports are automatically debated in Parliament
The Public Accounts Committee selects only a fraction of CAG reports for examination
The CAG's expenditure is voted through the Demand for Grants process
The Election Commission's reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee
questions.solution: The lesson notes that the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) selects only a fraction of CAG reports for detailed examination, and many reports languish without discussion. CAG reports are not automatically debated; the PAC decides which to take up. The CAG's expenditure is charged on the Consolidated Fund and does not go through the Demand for Grants. The Election Commission's expenditure is similarly charged, and its reports are not examined by the PAC. Therefore, option B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court ruled that the Speaker's decision on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is:
questions.a: Subject to judicial review for mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice
opts: Final and not subject to judicial review
Subject to judicial review for mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice
Only reviewable by the High Court
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan explicitly restored judicial review of the Speaker's adjudicatory decisions under the Tenth Schedule. The Court held that such decisions are subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice. The decision is not final and unreviewable, nor is it limited to High Court review only, and it does not bind the Election Commission. Thus, option B correctly states the Court's ruling.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the parliamentary approval requirement for a Proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 of the Constitution?
opts: Simple majority in Lok Sabha only
Special majority in Lok Sabha and simple majority in Rajya Sabha
questions.solution: Article 352 requires that a Proclamation of National Emergency be approved by both Houses of Parliament by a special majority (a majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting). This is distinct from Article 356 (President's Rule) and Article 360 (Financial Emergency), which require only a simple majority. The 44th Amendment introduced this special majority requirement to prevent executive misuse. Therefore, option B is correct.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the appointment and tenure of the Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: Appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Speaker and holds office until the age of 60 years or resignation, whichever is earlier.
opts: Appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendation of the Speaker for a fixed term of five years.
Appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Speaker and holds office until the age of 60 years or resignation, whichever is earlier.
Appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Prime Minister and holds office during the pleasure of the President.
Appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and holds office until the dissolution of the House.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "The Secretary‑General of the Lok Sabha and the Secretary‑General of the Rajya Sabha are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the respective Presiding Officers, and they hold office until the age of 60 years or until they resign, whichever is earlier." Option A incorrectly assigns the appointing authority to the Prime Minister and a fixed five-year term. Option C incorrectly assigns the recommendation to the Prime Minister and tenure to the President's pleasure. Option D incorrectly assigns the appointment to the Speaker and tenure to the House's dissolution. Only Option B matches the constitutional provision described in the text.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of negative resolution procedure for delegated legislation, what is the consequence if Parliament takes no action within the stipulated period?
questions.a: The delegated legislation is deemed to have been approved and continues in force.
opts: The delegated legislation lapses and ceases to have effect.
The delegated legislation is deemed to have been approved and continues in force.
The matter is automatically referred to the Committee on Subordinate Legislation for detailed scrutiny.
The government is required to re-promulgate the legislation with modifications.
questions.solution: The lesson's 'Common Errors' section clarifies: "Believing that negative resolution on delegated legislation requires a positive vote to annul; it only needs a disapproval motion, and silence implies consent." This means under negative resolution, the delegated legislation comes into force unless Parliament actively passes a motion to annul it (disapproval). If no action is taken (silence), it is deemed approved and continues in force. Option A describes affirmative resolution (where positive approval is needed). Option C and D are procedural inventions not supported by the text. The key principle is 'silence implies consent' for negative resolution.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides for free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years?
questions.solution: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, provides the Right to Education for children aged 6–14. Article 45 (Directive Principle) covers early childhood care below age 6. (Source: Constitution, 86th Amendment Act, 2002)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: MGNREGA guarantees how many days of wage employment per rural household per year?
questions.solution: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment per rural household per financial year. (Source: MGNREGA, 2005, Sec. 3)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is a Directive Principle (non-justiciable), not a Fundamental Right?
questions.a: Promotion of educational interests of SCs and STs
opts: Promotion of educational interests of SCs and STs
questions.solution: Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, and weaker sections) is a Directive Principle. Articles 17 (untouchability), 21A (education), and 24 (child labour) are justiciable rights. (Source: Constitution, Part III vs Part IV)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The National Food Security Act, 2013 covers up to what percentage of the rural population under TPDS?
questions.solution: NFSA covers up to 75% of the rural population and up to 50% of the urban population under the Targeted Public Distribution System. (Source: NFSA, 2013, Sec. 3)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Supreme Court judgement recognised the right of transgender persons to self-identify their gender?
opts: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)
questions.solution: NALSA v. Union of India (2014) recognised transgender persons as 'third gender' and affirmed their right to self-identification. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised homosexuality (Sec. 377). (Source: Writ Petition (Civil) No. 604 of 2013, decided 15 April 2014)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Ayushman Bharat PMJAY provides health insurance cover of how much per family per year?
questions.solution: PMJAY provides ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation. Based on SECC 2011 deprivation criteria (D1-D5, D7). (Source: PMJAY Operational Guidelines, NHA)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to which body?
questions.solution: 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Article 338B, giving constitutional status to NCBC. 105th Amendment (2021) restored State power to identify OBCs. (Source: Constitution, 102nd & 105th Amendment Acts)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the National Health Mission (NHM)?
opts: Flexipool for NCDs and Health Systems
questions.solution: NHM (launched 2013) subsumes NRHM and NUHM. PMJAY is a separate scheme under Ayushman Bharat (launched 2018), not a component of NHM. (Source: MoHFW, NHM Framework Document)
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under Article 74 of the Constitution, what is the extent of the President's discretion regarding the advice of the Council of Ministers?
questions.a: The President must act on the advice but may require the Council to reconsider it once.
opts: The President may reject the advice outright and act independently.
The President must act on the advice but may require the Council to reconsider it once.
The President can act independently in all matters except financial bills.
The advice of the Council of Ministers is not binding on the President.
questions.solution: Article 74(1) mandates that the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers, making the advice binding. Article 74(2) provides a limited safeguard: the President may require the Council to reconsider its advice, but after such reconsideration the President must act in accordance with the advice tendered. Thus the President cannot reject the advice outright nor act independently; the only discretion is to send the advice back for a single reconsideration.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: How is the Vice‑President of India elected?
questions.a: By an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament.
opts: Directly by the people of India.
By an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament.
By the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
By the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies.
questions.solution: Article 66 provides that the Vice‑President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). The Vice‑President is not directly elected by the people, nor appointed by the President, nor elected by state legislatures. This electoral college reflects the federal character of the office while keeping it within the parliamentary framework.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What change did the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) make regarding the President's ordinance‑making power?
questions.a: Provided that an ordinance cannot be promulgated when both Houses of Parliament are in session.
opts: Extended the maximum life of an ordinance to six months.
Provided that an ordinance cannot be promulgated when both Houses of Parliament are in session.
Removed the President's power to promulgate ordinances altogether.
Allowed the President to issue ordinances without the advice of the Council of Ministers.
questions.solution: The The 44th Amendment restored the pre-Emergency constitutional position. It reinstated the binding nature of ministerial advice under Article 74(1) and, under Article 123, provided that the President cannot promulgate an ordinance when both Houses of Parliament are in session. The six-week limit after Parliament reassembles is from the original Constitution (Article 123(2)), not a change made by the 44th Amendment; no longer period had been introduced by the 42nd Amendment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) placed a ceiling on the size of the Union Council of Ministers. What is that ceiling?
questions.a: 15 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
opts: 10 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
15 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
20 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
No ceiling; the size is determined by the Prime Minister.
questions.solution: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), which caps the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, at fifteen percent of the total number of members of the House of the People (Lok Sabha). This provision was introduced to prevent oversized cabinets and to promote administrative efficiency and fiscal discipline.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the creation of All‑India Services, and which body recruits them?
opts: Article 320 – Department of Personnel and Training.
questions.solution: Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All‑India Services (such as the IAS, IPS and IFoS) common to the Union and the States. Recruitment to these services is conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) through the annual Civil Services Examination. Central Civil Services, by contrast, are created under Article 309 and are recruited through separate examinations such as the Combined Graduate Level Examination.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the ordinance-making power of the President under Article 123, which principle was laid down by the Supreme Court in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)?
questions.a: Repeated repromulgation of ordinances without legislative approval constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and an abuse of the ordinance-making power.
opts: The President's satisfaction regarding the necessity of immediate legislation is entirely subjective and non-justiciable.
An ordinance can be repromulgated indefinitely without legislative approval as long as the President deems it necessary.
Repeated repromulgation of ordinances without legislative approval constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and an abuse of the ordinance-making power.
Ordinances lapse automatically after six weeks of Parliament's reassembly only if both Houses pass a resolution disapproving them.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court struck down a series of repromulgated ordinances, holding that repeated re-issuance without legislative approval constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and an abuse of the ordinance-making power. The ordinance must be laid before both Houses within six weeks of reassembly; otherwise it lapses. The President's satisfaction is not immune from judicial scrutiny. Option A is incorrect because the satisfaction is subject to judicial review. Option B is incorrect because indefinite repromulgation was held unconstitutional. Option D is incorrect because the ordinance lapses automatically after six weeks if not approved, not only if a disapproval resolution is passed.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Cabinet Committees in India is correct?
questions.a: The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) includes the National Security Adviser (NSA) as a permanent invitee.
opts: Cabinet Committees are statutory bodies established under an Act of Parliament.
The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) includes the National Security Adviser (NSA) as a permanent invitee.
The Cabinet Secretariat has no role in the functioning of Cabinet Committees.
Ad-hoc Groups of Ministers (GoMs) submit their recommendations directly to the Prime Minister, bypassing standing Cabinet Committees.
questions.solution: The lesson states that Cabinet Committees are executive bodies under the Transaction of Business Rules, not statutory bodies. The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) is the apex security decision-making forum and includes the NSA as a permanent invitee. The Cabinet Secretariat provides secretarial support, minutes, and follow-up for these committees. Ad-hoc GoMs/EGoMs address cross-cutting issues and their recommendations feed into the appropriate standing Cabinet Committees, not directly to the Prime Minister bypassing them. Option A is incorrect because they are not statutory. Option C is incorrect because the Cabinet Secretariat provides essential support. Option D is incorrect because GoM recommendations feed into standing committees.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court issued directions to insulate civil services from political interference. Which of the following was NOT a direction given by the Court?
questions.a: Making the Civil Services Board's recommendations binding on the political executive with no discretion to deviate.
opts: Establishment of a Civil Services Board at the Centre and in each state to recommend transfers, postings, and disciplinary actions.
Mandating fixed tenures for key posts such as Director General of Police and Chief Secretary.
Requiring that any premature transfer be recorded with reasons.
Making the Civil Services Board's recommendations binding on the political executive with no discretion to deviate.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) directed the establishment of Civil Services Boards at the Centre and in states to recommend transfers, postings, and disciplinary actions; mandated fixed tenures for key posts like DGP and Chief Secretary; and required that any premature transfer be recorded with reasons. However, the lesson notes that the Centre's Civil Services Board functions largely in an advisory capacity, and compliance remains uneven. The Court did not make the Board's recommendations binding on the political executive with no discretion to deviate. Option D describes a direction that was not given.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding Article 143 of the Constitution, which statement is correct?
questions.a: The advisory opinion is not binding but carries significant persuasive authority.
opts: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion is binding on the President and the Council of Ministers.
The President may refer only questions of fact, not questions of law, to the Supreme Court.
The advisory opinion is not binding but carries significant persuasive authority.
The Supreme Court is constitutionally compelled to answer every reference made by the President.
questions.solution: Article 143 empowers the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion. The lesson explicitly states that the Court's advisory opinion is not binding on the President or the government, but it carries significant persuasive authority and has shaped executive action. The first reference in 1951 (Delhi Laws Act) and the 1998 Ayodhya reference illustrate this practice. The Court may also decline to answer a reference, as it did in the Ayodhya case. Hence, option C is the only accurate description.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) from the Cabinet Secretariat?
questions.a: The PMO is a political office, whereas the Cabinet Secretariat is a constitutional‑administrative body.
opts: Both are constitutional bodies established under Article 74 of the Constitution.
The PMO is a constitutional‑administrative body, while the Cabinet Secretariat is a political office.
The PMO is a political office, whereas the Cabinet Secretariat is a constitutional‑administrative body.
The two offices are functionally interchangeable and share identical accountability mechanisms.
questions.solution: The lesson highlights that the PMO is a political office serving the Prime Minister, while the Cabinet Secretariat is a constitutional‑administrative body responsible for inter‑ministerial coordination and recording Cabinet decisions. They have distinct origins, functions, and accountability structures; the PMO is not a constitutional body, and the Cabinet Secretariat is not a political office. The text warns against treating them as interchangeable. Therefore, option C correctly captures this institutional distinction.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the doctrine of pleasure (Article 310) and the safeguards of Article 311, which statement is accurate?
questions.a: Article 311 protections apply only after a servant has been appointed to a substantive post, not during probation.
opts: Article 311 protections apply to all civil servants from the date of recruitment, including probationers.
Article 311 protections apply only after a servant has been appointed to a substantive post, not during probation.
Parliament cannot modify the procedural safeguards of Article 311 through ordinary legislation.
The protections of Article 311 extend to employees of public sector undertakings and autonomous bodies.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly notes that Article 311 protections apply only after a servant has been appointed to a substantive post, not during probation. This is a key exception to the doctrine of pleasure under Article 310. Judicial expansion has added safeguards such as the right to be heard, but the threshold of substantive appointment remains. The protections do not automatically cover probationers, PSU employees, or autonomous body staff unless specifically extended. Hence, option B is the correct statement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What change did the Cadre Allocation Policy, 2017 introduce for All India Services officers?
questions.a: It introduced a zone‑based allocation requiring officers to serve in at least one cadre outside their home zone.
opts: It abolished the state‑cadre system and created a single national cadre pool.
It introduced a zone‑based allocation requiring officers to serve in at least one cadre outside their home zone.
It allowed officers to choose any state cadre solely on the basis of personal preference.
It removed the mandatory central deputation requirement for all AIS officers.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the 2017 policy introduced a "zone‑based" allocation, dividing states into five zones and requiring officers to serve in at least one cadre outside their home zone to promote national integration. It did not abolish the cadre system, nor did it grant unrestricted choice or remove deputation requirements. The policy works within the existing cadre framework and the All India Services Act, 1951. Therefore, option B accurately reflects the 2017 reform.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai mandated a floor test in the State Assembly within a reasonable time, preferably 48 hours, before imposition.
opts: The President's satisfaction is absolute and not subject to judicial review.
The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within one month.
The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai mandated a floor test in the State Assembly within a reasonable time, preferably 48 hours, before imposition.
The dissolution of the State Assembly is a mandatory and routine sequel to the proclamation.
questions.solution: The S.R. Bommai (1994) judgment established that the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is subject to judicial review and is not absolute. The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months, not one. Crucially, the nine-judge bench mandated a floor test in the Assembly within a reasonable time, preferably 48 hours, before imposing President's Rule. Subsequent rulings in Rameshwar Prasad (2006) clarified that dissolution of the Assembly cannot be a routine sequel to the proclamation.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the President's pardoning power under Article 72: 1. It is an absolute discretionary power of the President. 2. It is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. 3. It is immune from judicial review. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution: Article 72 power is not absolute; it is exercised by the President on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Statement 2 correct). The Supreme Court in cases like Maru Ram, Kehar Singh, and Epuru Sudhakar has held that this power is subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fides, and non-application of mind (Statement 3 incorrect). Therefore, Statement 1 is also incorrect as the power is not a personal discretion of the President.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the context of a minority government or a hung Parliament, which of the following accurately describes the President's discretion regarding the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: The President may refuse dissolution if a viable alternative government can be formed.
opts: The President is bound to dissolve the Lok Sabha immediately on the advice of the Prime Minister.
The President may refuse dissolution if a viable alternative government can be formed.
The President must refer the matter to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion before dissolving the House.
The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha only after a confidence motion is defeated on the floor of the House.
questions.solution: The President is not a mere rubber stamp regarding dissolution. While the President generally acts on ministerial advice, constitutional practice and judicial dicta recognize that the President may refuse dissolution if a viable alternative government exists and the House is not deadlocked. This discretion prevents the Prime Minister from using dissolution as a tool to avoid accountability when another ministry can command a majority. The President does not require a Supreme Court reference or a prior floor test defeat to exercise this discretion.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the 360-degree Performance Appraisal Report (PAR) under Mission Karmayogi is correct?
questions.a: It applies only from the Under Secretary level upward, while lower-level officers continue under the older ACR system.
opts: It applies to all civil servants from the level of Assistant Section Officer upwards.
It replaces the Annual Confidential Report (ACR) system for all Group A and Group B officers.
It applies only from the Under Secretary level upward, while lower-level officers continue under the older ACR system.
It is administered solely by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) without any role for the Capacity Building Commission.
questions.solution: Mission Karmayogi's 360-degree PAR is applicable from the Under Secretary level (Level 11) upwards. Officers below this level continue to be assessed under the traditional Annual Confidential Report (ACR) system. The Capacity Building Commission (CBC), not the DoPT, defines the competency framework and behavioural indicators for this appraisal. The PAR is conducted electronically on the iGOT platform covering six competency clusters.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: With reference to Financial Emergency under Article 360 of the Constitution, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.a: The provision has never been invoked since the commencement of the Constitution.
opts: It has been proclaimed once in 1991 during the balance of payments crisis.
During its operation, the President may direct the reduction of salaries of all persons serving in the State, including judges of the High Courts.
The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month.
The provision has never been invoked since the commencement of the Constitution.
questions.solution: Article 360 provides for Financial Emergency, but it has never been proclaimed in India's history, not even during the 1991 economic crisis. The proclamation must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate after two months unless approved by both Houses (not one month). While the President can direct reduction of salaries of persons serving the State, the constitutional protection of judges' salaries under Article 221 makes the inclusion of High Court judges in such a directive constitutionally contentious and untested.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held that the President's pleasure doctrine under Article 156 for removal of a Governor:
questions.a: Is not absolute; removal must not be arbitrary, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations
opts: Is absolute and not subject to judicial review on any ground
Is not absolute; removal must not be arbitrary, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations
Requires prior consultation with the Chief Minister of the concerned state
Requires a resolution passed by the State Legislative Assembly
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) explicitly ruled that the pleasure doctrine under Article 156 is not absolute. The Court held that removal of a Governor before completion of the five-year term cannot be arbitrary, mala fide, or based on extraneous considerations. The Court mandated that a removed Governor is entitled to a statement of reasons, and the decision is subject to judicial review for violation of constitutional morality. Option A is incorrect because the Court rejected absolute immunity. Option C is incorrect because while the Sarkaria Commission recommended consultation with the Chief Minister, this is not a constitutional requirement established by the judgment. Option D has no constitutional basis.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) derives its authority from:
questions.a: The executive's prerogative and the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules
opts: A specific parliamentary statute enacted under Article 77
The executive's prerogative and the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules
A resolution of the Union Cabinet passed in 1947
questions.solution: The lesson text explicitly states: "Unlike other Cabinet committees, the CCS does not have a statutory basis; it derives its authority from the executive's prerogative." The CCS is chaired by the Prime Minister and comprises Ministers of Defence, Home Affairs, Finance, and External Affairs as permanent members. The National Security Adviser serves as its secretary. It is not established by a parliamentary statute (Option A), nor by a specific constitutional provision (Option C), nor by a 1947 Cabinet resolution (Option D). Its authority flows from the executive's prerogative to constitute committees for efficient transaction of business under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the Union Public Service Commission's role in disciplinary matters against civil servants, which statement is correct?
questions.a: The UPSC's advice is advisory, but non-consultation can invalidate the disciplinary order
opts: The UPSC's advice is binding on the President
The UPSC's advice is advisory, but non-consultation can invalidate the disciplinary order
The UPSC has no role in disciplinary matters; it only conducts recruitment examinations
The UPSC's advice is required only for Group A officers, not for Group B or C
questions.solution: The lesson's "Common Misconceptions" section explicitly states: "Believing the UPSC's advice in disciplinary matters is binding; it is advisory, though non-consultation can invalidate the order." Article 320(3)(c) of the Constitution requires the UPSC to be consulted on disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India. While the advice is not binding (Option A is incorrect), the Supreme Court has held that failure to consult the UPSC where mandated renders the disciplinary order void. Option C is incorrect because the UPSC has a constitutional role in disciplinary matters beyond recruitment. Option D is incorrect because the consultation requirement applies based on the nature of the penalty and service conditions, not merely Group classification.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The post of Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister:
questions.a: Is created by executive order and derives authority from the Prime Minister's discretion
opts: Is a constitutional authority created under Article 77
Is created by executive order and derives authority from the Prime Minister's discretion
Has a fixed tenure of five years as per the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules
Is appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
questions.solution: The lesson's "Common Misconceptions" section states: "Treating the Principal Secretary to the PM as a constitutional authority; the post is created by executive order and derives authority from the Prime Minister's discretion." The PMO itself is not a constitutional body but an executive creation to assist the Prime Minister. The Principal Secretary is typically a senior civil servant appointed by the Prime Minister, not through a constitutional process (Option A), not with a fixed statutory tenure (Option C), and not through the ACC appointment process which applies to certain senior posts like Secretary to Government of India (Option D). The post's authority flows entirely from the Prime Minister's delegation of functions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Committee on Estimates differs from the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) in that:
questions.a: The Committee on Estimates examines proposed outlays for efficiency, while PAC audits past expenditure with the CAG
opts: The Committee on Estimates has 30 members from both Houses, while PAC has 22 members only from Lok Sabha
The Committee on Estimates examines proposed outlays for efficiency, while PAC audits past expenditure with the CAG
The Committee on Estimates can summon Ministers for evidence, while PAC can only call officials
The Committee on Estimates' reports are legally binding, while PAC's reports are only recommendatory
questions.solution: The lesson text clearly distinguishes: "Unlike the Public Accounts Committee (which audits past expenditure with the CAG), the Estimates Committee looks forward, evaluating the efficiency of proposed outlays." The Committee on Estimates has 30 members all from Lok Sabha (not both Houses), making Option A incorrect. Neither committee can summon Ministers (Option C is incorrect for both). Both committees' reports are recommendatory, not legally binding (Option D is incorrect). The key functional difference is temporal: Estimates Committee evaluates proposed expenditure (ex-ante), while PAC audits past expenditure (post-ante) with CAG assistance.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the domestic legal effect of an executive agreement concluded by the President on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers?
questions.a: It is binding under international law but has no direct domestic effect unless implemented by a statute.
opts: It automatically becomes part of domestic law without any legislative action.
It is binding under international law but has no direct domestic effect unless implemented by a statute.
It requires ratification by Parliament under Article 253 before it can bind the Union.
It can amend the Constitution without a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the executive may conclude executive agreements which are binding under international law but have no direct domestic effect unless implemented by statute. This distinguishes them from treaties that require domestic legislation under Article 253. Option A is incorrect because domestic effect requires legislation. Option C describes the treaty route, not executive agreements. Option D is contradicted by the Keshav Singh case, which held the President cannot ratify a treaty amending the Constitution without an Article 368 amendment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Regarding the appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), which statement is accurate in light of recent procedural developments?
questions.a: The President appoints the CAG on the advice of the Council of Ministers, but recent rules mandate a selection committee.
opts: The Prime Minister can unilaterally appoint the CAG without any consultative mechanism.
The President appoints the CAG on the advice of the Council of Ministers, but recent rules mandate a selection committee.
The CAG is appointed by a collegium of judges similar to the higher judiciary.
The appointment of the CAG requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that while the formal appointing authority is the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers (headed by the Prime Minister), recent rules mandate a selection committee for key constitutional posts such as the CAG and CEC. Option A reflects the outdated assumption the lesson warns against. Option C confuses the CAG with judicial appointments governed by the collegium. Option D is incorrect because no constitutional amendment is needed for the CAG's appointment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Cabinet Secretariat is best characterised as:
questions.a: A permanent civil‑service body governed by the Transaction of Business Rules.
opts: A political office akin to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).
A permanent civil‑service body governed by the Transaction of Business Rules.
A constitutional authority established under Article 77 of the Constitution.
An ad‑hoc body constituted only during national emergencies.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that the Cabinet Secretariat is a permanent civil‑service body governed by the Transaction of Business Rules, and warns against treating it as a political office akin to the PMO. It is not a constitutional authority under Article 77 (which deals with conduct of business), nor is it an ad‑hoc emergency body. Its role includes crisis management and inter‑ministerial coordination as a standing administrative structure.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: On what grounds can the Supreme Court strike down an ordinance promulgated by the President?
questions.a: For mala fides, re‑promulgation, or lack of urgency.
opts: Only if the ordinance is not ratified by Parliament within the six‑week window.
If the ordinance is promulgated without the subjective satisfaction of the President.
For mala fides, re‑promulgation, or lack of urgency.
Only if the ordinance violates the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution.
questions.solution: The lesson outlines the evolving judicial standards: the Supreme Court can strike down ordinances for mala fides, re‑promulgation, or lack of urgency, as seen in the D.C. Wadhwa and Krishna Kumar Singh cases. While non‑ratification leads to lapse, it is not a ground for judicial striking down. The Court does not examine the President's subjective satisfaction (which is non‑justiciable), and basic structure violation is a broader ground not limited to ordinances.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which statement correctly reflects the legal status of the Attorney General's advice to the Government of India?
questions.a: The Attorney General's advice is advisory; the government may reject it but must record reasons.
opts: The Attorney General's advice is binding on the executive and cannot be disregarded.
The Attorney General's advice is advisory; the government may reject it but must record reasons.
The Attorney General's opinion on judicial appointments overrides the collegium's recommendation.
The Attorney General is a member of the Cabinet and enjoys parliamentary privilege.
questions.solution: The lesson cites the 1998 State of Punjab v. Union of India case, which clarified that the AG's advice is not binding; the executive may reject it but must record reasons. Option A contradicts this principle. Option C is incorrect because the Third Judges case held the AG's opinion carries weight but does not override the collegium. Option D is false as the AG is not a Cabinet member and does not enjoy parliamentary privilege, though they may attend Cabinet meetings on legal issues.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under Article 85(1) of the Constitution, the President is obliged to summon each House of Parliament such that the maximum interval between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next session shall not exceed:
questions.solution: Article 85(1) explicitly mandates that six months shall not intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next session. This constitutional ceiling ensures legislative accountability and prevents the executive from indefinitely avoiding parliamentary scrutiny. The 2020 winter session gap of 176 days (approximately 5.8 months) was criticized but did not breach this six-month limit, hence no judicial intervention occurred. The President acts on ministerial advice for summoning, but may return the recommendation if the gap threatens to exceed this constitutional limit.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the National Security Council (NSC) constituted in 1998, who serves as the Secretary of the Council?
opts: The Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister
questions.solution: The lesson text states that the NSC is chaired by the Prime Minister and comprises key ministers, with the National Security Advisor (NSA) serving as its secretary. The NSA is the primary advisor to the Prime Minister on national security matters and coordinates the NSC's functioning. The Cabinet Secretary, while crucial for inter-ministerial coordination, is not the NSC Secretary. The NSC is an advisory body; the Prime Minister takes final decisions based on its recommendations.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: The Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) introduced in 1997 classified households into which categories based on a consumption-expenditure survey?
questions.a: Above Poverty Line (APL) and Below Poverty Line (BPL) only
opts: Above Poverty Line (APL) and Below Poverty Line (BPL) only
APL, BPL, and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) categories
Priority and Non-Priority households under NFSA
questions.solution: The lesson states that the TPDS adopted in 1997 'classified households into Above Poverty Line and Below Poverty Line categories based on a consumption‑expenditure survey.' The AAY category was introduced later (2000) as a subset of BPL, and the three-fold APL/BPL/AAY classification became formalised under TPDS by 2000-01, but the 1997 launch specifically mentions only APL and BPL. The other options refer to later frameworks (NFSA's priority/non-priority) or design typologies (universal/categorical/means-tested) not used for the 1997 TPDS classification.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which governance reform mechanism is mandated under both MGNREGA and NFSA to empower gram sabhas to scrutinise expenditure and verify beneficiary lists?
questions.solution: Section 5.3 explicitly states: 'Social audits, mandated under MGNREGA and NFSA, empower gram sabhas to scrutinise expenditure, verify beneficiary lists and demand corrective action.' This dual mandate is a key feature of the rights-based architecture. Outcome-based budgeting (section 5.2) is a central ministry tool, citizen engagement platforms are complementary digital tools, and performance-based grants are Finance Commission incentives to states - none are mandated for gram sabha-level scrutiny under both Acts.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the Supreme Court's 2018 ruling in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India regarding Aadhaar and welfare services?
questions.a: Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for services that are not backed by law, and alternative identifiers must be provided.
opts: Aadhaar must be made mandatory for all central and state welfare schemes.
Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for services that are not backed by law, and alternative identifiers must be provided.
Aadhaar authentication is optional only for Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) schemes.
Aadhaar is mandatory for all schemes except those explicitly exempted by the Finance Commission.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court held that Aadhaar cannot be compelled for services lacking statutory backing. Consequently, the government introduced alternative identifiers such as voter ID and ration card for certain schemes. This ruling directly limits mandatory Aadhaar use and mandates provision of alternatives, making option B the accurate reflection of the judgment.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), the cash benefit is conditioned on which specific health‑seeking behaviour?
questions.a: Institutional delivery in a public or accredited private health facility.
opts: Institutional delivery in a public or accredited private health facility.
Early registration of pregnancy within the first trimester.
Immunisation of the newborn within six weeks.
questions.solution: JSY is designed to promote safe motherhood by providing cash assistance conditional on the beneficiary delivering in an institution (public or accredited private). The scheme does not require completion of antenatal visits, early registration, or newborn immunisation as the triggering condition; those are features of other programmes such as PMMVY. Hence, option B correctly identifies the JSY conditionality.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: What is the nature of the social audit requirement under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) and the National Food Security Act (NFSA)?
questions.a: A mandatory periodic process that must be carried out at regular intervals.
opts: A one‑time audit conducted at the end of each financial year.
A mandatory periodic process that must be carried out at regular intervals.
An optional exercise left to the discretion of the Gram Panchayat.
A central government‑led audit with no role for local institutions.
questions.solution: Both MGNREGA and NFSA institutionalise social audit as a recurring, mandatory exercise — not a single event. The legislation prescribes regular social audits (e.g., every six months under MGNREGA) to ensure continuous community oversight of implementation. Treating it as a one‑time or optional activity contradicts the statutory design. Therefore, option B accurately describes the mandatory periodic nature of social audits.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: For Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), what is the standard Centre‑State funding ratio for general category states?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the typical funding pattern for CSS follows a 60:40 Centre‑State split for general category states, while special category states (North‑East, Himalayan) receive a 90:10 split. This ratio determines the fiscal space available to states for scheme implementation. Option B matches the prescribed 60:40 sharing arrangement.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which provisions were introduced by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 to govern data use in digital welfare delivery?
questions.a: Purpose limitation, data minimisation, and establishment of a Data Protection Board.
opts: Mandatory Aadhaar linkage for all welfare databases and unrestricted data sharing.
Purpose limitation, data minimisation, and establishment of a Data Protection Board.
Removal of consent requirements for government agencies accessing citizen data.
Automatic deletion of all welfare data after one year.
questions.solution: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 brings in core data‑protection principles such as purpose limitation (data used only for specified purposes), data minimisation (collecting only what is necessary), and creates a Data Protection Board to oversee compliance. These safeguards directly address privacy concerns arising from the concentration of welfare data in central repositories. Option B correctly lists the Act's key provisions.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: Which of the following measures was introduced by the Ministry of Women and Child Development in 2022 to rationalise the workload of Anganwadi Workers?
questions.a: Capping AWW responsibilities at 30 core activities and removing non‑core duties such as election work.
opts: Mandatory 10‑day annual residential training certified by NIRD.
Capping AWW responsibilities at 30 core activities and removing non‑core duties such as election work.
Linking frontline workers to a portable pension‑cum‑insurance scheme financed by a 0.5 % cess.
Establishing a unified grievance redressal mechanism for frontline workers.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the 2022 Ministry of Women and Child Development directive capped AWW responsibilities at 30 core activities, removing non‑core duties such as election work. This is a clear workload rationalisation measure. The other options refer to proposals under discussion (training, pension‑cum‑insurance, grievance mechanism) but were not the 2022 directive.
questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.q: In the Union Budget 2023‑24 Gender Budget Statement (Statement 13), how are gender‑neutral schemes treated?
questions.a: They are included but a gender audit is mandated for each line item.
opts: They are excluded from the Gender Budget Statement altogether.
They are classified as pro‑women schemes with a minimum 30 % allocation.
They are included but a gender audit is mandated for each line item.
They receive a 100 % earmarking for women‑specific components.
questions.solution: According to the lesson, the Gender Budget Statement classifies expenditures into three categories: women‑specific (100 %), pro‑women (≥30 %), and gender‑neutral schemes where a gender audit is mandated. Thus gender‑neutral schemes are not excluded nor automatically given a 30 % allocation; they require a gender audit.
