questions.q: According to the verification protocol for digital sources, which step is essential before citing a digital transcription?

The first and most fundamental step is to verify that a facsimile exists and to match it against the transcription, because OCR errors in Devanagari Dogri are frequent and metadata may be inconsistent. Downloading a PDF, relying solely on metadata, or assuming OCR accuracy would bypass this crucial cross‑check. Hence, the essential step is confirming facsimile availability and comparing image with transcription.

Demonstrate the direct influence of European modernist techniques without any indigenous narrative adaptation.
Replace the traditional frame narrative device entirely, marking a complete break from oral storytelling conventions.

The dissolution of the Dogri Sanstha due to script purism conflicts.

This cause-effect chain is presented as the model for high-scoring answers. Option B is incorrect because Takri standardization for digital archives (CIIL/IIT Jammu) occurred much later (2019 model). Option C describes a later development (translations facilitating comparative studies) not linked to the 1985 mandate. Option D is not mentioned; the text notes "tensions" between Sanstha and Academy, not dissolution.

questions.q: In the structuralist analysis of river imagery in Dogri poetry, what distinguishes the connotative level from the denotative level?
questions.a: The connotative level signifies concepts such as zindagi, behna, and parivartan
opts: The connotative level supplies concrete sensory details like sound of rapids and smell of wet clay
The connotative level signifies concepts such as zindagi, behna, and parivartan
The denotative level reflects the rise of environmental activism in the Jammu region
The denotative level operates as a lyrical conduit linking pastoral past to urban present
questions.solution: The lesson clearly distinguishes the two semiotic levels: at the denotative level, the river supplies concrete sensory details (sound of rapids, smell of wet clay, seasonal flood cycle), while at the connotative level, the river becomes a signifier for concepts such as zindagi (life), behna (flow), and parivartan (change). Option A describes the denotative level, while options C and D describe thematic evolutions, not the structuralist distinction between levels.

questions.q: Which characteristic of Dogri folk theatre is identified as its oral-performative core, distinguishing it from static scripts?
questions.a: Improvisation and audience interaction during performance
opts: Fixed textual manuscripts preserved by the Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages
Improvisation and audience interaction during performance
Use of traditional dholak patterns as background music
Dramatised readings broadcast on All India Radio's Dogri Kahani programme
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states in the 'common pitfalls' section: 'Assuming folk theatre texts are static scripts; the oral-performative core resides in improvisation and audience interaction.' This directly identifies improvisation and audience interaction as the core. Option A refers to institutional preservation, option C describes radio production policy, and option D describes a radio programme format, not the folk theatre's core performative dimension.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly identifies the historiographical phase of Dogri literary criticism characterised by the application of post-structuralist, feminist, and ecocritical frameworks alongside the digitisation of manuscripts on the CIIL Dogri Online portal?
questions.a: The contemporary theoretical phase beginning in the 1990s with scholars affiliated to CIIL and university departments
opts: The colonial linguistic survey phase represented by Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India (1919)
The institutional patronage phase following the establishment of the Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages (1958)
The contemporary theoretical phase beginning in the 1990s with scholars affiliated to CIIL and university departments
The nation-building phase of the 1970s reflected in Dogri Sahitya Akademi award citations
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly outlines three phases: (1) colonial surveys (Grierson 1919), (2) post-1947 institutional patronage (Academy 1958, Akademi 1978), and (3) a third phase beginning in the 1990s marked by post-structuralist/feminist/ecocritical frameworks, CIIL affiliation, translation projects, digitisation on the CIIL Dogri Online portal, and comparative studies. Option 3 matches this description exactly. Option 1 describes phase 1, option 2 describes phase 2, and option 4 describes a specific aspect of phase 2 (1970s nation-building agenda).

questions.q: In the Comparative Textual Methodology for Paper II, what is the third stage after genre-specific coding and thematic clustering?
questions.a: Inter-generic dialogue: tracing how a motif transforms when it migrates across genres
opts: Inter-generic dialogue: tracing how a motif transforms when it migrates across genres
Critical edition preparation: constructing a stemma codicum for multiple witnesses
Digital imaging and transcription: capturing high-resolution images at 600 dpi
Conservation prioritisation: applying the IFLA risk assessment matrix

opts: IFLA (International Federation of Library Associations) risk assessment matrix
FADGI (Federal Agencies Digital Guidelines Initiative) four-star standard
Lachmannian stemmatic method for archetype reconstruction

questions.q: In the 1972 anthology "Dogri Poetry in Translation" edited by Ved Rahi, which thematic content was omitted or softened to align with a nationalist narrative of regional integration?
questions.a: Verses referencing the 1947 Partition displacement of Dogri-speaking communities
opts: Poems celebrating the Chenab valley's pastoral imagery
Verses referencing the 1947 Partition displacement of Dogri-speaking communities
Poems employing folk-song refrains as structural leitmotifs
Verses critiquing the purdah system through domestic ritual description
questions.solution: The lesson states that the 1972 anthology retained poems dealing with the Chenab valley's pastoral imagery but omitted or softened verses referencing the 1947 Partition displacement of Dogri-speaking communities. This editorial decision aligned with the Centre's cultural policy of the 1970s, framing the collection as a "bridge between the hills and the plains."

questions.q: Which narrative strategy in Dogri women's autobiographical writing involves the recurring folk-song refrain "Chann ve chann" functioning as both a mnemonic device and a subversive echo of oral tradition?
questions.a: Use of the folk-song refrain as a structural leitmotif
opts: Interleaving domestic ritual description with meta-commentary on writing
Use of the folk-song refrain as a structural leitmotif
Direct address to the reader in confessional mode
Incorporation of archival photographs and manuscript facsimiles
questions.solution: The lesson identifies the use of the folk-song refrain as a structural leitmotif as a second strategy, citing the recurring line "Chann ve chann" which functions both as a mnemonic device linking episodic memories and as a subversive echo of the oral tradition that historically excluded women's voices.
questions.subject: Dogri Literature

questions.q: In the 1998 anthology "Voices from the Jammu Plains," the Dogri term "kotha" is rendered as "mansion" with a footnote explaining "traditional courtyard house." What does this gloss reveal about the translator's ideological positioning?
questions.a: It enacts a cultural substitution that replaces a multi-generational household concept with an elite English connotation
opts: It prioritizes semantic precision by preserving the culturally specific architectural term
It enacts a cultural substitution that replaces a multi-generational household concept with an elite English connotation
It demonstrates the translator's adherence to the Sahitya Akademi's 1965 grant scheme guidelines
It reflects the influence of the Progressive Writers' Association on translation policy
questions.solution: The gloss replaces the culturally specific term "kotha" (denoting a multi-generational household centred on a courtyard) with "mansion," a word connoting elite residence, thereby shifting the semantic field. This cultural substitution reveals the translator's ideological positioning by privileging a target-language term that erases the indigenous social structure embedded in the source term.
questions.subject: Dogri Literature

questions.q: The inaugural Sahitya Akademi Dogri language award in 1971 was given to Padma Sachdev for which work, establishing a precedent for honouring poetry blending folk idiom with modernist form?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the inaugural award (1971) went to Padma Sachdev for "Mithi Deewar," establishing a precedent for honouring poetry that blends folk idiom with modernist form. The other works are associated with later awardees: Shiv Nath Shastri's "Pita Putra" (1975), Ved Rahi's "Kahani Sangrah" (1980), and "Ghar Ki Baat" is a serialized memoir from 1992-94.

questions.q: Which element of a Dogri manuscript colophon is primarily used by scholars to reconstruct networks of scribal families?
questions.solution: The colophon records the scribe, patron, date, and place, but the scribe's name together with his lineage (e.g., "Likhita Lakhmi Chand, shishya of Pandit Ram Das") allows scholars to trace scribal families such as the Lakhmi Chand, Gopal Das, and Hari Ram lineages across the Jammu‑Kashmir hills and Punjab plains. Patron names, dates, and places provide contextual metadata but do not directly reveal the transmission network of scribes.

questions.q: The money multiplier is higher when:
questions.solution: M = (1 + c)/(c + r). A fall in the currency–deposit ratio (c) raises the multiplier; higher reserves (r) lower it.

questions.q: The Solow growth model predicts that, in the long run, output per worker depends on:
questions.solution: In the Solow model, steady-state output per worker depends on capital per worker (saving, depreciation, population growth) and on technology (TFP).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: A public good is characterised by:
questions.solution: Public goods are non-rival (one person’s use does not reduce another’s) and non-excludable (no one can be kept out), causing market failure.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The ‘drain theory’ in Indian economic history referred to:
questions.a: Transfer of wealth from India to Britain
opts: Transfer of wealth from India to Britain
questions.solution: Dadabhai Naoroji’s drain theory described the unrequited transfer of Indian wealth to Britain through trade surpluses, home charges and services.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The Phillips curve shows the short-run relationship between:
questions.solution: The Phillips curve shows the inverse short-run relationship between inflation and unemployment; the expectations-augmented version explains stagflation.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the context of natural monopolies, if a regulator applies the Ramsey-Boiteux Pricing rule to minimize deadweight loss while ensuring cost coverage, what is the mathematical condition for price setting across different products?
questions.a: (P_i - MC_i) / P_i = λ where λ is a constant across all products
opts: (P_i - MC_i) / P_i = λ where λ is a constant across all products
questions.solution: The standard monopoly condition MR=MC leads to significant deadweight loss. The Ramsey-Boiteux rule is an advanced pricing strategy specifically designed for natural monopolies under regulation. It dictates that the firm should not set price equal to marginal cost (which would fail to cover costs) nor engage in perfect price discrimination. Instead, it requires setting prices such that the inverse elasticity markup is constant across all products. Mathematically, this is expressed as (P_i - MC_i) / P_i = λ, where λ represents a uniform constant determined by the need to cover total fixed costs. This minimizes welfare loss compared to a single-price monopoly while ensuring financial viability.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Consider an economy at full employment (Vertical AS curve). If the Central Bank implements an expansionary monetary policy by increasing the Money Supply, what is the final outcome regarding output and interest rates according to the IS-LM-AS framework?
questions.a: Output remains stuck at Y^* while interest rates rise back to original levels
opts: Output rises above potential GDP and interest rates fall
Output remains stuck at Y^* while interest rates rise back to original levels
Output falls due to a liquidity trap and interest rates remain unchanged
Interest rates fall permanently while output fluctuates randomly
questions.solution: When an economy is at full employment, the Aggregate Supply (AS) curve is vertical at potential GDP (Y^*). An expansionary monetary policy initially shifts the LM curve to the right. In the short run, this lowers interest rates and stimulates investment, pushing output toward Y^*. However, because the AS curve is vertical, any further increase in aggregate demand cannot raise real output; instead, it manifests as higher prices. As price levels rise, the real money supply effectively contracts or expectations adjust, causing the LM curve to shift back until it intersects the IS and AS curves at Y^*. Consequently, output remains stuck at its potential level, and interest rates return to (or slightly exceed) their original equilibrium level.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: According to the Ramsey Rule for optimal commodity taxation, how should taxes be structured across different goods to minimize deadweight loss?
questions.a: Taxes should be inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand
opts: Taxes should be proportional to the price of the good
Taxes should be inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand
Taxes should be higher on essential goods like salt and tobacco
Taxes should be zero for all luxury goods
questions.solution: The Ramsey Rule provides a guideline for optimal taxation in public economics. It states that to minimize the efficiency cost (deadweight loss) of taxation, taxes should be inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand for different goods. Mathematically, t_i ∝ 1/ε_i. Goods with high elasticity (where consumers are sensitive to price changes, like luxury cars) should bear lower tax rates because a high tax would cause a large reduction in quantity demanded, creating significant welfare loss. Conversely, goods with low elasticity (inelastic demand, like salt or tobacco) can sustain higher taxes without causing a drastic drop in consumption, thereby minimizing the overall deadweight loss to society.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: India's economic transition from agriculture to services rather than manufacturing challenges which specific assumption of the classic Lewis Model?
questions.a: The assumption that capital accumulation automatically creates enough jobs for migrating labor
opts: The assumption that capital accumulation automatically creates enough jobs for migrating labor
The assumption that surplus labor exists in agriculture
The assumption that wages are constant until full employment is reached
The assumption that industrialization leads to absolute convergence
questions.solution: The classic Lewis Dual Sector Model posits that as capital accumulates in the industrial sector, it absorbs surplus labor from the traditional agricultural sector. A critical underlying assumption is that this capital accumulation automatically generates sufficient employment opportunities for the migrating workforce. India's recent experience of 'Premature De-industrialization,' where the economy shifted rapidly to services while manufacturing employment elasticity remained low, directly challenges this assumption. The data shows that despite GDP growth and capital deepening, the structural transformation did not create enough labor-intensive jobs in manufacturing to absorb the surplus agricultural labor, leading to a divergence from the Lewis Model's prediction of rapid industrialization and job creation.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In analyzing the inflation-unemployment trade-off using the Phillips Curve, why is it considered a fatal error to ignore the expectations-augmented version or supply shocks?
questions.a: Because ignoring them leads to incorrect policy recommendations during stagflation
opts: Because the original curve suggests a permanent trade-off exists
Because ignoring them leads to incorrect policy recommendations during stagflation
Because the natural rate hypothesis was never proposed
Because inflation targeting frameworks do not exist
questions.solution: Static analysis of the Phillips Curve often depicts a stable negative relationship between inflation and unemployment. However, advanced analysis requires incorporating the expectations-augmented version (Friedman-Phelps) and supply shocks. Ignoring these factors is fatal because if policymakers try to exploit the static trade-off by keeping unemployment below the natural rate, inflation expectations will rise, shifting the curve upward. This can lead to stagflation—a scenario of high inflation combined with high unemployment caused by adverse supply shocks (like an oil price hike). Failing to mention these dynamics results in a superficial understanding that could lead to disastrous policy recommendations, such as increasing demand during a supply shock, which would worsen both inflation and output gaps.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In a large‑country model, the optimal tariff that maximizes national welfare is given by which formula, where ε* is the foreign export‑supply elasticity?
questions.solution: The optimal‑tariff formula derived from the large‑country welfare decomposition is τ* = 1/(ε* – 1). A large country can influence its terms of trade; the tariff that equates the marginal terms‑of‑trade gain to the marginal deadweight loss yields this expression. The denominator uses the foreign export‑supply elasticity minus one, not plus one, and the tariff is the reciprocal of that term. Options A, C, and D misstate the algebraic relationship.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) used which variable as an instrument for early property‑rights institutions in their “colonial origins” study?
questions.solution: The seminal AJR (2001) paper argues that European settler mortality rates during colonisation determined whether colonisers established extractive or inclusive institutions. Because mortality is exogenous to current income, it serves as a valid instrument for the historical property‑rights institutions that persist today. The other variables are either outcomes or correlated with geography but were not used as the primary instrument in that study.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: When valuing a non‑market environmental good, which technique relies on observing actual behaviour in related markets rather than on survey‑based stated preferences?
questions.solution: Hedonic pricing is a revealed‑preference method that infers the value of environmental attributes (e.g., air quality) from observed price differentials in housing or labour markets. Contingent valuation and choice experiments are stated‑preference approaches that ask respondents directly about willingness to pay. Benefit transfer applies values from existing studies to a new context and does not generate primary behavioural data.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The joint‑hypothesis problem in tests of market efficiency implies that a rejection of the CAPM could be due to either market inefficiency or which of the following?
questions.solution: Fama (1970) highlighted that any test of market efficiency is a joint test of efficiency and the asset‑pricing model used to define “normal” returns. If the CAPM is rejected, it may be because markets are inefficient or because the CAPM itself is misspecified (e.g., missing risk factors). The other options are potential empirical issues but do not capture the core joint‑hypothesis distinction.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Randomised controlled trials of automatic enrolment in retirement savings plans have shown that participation rates rise from roughly 40 % to above what level?
questions.solution: Empirical evaluations cited in the lesson report that default enrolment (a nudge) lifts participation from about 40 % to over 90 %. This large jump illustrates the power of the default effect, a core prediction of bounded‑rationality and nudge theory. The other percentages understate the documented impact.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: According to the optimal tariff formula τ* = 1/(ε* – 1), what happens to the optimal tariff for a small country where foreign export supply elasticity (ε*) approaches infinity?
questions.solution: The optimal tariff formula τ* = 1/(ε* – 1) shows that the optimal tariff depends inversely on the foreign export supply elasticity ε*. For a small country, the foreign export supply is perfectly elastic, so ε* → ∞. Substituting ε* → ∞ into the formula gives τ* = 1/(∞ – 1) = 0. Thus, a small country cannot improve its terms of trade through a tariff; any tariff only creates deadweight loss.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the Lucas (1988) endogenous growth model, the long-run growth rate of output per worker is determined by:
questions.a: The fraction of time devoted to education (u) and the productivity of schooling (φ)
opts: The fraction of time devoted to education (u) and the productivity of schooling (φ)
The rate of exogenous technological progress
The depreciation rate of physical capital
questions.solution: In the Lucas (1988) model, human capital accumulates according to Ḣ = φ u H, where u is the fraction of time spent on education and φ is the productivity of schooling. The long-run growth rate of output per worker equals the growth rate of human capital, which is φ u. This growth rate is endogenous and depends on policy choices that affect u and φ, unlike the Solow model where long-run growth is exogenous.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Which of the following is a key requirement of the NOAA guidelines for contingent valuation studies?
questions.a: Use of a referendum format and pre-testing for hypothetical bias
opts: Use of a referendum format and pre-testing for hypothetical bias
Reliance solely on revealed preference methods
questions.solution: The NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) guidelines for contingent valuation studies were established to improve reliability. Key requirements include using a referendum (dichotomous choice) format rather than open-ended questions, conducting extensive pre-testing, and correcting for hypothetical bias through careful survey design. The guidelines also recommend conservative design choices. Option C correctly captures the referendum format and hypothetical bias correction.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the Brander-Spencer model of strategic trade policy, what is a key assumption regarding the timing of the government's export subsidy?
questions.a: The government can commit to the subsidy before firms choose output
opts: The subsidy is announced after firms choose output
The government can commit to the subsidy before firms choose output
The subsidy is set simultaneously with foreign government policy
The subsidy is adjusted continuously based on market shares
questions.solution: The Brander-Spencer model analyzes strategic trade policy in a Cournot duopoly. A critical assumption is that the domestic government acts as a Stackelberg leader by committing to an export subsidy before firms choose their output levels. This commitment allows the domestic firm to expand output credibly, shifting profits from the foreign rival. If the subsidy were announced after output choices, the profit-shifting effect would not occur.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: What is the vertical devolution share of States in the divisible pool as per the 15th Finance Commission (2021-26)?
questions.solution: The 15th Finance Commission (2021-26) recommended that 41% of the divisible pool of central taxes be devolved to the states as vertical devolution. This is a reduction from the 42% recommended by the 14th Finance Commission. The horizontal distribution among states uses criteria with weights: income distance (45%), population (15%), area (15%), forest and ecology (10%), demographic performance (12.5%), and tax effort (2.5%).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the discrete‑time debt dynamics equation Δd = (r – g) d – p, the debt‑stabilising primary balance p* is given by:
questions.solution: Setting the change in the debt‑to‑GDP ratio to zero (Δd = 0) for a stable debt path gives 0 = (r – g) d – p. Rearranging yields p = (r – g) d. This primary surplus exactly offsets the automatic increase in the debt ratio when the nominal interest rate exceeds nominal GDP growth. If r > g, a positive primary surplus is required; if g > r, a primary deficit can be compatible with a falling debt ratio. The formula p* = (r – g) d is therefore the debt‑stabilising primary balance.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The Shapiro‑Stiglitz efficiency‑wage (no‑shirking) condition requires specification of which two parameters?
questions.solution: In the Shapiro‑Stiglitz model, workers choose effort to avoid being caught shirking. The no‑shirking condition equates the expected cost of shirking (probability of detection multiplied by the penalty, which is the loss of the wage rent) to the disutility of effort. Therefore the condition explicitly requires the detection probability and the effort cost (or disutility of effort). The other pairs belong to the DMP matching framework or to general macro parameters, not to the Shapiro‑Stiglitz no‑shirking condition.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the New Keynesian Phillips curve πₜ = β Eₜ[πₜ₊₁] + κ ŷₜ, the slope κ becomes steeper when:
opts: The Calvo price‑stickiness parameter θ increases
The household discount factor β decreases
The degree of price stickiness rises
questions.solution: The slope κ is proportional to (1‑θ)(1‑βθ)/θ. A lower θ means firms reset prices more frequently, reducing price stickiness and increasing the responsiveness of current inflation to the output gap. Hence decreasing θ steepens the Phillips curve, while increasing θ or raising price stickiness flattens it.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the financial accelerator framework, which parameter captures the cost incurred by lenders to monitor borrowers’ returns?
questions.solution: The financial accelerator model introduces a monitoring cost parameter (often denoted μ) that represents the resources lenders must expend to verify the realized returns of borrowers. This friction creates an external finance premium. The loan‑to‑value ratio, capital adequacy ratio, and deposit insurance premium are distinct regulatory or contractual variables, not the monitoring cost itself.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the Grossman‑Helpman protection‑for‑sale model, the equilibrium tariff for an organised sector tᵢ* = (1/a)(∂W/∂tᵢ)/(∂πᵢ/∂tᵢ) rises when:
questions.a: The marginal effect of the tariff on social welfare ∂W/∂tᵢ increases
opts: The weight on social welfare a increases
The marginal profit of the lobby from the tariff ∂πᵢ/∂tᵢ increases
The marginal effect of the tariff on social welfare ∂W/∂tᵢ increases
The number of unorganised sectors rises
questions.solution: From the equilibrium condition tᵢ* = (1/a)·(∂W/∂tᵢ)/(∂πᵢ/∂tᵢ), the tariff is directly proportional to the marginal impact of the tariff on aggregate welfare (∂W/∂tᵢ) and inversely proportional to both the welfare weight a and the lobby’s marginal profit sensitivity (∂πᵢ/∂tᵢ). Hence an increase in ∂W/∂tᵢ raises the equilibrium tariff.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of perfect competition?
questions.solution: Perfect competition assumes many buyers & sellers, homogeneous products, free entry & exit, perfect information, NO market power (price takers).

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of monopolistic competition?
questions.solution: Monopolistic competition has many sellers, differentiated products, free entry & exit - all three characteristics.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a condition for Pareto efficiency?
questions.solution: Pareto efficiency requires exchange efficiency, production efficiency, & product mix efficiency - NOT income equality (equity vs efficiency trade-off).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of perfect competition?
questions.solution: Perfect competition has many buyers & sellers, homogeneous products, free entry & exit - all three characteristics.

questions.q: The Lerner Index measures:
questions.solution: Lerner Index L = (P - MC)/P = -1/|e| measures degree of monopoly power (market power). Higher L = more monopoly power.

questions.q: What does the Sonnenschein‑Mantel‑Debreu (SMD) theorem state about the aggregate excess‑demand function?
questions.a: Any continuous function satisfying Walras' law and homogeneity of degree zero can be an aggregate excess‑demand function.
opts: It must be downward sloping and globally stable.
Any continuous function satisfying Walras' law and homogeneity of degree zero can be an aggregate excess‑demand function.
It guarantees the uniqueness of competitive equilibrium.
It requires all individual excess‑demand functions to be derived from convex preferences.
questions.solution: The SMD theorem shows that the only restrictions on aggregate excess demand are continuity, homogeneity of degree zero, and Walras' law. No further structure (such as the law of demand or convexity) is implied. Therefore, any function meeting those three conditions can arise as the aggregate excess‑demand function of some economy, implying that multiple equilibria, cycles, or chaotic dynamics are theoretically possible. Option B captures this exact statement.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the Diamond OLG model with Cobb‑Douglas production Y = K^α (AL)^(1‑α) and log utility, the steady‑state capital per worker k* is given by which expression?
questions.solution: The lesson provides the steady‑state condition k* = [αβ / (1 + n)]^(1/(1‑α)), where α is the capital share, β the discount factor, and n the population growth rate. This follows from the saving function derived from log utility and the Cobb‑Douglas production function. Option A matches the formula exactly.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the Mirrlees optimal nonlinear income tax formula presented, the optimal marginal tax rate T'(y) depends on which variables?
questions.a: The social marginal welfare weight G(y), the local Pareto parameter α(y), and the elasticity of taxable income ε(y).
opts: Only the social marginal welfare weight G(y).
The social marginal welfare weight G(y), the local Pareto parameter α(y), and the elasticity of taxable income ε(y).
The Ramsey inverse‑elasticity rule applied to labour income.
questions.solution: The lesson gives the Mirrlees formula T'(y) = (1 - G(y)) / (1 - G(y) + α(y) ε(y)), where G(y) is the social marginal welfare weight, α(y) the local Pareto parameter of the income distribution, and ε(y) the elasticity of taxable income. Thus the optimal marginal tax rate depends on all three variables. Option B lists them correctly.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The Tiebout model's conclusion that local public goods are efficiently provided relies on which set of assumptions?
questions.a: A continuum of communities, zero moving costs, and perfect information.
opts: A small number of jurisdictions, positive moving costs, and imperfect information.
A continuum of communities, zero moving costs, and perfect information.
Centralized tax collection and uniform preferences across jurisdictions.
Presence of significant spillovers and heterogeneous preferences.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Tiebout theorem assumes a continuum of communities, zero moving costs, and perfect information — conditions rarely met in practice. These assumptions allow households to "vote with their feet" and achieve efficient provision of local public goods. Option B matches the required assumptions.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In an infinitely repeated game, the folk theorem shows that cooperation can be sustained as a subgame‑perfect equilibrium only if which condition holds?
questions.a: The discount factor is sufficiently high
opts: The discount factor is sufficiently high
The game has a finite horizon
Players are myopic and ignore future payoffs
The stage game possesses multiple Nash equilibria
questions.solution: The folk theorem states that any feasible, individually rational payoff vector can be sustained as a subgame‑perfect equilibrium in an infinitely repeated game provided the discount factor δ is sufficiently high. A high δ means players value future payoffs enough to make the threat of future punishment credible, deterring unilateral deviation. A finite horizon, myopic players, or multiple stage‑game Nash equilibria are not sufficient for the folk theorem; the key requirement is a high enough discount factor.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: According to the Taylor principle, the coefficient on inflation in the Taylor rule must satisfy which inequality to ensure determinacy?
questions.solution: The Taylor principle requires the central bank to raise the nominal interest rate more than one‑for‑one with an increase in inflation, i.e., the inflation coefficient must be greater than 1. If the coefficient is ≤ 1, a rise in inflation lowers the real interest rate, leading to indeterminacy and multiple equilibria. Therefore, to anchor inflation expectations and achieve a unique rational expectations equilibrium, the coefficient on inflation must exceed unity.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The modern micro‑founded gravity equation includes multilateral resistance terms. What do these terms capture?
questions.a: The effect of third‑country trade costs on bilateral trade flows
opts: Only bilateral tariffs between the two trading partners
The effect of third‑country trade costs on bilateral trade flows
Exchange rate volatility between the two countries
Domestic subsidy rates in the exporting country
questions.solution: Anderson and van Wincoop (2003) derived the gravity equation from a CES demand system, showing that bilateral trade depends not only on bilateral barriers but also on each country's average trade barriers with all partners — the multilateral resistance terms. These terms reflect how third‑country trade costs affect the relative attractiveness of trading with a specific partner. They are distinct from bilateral tariffs alone, exchange rate volatility, or domestic subsidies.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: The Solow model predicts conditional convergence. This means that poorer countries grow faster than richer ones only after controlling for which set of variables?
questions.a: Savings rate, population growth, and technology
opts: Savings rate, population growth, and technology
Inflation rate and exchange rate regime
Trade openness and foreign direct investment
questions.solution: In the Solow framework, each country converges to its own steady state determined by its savings rate, population growth rate, and level of technology (total factor productivity). Conditional convergence holds when these determinants are held constant; unconditional convergence across all countries does not occur because steady states differ. Thus the correct conditioning variables are the savings rate, population growth, and technology.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Weitzman (1974) compares an emission tax with a tradable‑permit (cap) system under uncertainty. If the marginal damage (MD) curve is steeper than the marginal abatement cost (MAC) curve, which instrument is welfare‑superior?
questions.solution: Weitzman's rule states that the choice between a price instrument (tax) and a quantity instrument (cap) depends on the relative slopes of the marginal damage and marginal abatement cost curves. When the MD curve is steeper than the MAC curve, the welfare loss from quantity errors (under a cap) exceeds that from price errors (under a tax). Hence a tax, which fixes the price of emissions, is preferred. Conversely, if MAC is steeper, a cap is superior.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Under perfect capital mobility, which policy becomes ineffective when a country maintains a fixed exchange rate according to the Mundell‑Fleming model?
questions.solution: In the Mundell‑Fleming framework with perfect capital mobility, a fixed exchange rate forces the domestic interest rate to equal the world interest rate. Any attempt by the central bank to change the money supply triggers offsetting capital flows that restore the interest parity, leaving output unchanged. Hence monetary policy loses its effectiveness, while fiscal policy remains potent because the central bank must accommodate the resulting capital flows to keep the exchange rate fixed.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In a Cournot duopoly with linear inverse demand P = a − bQ and identical constant marginal cost c, what is each firm's Nash equilibrium output?
questions.solution: Each firm's reaction function is q_i = (a − c − b q_j) / (2b). Imposing symmetry (q_i = q_j = q*) gives q* = (a − c − b q*) / (2b). Solving yields 2b q* = a − c − b q* → 3b q* = a − c → q* = (a − c) / (3b). This is the Cournot‑Nash equilibrium quantity for each firm.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: What is a major econometric concern when interpreting the Mincer coefficient on schooling as a causal return to education?
questions.solution: The Mincer equation regresses log wages on schooling and experience. If innate ability is positively correlated with both schooling and earnings, omitting ability from the regression causes omitted‑variable bias. The estimated schooling coefficient then captures both the true return to education and the effect of ability, overstating the causal return. Addressing this requires instrumental variables, sibling fixed effects, or other strategies to isolate the exogenous variation in schooling.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: According to the New Institutional Framework, why may the Coase theorem fail to achieve efficient outcomes in practice?
questions.a: Because transaction costs such as asymmetric information and hold‑up exist
opts: Because property rights are always well defined
Because transaction costs such as asymmetric information and hold‑up exist
Because government intervention is always required
questions.solution: The Coase theorem states that with zero transaction costs and well‑defined property rights, bargaining leads to an efficient allocation regardless of the initial rights assignment. In reality, transaction costs — including asymmetric information, hold‑up problems, and enforcement costs — are positive. These costs impede bargaining, prevent the full internalisation of externalities, and thus cause the theorem's predictions to break down, justifying institutional arrangements that reduce such costs.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: What distinguishes a nudge from a paternalistic mandate in behavioural policy design?
questions.a: Nudges preserve freedom of choice, mandates do not
opts: Nudges restrict options, mandates do not
Nudges preserve freedom of choice, mandates do not
Nudges are legally binding, mandates are not
Nudges require financial incentives, mandates do not
questions.solution: Nudge theory, or libertarian paternalism, designs choice architecture that steers individuals toward welfare‑improving decisions while leaving all options available (e.g., automatic enrolment with opt‑out). A paternalistic mandate, by contrast, removes or compels specific choices (e.g., a ban on a product). The defining feature of a nudge is that it preserves the decision‑maker's freedom to choose, whereas a mandate eliminates that freedom.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: Under a fixed exchange rate regime with perfect capital mobility in the Mundell‑Fleming model, how does the fiscal multiplier compare with the closed‑economy multiplier?
questions.solution: In the Mundell‑Fleming framework with a fixed exchange rate, an expansionary fiscal policy raises output and the domestic interest rate. Capital inflows force the central bank to buy foreign reserves, automatically expanding the money supply. This monetary accommodation exactly offsets the interest‑rate rise, leaving the LM* curve to shift rightward until the domestic rate equals the world rate. Consequently, the fiscal multiplier is the same as in a closed economy where monetary policy is passive. The monetary multiplier, by contrast, is zero because the money supply is endogenous.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: What is the impact of a sterilised foreign‑exchange intervention on the LM* curve in a managed‑float regime?
opts: Shifts the LM* curve to the right
Shifts the LM* curve to the left
questions.solution: Sterilised intervention means the central bank offsets the reserve change with an open‑market operation, keeping the domestic money supply constant. Since the LM* curve represents money‑market equilibrium (M/P = L(Y,r)), an unchanged money supply implies no shift in LM*. The intervention can only affect the exchange rate temporarily, unless it signals a future change in monetary policy. This is a standard result in the Mundell‑Fleming‑Dornbusch literature on managed floats.

questions.q: If the actual primary balance is tighter (i.e., a larger surplus) than the debt‑stabilising primary balance pd* = (g − r)b, what happens to the debt‑to‑GDP ratio?
questions.solution: The debt dynamics equation is Δb = (r − g)b + pd. Setting Δb = 0 gives the debt‑stabilising primary surplus pd* = (g − r)b. If the actual primary balance pd is more negative (a larger surplus) than pd*, then pd pd*) makes Δb > 0 and the debt ratio rises.

questions.q: Which strategic variable fundamentally distinguishes the Cournot equilibrium from the Bertrand equilibrium in oligopoly theory?
questions.a: Firms choose quantities in Cournot and prices in Bertrand
opts: Firms choose quantities in Cournot and prices in Bertrand
Firms choose capacities in Cournot and outputs in Bertrand
Firms choose costs in Cournot and demands in Bertrand
Firms choose entry in Cournot and exit in Bertrand
questions.solution: In the Cournot model each firm selects its output quantity, taking rivals’ quantities as given; the reaction function maps a firm’s optimal quantity to the rivals’ quantities. In the Bertrand model firms set prices, and the reaction function maps optimal price to rivals’ prices. Because the strategic variable differs (quantity vs. price), the resulting equilibria differ dramatically: Cournot yields positive mark‑ups, while Bertrand with homogeneous products drives price to marginal cost. This distinction is central to industrial organization analysis.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism through which the portfolio-balance channel of quantitative easing lowers long-term yields?
questions.a: Removing safe, long-duration assets from private portfolios, forcing rebalancing into riskier securities and compressing term premiums.
opts: Lowering expected future short-term rates through central bank communication.
Removing safe, long-duration assets from private portfolios, forcing rebalancing into riskier securities and compressing term premiums.
Charging banks on excess reserves to push short-term market rates below zero.
Coordinating with fiscal authorities to raise inflation expectations and reduce real rates.
questions.solution: The portfolio-balance channel operates through asset supply effects. By purchasing long-term bonds, the central bank reduces the quantity of safe, long-duration assets held by the private sector. Investors must rebalance into riskier assets, which compresses term premiums and lowers long-term yields. This is distinct from the signalling channel (Option A), which works via expectations of future policy rates. Negative interest rate policy (Option C) and fiscal coordination (Option D) are separate unconventional tools.

questions.q: In Tullock's rent-seeking theory, what determines the total resources dissipated in a rent-seeking contest?
questions.a: The dissipation depends on the number of contestants and the specific contest success function.
opts: The total dissipation always equals the full value of the rent being contested.
The dissipation is zero under conditions of perfect competition among rent-seekers.
The dissipation depends on the number of contestants and the specific contest success function.
The dissipation is determined solely by the price elasticity of demand for the privileged position.
questions.solution: Tullock's analysis shows that rent-seeking expenditure (dissipation) is not automatically equal to the rent value. In imperfect competition, the equilibrium dissipation depends on the number of contestants and the contest success function, which maps individual effort to the probability of winning. Dissipation can be lower or higher than the rent value depending on these parameters. It is not necessarily equal to the rent (Option A), nor zero in perfect competition (Option B), nor determined solely by demand elasticity (Option D).

questions.q: How does loss aversion differ from risk aversion in reference-dependent preference models?
questions.a: Loss aversion is characterized by a kink in the value function at the reference point, making losses loom larger than gains.
opts: Loss aversion implies a concave utility function over final wealth levels.
Loss aversion is characterized by a kink in the value function at the reference point, making losses loom larger than gains.
Risk aversion arises from a kink in the utility function at the reference point.
Both concepts describe the curvature of the utility function over final wealth.
questions.solution: In prospect theory, loss aversion refers to the asymmetry where the value function is steeper for losses than for gains, creating a distinct kink at the reference point. Risk aversion, by contrast, is traditionally modeled as the concavity (curvature) of the utility function over final wealth levels. Option A describes risk aversion, not loss aversion. Option C incorrectly attributes the kink to risk aversion. Option D conflates the two distinct phenomena.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: What does the joint-hypothesis problem imply for the interpretation of asset pricing anomalies such as the CAPM beta anomaly?
questions.a: Anomalies may reflect a misspecified risk model or missing risk factors rather than genuine market inefficiency.
opts: Anomalies provide conclusive proof of market inefficiency and exploitable profit opportunities.
Anomalies may reflect a misspecified risk model or missing risk factors rather than genuine market inefficiency.
The CAPM is the only theoretically valid benchmark for testing market efficiency.
Event-study methodology cannot be used to test market efficiency due to this problem.
questions.solution: The joint-hypothesis problem (Fama, 1970) states that testing market efficiency requires a model of equilibrium pricing (e.g., CAPM). An observed anomaly — abnormal returns relative to the model — could indicate either market inefficiency or a misspecified asset pricing model (e.g., omitted risk factors). Therefore, anomalies cannot be automatically equated with inefficiency (Option A). The CAPM is not the only benchmark (Option C), and event studies remain valid with appropriate benchmarks (Option D).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: What is the 'balance-sheet effect' emphasized in the sudden-stop literature?
questions.a: An increase in the domestic-currency value of foreign-currency debt due to exchange rate depreciation, triggering bankruptcies.
opts: An improvement in corporate balance sheets caused by currency appreciation during capital inflow surges.
A contraction in domestic absorption resulting from a sharp rise in domestic interest rates.
An increase in the domestic-currency value of foreign-currency debt due to exchange rate depreciation, triggering bankruptcies.
An increase in the real value of domestic-currency denominated debt due to unexpected deflation.
questions.solution: The sudden-stop literature (Calvo, 1998) highlights liability dollarization: firms and banks borrow in foreign currency. When a sudden stop triggers a sharp nominal depreciation, the domestic-currency burden of this foreign-currency debt increases dramatically. This deteriorates balance sheets, causes bankruptcies, and induces a credit crunch — the balance-sheet effect. Option C correctly describes this currency mismatch channel. Option A describes the opposite scenario. Option B describes a monetary contraction channel. Option D refers to domestic-currency debt and deflation, not the sudden-stop currency mismatch.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.q: In the Mirrlees optimal income tax model, why can a positive marginal tax rate at the top of the income distribution be optimal even when the social planner assigns zero welfare weight to the highest-ability individuals?
questions.a: Because raising the top rate reduces information rents for high-ability types, allowing lower distortions for middle-income earners
opts: Because high-ability individuals have perfectly inelastic labor supply
Because raising the top rate reduces information rents for high-ability types, allowing lower distortions for middle-income earners
Because the Ramsey inverse-elasticity rule requires positive rates at all income levels
Because behavioral biases cause high-ability individuals to overestimate their tax liability
questions.solution: The Mirrlees model incorporates incentive-compatibility constraints: high-ability individuals can mimic lower-ability ones. A positive top marginal tax rate reduces the information rent (the utility gain from mimicking) that high-ability types would otherwise capture. This relaxation of incentive constraints allows the planner to reduce distortions on middle-income earners, raising overall welfare even if the planner values the rich at zero. The Ramsey rule applies to commodity taxation with a representative agent, not to nonlinear income taxation with heterogeneous abilities. Behavioral biases are extensions, not the core mechanism in the standard Mirrlees framework.

opts: A) 3 % CPI inflation with a tolerance band of ±1 %.

C) Remittances and services belong to the Current Account, while FDI and portfolio flows belong to the Financial Account.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the 'escape clause' from the 'flexibility clause' under the FRBM Act as amended in 2018?
questions.a: Escape clause requires parliamentary approval and is triggered by exogenous shocks; flexibility clause is a built-in 0.5% margin for reform-linked expenditure.
opts: Escape clause allows 0.5% deviation for structural reforms; flexibility clause allows breach for national calamity.
Escape clause requires parliamentary approval and is triggered by exogenous shocks; flexibility clause is a built-in 0.5% margin for reform-linked expenditure.
Both clauses require CAG certification but only escape clause requires Finance Commission assessment.
Flexibility clause was invoked during COVID-19; escape clause is used for routine fiscal slippage.
questions.solution: The FRBM Act amendments distinguish between the 'escape clause' (Section 4(2)) and the 'flexibility clause'. The escape clause permits a breach of the fiscal deficit target by up to 0.5% of GDP due to exogenous shocks like national security, war, calamity, or a sharp output decline, and mandates parliamentary approval and CAG certification. It was invoked in 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2023-24. Conversely, the flexibility clause is a permanent 0.5% allowance built into the fiscal glide path for structural reform-linked expenditure, not triggered by shocks. Option B captures this distinction accurately. Option A reverses the triggers. Option C incorrectly states both require CAG certification (only escape clause does). Option D misattributes the COVID invocation to the flexibility clause.

questions.q: Regarding India's capital account management and sovereign rating assessment, which statement is accurate?
questions.a: The SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 impose a 10% limit on a single FPI's holding in a listed company and sectoral caps for corporate debt.
opts: India maintains full capital account convertibility with no sectoral limits on FPI investments in corporate debt.
Sovereign rating agencies primarily assess the Centre's FRBM debt ceiling of 60% of GDP as the key debt sustainability metric.
The SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 impose a 10% limit on a single FPI's holding in a listed company and sectoral caps for corporate debt.
External Commercial Borrowings are fully deregulated and do not require RBI approval under the revised framework.
questions.solution: India's capital account is partially liberalized. The SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 explicitly impose a 10% limit on a single Foreign Portfolio Investor's holding in a listed company and sectoral caps for investments in corporate debt. Option A is incorrect because India retains capital flow management measures (CFMs) and sectoral limits; full convertibility does not exist. Option B is a common trap: rating agencies assess the combined general government debt (~90% of GDP), not the Centre's standalone FRBM ceiling of 60% of GDP. Option D is false as ECBs remain regulated under the RBI's revised framework with tracks based on maturity and end-use.

questions.q: Under the Code on Wages, 2019, what is the significance of the 'floor wage' fixed by the Central Government?
questions.a: It acts as a national lower bound below which state governments cannot fix minimum wages for scheduled employments.

It acts as a national lower bound below which state governments cannot fix minimum wages for scheduled employments.
It is applicable only to the organized sector workers covered under the Industrial Relations Code.
It is determined by the Minimum Wages Advisory Board and is binding on the Central Government only.
questions.solution: The Code on Wages, 2019 empowers the Central Government to fix a 'floor wage' taking into account minimum living standards. This floor wage serves as a national lower bound; state governments cannot fix minimum wages for scheduled employments below this floor wage. It does not replace state-level minimum wages (Option A), nor is it limited to the organized sector (Option C). While advisory boards exist, the floor wage is fixed by the Central Government, not the board (Option D).

100% of their net profit after tax as dividends.
A minimum of 75% of the asset valuation gains realized during the financial year.

opts: e₹-W uses a token-based architecture for consumer payments, while e₹-R uses an account-based architecture for inter-bank settlement.
