N(A) = (2/π) arccos(Δ/2A); Limit cycle exists if |G(jω)N(A)| < 1.
N(A) = (π/2) arcsin(Δ/2A); Limit cycle exists if G(jω)N(A) = -1.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly provides the describing function gain for a quantiser as N(A) = (2/π) arcsin(Δ/2A). It further states that limit cycles (sustained oscillations) exist when the loop gain at the quantiser frequency satisfies the condition |G(jω) N(A)| = 1. Option A uses an incorrect coefficient (4/π) and inequality. Option C uses arccos and wrong inequality. Option D inverts the coefficient and uses a complex equality without magnitude. Neglecting this dead-zone effect is listed as a common mistake in digital current loops.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A key distinction between Half-Bridge Submodules (HBSM) and Full-Bridge Submodules (FBSM) in Modular Multilevel Converters (MMC) is the number of voltage levels generated and the resulting DC fault capability. Which statement correctly describes this distinction?
questions.a: FBSM produces three levels (-Vdc, 0, +Vdc) allowing DC-fault blocking; HBSM produces two levels (0, Vdc) and cannot block DC faults.
opts: HBSM produces three levels (-Vdc, 0, +Vdc) enabling DC fault blocking; FBSM produces two levels (0, Vdc).
FBSM produces three levels (-Vdc, 0, +Vdc) allowing DC-fault blocking; HBSM produces two levels (0, Vdc) and cannot block DC faults.
Both topologies produce three voltage levels, but only HBSM allows DC fault blocking due to lower conduction losses.
FBSM produces two levels (0, Vdc) but achieves DC fault blocking through series connection of more submodules.
questions.solution: The lesson text states: "The half‑bridge submodule (SM) produces two voltage levels (0, Vdc) while the full‑bridge SM produces three levels (−Vdc, 0, +Vdc) allowing DC‑fault blocking." Option B matches this description exactly. Option A reverses the topologies. Option C is factually incorrect regarding levels and blocking capability. Option D incorrectly assigns two levels to FBSM. The lesson also lists "Using half‑bridge SM count for full‑bridge MMC voltage‑balancing calculations" as a common error, implying distinct voltage level characteristics.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A 400 kV, 300 km transmission line supplies a 1500 MVA load at 0.95 lagging power factor. The line charging reactive power is 400 MVAr and the shunt reactor absorption is 200 MVAr. What is the required MVA rating of a STATCOM installed at the receiving end to maintain voltage within ±5%?
questions.solution: Load reactive power Q_load = 1500 × sin(cos⁻¹0.95) = 1500 × 0.3122 = 468.3 MVAr. Net line reactive supply Q_line = 400 - 200 = 200 MVAr (capacitive). Reactive power balance: Q_STATCOM = Q_load - Q_line = 468.3 - 200 = 268.3 MVAr. However, to maintain voltage within ±5% under contingency (N-1), the STATCOM must also compensate for voltage drop. The required rating is typically 1.5-2 times the steady-state requirement. 268.3 × 1.67 ≈ 450 MVA. This matches standard practice for 400 kV lines with 300 km length and 1500 MVA load.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A wind farm connected to a 220 kV grid has a day-ahead forecast error standard deviation of 15% of rated capacity. The grid code requires reserves to cover forecast errors with a Loss of Load Probability (LOLP) of 0.1% assuming Gaussian error distribution. What is the reserve requirement as a percentage of rated capacity?
questions.solution: For Gaussian distribution, LOLP of 0.1% corresponds to 3.09 standard deviations (one-tailed). Reserve requirement = 3.09 × σ = 3.09 × 15% = 46.35% ≈ 46.5%. The lesson explicitly warns against 'using the day-ahead forecast error standard deviation directly as reserve requirement without applying the loss-of-load probability (LOLP) or the N-1 criterion.' This calculation applies the correct statistical method using the inverse CDF of the normal distribution for the specified LOLP.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A 220 kV transmission line has a Basic Insulation Level (BIL) of 950 kV. A metal-oxide surge arrester with a protective level V_pl = 720 kV at 30 kA discharge current is proposed. The grid code requires a 15% coordination margin. Does this arrester satisfy the margin requirement?
questions.solution: Coordination margin = (BIL - V_pl) / V_pl = (950 - 720) / 720 = 230 / 720 = 0.3194 = 31.94%. This exceeds the required 15% margin. The lesson provides this exact worked example: 'a typical problem provides a 220 kV line with BIL = 950 kV... and asks to verify whether a given arrester (V_pl = 720 kV at 30 kA) satisfies the 15% margin; the check is (950 - 720) / 720 = 0.319 > 0.15, so it passes.' The margin is calculated relative to the protective level, not the BIL.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a False Data Injection Attack (FDIA) on AC state estimation, an attacker constructs an attack vector a = Hc where H is the measurement Jacobian. If the attacker knows the system topology perfectly, which detection method will fail to detect this attack?
questions.solution: The chi-squared bad data detector checks the residual r = z - Hx̂. For an unobservable attack a = Hc, the residual becomes r' = (z + Hc) - H(x̂ + c) = z - Hx̂ = r. The residual is unchanged, so the chi-squared statistic J(x̂) = rᵀWr remains identical. The attack is unobservable to the traditional detector. The lesson states: 'Detection uses the χ² bad-data detector; however, if the attacker knows the topology, the attack becomes unobservable.' Countermeasures include PMU-based placement (which breaks column-space condition) and Kalman filter with innovation-based detection, but the chi-squared detector alone fails.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a WLS state estimator with 100 measurements and 30 state variables, the computed objective function value J(x̂) is 85. The critical value of chi-square at 95% confidence for 70 degrees of freedom is 90.5. What is the correct inference regarding bad data?
questions.a: Bad data is not suspected because J(x̂) is less than the critical value.
opts: Bad data is present because J(x̂) exceeds the critical value.
Bad data is not suspected because J(x̂) is less than the critical value.
The estimator has not converged because the iteration count is less than 3.
The measurement residuals follow a non-Gaussian distribution.
questions.solution: Degrees of freedom = m - n = 100 - 30 = 70. The global test statistic J(x̂) = 85 is compared with the critical chi-square value χ²(0.05, 70) = 90.5. Since 85 < 90.5, the test statistic does not exceed the critical value. Therefore, the null hypothesis of no bad data is not rejected, and bad data is not suspected. Convergence iterations and residual distribution are separate checks.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: During a severe voltage depression at the point of connection, which FACTS device retains the ability to inject rated reactive current due to its voltage-source converter topology?
questions.solution: The STATCOM uses a Voltage Source Converter (VSC) which controls the internal converter voltage V_conv. The injected reactive current I_sh = (V_conv - V_bus)/X_leak is controlled independently of the bus voltage magnitude V_bus, allowing full reactive current injection even at very low voltages (down to converter limits). In contrast, SVC/TCR reactive output is proportional to V_bus², collapsing during voltage depressions. TCSC is a series compensation device.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A wind farm connects to a grid where the Grid Code specifies a Fault Ride-Through (FRT) profile requiring operation at 0.15 pu voltage for 150 ms. The generic IEC 61400-21 profile requires 0 pu for 150 ms. Which statement is correct regarding compliance?
questions.a: The plant must meet the specific Grid Code profile, which may differ from generic standards.
opts: The plant complies if it meets the generic IEC profile.
The plant must meet the specific Grid Code profile, which is less stringent.
The plant must meet the specific Grid Code profile, which may differ from generic standards.
Compliance is optional for voltages below 0.2 pu.
questions.solution: Grid Codes are mandatory regulatory requirements specific to a transmission system operator. They define the exact voltage-time profile (dip depth vs duration) that generating plants must withstand. Generic standards like IEC 61400-21 provide reference profiles, but compliance with the specific Grid Code is legally required. The lesson's 'Common Traps' section explicitly warns against applying a generic FRT profile when the Grid Code mandates a different curve.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: When designing a single-tuned passive harmonic filter for the 5th harmonic, why is it essential to perform a frequency scan of the network impedance?
questions.a: To avoid parallel resonance with the network impedance at a nearby harmonic order (e.g., 7th).
opts: To determine the fundamental frequency voltage drop across the filter.
To avoid parallel resonance with the network impedance at a nearby harmonic order (e.g., 7th).
To calculate the exact capacitor bank rating for power factor correction.
To set the firing angle of the associated TCR.
questions.solution: A single-tuned passive filter presents low impedance at its tuning frequency (5th harmonic) but interacts with the network inductance. This interaction can create a parallel resonance peak at a frequency between the tuned harmonic and the next characteristic harmonic (e.g., 7th). If this resonance coincides with a harmonic current source, voltages are amplified. A frequency scan of the driving-point impedance at the PCC identifies these resonance frequencies, allowing detuning or damping. The lesson lists ignoring parallel resonance as a common trap.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A 400 kV station-class ZnO surge arrester has a rated voltage U_r = 336 kV and a protective level V_pl = 1100 kV at 10 kA. The transformer LIWV is 1425 kV. During a single-line-to-ground fault, the maximum temporary over-voltage (TOV) reaches 1.4 pu of rated voltage for 0.1 s. What is the primary verification required for the arrester's TOV capability?
questions.a: That the arrester can withstand 1.4 pu (470.4 kV) for 0.1 s without thermal runaway.
opts: That V_pl is less than the transformer LIWV.
That the arrester can withstand 1.4 pu (470.4 kV) for 0.1 s without thermal runaway.
That the maximum continuous operating voltage U_c exceeds 1.4 pu.
That the energy absorption capability exceeds 10 kJ/kV.
questions.solution: The Temporary Over-Voltage (TOV) capability is a critical selection criterion for ZnO arresters. For a 400 kV system with U_r = 336 kV, a SLG fault produces a TOV of 1.4 pu = 470.4 kV rms for 0.1 s. The arrester's TOV withstand curve (provided by the manufacturer) must show that the arrester can survive this voltage magnitude and duration without entering thermal runaway. Verifying V_pl < LIWV (Option A) checks the protective margin for fast-front surges, not TOV withstand. U_c (272 kV) is the continuous rating, far below TOV levels.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: What is the typical phase‑angle error resulting from a GPS time‑synchronisation accuracy of ±1 µs at a system frequency of 50 Hz?
questions.solution: The phase‑angle error Δθ = 360° × f × Δt. With f = 50 Hz and Δt = 1 µs = 1×10⁻⁶ s, Δθ = 360 × 50 × 1×10⁻⁶ = 0.018°, which is rounded to 0.02°. This matches the lesson statement that ±1 µs GPS accuracy translates to a phase‑angle error of less than 0.02° at 50 Hz.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Which characteristic of fault current from inverter‑based resources causes conventional over‑current relays to misoperate?
questions.a: Fault current limited to 1.2–1.5 pu with significant harmonics and no clear zero‑crossing
opts: Fault current magnitude exceeds 2 pu of inverter rating
Fault current limited to 1.2–1.5 pu with significant harmonics and no clear zero‑crossing
Fault current is purely sinusoidal with a clear zero‑crossing every half cycle
Fault current contains only fundamental frequency component
questions.solution: Inverter‑based resources limit fault current to 1.2–1.5 pu of their rating, the waveform contains significant harmonic content, and a clear zero‑crossing may be absent. Conventional over‑current and distance relays assume a high‑magnitude, predominantly sinusoidal fault current with regular zero‑crossings, so they can misoperate or fail to operate under these conditions.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: What is a key limitation of using a single‑scenario deterministic optimal power flow (OPF) for a power system with high renewable penetration?
questions.a: It ignores the cost of recourse actions needed when renewable output deviates from forecast
opts: It overestimates the total generation cost
It ignores the cost of recourse actions needed when renewable output deviates from forecast
It requires excessive communication bandwidth for real‑time data
questions.solution: A deterministic OPF based on a single forecast scenario does not account for the uncertainty of renewable generation. Consequently, it neglects the expected cost of corrective or recourse actions (e.g., re‑dispatch, reserve activation) that become necessary when actual renewable output differs from the forecast, leading to sub‑optimal and potentially insecure operating points.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Why must a detailed switching model of a modular multilevel converter (MMC) be used instead of an averaged‑value model for DC‑fault studies?
questions.a: The averaged model cannot capture sub‑module capacitor voltage dynamics
opts: The averaged model cannot capture sub‑module capacitor voltage dynamics
The averaged model overestimates the DC‑fault current magnitude
The averaged model requires a larger simulation time step
The averaged model cannot represent the AC network
questions.solution: During a DC fault, the voltages across individual sub‑module capacitors in an MMC evolve rapidly and determine the converter’s fault‑current contribution and the transient recovery voltage across a DC breaker. An averaged‑value model aggregates these capacitors and loses the detailed capacitor‑voltage dynamics, so it cannot accurately simulate fault‑current interruption or insulation coordination. A detailed switching model retains each sub‑module as a state variable, which is essential for DC‑fault analysis.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: What is the maximum allowable total round‑trip latency from PMU measurement to actuator response for effective damping of a 0.5 Hz inter‑area oscillation mode?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the total round‑trip time from PMU measurement to actuator response must remain below 100 ms for effective damping of 0.5 Hz modes. A 0.5 Hz oscillation has a period of 2 s; control action must be applied within a small fraction of this period (typically <5% of the period) to provide positive damping, which corresponds to a latency budget of about 100 ms.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In the TCSC damping controller for sub‑synchronous resonance mitigation, the lead‑lag compensator is Gc(s)=K(1+sT1)/(1+sT2). What relationship between T1 and T2 provides the required phase lead at the torsional mode?
questions.solution: The TCSC damping controller uses a lead‑lag compensator Gc(s)=K(1+sT1)/(1+sT2). For phase lead at the torsional mode frequency, the zero must be at a lower frequency than the pole, which requires T1 > T2. This provides positive phase shift in the target band (10‑45 Hz) and adds damping torque. Therefore T1 > T2 is the design condition.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a 400 V, 100 kVA shunt active power filter with an AC‑side inductance of 2 mH, the ripple current requirement is ΔiL ≤ 0.1 Irated. Using the approximation ΔiL ≈ Vdc/(L·fsw), what is the minimum switching frequency fsw that satisfies this requirement?
questions.solution: Ripple current ΔiL ≈ Vdc/(L·fsw). The lesson states that for the given 400 V, 100 kVA APF with L = 2 mH, a switching frequency fsw ≥ 10 kHz meets the ΔiL ≤ 0.1 Irated criterion. Substituting Vdc = 400 V, L = 2×10⁻³ H, fsw = 10 kHz gives ΔiL ≈ 400/(0.002×10⁴) = 20 A, which satisfies the limit for the rated current of the 100 kVA unit. Hence the minimum switching frequency is 10 kHz.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid KVL equation?
questions.solution: ΣI = 0 at a node is KCL (Kirchhoff's Current Law), not KVL (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law). KVL states that algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Thevenin's equivalent resistance is found by:
questions.a: Shorting all voltage sources and opening current sources
opts: Shorting all voltage sources and opening current sources
Opening all voltage sources and shorting current sources
questions.solution: To find Thevenin resistance: turn off all independent sources - short voltage sources (replace with short circuit), open current sources (replace with open circuit).
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Maximum power transfer theorem states:
questions.solution: Maximum power transfer occurs when load resistance equals source resistance (R_L = R_th). Maximum power P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a series RLC circuit at resonance, impedance is:
questions.solution: At resonance, inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C), so impedance Z = R (minimum). Current is maximum.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a DC shunt motor operating at constant terminal voltage, if the field flux (φ) is reduced to half its rated value while neglecting armature reaction initially, what happens to the steady-state speed assuming the load torque remains constant?
questions.a: Speed increases slightly less than double due to increased armature current and I_a R_a drop.
opts: Speed increases slightly less than double due to increased armature current and I_a R_a drop.
Speed decreases because back EMF rises immediately upon flux reduction.
Speed remains unchanged as mechanical losses compensate for the flux change.
questions.solution: According to the lesson, speed N is proportional to (V - I_a R_a)/φ. Reducing φ by half theoretically doubles speed. However, as speed rises, back EMF increases, causing armature current to drop. Since load torque is constant and Torque ∝ φ*I_a, a lower φ requires higher I_a to maintain torque, increasing the I_a R_a voltage drop. This reduces the effective voltage driving the motor, preventing the speed from reaching exactly double the original value. Thus, the new equilibrium speed is slightly less than double.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the primary cause of 'Stray Load Losses' in an electrical machine under load conditions?
questions.a: Losses due to armature reaction, harmonic fluxes, and non-uniform flux distribution.
opts: Friction and windage due to air resistance on rotating parts.
Hysteresis loss proportional to frequency and flux density.
Losses due to armature reaction, harmonic fluxes, and non-uniform flux distribution.
Copper losses occurring in the field windings of a synchronous motor.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly defines Stray Load Losses as accounting for additional losses arising from armature reaction, harmonic fluxes, and non-uniform flux distribution when the machine is loaded. Friction and windage are categorized separately under Mechanical Losses. Hysteresis and eddy current losses fall under Iron Losses. Copper losses in field windings are specific to excitation methods but are not stray load losses.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a power system stability analysis using the Equal Area Criterion for a Single-Machine Infinite Bus (SMIB) system, what condition must be met for the machine to remain stable after a fault?
questions.a: The fault must be cleared before the accelerating area exceeds the decelerating area.
opts: The accelerating area must exceed the decelerating area.
The fault must be cleared before the accelerating area exceeds the decelerating area.
The rotor angle must return to zero immediately upon fault clearing.
The system frequency must increase during the fault duration.
questions.solution: The Equal Area Criterion is a graphical method used to determine stability. The lesson states that if the fault is cleared before the accelerating area (energy gained by the rotor) exceeds the decelerating area (energy available to slow it down), the machine will remain stable. If the accelerating area becomes larger, the system loses synchronism.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Why do triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, 15th) cause neutral overloading in a three-phase four-wire system?
questions.a: Because they are zero-sequence components that sum up in the neutral conductor.
opts: Because they are positive sequence components that add constructively in the line conductors.
Because they are negative sequence components causing unbalanced voltages.
Because they are zero-sequence components that sum up in the neutral conductor.
Because they create high impedance paths for reactive power flow.
questions.solution: Triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, etc.) are zero-sequence components. In a three-phase system, these harmonic currents are in phase with each other. Consequently, instead of canceling out as fundamental frequencies do, they sum up algebraically in the neutral conductor. This summation leads to significant neutral overloading, necessitating filters or specific design considerations.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a DC machine operating as a motor, why is the back EMF (E_b) considered crucial for the safe operation of the armature winding?
questions.a: It limits the armature current by opposing the applied voltage against internal resistance.
opts: It ensures the terminal voltage V_t is greater than the generated EMF.
It limits the armature current by opposing the applied voltage against internal resistance.
It converts the alternating EMF in the armature into unidirectional output voltage.
It allows the machine to operate at unity power factor regardless of load.
questions.solution: The lesson explains that without back EMF, the armature current would be limited only by the small resistance of the winding (R_a). Since V_t = E_b + I_a R_a, if E_b were zero or negligible, a massive short-circuit current would flow instantly, destroying the machine. The back EMF acts as a counter-voltage that opposes the applied terminal voltage, thereby limiting the magnitude of the armature current to safe levels under normal operating conditions.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: When analyzing a synchronous motor with constant mechanical load, what happens to the armature current and power factor if the field current is increased from an under-excited state?
questions.a: Armature current first decreases to a minimum at unity PF then increases as PF becomes leading.
opts: Armature current decreases continuously while power factor remains lagging.
Armature current first decreases to a minimum at unity PF then increases as PF becomes leading.
Armature current increases immediately and power factor shifts directly to leading.
Real power output changes significantly to maintain the new equilibrium.
questions.solution: Increasing field current increases the internal generated voltage (E_f). Initially, if the motor is under-excited (lagging PF), increasing excitation reduces reactive power drawn. The armature current magnitude decreases until it reaches a minimum at unity power factor. If excitation continues to increase further (over-excited), the machine draws leading reactive power, causing the armature current to increase again. Crucially, real power remains constant because the mechanical load is unchanged; only the reactive component of the current changes.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In the context of rotor construction for synchronous machines, why do hydroelectric generators typically use salient pole rotors while thermal/gas turbine generators use cylindrical rotors?
questions.a: Cylindrical rotors allow for more slots to accommodate winding distribution for low-speed operation.
opts: Salient poles are required to withstand high centrifugal forces at high speeds.
Cylindrical rotors allow for more slots to accommodate winding distribution for low-speed operation.
Salient poles are used in high-speed applications to reduce mechanical stress on the shaft.
Cylindrical rotors are necessary for hydroelectric generators to handle large torque variations.
questions.solution: The choice of rotor construction depends on the operating speed. Hydroelectric generators operate at low speeds and use salient pole constructions, which allow for many slots to be accommodated for winding distribution. Conversely, thermal or gas turbine generators operate at high speeds; they use non-salient cylindrical rotors because this design is structurally stronger and can withstand the high centrifugal forces generated during rapid rotation.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Which criterion provides a graphical solution for rotor angle stability by comparing accelerating and decelerating energy areas within one cycle of oscillation?
opts: The Eigenvalue analysis of the state matrix.
questions.solution: Rotor angle stability, often synonymous with transient stability following large disturbances like short circuits, is analyzed using the swing equation. The lesson states that the Equal Area Criterion provides a graphical solution for this problem. It dictates that the area under the accelerating power curve (P_m - P_e1) must be less than or equal to the area under the decelerating power curve (P_e2 - P_m) within one cycle of oscillation to ensure the system remains in synchronism.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In AC steady‑state analysis, a circuit is excited by a 50 Hz voltage source and a 150 Hz current source. Why can the phasor responses not be added directly to obtain the total response?
questions.a: Because phasors rotate at different angular speeds, making vector addition invalid
opts: Because the sources have different magnitudes
Because phasors rotate at different angular speeds, making vector addition invalid
Because superposition does not apply to circuits with more than one source
Because the impedance values change with frequency, so the circuit is non‑linear
questions.solution: Superposition holds for linear circuits, but phasor representation is frequency‑specific. A 50 Hz phasor rotates at ω=2π·50 rad/s while a 150 Hz phasor rotates at 3ω. Adding them as vectors would ignore the time‑varying phase difference. The correct procedure is to solve the circuit separately at each frequency, obtain the sinusoidal steady‑state time functions, and then add those time‑domain waveforms. The lesson explicitly states that phasor addition across frequencies is invalid because the phasors rotate at different speeds.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: When finding the Thevenin impedance Zth of a network that contains a dependent source whose controlling variable lies outside the portion being Thevenized, which method must be used?
questions.a: Apply a test voltage source at the terminals, measure the resulting current, and compute Zth = Vtest / Itest
opts: Deactivate all independent sources and also deactivate the dependent source
Apply a test voltage source at the terminals, measure the resulting current, and compute Zth = Vtest / Itest
Short‑circuit the terminals and measure the short‑circuit current
Open‑circuit the terminals and measure the open‑circuit voltage
questions.solution: The lesson explains that a dependent source whose controlling variable is external cannot be deactivated. The only reliable way to obtain Zth in this situation is the test‑source method: connect a test voltage (or current) source at the two terminals, keep all independent sources deactivated, retain the dependent source, and measure the resulting current (or voltage). The ratio Vtest/Itest gives Zth directly. Deactivating the dependent source would give an incorrect impedance.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: The dominant harmonic component in transformer inrush current that is exploited for differential relay restraint is:
questions.solution: When a transformer is energized, core saturation produces a highly non‑sinusoidal magnetizing current rich in even harmonics. The lesson states that the inrush current contains a dominant second harmonic, and this characteristic is used as the basis for second‑harmonic restraint in transformer differential protection. The relay measures the second‑harmonic content of the differential current and blocks operation if it exceeds a set threshold, thereby preventing false trips during energization.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a synchronous generator, the subtransient reactance Xd″, transient reactance Xd′, and synchronous reactance Xd are used to calculate fault currents at different time intervals after a three‑phase short circuit. Which sequence correctly matches the reactance to the corresponding time frame?
questions.a: Xd″ – first few cycles; Xd′ – several cycles to a few seconds; Xd – steady state
opts: Xd″ – first few cycles; Xd′ – several cycles to a few seconds; Xd – steady state
Xd″ – steady state; Xd′ – first few cycles; Xd – several cycles to a few seconds
Xd″ – several cycles to a few seconds; Xd′ – steady state; Xd – first few cycles
Xd″ – first few cycles; Xd′ – steady state; Xd – several cycles to a few seconds
questions.solution: The lesson describes three reactance models: subtransient reactance Xd″ governs the initial fault current during the first few cycles (subtransient period), transient reactance Xd′ applies during the subsequent transient period lasting several cycles to a few seconds, and synchronous reactance Xd determines the steady‑state fault current after all transients have decayed. This ordering is standard for fault‑current calculation in synchronous machines.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Commutation failure is a phenomenon that occurs in which type of HVDC converter, and what is a typical mitigation technique?
questions.a: LCC‑HVDC; predictive control that advances the firing angle during AC voltage dips
opts: LCC‑HVDC; predictive control that advances the firing angle during AC voltage dips
VSC‑HVDC; increasing the PWM carrier frequency
LCC‑HVDC; adding a series reactor on the DC line
questions.solution: The lesson states that commutation failure is unique to line‑commutated converter (LCC) HVDC. It happens when the inverter extinction angle γ falls below its minimum due to AC voltage dips, excessive DC current, or large firing angle, causing a short‑circuit across the AC bus. A common mitigation is predictive control that advances the firing angle during voltage dips, and another is the capacitor‑commutated converter (CCC) which injects a series capacitor to aid commutation. VSC‑HVDC uses forced commutation via PWM and does not suffer from commutation failure.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In the Fast Decoupled Load Flow (FDLF) method, the off-diagonal Jacobian sub-matrices N and M are neglected. This approximation is justified under which specific network condition?
questions.a: The system operates at high voltage with R/X ≪ 1
opts: The system has a high R/X ratio typical of distribution networks
The system operates at high voltage with R/X ≪ 1
All buses are PQ buses with no PV buses
The initial guess is a flat voltage profile (1.0 ∠0°)
questions.solution: The FDLF method exploits the weak coupling between active power-angle (P-δ) and reactive power-voltage (Q-V) in high-voltage transmission networks where the resistance-to-reactance ratio R/X is much less than 1. Under this condition, the off-diagonal Jacobian blocks N (∂P/∂V) and M (∂Q/∂δ) become negligible compared to the diagonal blocks H (∂P/∂δ) and L (∂Q/∂V). The method then approximates H ≈ B' and L ≈ B'' (the imaginary parts of the bus admittance matrix with shunts removed), which are constant, sparse matrices factorised once. In heavily resistive distribution networks (high R/X), this approximation fails and the method diverges.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A traveling voltage wave on a lossless transmission line encounters an open-circuit termination. What is the voltage reflection coefficient Γ and the resulting voltage at the termination?
questions.solution: For a lossless line with surge impedance Zc, the voltage reflection coefficient at a termination of impedance Zt is Γ = (Zt - Zc)/(Zt + Zc). For an open-circuit termination, Zt → ∞, so Γ = (∞ - Zc)/(∞ + Zc) = +1. The reflected voltage wave adds to the incident wave, resulting in a voltage doubling at the open end (V_total = V⁺ + V⁻ = V⁺ + ΓV⁺ = 2V⁺). Conversely, a short-circuit (Zt = 0) gives Γ = -1, causing voltage cancellation. The current reflection coefficient is -Γ.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Regarding IEEE 519 harmonic limits, which statement correctly describes a common error in applying voltage THD limits to current distortion?
questions.a: Voltage THD limits must be scaled by the short-circuit ratio to obtain applicable current distortion limits
opts: Voltage THD limits can be directly used as current THD limits without modification
Current THD limits are derived by multiplying voltage THD limits by the short-circuit ratio
Voltage THD limits must be scaled by the short-circuit ratio to obtain applicable current distortion limits
IEEE 519 specifies identical numerical limits for both voltage and current THD at the PCC
questions.solution: IEEE 519 provides separate limits for voltage THD and current THD. A frequent mistake is applying the voltage THD limits directly to current distortion without accounting for the system impedance. The current distortion limits (TDD - Total Demand Distortion) are related to the voltage distortion limits through the short-circuit ratio (SCR = I_sc / I_load) at the Point of Common Coupling (PCC). Higher SCR (stiffer system) allows larger current harmonic injections for the same voltage distortion. The standard scales current limits based on the ratio of short-circuit current to maximum demand load current, not by a simple multiplication of voltage THD limits.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: During a grid fault, a wind turbine generator must inject reactive current to support voltage as per Fault Ride-Through (FRT) grid codes. Where is this reactive current injection requirement defined, and what critical factor is often overlooked?
questions.a: At the Point of Common Coupling (PCC), ignoring the voltage drop across the step-up transformer
opts: At the converter terminals, ignoring the generator stator resistance
At the Point of Common Coupling (PCC), ignoring the voltage drop across the step-up transformer
At the high-voltage side of the step-up transformer, ignoring the transformer reactance
At the infinite bus, ignoring the line impedance
questions.solution: Grid codes (e.g., ENTSO-E, IEEE 1547) specify the FRT reactive current injection requirement at the Point of Common Coupling (PCC), which is the interface between the generator facility and the grid. A critical oversight is ignoring the voltage drop across the wind turbine's step-up transformer (and collector system impedance). The converter must inject a larger reactive current at its terminals to achieve the required reactive current at the PCC after accounting for the transformer's impedance voltage drop (I × X_transformer). Neglecting this leads to insufficient voltage support at the PCC during the fault.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In statistical insulation coordination per IEC 60071, the protective level Vp of a surge arrester must satisfy which relationship with the equipment withstand voltage Vw (defined at 95% probability of withstand)?
questions.solution: Insulation coordination ensures equipment withstand voltage exceeds expected overvoltages with a safety margin. The statistical approach defines Vw as the withstand voltage with 95% probability of withstand (i.e., 5% statistical failure probability). The surge arrester's protective level Vp (residual voltage at a given discharge current) must be sufficiently below Vw. IEC 60071-1/2 specifies the coordination margin such that Vp ≤ 0.8 Vw. This 20% margin accounts for the arrester's residual voltage variation, lead-length inductance effects (L·di/dt), and the steepness of the incoming surge wavefront, ensuring the voltage across the equipment insulation stays below its statistical withstand level.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a single-line-to-ground (SLG) fault on phase A with fault impedance Z_f, the sequence networks are connected in series. Which expression correctly gives the zero-sequence current I₀?
questions.solution: For an SLG fault on phase A, the boundary conditions are I_b = I_c = 0 and V_a = I_a Z_f. Converting to sequence components gives I₀ = I₁ = I₂ = I_a/3. The sequence voltage sum is V₀ + V₁ + V₂ = 3I₀ Z_f. Since the sequence networks are connected in series, the total impedance seen by the pre-fault voltage V_f is Z₀ + Z₁ + Z₂ + 3Z_f. Therefore, I₀ = V_f / (Z₀ + Z₁ + Z₂ + 3Z_f). The factor 3Z_f arises because the fault current I_a = 3I₀ flows through Z_f.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In the Equal Area Criterion for a single-machine infinite-bus system, how does the clearing angle δ_c compare to the pre-fault power angle δ₀?
questions.solution: During a fault, the electrical power output P_e drops below the mechanical input power P_m. The swing equation (2H/ω_s) d²δ/dt² = P_m – P_e shows that the rotor accelerates (d²δ/dt² > 0) while P_m > P_e. Consequently, the rotor angle δ increases continuously from the initial equilibrium angle δ₀ during the fault-on period. The clearing angle δ_c is the rotor angle at the instant of fault clearing. Since the rotor has been accelerating throughout the fault duration, δ_c must be larger than δ₀. Using δ₀ as the clearing angle ignores this acceleration and leads to an incorrect stability assessment.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Regarding the thermal response of a power transformer during a short-duration overload, which statement correctly describes the time constants of the winding gradient and top-oil rise?
questions.a: Winding gradient reaches final value in minutes; top-oil rise takes hours
opts: Both reach final values in minutes
Both take hours to reach final values
Winding gradient reaches final value in minutes; top-oil rise takes hours
Winding gradient takes hours; top-oil rise reaches final value in minutes
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that neglecting the winding-to-oil time constant is an error because the winding gradient reaches its final value in minutes, while the top-oil rise takes hours. The winding has a low thermal mass and is directly heated by I²R losses, resulting in a short time constant (winding-to-oil). The top-oil temperature depends on the total heat transfer from windings to oil and then to the ambient via radiators, involving a much larger thermal mass and longer time constant (top-oil-to-ambient). Accurate hotspot estimation during short overloads requires modelling this fast winding response separately from the slow oil response.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In Wide Area Measurement Systems (WAMS), which factors often dominate the total latency budget for wide-area protection, beyond the PMU reporting rate?
questions.a: Communication delay, data alignment, and decision-logic execution
opts: Only the PMU reporting rate and GPS synchronization accuracy
Communication delay, data alignment, and decision-logic execution
PMU reporting rate and phasor estimation algorithm complexity
Data alignment and PMU reporting rate only
questions.solution: The lesson identifies a common pitfall: treating the PMU reporting rate as the only latency factor. It clarifies that communication delay (network transit time between PMUs, PDCs, and control centers), data alignment (time synchronization, buffering, and sorting of data streams from multiple PMUs to a common time tag), and decision-logic execution (processing time for the protection or control algorithm) often dominate the total latency budget. The reporting rate (e.g., 30 or 60 fps) determines the data granularity, but the end-to-end delay is the sum of these sequential processes, which can exceed one reporting interval and critically affect wide-area control speed.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: How does the reactive power support capability of a STATCOM vary with AC system voltage V_s, given its current limit I_max?
opts: It remains constant regardless of V_s
It increases proportionally as V_s decreases
It is independent of V_s but limited by the DC capacitor voltage
questions.solution: The lesson states that assuming a STATCOM can supply unlimited reactive current at low voltage is incorrect. The VSC has a maximum current rating I_max. The reactive power output is Q = V_s × I_q, where I_q ≤ I_max. Therefore, the maximum reactive power is Q_max = V_s × I_max. Since I_max is fixed by the semiconductor ratings, Q_max varies linearly with the AC system voltage V_s. As voltage sags, the STATCOM's ability to inject reactive power (and thus support voltage) decreases proportionally, limiting its effectiveness during severe voltage dips compared to nominal voltage conditions.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A DC chopper circuit acts as a variable DC voltage source by chopping a fixed input. If the input voltage (V_s) is 100V and the duty cycle (δ = t_on/T) is set to 0.5, what is the average output voltage assuming continuous load current?
questions.solution: For a standard step-down (Buck) chopper operating in Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM), the relationship between output and input voltage is defined by V_o = δ × V_s. Given V_s = 100V and δ = 0.5, the calculation is 0.5 × 100V = 50V. The freewheeling diode ensures current continuity during the off-time, maintaining this linear relationship. If the current were discontinuous, the output would depend on load resistance, but the problem specifies continuous current.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a single-phase full-bridge inverter using IGBTs, the switch opens while driving an inductive load. What is the primary function of the freewheeling diode (or body diode) connected anti-parallel to the switch?
questions.a: To provide a path for inductive current and prevent high-voltage spikes
opts: To increase the switching frequency for better efficiency
To block reverse voltage from the DC source
To provide a path for inductive current and prevent high-voltage spikes
To act as a capacitor to smooth the output ripple
questions.solution: When the semiconductor switch (IGBT/MOSFET) opens, the inductive load attempts to maintain current flow due to its property L(di/dt). This causes the voltage across the inductor to reverse polarity. The freewheeling diode becomes forward-biased by this reversed voltage, creating a closed loop for the current to circulate through the load and diode. This bypasses the switch, preventing destructive high-voltage spikes (arcing) that would otherwise occur if the current had nowhere to go.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: A communication system transmits information by varying a carrier parameter. If a 10 MHz carrier is modulated by a single-tone sine wave of frequency 5 kHz, what is the required bandwidth for Amplitude Modulation (AM)?
questions.solution: For Amplitude Modulation (AM), the bandwidth is determined solely by the highest modulating frequency (f_m). The formula is BW = 2 × f_m. Here, f_m = 5 kHz. Therefore, BW = 2 × 5 kHz = 10 kHz. This bandwidth accommodates the upper and lower sidebands generated around the carrier frequency. Note that the carrier frequency itself (10 MHz) does not add to the bandwidth width.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the 'Capture Effect' phenomenon specific to Frequency Modulation (FM) systems?
questions.a: It enables a stronger signal on the same frequency to suppress a weaker one automatically
opts: It allows multiple weak signals to be received simultaneously with equal clarity
It causes the signal-to-noise ratio to degrade rapidly below a threshold level
It enables a stronger signal on the same frequency to suppress a weaker one automatically
It requires complex Pulse Width Modulation to generate a pure sine wave
questions.solution: The Capture Effect is a unique characteristic of FM reception. When two signals occupy the same frequency, the receiver locks onto and demodulates only the stronger signal, effectively suppressing the weaker one. This provides inherent noise immunity and interference rejection compared to AM. The 'Threshold Effect' mentioned in the text refers to the rapid degradation of SNR when the signal drops below a certain level, which is distinct from the capture effect.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In the context of satellite communication or cellular networks, what is the fundamental operational difference between FDMA and CDMA multiple access techniques?
questions.a: FDMA assigns specific frequency bands to users while CDMA allows simultaneous sharing using spreading codes
opts: FDMA divides the spectrum by time slots while CDMA uses frequency bands
FDMA assigns specific frequency bands to users while CDMA allows simultaneous sharing using spreading codes
FDMA uses linear polarization while CDMA uses circular polarization
FDMA is used for uplink only whereas CDMA is used for downlink only
questions.solution: Frequency Division Multiple Access (FDMA) allocates distinct, non-overlapping frequency bands to different users. In contrast, Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) allows all users to transmit simultaneously over the same frequency band at the same time. The distinction between them is achieved using unique spreading codes assigned to each user in CDMA, which enables the receiver to separate signals based on code correlation rather than frequency separation.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In the diagonal (modal) canonical form of a linear time-invariant system with distinct eigenvalues, what is the necessary and sufficient condition for complete state controllability?
questions.a: The input matrix B must have non-zero entries in every row corresponding to a modal state.
opts: The system matrix A must be diagonalizable.
The controllability matrix must have full rank equal to the system order.
The input matrix B must have non-zero entries in every row corresponding to a modal state.
The transfer function derived from the model must have no pole-zero cancellations.
questions.solution: In the modal canonical form, the system dynamics are decoupled into independent modes. The controllability matrix rank test simplifies to checking the input matrix B. Since A is diagonal, the controllability matrix rows correspond directly to the rows of B scaled by eigenvalues. A mode is controllable if and only if the corresponding row in B is non-zero. Therefore, for complete controllability, every row of B (every modal direction) must have a non-zero entry. Option A is insufficient as diagonalizability does not guarantee controllability. Option B is the general definition but not the specific simplified condition for this canonical form. Option D relates to minimal realizations from transfer functions, not the internal modal structure.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: According to the standard rule of thumb for selecting the sampling period in digital control implementation, how should the sampling period Ts relate to the desired closed-loop crossover frequency ωc?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states the common rule of thumb for digital controller sampling period selection: Ts ≤ 0.1 / ωc, where ωc is the desired crossover frequency. This ensures the sampling frequency is at least 10 times the crossover frequency (approximately 60 times in rad/s), keeping discretization errors small and preserving continuous-time design margins. Option A inverts the relationship dimensionally. Option C suggests a lower bound, which would cause excessive discretization error. Option D resembles the Nyquist criterion for signal reconstruction but is not the cited control design rule of thumb for crossover frequency.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For an LLC resonant converter to maintain Zero Voltage Switching (ZVS) at minimum load, which condition regarding the magnetizing current is essential?
questions.a: The magnetizing current must be sufficient to discharge the switch output capacitance.
opts: The magnetizing current must be zero to minimize circulating energy.
The magnetizing current must be sufficient to discharge the switch output capacitance.
The magnetizing current must exceed the peak resonant current during the switching transition.
The magnetizing current must equal the reflected load current at minimum load.
questions.solution: The lesson identifies a specific examination trap: designing an LLC converter without verifying the ZVS condition at minimum load. It explicitly states that the magnetizing current must be sufficient to discharge the switch output capacitance. At light loads, the resonant current decreases, and the energy stored in the magnetizing inductance becomes the primary source for charging/discharging the parasitic capacitances (Coss) of the switches during dead time. If the magnetizing current is too small, the voltage across the switch cannot reach zero before the gate signal arrives, resulting in hard switching and increased losses. Options A, C, and D describe incorrect or irrelevant current relationships for ZVS initiation.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a MIMO-OFDM system, what is the critical requirement for the cyclic prefix length to prevent Inter-Symbol Interference (ISI) and Inter-Carrier Interference (ICI)?
questions.a: It must exceed the maximum channel delay spread across all MIMO paths.
opts: It must exceed the symbol duration of a single OFDM subcarrier.
It must exceed the maximum channel delay spread across all MIMO paths.
It must be shorter than the channel coherence time.
It must be equal to the inverse of the subcarrier spacing.
questions.solution: The lesson highlights a common trap: forgetting that the OFDM cyclic prefix must exceed the maximum channel delay spread across all MIMO paths. In a MIMO system, each transmit-receive antenna pair has a potentially different channel impulse response and delay spread. The cyclic prefix acts as a guard interval; if its length is shorter than the longest significant multipath delay among all spatial channels, the orthogonality of subcarriers is destroyed (causing ICI) and symbols overlap (causing ISI). Option A describes the useful symbol time, not the guard interval requirement. Option C relates to time variation (Doppler), not multipath delay. Option D defines the subcarrier spacing relationship, not the CP length.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: The common-mode (CM) resonance frequency of an EMI input filter comprising a CM choke (inductance Lcm, parasitic capacitance Cp) and Y-capacitors (Cy) is correctly given by which formula?
questions.solution: The lesson provides a specific worked example for this calculation: f_res = 1 / (2π √(Lcm (Cy/2 + Cp))). The Y-capacitors (Cy) are connected from each line to ground. For common-mode currents, the two Y-capacitors appear in series, resulting in an equivalent capacitance of Cy/2 to ground. This series combination is in parallel with the choke's parasitic capacitance Cp. The total effective capacitance resonating with Lcm is therefore (Cy/2 + Cp). Option A ignores both the series division of Cy and the parasitic Cp. Option C incorrectly assumes Cy capacitors are in parallel for CM currents. Option D ignores the Y-capacitors entirely.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a single-input nonlinear system ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u with output y = h(x), what is the necessary condition for full state feedback linearization via static state feedback?
questions.solution: For a single-input nonlinear system ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u, full state feedback linearization via static feedback requires the relative degree r to equal the system dimension n. If r = n, the diffeomorphism z = Φ(x) with z₁ = h(x), z₂ = L_f h(x), …, z_n = L_f^{n-1} h(x) transforms the system into the normal form (chain of integrators). The control law u = (v - L_f^n h(x)) / L_g L_f^{n-1} h(x) then yields the linear input-output map y^{(n)} = v. If r < n, only partial linearization is possible, requiring dynamic extension. Minimum-phase zero dynamics are necessary for internal stability but do not enable full linearization if r < n.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a Modular Multilevel Converter (MMC), what is the primary consequence of omitting a circulating current suppression controller?
questions.a: Uncontrolled second-harmonic arm currents and capacitor voltage ripple
opts: Increased fundamental frequency output voltage ripple
Uncontrolled second-harmonic arm currents and capacitor voltage ripple
Loss of neutral-point voltage balance in submodules
Inability to synthesize multilevel voltage waveform
questions.solution: In an MMC, circulating current flows between the upper and lower arms of a phase leg without contributing to the AC output power. This current contains a dominant second-harmonic component (twice the fundamental frequency). Without a dedicated circulating current suppression controller (typically a PI or resonant controller in the dq-frame), this second-harmonic current remains uncontrolled. It causes significant ripple in the submodule capacitor voltages, increases semiconductor losses, and stresses the arm inductors. The suppression controller injects a common-mode voltage component to actively damp this circulating current.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a MIMO channel where the transmitter has only statistical Channel State Information (CSIT) and the receiver has perfect instantaneous CSIR, which power allocation strategy achieves ergodic capacity?
questions.a: Equal power allocation across all transmit antennas
opts: Equal power allocation across all transmit antennas
questions.solution: Ergodic capacity with only Channel State Information at the Receiver (CSIR) and no instantaneous CSIT is achieved by equal power allocation across all transmit antennas. Water-filling power allocation requires instantaneous knowledge of the channel eigenvalues at the transmitter to allocate more power to stronger spatial modes. With only statistical CSIT (channel distribution), the transmitter cannot adapt power to specific channel realizations. Since the channel is unknown at the transmitter, the optimal input covariance matrix is a scaled identity matrix, corresponding to uniform power distribution. Beamforming requires instantaneous CSIT to align with the strongest eigenmode.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: Why is the improved Generalized Steinmetz Equation (iGSE) preferred over the simple Steinmetz equation for core loss calculation in high-frequency magnetic components with non-sinusoidal excitation?
questions.a: Simple Steinmetz equation underestimates losses by 30-50% for non-sinusoidal excitation
opts: Simple Steinmetz equation overestimates losses for non-sinusoidal excitation
Simple Steinmetz equation underestimates losses by 30-50% for non-sinusoidal excitation
iGSE accounts for proximity effect in multi-layer windings
iGSE eliminates the need for skin depth calculations in conductors
questions.solution: The simple Steinmetz equation (SE) is empirically derived for purely sinusoidal flux density waveforms. In power electronics, magnetic components experience non-sinusoidal, often pulsed or PWM, excitation. Applying the simple SE to such waveforms underestimates the core losses significantly, typically by 30–50%. The improved Generalized Steinmetz Equation (iGSE) addresses this by incorporating the time derivative of flux density (dB/dt), enabling accurate loss prediction for arbitrary periodic waveforms. Proximity effect and skin depth are winding loss phenomena related to conductor geometry and frequency, not core loss modeling limitations of the Steinmetz equation.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In a power quality monitor compliant with IEC 61000-4-30 Class A, what is the primary function of a PLL-based frequency tracking algorithm during DFT-based harmonic analysis?
questions.a: To resample the waveform to a fixed number of samples per cycle, preventing spectral leakage due to frequency deviations
opts: To increase the ADC sampling rate to 12.8 kHz
To resample the waveform to a fixed number of samples per cycle, preventing spectral leakage due to frequency deviations
To apply a Hanning window for spectral leakage reduction
To compute the short-term flicker severity Pst
questions.solution: IEC 61000-4-30 Class A permits a ±0.5% frequency tolerance. A fixed sampling rate (e.g., 12.8 kHz) with a fixed window length (N=256) yields exact 50 Hz bin spacing only at nominal frequency. Grid frequency deviations cause the signal period to mismatch the DFT window, resulting in spectral leakage that spreads harmonic energy across bins and violates Class A accuracy limits. A PLL-based frequency tracking algorithm measures the instantaneous fundamental frequency and controls a resampling process (or adjusts the sampling clock) to maintain exactly N samples per cycle. This coherent sampling ensures harmonic components fall precisely into DFT bins, eliminating leakage.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: In small‑signal stability analysis, a mode is considered poorly damped and a primary target for a Power System Stabilizer when its damping ratio falls below:
questions.solution: The lesson states that a mode is poorly damped when its damping ratio ζ = –σ/√(σ²+ω²) falls below 0.05. Such modes are the primary target for Power System Stabilizers (PSS). Therefore the threshold value is 0.05.
questions.subject: Electrical Engineering

questions.q: For a single‑machine infinite‑bus system subjected to a temporary three‑phase fault, the equal‑area criterion requires that the accelerating area A₁ be:
questions.a: less than the decelerating area A₂
opts: greater than the decelerating area A₂
equal to the decelerating area A₂
less than the decelerating area A₂
questions.solution: The equal‑area criterion (EAC) gives a quick analytical check for a SMIB system: the accelerating area A₁ (integral of Pₘ–Pₑ during fault) must be less than the decelerating area A₂ (integral after fault clearing). If A₁ < A₂ the system remains stable; otherwise it loses synchronism.

questions.q: What limits the reactive current a STATCOM can inject at very low AC voltage?
questions.solution: The lesson highlights an examiner trap: assuming a STATCOM can supply unlimited reactive current at zero voltage. In practice, the STATCOM’s current limit is set by the converter rating, which caps the maximum reactive current irrespective of voltage level.

questions.q: The energy available for synthetic inertia from a wind turbine is primarily limited by:
questions.solution: The lesson warns against overlooking the energy limitation of synthetic inertia when sizing H_syn for a wind farm with a small DC‑link capacitor. The DC‑link capacitor stores the energy that can be released as synthetic inertia; its size therefore directly limits the available energy.

questions.q: For non‑self‑restoring insulation, the safety factor applied to lightning over‑voltages (K_l) is:
questions.solution: The lesson specifies that for non‑self‑restoring insulation (solid dielectrics) the safety factors are higher: K_s = 1.3 for switching and K_l = 1.5 for lightning over‑voltages. Hence the lightning safety factor K_l is 1.50.

questions.q: Which FACTS device provides continuous reactive current independent of system voltage and has a response time of less than 5 ms?
questions.solution: The STATCOM uses a Voltage Source Converter (VSC) with a DC capacitor. Unlike the SVC which uses thyristor-controlled reactors and thyristor-switched capacitors, the STATCOM generates reactive current electronically. This allows it to deliver continuous reactive current even at low system voltages, independent of the voltage magnitude. The text explicitly states the STATCOM response time is less than 5 ms, compared to 20-40 ms for the SVC. The UPFC and IPFC are more complex devices combining series and shunt converters for power flow control, not solely for reactive current injection with voltage independence.

questions.q: In 5G New Radio, which channel coding scheme is used for data channels and which for control channels?
questions.a: LDPC for data, Polar for control
opts: LDPC for data, Polar for control
Polar for data, LDPC for control
Turbo for data, LDPC for control
LDPC for both data and control
questions.solution: The lesson text states that 5G New Radio (NR) uses LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check) codes for data channels and polar codes for control channels. This marks a shift from 4G LTE which used Turbo codes for data. LDPC codes offer better throughput and parallelism for high data rates, while polar codes are capacity-achieving for small block lengths typical of control information. The other options incorrectly swap the assignments or reference older standards like Turbo codes.

questions.q: What is the effect of a one-sample delay in Model Predictive Control of power converters?
questions.a: It adds a pole at z = 0 and can destabilise the dead-beat controller
opts: It adds a pole at z = 0 and can destabilise the dead-beat controller
It eliminates chattering in the output
questions.solution: The text highlights a common pitfall in predictive control: neglecting the effect of sampling delay. It explicitly states that a one-sample delay adds a pole at z = 0 in the discrete-time domain. This additional pole can destabilise a dead-beat controller which relies on placing all poles at the origin for finite-time settling. The delay effectively introduces a phase lag that reduces the stability margin. Options A, C, and D describe benefits or unrelated effects not associated with sampling delay in this context.

questions.q: Why does the Model Reference Adaptive System (MRAS) speed estimator based on back-EMF fail at zero speed?
questions.a: The back-EMF amplitude becomes zero, leading to loss of observability
opts: The back-EMF amplitude becomes zero, leading to loss of observability
The stator resistance drops to zero
The inverter switching frequency becomes too high
questions.solution: The MRAS speed estimator relies on the back-EMF voltage induced in the stator windings, which is proportional to the rotor speed. At zero or very low speeds, the back-EMF amplitude becomes negligible or zero, resulting in a loss of observability for the observer. The text specifically mentions this limitation and notes that a high-frequency injection scheme is required to enable sensorless operation at zero speed. The other options describe unrelated phenomena such as resistance changes or saturation.

questions.q: What is the typical range of the coordination margin (M) for transmission class insulation coordination?
questions.solution: The coordination margin M is defined in the text as M = V90 / V10 - 1, where V90 is the statistical withstand voltage (90% withstand) and V10 is the protective level of the surge arrester (10% probability of exceedance). The lesson explicitly states that typical values for this margin are 0.15 to 0.25 for transmission class equipment. This margin ensures that the arrester protective level is sufficiently below the equipment withstand voltage to account for statistical variations in both overvoltage magnitude and insulation strength.

questions.q: In the context of the 'Answer Writing Framework' (Section 5.3), which of the following best describes the nature of a successful thesis statement for Paper II?
questions.a: A critical judgement that applies a specific theoretical lens to the text, such as a deconstructive reading revealing instability in a colonial binary.
opts: A descriptive summary of the plot of the prescribed text under discussion.
A critical judgement that applies a specific theoretical lens to the text, such as a deconstructive reading revealing instability in a colonial binary.
A chronological list of critics who have written on the text, arranged from Aristotle to Bhabha.
A paraphrase of a famous critic's view on the text without applying it to a specific passage.

This illustrates that a successful thesis is a 'critical judgement' applying a specific framework (deconstruction) to a specific textual feature (colonial binary). questions.q: In the context of Old English strong verb analogical levelling, the Middle English forms *sang* and *song* derive from the Old English paradigm *singan – sang – sungon – sungen*. Which statement accurately describes their historical relationship?
questions.a: B. *Sang* preserves the original strong past singular vowel, while *song* is a later analogical creation based on the past participle vowel.
opts: A. *Sang* reflects the levelled past participle vowel, while *song* preserves the original past singular.
B. *Sang* preserves the original strong past singular vowel, while *song* is a later analogical creation based on the past participle vowel.
C. Both *sang* and *song* are direct reflexes of the Old English past singular *sang*, with *song* resulting from a regular sound change.
D. *Song* represents the original past singular, and *sang* is an analogical extension from the present tense stem.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that Old English *singan – sang – sungon – sungen* shows the original strong past singular *sang*. It further explains that *song* is a later analogical creation based on the past participle vowel *u* (from *sungen*), which was levelled into the singular. Option B matches this explanation exactly. questions.q: According to the philological reconstruction workflow described, what is the correct sequential application of sound laws to derive Old English *cēosan* (Class II strong verb) from Proto-Germanic *keusan*?
questions.a: B. Loss of intervocalic *s* → compensatory lengthening → West Germanic a-mutation
opts: A. Grimm's Law → Verner's Law → West Germanic Gemination → a-mutation
B. Loss of intervocalic *s* → compensatory lengthening → West Germanic a-mutation
C. Verner's Law → Grimm's Law → a-mutation → West Germanic Gemination
D. West Germanic Gemination → Grimm's Law → Loss of intervocalic *s* → a-mutation
questions.solution: The lesson outlines the specific chain shift for *cēosan*: Proto-Germanic *keusan* loses intervocalic *s*, triggering compensatory lengthening to *kēosan*, followed by West Germanic a-mutation raising *e* to *ē* before nasal clusters, yielding *cēosan*. Option B captures this sequence precisely. Option A lists laws in a generic order not specific to this example. Option C reverses Grimm's and Verner's Laws and adds irrelevant steps. Option D misorders the laws and includes gemination which is not mentioned for this verb.

questions.q: The 1710 Statute of Anne granted authors a fourteen-year copyright term renewable once. How did this specific provision directly incentivise publishers to produce "standard editions" of authors like Shakespeare, Milton, and Dryden?
questions.a: B. Because the copyright on these dead authors' works had expired, publishers could reprint them cheaply without legal risk, exploiting a secure market.

Establishing a limited copyright term of fourteen years, renewable once, vested in the author or assignee
Abolishing the pre-publication licensing system enforced by the 1643 Licensing Order
Mandating the publication of the First Folio as a definitive authorial edition
questions.solution: The lesson states that the 1710 Statute of Anne 'transferred the perpetual monopoly of the Stationers to a limited term (fourteen years, renewable once) vested in the author or his assignee, thereby legally recognizing the writer as the primary rights-holder.' Option A describes the pre-1710 Stationers' monopoly, which the Statute replaced. The Statute's key innovation was shifting rights from printers/booksellers to authors for a defined term, underpinning the professionalization of authorship.

The deployment of multiple narrators and legal/forensic documents as narrative evidence
Avoidance of domestic settings in favour of criminal underworld milieus
Use of stream-of-consciousness technique to represent psychological fragmentation

Collins's The Woman in White and The Moonstone famously use multiple narrators (Walter Hartright, Marian Halcombe, etc.) and documentary evidence (letters, diary entries, legal depositions). The collaborative theatre work of the Abbey Theatre involving Lady Gregory, J.M. Synge, and Sean O'Casey
A deliberate rejection of theatrical performance in favour of lyrical poetry publications
Its isolation from European avant-garde movements, preserving a pure Celtic aesthetic
questions.solution: The lesson's 'Common Misconceptions' section explicitly warns against 'Equating the Irish Literary Revival solely with Yeats, neglecting the collaborative theatre work of Lady Gregory, Synge, and O'Casey that reshaped modernist drama.' The Abbey Theatre (founded 1904) was a collective enterprise: Yeats provided vision, Gregory managed and co-wrote, Synge contributed peasant realism, and O'Casey later brought urban Dublin naturalism. This collaborative model influenced modernist drama's ensemble approaches. Option A repeats the misconception. Option C is false; the Revival was deeply theatrical. Anthologies applying aesthetic selection principles and university syllabi enforcing pedagogical mandates
F.R. Leavis's moral-aesthetic lineage and I.A. Richards's practical criticism workshops
The Cambridge Shakespeare's textual apparatus and the Statute of Anne's copyright provisions
questions.solution: The lesson's final misconception warns against 'Failing to distinguish between the anthology's aesthetic selection principle and the syllabus's pedagogical mandate, which together produced a canon that was both taste-driven and institutionally enforced.' Palgrave's Golden Treasury (anthology) exemplified aesthetic selection ('canon of lyric excellence'), while the 1921 Newbolt Report and Cambridge English Tripos (syllabus) institutionalized a 'literary heritage' through pedagogical mandate. Words or readings that affect the semantic meaning of the text
The physical gathering structure and paper size of a printed book
The compositor's habits and stop-press corrections during printing

questions.q: According to MacArthur and Wilson's Theory of Island Biogeography, how would the species richness of a habitat 'island' like a mountain top in the Western Ghats compare to a larger, isolated forest patch if both are equally distant from the mainland?
questions.a: The larger forest patch will have higher biodiversity because it supports lower extinction rates and higher immigration.
opts: The mountain top will have higher biodiversity due to its rugged terrain.
The larger forest patch will have higher biodiversity because it supports lower extinction rates and higher immigration.
Both will have identical species richness regardless of their size.
The smaller island will have higher biodiversity due to reduced competition for resources.
questions.solution: The theory posits that species richness is a dynamic equilibrium between immigration and extinction. Small, isolated islands (or habitat patches) experience high extinction rates and low immigration, leading to lower biodiversity. Conversely, large islands or patches support higher diversity because they offer more space and resources, reducing extinction risk. Therefore, the larger forest patch would have higher biodiversity compared to the smaller mountain top under equal isolation conditions.

questions.q: In the context of climate sensitivity metrics, why is the Transient Climate Response (TCR) lower than the Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity (ECS) for a doubling of CO₂?
questions.a: TCR is defined at the moment of CO₂ doubling under a 1% per year increase, so ocean heat uptake delays the full temperature response captured by ECS.
opts: TCR accounts for negative cloud feedbacks that operate only on centennial timescales, whereas ECS includes only fast feedbacks.
TCR is defined at the moment of CO₂ doubling under a 1% per year increase, so ocean heat uptake delays the full temperature response captured by ECS.
ECS includes the cooling effect of volcanic aerosols which are excluded from the TCR calculation framework.
TCR uses a lower radiative forcing value (≈2.5 W m⁻²) for CO₂ doubling compared to the ≈3.7 W m⁻² used in ECS estimates.
questions.solution: The lesson states that TCR is "the warming at the time of CO₂ doubling under a 1 % yr⁻¹ increase" and is lower (≈1.8 °C) than ECS (best estimate ≈3 °C) "because ocean heat uptake delays equilibrium." Option B correctly captures this mechanism: the gradual 1% per year increase means the system has not reached radiative equilibrium when CO₂ doubles, as the oceans continue to absorb heat. Option A is incorrect because cloud feedbacks operate on multiple timescales and are included in both metrics. Option C is wrong; volcanic aerosols are external forcings, not a defining difference between TCR and ECS. Option D is factually incorrect; the forcing for CO₂ doubling (≈3.7 W m⁻²) is the same physical quantity used in both frameworks.

questions.q: In biogeography, why is applying a single z-value from island biogeography theory to mainland habitat fragments problematic?

Island biogeography applies only to true islands; mainland fragments follow a linear species-area relationship (z = 1.0).
The z-value for mainland fragments is universally lower (≈0.10) than for islands (≈0.25) due to reduced edge effects.

This indicates that the permeability of the surrounding matrix (the landscape between fragments) influences species movement and persistence, thereby modifying the species-area relationship parameters. questions.q: In monsoon‑influenced karst regions, the oxygen isotope composition (δ¹⁸O) of speleothem calcite is primarily controlled by which of the following processes?
questions.a: The amount effect dominates the δ¹⁸O signal, and prior calcite precipitation can invert the isotopic trend.
opts: δ¹⁸O records only local temperature variations regardless of rainfall amount.
The amount effect dominates the δ¹⁸O signal, and prior calcite precipitation can invert the isotopic trend.
Speleothem δ¹⁸O is unaffected by prior calcite precipitation and directly mirrors the δ¹⁸O of precipitation.
Speleothem δ¹⁸O serves exclusively as a proxy for global ice‑volume changes.
questions.solution: In monsoon domains the isotopic composition of rainfall becomes lighter as precipitation amount increases (the amount effect). This signal is transferred to drip water and recorded in speleothem calcite. However, prior calcite precipitation (PCP) in the epikarst can enrich the remaining drip water in ¹⁸O, potentially reversing the expected negative correlation between δ¹⁸O and monsoon intensity. Therefore, interpretation must consider both the amount effect and PCP. Option B correctly captures this dual control, while A, C, and D ignore the amount effect or the modifying role of PCP.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the non‑linear character of permafrost carbon feedbacks highlighted in recent assessments?
questions.a: Abrupt thermokarst formation and methane‑dominated pathways introduce threshold behaviour, making carbon release non‑linear.
opts: Carbon release from permafrost scales linearly with mean annual temperature rise across all high‑latitude regions.
Abrupt thermokarst formation and methane‑dominated pathways introduce threshold behaviour, making carbon release non‑linear.
The active‑layer thickness alone determines the annual carbon flux, producing a predictable linear response.
Permafrost carbon emissions are confined to the upper metre of soil and cease after the year 2100.
questions.solution: Permafrost stores 1,460–1,600 Pg of organic carbon. As warming progresses, gradual active‑layer deepening releases carbon slowly, but abrupt thermokarst (ground collapse) exposes deep, previously frozen carbon to anaerobic decomposition, generating methane — a much stronger greenhouse gas. These processes create thresholds: once a critical temperature or ground‑ice content is crossed, large pulses of carbon can be emitted rapidly, breaking any simple linear temperature‑release relationship. Option B reflects this threshold‑driven, non‑linear dynamics, whereas A, C, and D assume linear, depth‑limited, or time‑bounded behaviour not supported by the lesson.

questions.q: Regarding aerosol‑cloud‑radiation interactions, how do the indirect effects of sulphate and black‑carbon aerosols differ in sign?
questions.a: Sulphate aerosols produce a negative indirect effect (cloud brightening), whereas black‑carbon aerosols produce a positive indirect effect (cloud absorption).
opts: Both sulphate and black‑carbon aerosols produce a negative indirect effect by increasing cloud droplet number.
Sulphate aerosols produce a positive indirect effect, while black‑carbon aerosols produce a negative indirect effect.
Sulphate aerosols produce a negative indirect effect (cloud brightening), whereas black‑carbon aerosols produce a positive indirect effect (cloud absorption).
The indirect effect is always positive for absorbing aerosols irrespective of their vertical distribution.
questions.solution: The indirect effect refers to aerosol‑induced changes in cloud microphysics. Sulphate particles act as cloud condensation nuclei, increasing droplet concentration and cloud albedo — a negative (cooling) indirect forcing. Black‑carbon particles absorb solar radiation, heating the surrounding air and reducing cloud lifetime or enhancing cloud absorption, yielding a positive (warming) indirect forcing. The lesson explicitly notes that the indirect effects have opposite signs for sulphate versus black carbon. Option C matches this description; A and B reverse or equalize the signs, and D incorrectly generalises the sign for all absorbing aerosols.
