questions.q: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 primarily extended which powers into peacetime?
questions.a: Wartime emergency powers allowing detention without trial
opts: Powers to impose martial law in disturbed districts
Wartime emergency powers allowing detention without trial
Powers to censor the vernacular press
Powers to recruit Indians for the British Indian Army
questions.solution: The text states: "The Rowlatt Act, passed in March 1919, extended wartime emergency powers into peacetime, allowing detention without trial and restricting civil liberties." Option B accurately reflects this specific provision. Option A (martial law) is not specified as the Act's primary extension. Option C (press censorship) relates to the 1908 and 1910 Press Acts mentioned in the Swadeshi context. Option D (recruitment) is unrelated to the Rowlatt Act.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: When did the Constituent Assembly adopt the Constitution of India?
questions.solution: The text states: "The Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into force on 26 January 1950." Option B is the adoption date. Option A is the commencement (enforcement) date. Option C is the date of Independence. Option D is the date of the first sitting of the Constituent Assembly (not explicitly in text but general knowledge), neither of which is the adoption date mentioned in the lesson.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: What was a major fiscal consequence of the 'guarantee system' (5% return on capital) for railway construction in colonial India?
questions.a: It fixed the colonial state's fiscal obligations, limiting investment in irrigation or education
opts: It enabled the Government of India to rapidly expand irrigation networks
It fixed the colonial state's fiscal obligations, limiting investment in irrigation or education
It led to the immediate nationalisation of all railway lines by 1880
It resulted in lower freight rates for Indian merchants compared to British traders
questions.solution: The text states: "The guarantee system attracted London capital but also fixed the colonial state's fiscal obligations, limiting its ability to invest in irrigation or education." Option B paraphrases this consequence accurately. Option A contradicts the text. Option C is false; the 1921-23 reorganisation merged companies, but nationalisation occurred post-independence. Option D is not mentioned; the text notes freight policy prioritised export raw materials and passenger fares were kept relatively high.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the kudavolai method as recorded in the Uttaramerur inscriptions?
questions.a: It involved writing names on palm‑leaf tickets placed in a pot and drawn by a child.
opts: It was a system of hereditary succession for committee members.
It involved writing names on palm‑leaf tickets placed in a pot and drawn by a child.
It required candidates to pass a written examination on Dharmashastras.
It was a method of revenue assessment for village lands.
questions.solution: The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I detail the kudavolai (pot‑ticket) election procedure for the sabha and ur. Eligible voters wrote candidate names on palm‑leaf tickets, placed them in a pot, and a child drew the tickets to ensure impartial selection. This method is distinct from the variyam committee system, which refers to the standing administrative committees (garden, tank, gold, annual) that managed village affairs after the election.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly deliberately chose the phrase 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 instead of 'due process' to:
questions.a: Limit judicial review and give primacy to legislative authority.
opts: Expand judicial review over legislative actions.
Limit judicial review and give primacy to legislative authority.
Align the Constitution with the American Bill of Rights.
Ensure that fundamental rights could be suspended during emergencies.
questions.solution: During the Fundamental Rights Committee debates, the Assembly rejected the American 'due process' clause because it would empower courts to scrutinise the fairness of legislation. By adopting 'procedure established by law', the framers intended to restrict judicial review to whether a law was enacted by a competent legislature following the prescribed procedure, thereby preserving legislative supremacy over the content of laws affecting life and personal liberty.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which historiographical school explicitly seeks to recover the autonomous politics of peasants, tribals and lower‑caste groups, arguing that their consciousness cannot be reduced to nationalist or Marxist categories?
questions.solution: The Subaltern Studies collective, led by Ranajit Guha, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak and Dipesh Chakrabarty, challenges elite‑centric narratives by recovering the autonomous politics of peasants, tribals and lower‑caste groups. The Nationalist school emphasises unity of the anti‑colonial struggle, the Marxist school foregrounds class contradictions, and the Cambridge school stresses British imperial strategy and collaborationist elites. Therefore, the correct answer is the Subaltern Studies collective.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which constitutional reform introduced separate electorates for Muslims, thereby institutionalising communal representation?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Morley‑Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims, institutionalising communal representation — a precedent that shaped later communal politics. The 1892 Act only allowed limited indirect election, the 1919 Act established dyarchy, and the 1935 Act provided provincial autonomy and a federal structure but did not introduce separate electorates for the first time.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which commission, appointed in 1948, recommended the reorganisation of states on the basis of administrative convenience rather than linguistic principles?
questions.solution: The Dhar Commission (1948) was appointed to examine the feasibility of linguistic states. It recommended reorganisation based on administrative convenience, financial viability, and geographical continuity rather than language. This contrasted with the JVP Committee (1949) which later conceded the linguistic principle. The States Reorganisation Commission (1953-55) under Fazal Ali ultimately recommended linguistic reorganisation which was implemented by the 1956 Act.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which institution was established in 1965 specifically for the procurement of foodgrains at Minimum Support Prices (MSP) to support the Green Revolution?
questions.solution: The Food Corporation of India (FCI) was established in 1965 under the Food Corporations Act to undertake procurement of foodgrains at Minimum Support Prices (MSP), maintain buffer stocks, and ensure distribution through the Public Distribution System. The National Seeds Corporation (1963) handled seed production, while Regional Rural Banks (1975) provided credit. The Agricultural Prices Commission (later CACP) recommended MSPs but did not conduct procurement.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act (1978), enacted after the Emergency, introduced which key procedural safeguard for the proclamation of a National Emergency under Article 352?
questions.a: Requirement of written advice from the Union Cabinet to the President
opts: Mandatory approval by a two-thirds majority of State Legislatures
Requirement of written advice from the Union Cabinet to the President
Extension of the period for parliamentary approval to six months
Removal of judicial review for emergency proclamations
questions.solution: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) was passed by the Janata Party government to reverse the authoritarian changes of the 42nd Amendment. It restored judicial review of emergency proclamations, replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" as grounds for Emergency, mandated written Cabinet advice for proclamation, and required parliamentary approval within one month. These procedural safeguards aimed to prevent misuse of Article 352.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: What was the official designation given by the Government of India to the 1974 nuclear test conducted at Pokhran?
questions.solution: India's first nuclear test on 18 May 1974 at Pokhran was officially designated a "Peaceful Nuclear Explosion" (PNE) by the government, claiming it was for peaceful purposes like excavation. The device was not weaponised or deployed. The 1998 tests (Operation Shakti/Pokhran-II) were openly declared as weapon tests. The 1974 test triggered the formation of the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) in 1975, leading to technology denial regimes against India.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which of the following accurately distinguishes the strategic orientation of the Dalit Panthers (1972) from the Bahujan Samaj Party (1984)?
questions.a: The Dalit Panthers adopted a Marxist-inspired radical cultural resistance while the BSP pursued electoral pragmatism and social engineering
opts: The Dalit Panthers focused on electoral alliances with upper castes while the BSP pursued radical cultural resistance
The Dalit Panthers adopted a Marxist-inspired radical cultural resistance while the BSP pursued electoral pragmatism and social engineering
Both organisations prioritised parliamentary politics over mass mobilisation
The BSP emerged as a splinter group of the Dalit Panthers in the 1980s
questions.solution: The Dalit Panthers, founded in Maharashtra in 1972 by Namdeo Dhasal and others, adopted a radical, Marxist-inspired approach focusing on cultural resistance, literary assertion (Dalit Manifesto), and direct action against caste oppression. In contrast, the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984, pursued electoral pragmatism, cadre-based organisation, and "social engineering" — forging tactical alliances with upper castes (notably Brahmins) to capture state power, exemplified by Mayawati's chief ministership in Uttar Pradesh (1995).
questions.subject: History

questions.q: The Women's Indian Association (WIA), founded in 1917, linked which specific demand to nationalist objectives in its petition to the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms?
questions.solution: The lesson text explicitly states: "The Women's Indian Association (WIA), founded in 1917 by Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins, and Dorothy Jinarajadasa, linked suffrage to nationalist demands and petitioned the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms for limited franchise." Property rights and child marriage were later focuses of the All India Women's Conference (AIWC). Temple entry is not mentioned in connection with the WIA's 1917 petition. Therefore, suffrage is the correct answer.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: Which historiographical phase questioned the "woman as victim" narrative and emphasized how peasant and tribal women negotiated colonial law, forest policy, and patriarchal community norms simultaneously?
questions.solution: The text outlines three historiographical phases. Early nationalist histories (e.g., B.R. Nanda) portrayed women as supportive symbols. The 1980s feminist turn (Forbes, Sangari & Vaid) recovered autonomous agency and highlighted tension between gender reform and nationalist priorities. Subaltern Studies (Guha, Chatterjee) specifically "questioned the 'woman as victim' narrative, emphasising how peasant and tribal women negotiated colonial law, forest policy, and patriarchal community norms simultaneously." Contemporary scholarship stresses intersectionality. Thus, Subaltern Studies matches the description.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) was originally established in 1911 under which name?
questions.solution: The lesson text states: "Parallel to IISc, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), established in 1911 as the Indian Research Fund Association, coordinated tropical disease research...". The other options are not mentioned as the original name. The Haffkine Institute is noted for plague vaccine trials (1899), but it is a separate institution. Therefore, Indian Research Fund Association is the correct founding name.
questions.subject: History

questions.q: According to the historiographical discussion on the 1857 Revolt, the evidential basis for assessment includes which of the following sources?

Transferred subjects (education, public health, agriculture, local self-government) were administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislative council. Reserved subjects (law and order, finance, land revenue, irrigation) remained under the Governor's executive councillors. The text explicitly lists 'law and order' as a Reserved subject.

questions.q: In the context of the 'Mechanism of Shift' described by critics like K.S. Narasimhaswamy, how does the critical approach change when moving from classical texts to modernist works like U.R. Ananthamurthy's Samskara?
questions.a: The critic must shift from analyzing theological consistency and gunas to examining psychological contradictions and existentialism.
opts: The critic must shift from analyzing theological consistency and gunas to examining psychological contradictions and existentialism.
The critic must abandon the study of alamkara entirely in favor of only structuralist analysis.
The critic should focus solely on the fourth wall breaking techniques found in Girish Karnad's plays.
The critic must prioritize the use of Sanskrit metres over vernacular dialects to maintain traditional purity.
questions.solution: The lesson explains that critics like K.S. Narasimhaswamy argue for a shift from alamkara to psychological realism. Specifically, it contrasts Pampa's static, idealized heroes with Ananthamurthy's complex, flawed characters. The critical approach must therefore move from analyzing theological consistency (guna) in classical texts to examining psychological contradictions in modernist works like Samskara. Option 0 accurately captures this transition. Options 1, 2, and 3 are either too extreme or refer to specific examples (like Karnad's fourth wall breaking) rather than the general shift described for Ananthamurthy.

questions.q: In the intertextual dialogue between classical epics and Navodaya novels, which of the following is NOT identified as one of the three operating mechanisms?
questions.a: Complete rejection of epic characters in favour of entirely new fictional protagonists
opts: Structural borrowing where the novel's chapter division mirrors the epic's Parva
Thematic inversion where the epic's dharma becomes a site of critique
Linguistic hybridity where Sanskritised diction coexists with colloquial Kannada
Complete rejection of epic characters in favour of entirely new fictional protagonists
questions.solution: The lesson clearly outlines three mechanisms: (1) structural borrowing (chapter division mirrors Parva), (2) thematic inversion (dharma becomes critique site), and (3) linguistic hybridity (Sanskritised and colloquial coexistence). Option D describes a complete rejection of epic characters, which contradicts the lesson's emphasis on re-contextualising characters, episodes, and moral dilemmas. The Navodaya writers treat epics as 'intertextual fields' for re-engagement, not rejection.

questions.q: A.K. Ramanujan's translations of Vachana poetry in 'Speaking of Siva' (1973) and 'Hymns for the Drowning' (1981) established a canonical hierarchy among Vachanakaras primarily through selection criteria emphasizing:
questions.a: Linguistic accessibility, thematic universality, and perceived philosophical depth
opts: Linguistic accessibility, thematic universality, and perceived philosophical depth
Chronological authenticity, metrical complexity, and sectarian orthodoxy
Folk performativity, oral transmission fidelity, and regional dialect purity
Sanskritised vocabulary, courtly patronage records, and manuscript antiquity
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that Ramanujan's selection criteria — 'linguistic accessibility, thematic universality, and perceived philosophical depth' — privileged Basavanna and Akka Mahadevi over Allama Prabhu and Siddharama, shaping the Vachana canon for decades. Option B describes traditional philological criteria not mentioned. Option C focuses on folk/oral aspects that Ramanujan's anthologies marginalised. Option D reflects the Sanskritised courtly aesthetic of earlier anthologies like B.M. Srikantaiah's 1915 collection, not Ramanujan's modernist editorial judgement.

questions.q: D.R. Nagaraj's essay 'The Colonial Construction of Kannada Literature' (1991) employs which specific postcolonial concept to argue that British classification created a persistent hierarchy in university curricula?
questions.solution: The lesson identifies two phases: the 1980s phase where scholars like Nagaraj appropriated 'Edward Said's Orientalism and Homi Bhabha's concepts of hybridity', and the late 1990s phase incorporating subaltern studies (Guha, Spivak). Nagaraj's 1991 essay specifically argued that 'British classification of Kannada texts into "classical" and "folk" categories produced a hierarchy' — a classic Orientalist taxonomic operation. While Bhabha's hybridity is mentioned as part of the first phase toolkit, the classification hierarchy maps directly onto Said's Orientalist discourse. Guha and Spivak belong to the second phase applied to caste/gender in Bhakti corpus.

questions.q: The Navodaya novelists Kuvempu and Shivarama Karanth adapted the realist template for local agrarian settings primarily through engagement with translations of:

opts: English modernist criticism (T.S. Eliot, Virginia Woolf)

Tamil Sangam poetry rendered into modern Kannada prose

Option A describes the later Navya movement (Ananthamurthy's Samskara) which engaged English modernist techniques via translated criticism. questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a contemporary Kannada poet with the specific dialect feature they employ to foreground caste-specific or regional experience?

opts: Siddalingaiah — Kundapura vowel shifts (a → e) and lexical items like 'moggu'

Siddalingaiah — Holeya dialect kinship terms (anna, akka) with standard grammar

(2) 'The coastal poet K.V. Subbanna ... employs the Kundapura dialect's vowel shifts (a → e) and lexical items (moggu for "bud") to evoke the maritime landscape.' Option C matches Siddalingaiah with Holeya kinship terms correctly. Option A swaps the poets. Option B swaps the dialect features. Option D invents 'Malnad region' for Subbanna, who is explicitly 'coastal' (Kundapura).

questions.q: The corrective wave of Kannada anthologies in the 1990s, exemplified by the Dalit Sahitya Akademi's 'Dalit Kavya Sangraha' (1994) and the Bandaya anthology 'Virodhi Kavya' (1998), differed from earlier colonial and post-independence anthologies primarily in their:

Deliberate assembly of excluded writers with editorial introductions framing selections as political interventions
Reproduction of a Sanskritised aesthetic as the normative standard for literary value
Establishment of a 'golden age' narrative privileging court poets like Pampa, Ranna, and Janna
questions.solution: The lesson contrasts three anthology moments: (1) 1915 B.M. Srikantaiah — 'golden age' narrative privileging court poets (Option D). (2) Post-independence (1965, 1972) — 'reproduced this hierarchy, reinforcing a Sanskritised aesthetic' (Option C). (3) 1990s corrective wave — 'deliberately assembled poems by writers excluded from mainstream volumes, providing editorial introductions that framed the selections as political interventions' (Option B). Option A describes the 2021 digital 'Open Anthology' project, not the 1990s print anthologies. The 1990s anthologies are explicitly defined by their political interventionism against the preceding consensus canon.

questions.q: Which translation work by B. M. Srikantaiah introduced the sonnet and lyric stanza to Kannada readers in 1914, influencing poets like Kuvempu and D. R. Bendre?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that B.M. Srikantaiah's 1914 translation "English Geethegalu" introduced the sonnet and lyric stanza to Kannada readers, prompting poets such as Kuvempu and D. R. Bendre to experiment with metrical regularity and personal voice. Ramanujan's "Speaking of Siva" (1973) and "The Interior Landscape" (1990) translated Vachana poetry much later. "Samskara" is a novel by U.R. Ananthamurthy translated by Ramanujan in 1976. Therefore, only "English Geethegalu" matches the description.

questions.q: The episodic, cliff-hanger structure of which performance tradition's prasanga informed the chapter design of early Navodaya novels such as "Chomana Dudi"?
questions.solution: The lesson identifies three feedback mechanisms from performance traditions to written literature. The first is narrative pacing: "the episodic, cliff‑hanger structure of Yakshagana prasanga informs the chapter design of early Navodaya novels such as 'Chomana Dudi'". Bayalata contributed stylised dialogic technique, while Harikatha contributed performative rhetoric like direct address. Dollu Kunitha is not mentioned in the lesson. Thus, Yakshagana is the correct answer.

questions.q: Critics such as Keerthinath Kurtakoti and G. S. Amur have argued that the Karnataka Sahitya Academy's selection committees historically favoured which group of writers?
opts: Translators and scholars of Sanskrit classics
Folk performers and oral tradition bearers
questions.solution: The lesson states that critics like Keerthinath Kurtakoti and G. S. Amur argued the Academy's selection committees "historically favoured dominant-caste, male, and urban writers, marginalising Dalit, tribal, and women's voices until the 1990s." The Academy commissioned translations of major novels but did not exclusively reward translators. It did not prioritize folk performers as a policy, nor did it favor Dalit/tribal/women writers historically — rather, it marginalized them. Option B directly reflects the cited criticism.

questions.q: The Appiko movement (1983) in Uttara Kannada, led by Panduranga Hegde, finds poetic resonance in the works of which poet?

questions.q: Devanur Mahadeva's Dalit short story "Kusuma Bale" (1990) is noted for deploying which narrative strategy to articulate community trauma?

Limited third-person focalisation and stream-of-consciousness passages

Option A describes the early modernist phase (Masti, A.N. Krishna Rao). Option B describes the Navya period (Lankesh, Chittal). Option D describes postmodern strategies (Vasudhendra, Banu Mushtaq). G. S. Shivarudrappa (1975) – tatsama vocabulary reflecting nationalist cultural retrieval

questions.q: In the context of Navodaya short stories, Masti Venkatesha Iyengar's "Kavalu" (1935) is cited as a prime example of linguistic experimentation primarily because it:
questions.a: employs a shatpadi-style invocation before shifting into dialogue rendered in the Mysuru dialect
opts: adopts a purely colloquial Mysuru dialect throughout to reject classical conventions
employs a shatpadi-style invocation before shifting into dialogue rendered in the Mysuru dialect
introduces blank verse and sonnet forms into Kannada prose narrative for the first time
embeds a translated fragment from Kafka's The Metamorphosis to foreground existential alienation
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Masti's 'Kavalu' (1935) opens with a shatpadi-style invocation before shifting into a dialogue rendered in the Mysuru dialect, illustrating a deliberate code-switching." This juxtaposition of classical champu cadences (shatpadi) with emerging colloquial speech (Mysuru dialect) exemplifies the Navodaya short story's role as a laboratory for testing expressive limits. Option A is incorrect because the story does not use dialect throughout; it begins classically. Option C describes the metrical innovations in poetry (Kuvempu/Bendre), not prose. Option D refers to P. Lankesh's Navya story "Matsyagandhi" (1970), not Masti's Navodaya story.

questions.q: According to the sociological periodisation of Kannada literary history advanced by D. R. Nagaraj and Janaki Nair, the "Modern" period is inaugurated by:
questions.a: the colonial print-public sphere and the rise of the novel
opts: the Halmidi inscription (c. 450 CE) marking the advent of written Kannada
the twelfth-century Vachana movement creating a non-Brahminical literary public sphere
the colonial print-public sphere and the rise of the novel
the formal shift from champu to Navodaya free verse initiated by B. M. Srikantaiah
questions.solution: The lesson clearly outlines three periodisation schemata. The sociological model, advanced by D. R. Nagaraj (1998) and Janaki Nair (2003), proposes a "Bhakti-Modern" break around the twelfth-century Vachana movement (Option B describes the rupture, not the Modern period's start). Crucially, it states: "while the 'Modern' period is inaugurated by the colonial print-public sphere and the rise of the novel." Option A is the philological marker for the Old period (Narasimhachar). Option D is the aesthetic marker for the Modern period (Subbanna). Option C is the correct sociological marker for the Modern period's inauguration.

questions.q: The editorial policy of preserving dialect spellings in the 1995 anthology Dalit Kavya, edited by K. B. Siddaiah, is significant for Paper II answers on "language politics in contemporary Kannada poetry" because it demonstrates:

the institutionalisation of the Karnataka Sahitya Academy's standardisation norms
a strategic "linguistic reclamation" turning stigmatised vocabulary into poetic capital
the continued dominance of the champu metre in post-independence Dalit writing

Krishnappa's (1990) argument that such strategic code-mixing performs a "linguistic reclamation", turning stigmatised vocabulary into poetic capital. This is directly cited as material for essay answers on "language politics in contemporary Kannada poetry." Option A contradicts the move away from tatsama toward dialect/tadbhava. Option B is incorrect as the Academy's Anuvada Granthamale focused on translation, not dialect preservation in Dalit poetry. Option D is factually wrong; Dalit poetry is associated with free verse and dialect, not the classical champu metre.

questions.q: The Kannada Sahitya Parishat's 1958 declaration of Pampa, Ranna, and Janna as 'Mahakavis' is significant for Paper II preparation because it:

Directly influenced the prescribed-text list and essay questions on canon formation
Marked the Parishat's shift from manuscript collation to digital archiving

questions.q: In the classical vakh form employed by Lal Ded and Nund Rishi, which of the following accurately describes the mandatory metrical structure?
questions.a: Four lines of 14 matras each with a 7+7 split, caesura after the 7th matra, and aaba rhyme
opts: Four lines of 14 matras each with a 6+8 split and aaba rhyme
Four lines of 14 matras each with a 7+7 split, caesura after the 7th matra, and aaba rhyme
Four lines of variable matras (12-16) with free caesura and abab rhyme
Four lines of 14 matras each with a 7+7 split, caesura after the 7th matra, and abab rhyme
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'A classical vakh consists of four lines (pādas) each bearing fourteen matras (morae) arranged in a 7 + 7 pattern with a mandatory caesura after the seventh matra. The rhyme scheme is typically a a b a'. Option B matches all three defining features: 14 matras per line, 7+7 split with mandatory caesura after the 7th matra, and aaba rhyme. Option A incorrectly states 6+8 split (a Mahjoor innovation). Option C describes post-1990 adaptations (variable matras, free caesura). questions.q: Which feature distinguishes the Kashmiri qasida's adaptation of the Persian hazaj meter from its prototype?

Retention of hazaj meter but adaptation to Kashmiri stress patterns
Abandonment of monorhyme in favor of the ghazal's qafiya-radif structure
Substitution of the radif with a native Kashmiri refrain in every bayt
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that in the Kashmiri qasida, 'the quantitative meter hazaj (⏑ – ⏑ – ⏑ – ⏑ –) ... is retained' but 'the adaptation of the hazaj meter to Kashmiri stress patterns' is a key feature. Option B correctly captures this retention-with-adaptation. Option A is incorrect because the meter remains quantitative (hazaj), not replaced by stress-based. Option C confuses qasida's monorhyme (aa ba ca da...) with ghazal's qafiya-radif; the lesson notes this confusion as a trap. Option D is incorrect because the radif (e.g., '-e ya Rab') is retained from Persian, not substituted with a native refrain in every bayt.

questions.q: A Kashmiri verb form 'farāmōsh‑karun' (to forget) illustrates which morphological integration pathway for Persian loans?

Re-analysis as a compound verb with the light verb 'karun'
Retention of Persian infinitival endings in learned registers
Phonological nativisation with final vowel shortening and dentalisation
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'Verbs borrowed as infinitives (e.g., "farāmōsh" → "farāmōsh‑karun") are re‑analysed as compound verbs with the light verb "karun" (to do), a productive pattern also seen with Sanskrit loans such as "adhikār‑karun".' Option B matches this exact description. Option A describes Persian noun integration (e.g., 'kitāb-as'). Option C describes Sanskrit tatsama behavior, not Persian verbs. questions.q: Which institution's editorial board minutes are cited as primary evidence for linking state patronage to the canonisation of Mahjoor, Abdul Ahad Azad, and Rahman Rahi in the Paper II prescribed list?

opts: Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages (1958)
Kashmiri Research Department, University of Delhi (1955)
Kashmiri Manuscript Project, University of Kashmir (2012)
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that 'a strong answer links the Academy's editorial board minutes (published in its annual reports) to the canonisation of Mahjoor, Abdul Ahad Azad, and Rahman Rahi.' The Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages, established in 1958, produced the Kashir Encyclopedia and Kashmiri-English Dictionary (edited by G.M. Koul) which became de-facto reference works. The Kashmir Sahitya Parishad (1935) initiated the movement but the Academy's minutes are the specific evidence cited for canonisation. The University of Delhi department and the Manuscript Project are later developments unrelated to this specific canon-formation process.

questions.q: In Rahman Rahi's couplet 'Chinar-i pāt girān hō yim dil tchhu vuchhun / Gul-e-rang-e-dil-e-nāzuk-e-shām-e-bahār', which feature demonstrates the retention of the indigenous vakh metre in the first hemistich?
questions.a: The 7 + 7 matra rhythm in the first line
opts: The use of the radif '-e-dil' in the second hemistich
The 7 + 7 matra rhythm in the first line
The qafiya pattern '-ān / -ūn' across both hemistichs
questions.solution: The worked comparative annotation in the lesson explicitly states in Step 4: 'Rahi retains the vakh's 7 + 7 matra rhythm in the first line while adopting the ghazal's monorhyme in the second.' The first hemistich 'Chinar-i pāt girān hō yim dil tchhu vuchhun' follows the indigenous vakh metre of 7+7 matras. The radif '-e-dil' and qafiya '-ān/-ūn' are ghazal conventions (Urdu/Persian), and the Persianised compound is characteristic of Urdu ghazal diction. The hybrid form precisely consists of maintaining the vakh rhythm in the first line while adopting ghazal structures in the second.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of the three-stage editorial protocol established by the Kashmiri Manuscript Project for philological reconstruction of Sharada manuscripts?
questions.a: Paleographic collation → Orthographic normalisation → Stemmatic reconstruction
opts: Stemmatic reconstruction → Paleographic collation → Orthographic normalisation
Paleographic collation → Orthographic normalisation → Stemmatic reconstruction
Orthographic normalisation → Stemmatic reconstruction → Paleographic collation
Paleographic collation → Stemmatic reconstruction → Orthographic normalisation
questions.solution: The lesson clearly outlines the three-stage protocol in sequence: '(1) paleographic collation of multiple folios to resolve ligature ambiguities...; (2) orthographic normalisation to the modern Devanagari-based script while preserving archaic vowel markers...; (3) stemmatic reconstruction using shared scribal errors to posit a lost archetype.' This order is logical: first collate physical manuscripts to establish readings, then normalise orthography for modern accessibility, finally reconstruct the stemma/archetype. The example of resolving 'kōr' (Sharada) vs 'kor' (Persian script) in the vakh 'Shiv-chhu kōr kōr' demonstrates the collation-normalisation process preceding stemmatic analysis.

questions.q: What is the key constitutional distinction between Kashmiri's inclusion in the Eighth Schedule (1950) and its acquisition of official language status in the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir?
questions.a: Eighth Schedule provides symbolic recognition, while functional official language status required the 2020 Official Languages Act.
opts: Eighth Schedule inclusion automatically conferred official language status at the state level.
Eighth Schedule provides symbolic recognition, while functional official language status required the 2020 Official Languages Act.
Official language status derives from Article 351, whereas Eighth Schedule listing falls under Article 344.
The 2020 Act removed Kashmiri from the Eighth Schedule and granted it official language status instead.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that a typical examiner twist tests whether Eighth Schedule entry alone guarantees 'official language' status. The correct distinction is that scheduled status is a symbolic recognition, while official language status is a functional mandate for governance that only became operative for Kashmiri in the UT of J&K through the 2020 amendment to the Official Languages Act, 1963. The former State Constitution (1957) had designated Urdu as the sole official language, rendering the Eighth Schedule placement administratively inert until the post-2019 reorganization brought central legislation into force.

questions.q: In Kashmiri's split-ergative system, the ergative marker 'an' (or its allomorph 'n') appears on the subject of a transitive verb under which specific grammatical condition?
opts: In all transitive clauses irrespective of tense or aspect.
Only in the imperfective aspect (habitual, progressive, future).
In both perfective and imperfective aspects for intransitive subjects.
questions.solution: The lesson defines Kashmiri's split-ergative alignment as conditioned by aspect: in the perfective aspect, the transitive subject receives the ergative marker 'an' (or 'n' after vowels), while the intransitive subject and transitive object appear in the absolutive (unmarked) case. In the imperfective aspect, the system shifts to nominative-accusative alignment with the object marked by the dative-accusative suffix '-as'. A common error noted is assuming ergative marking applies uniformly across all tenses rather than being aspect-sensitive.

questions.q: Which evolutionary shift characterizes the Kashmiri short story tradition as outlined in the syllabus?
questions.a: A shift from realist modes to fragmented post-conflict narratives.
opts: A transition from romanticism to classical realism in the mid-20th century.
A shift from realist modes to fragmented post-conflict narratives.
A movement from oral storytelling traditions to exclusively written literary forms.
A replacement of Persian-influenced themes with Sanskritized vocabulary.
questions.solution: The syllabus heading 'The Kashmiri Short Story Tradition: From Early Modern to Post‑Conflict Narratives' and the listed common error — 'Treating the short story tradition as monolithic, ignoring the shift from realist to fragmented post‑conflict modes' — directly identify this trajectory. Early modern writers such as Akhtar Mohiuddin and Amin Kamil employed realist techniques, while post-1990 conflict narratives exhibit fragmentation, meta-fiction, and trauma-focused non-linear structures reflecting the rupture in Kashmiri society.

questions.q: A distinctive narrative strategy of the Kashmiri novel, differentiating it from the short story form, is the interweaving of history and myth through which technique?
questions.a: Polyphony and magical realism allowing multiple voices and temporal planes.
opts: Strict linear chronological narration with a single authoritative narrator.
Polyphony and magical realism allowing multiple voices and temporal planes.
Exclusive use of the ergative case to foreground narrative agency.
Deliberate avoidance of historical events in favour of purely mythological themes.
questions.solution: The syllabus section 'Narrative Strategies in the Kashmiri Novel: Interweaving History and Myth' and the common error 'Attributing novelistic techniques such as polyphony to the short story form' confirm that polyphony (multiple narrative voices) and magical realism (blending mythic/magical elements with historical reality) are novelistic strategies. The lack of any Konkani-language periodicals published outside India.
The prohibition of code-mixing in texts submitted for the Konkani Sahitya Akademi Award.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly notes: 'The candidate should also note the institutional gap: the Sahitya Akademi's award categories have yet to create a dedicated diaspora section, a point that can be raised in a critical evaluation of "institutional patronage."' Option B directly reflects this. Option A is incorrect; the lesson mentions community associations publishing newsletters and anthologies, with no mention of Academy funding refusal. Option C is false; Konkani Voice (Toronto) and other periodicals are cited. Option D is unsupported; the lesson highlights code-mixing as a formal feature of diaspora writing (Konkani, English, Arabic) without mentioning any prohibition.
questions.subject: Konkani Literature

questions.q: The first Konkani book to survive Portuguese censorship, Doutrina Christam (1622), was characterized by which of the following features?
questions.a: A catechism printed in Roman script under Jesuit supervision
opts: A secular folk narrative printed in Devanagari script
A catechism printed in Roman script under Jesuit supervision
An epic poem in ovi metre composed by Thomas Stephens
A manuscript preserved from the Auto da Fé of 1560
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that Doutrina Christam (1622) was 'a catechism printed in the Roman script under the supervision of the Jesuit missionary Thomas Stephens.' Option A is incorrect because it was religious, not secular, and used Roman script, not Devanagari. Option C describes Krista Purana (1616), not Doutrina Christam. Option D is incorrect because the Auto da Fé of 1560 destroyed manuscripts; Doutrina Christam was a printed book that survived the censorship regime.
questions.subject: Konkani Literature

questions.q: The 1974 seminar "Literature and Society in Goa" organized by Goa University's Department of Konkani produced a volume edited by R.V. Pandit that applied base-superstructure analysis to which short story?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the 1974 seminar volume edited by R.V. Pandit 'applied base‑superstructure analysis to the short story "Kavlem", arguing that the village festival functions as an ideological apparatus masking agrarian exploitation.' Acchev is mentioned later as a novel with stylistic discontinuities detected by computational analysis. Bhagavad-Gita Konkani is an 18th-century manuscript attributed to Miguel de Almeida. Krista Purana is Thomas Stephens' 1616 epic poem.
questions.subject: Konkani Literature

questions.q: Which three domains constitute Paper I of the Law Optional examination?
questions.a: Constitutional Law, Administrative Law, International Law
opts: Constitutional Law, Administrative Law, International Law
Constitutional Law, Criminal Law, International Law
Administrative Law, Contract Law, International Law
Constitutional Law, Administrative Law, Labour Law
questions.solution: The lesson states that Paper I carries 250 marks and is divided into three broad domains: constitutional law, administrative law and international law. This directly matches option A. The other options substitute criminal law, contract law or labour law, which belong to Paper II or are not listed as Paper I domains.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: How many major clusters are identified for Paper II in the syllabus map?
questions.solution: The lesson enumerates six major clusters for Paper II: (1) law of contracts and mercantile statutes, (2) law of crimes, (3) law of torts, (4) family law, (5) property law, and (6) industrial and labour law. Therefore the correct count is six, corresponding to option C.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which constitutional articles are mentioned as frequently surfacing in administrative law questions and informing statutory rights in contract, tort and labour disputes?
questions.solution: The interrelationship section explicitly notes that constitutional provisions such as Article 14, Article 19 and Article 21 frequently surface in administrative law questions and also inform the interpretation of statutory rights in contract, tort and labour disputes. This matches option B.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: According to the answer‑writing technique described, how many paragraphs should a legal answer contain and what is the function of the third paragraph?
questions.a: Four paragraphs; the third applies the rule to the facts
opts: Three paragraphs; the third states the conclusion
Four paragraphs; the third applies the rule to the facts
Four paragraphs; the third states the applicable rule
Five paragraphs; the third integrates authorities
questions.solution: The lesson outlines a four‑paragraph structure: (1) identify legal issues, (2) state the rule with authority, (3) apply the rule to the facts, and (4) deliver a clear conclusion. Hence the answer has four paragraphs and the third paragraph applies the rule to the facts, which is option B.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: What is the duration and focus of the second phase of the recommended nine‑month study plan?
questions.a: Three months; answer writing practice with timed questions
opts: Two months; comprehensive reading of primary textbooks
Three months; answer writing practice with timed questions
Four months; intensive revision and mock tests
Three months; only current legal developments
questions.solution: The study plan divides the nine months into three phases. The first phase lasts four months for comprehensive reading. The second phase lasts three months and focuses on answer writing practice, attempting at least two full‑length questions per day timed to twenty minutes each. The third phase of two months is for revision and mock tests. Thus option B correctly describes the second phase.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: According to the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Ram Singh (2000), when does a policy statement create a substantive legitimate expectation enforceable against the State?
questions.a: Only a clear, unambiguous promise accompanied by reliance creates a substantive legitimate expectation.
opts: Any policy statement automatically creates a substantive legitimate expectation.
Only a clear, unambiguous promise accompanied by reliance creates a substantive legitimate expectation.
A policy statement made by a Minister in Parliament creates a substantive legitimate expectation.
Substantive legitimate expectation arises only when the policy is codified in a statute.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that in State of Punjab v. Ram Singh (2000) the Court held that a mere policy statement without a clear, unambiguous promise does not create a substantive expectation enforceable against the State. Substantive legitimate expectation is narrowly confined and requires a definite promise and reliance. Option B reflects this requirement, whereas the other options either overstate the effect of policy statements or impose an incorrect statutory codification condition.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Under the ILC Articles on State Responsibility, which test is required for attributing the conduct of non‑State actors to the State?
questions.a: Effective control test as per the Nicaragua case.
opts: Effective control test as per the Nicaragua case.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly warns against applying the "overall control" test and states that the ILC Articles require the "effective control" test per the Nicaragua judgment for attribution of non‑State actors' conduct to the State. This is a distinct legal standard from the due‑diligence obligation to prevent private violations. Option B correctly identifies the effective control test, while the other options represent tests not endorsed by the ILC Articles as described.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which safeguard against judicial overreach in Public Interest Litigation is highlighted by the Supreme Court in Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008)?
questions.a: Continuing mandamus must be time‑bound and courts should avoid prescribing detailed policy.
opts: Continuing mandamus must be time‑bound and courts should avoid prescribing detailed policy.
Courts should assume full legislative powers to ensure justice.
PIL should be entertained on all policy matters including farm‑law repeal.
Judicial activism is synonymous with any expansive PIL order.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that in Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008) the Court cautioned against "judicial overreach" and emphasised that continuing mandamus must be time‑bound, the Court should avoid prescribing detailed policy, and it must respect the domain of elected branches. Option A reproduces these safeguards. The other options either advocate unlimited judicial power, expand PIL indiscriminately, or conflate activism with any expansive order, all contrary to the Court's stated limits.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the temporal scope of the doctrine of eclipse as laid down by the Supreme Court?
questions.a: It applies only to laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950.
opts: It applies to both pre‑Constitutional and post‑Constitutional laws.
It applies only to laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950.
It applies only to laws enacted after the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951.
It applies only to laws that have been re‑enacted after 1973.
questions.solution: The doctrine of eclipse was first articulated in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) and later clarified in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974). The Court held that a pre‑Constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right is not void ab initio but merely eclipsed, and it revives when the constitutional impediment is removed. Post‑Constitutional laws violating fundamental rights are void under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by amendment. Therefore, the doctrine applies exclusively to pre‑Constitutional statutes.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: At which levels does the doctrine of harmonious construction operate according to the Supreme Court's jurisprudence?
questions.a: At the intra‑statutory, inter‑statutory, and constitutional levels.
opts: At the intra‑statutory, inter‑statutory, and constitutional levels.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Keshav Mills Co. Ltd. v. Union of India (1973) stated that harmonious construction requires giving effect to both conflicting provisions. The doctrine operates at three levels: intra‑statutory (e.g., State of Rajasthan v. Gopi Kishan, 1992 reconciling sections of the same Act), inter‑statutory (e.g., M. S. M. Sharma v. Krishna Sinha, 1959 harmonising the Parliamentary Privileges Act with Article 194), and constitutional (underpinning the pith and substance test for statute‑Constitution conflicts). Hence, it functions across all three levels.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: How does the principle of proportionality in Indian administrative law differ from the Wednesbury reasonableness test?
questions.a: Proportionality demands a structured four‑stage analysis, whereas Wednesbury is a mere reasonableness review.
opts: Proportionality is identical to the Wednesbury test and requires only a subjective assessment.
Proportionality demands a structured four‑stage analysis, whereas Wednesbury is a mere reasonableness review.
Proportionality applies only to legislative actions, while Wednesbury applies to executive actions.
Proportionality is not recognised in Indian administrative law.
questions.solution: Indian courts have adopted a structured proportionality test comprising four stages: legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity (least restrictive means), and balancing (proportionality stricto sensu). This is distinct from the Wednesbury principle, which only asks whether a decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it. The lesson explicitly warns against treating proportionality as a mere reasonableness test, confirming that proportionality requires a rigorous four‑stage analysis.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Under the ILC Articles on State Responsibility, which condition must be satisfied for the defence of necessity to be invoked?
questions.a: Necessity requires an imminent peril, the absence of any alternative, and cannot justify violation of jus cogens.
opts: The state may invoke necessity to justify any emergency, including violation of jus cogens norms.
Necessity requires an imminent peril, the absence of any alternative, and cannot justify violation of jus cogens.
Necessity is available as a defence for countermeasures without any procedural prerequisites.
Necessity does not require proportionality between the act and the peril.
questions.solution: Article 25 of the ILC Articles permits necessity only when the act is the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril, and it does not seriously impair an essential interest of the other state. Crucially, necessity cannot be invoked to justify violation of peremptory norms (jus cogens). The lesson highlights that necessity demands an imminent peril, no alternative, and is barred for jus cogens breaches, distinguishing it from a blanket emergency defence.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: What is the correct scope of judicial review of legislative privileges under Articles 105 and 194 as established by the Supreme Court?
questions.a: The judiciary can review whether a particular act falls within the scope of the privilege and whether it complies with natural justice.
opts: The judiciary cannot review any exercise of legislative privilege.
The judiciary can review only the wisdom or propriety of the legislative decision.
The judiciary can review whether a particular act falls within the scope of the privilege and whether it complies with natural justice.
Legislative privileges are absolute and not subject to judicial review under Articles 32 and 226.
questions.solution: In Keshav Singh v. Speaker (1965) the Court held that judicial review extends to determining whether an act falls within the four corners of the privilege, but not to the wisdom of the decision. In Raja Ram Pal v. Speaker (2007) the Court further ruled that expulsion of members must conform to natural justice. The lesson emphasises a three‑step framework: identify the privilege, locate its constitutional/statutory source, and apply the review standard of jurisdictional correctness and procedural fairness. Thus, review is limited to scope and natural justice compliance.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: According to the 2016 ICRC Commentary on the Geneva Conventions, the 'continuous combat function' test is used to determine:
questions.a: Whether a person in a non-international armed conflict may be targeted as a fighter
opts: Whether a person in a non-international armed conflict may be targeted as a fighter
The threshold for applying Additional Protocol II based on intensity of violence
Whether a combatant in an international armed conflict has lost prisoner-of-war status
The legality of autonomous weapon systems under the principle of distinction
questions.solution: The 2016 ICRC Commentary clarifies that in non-international armed conflicts (NIACs), where combatant status does not exist, the 'continuous combat function' test determines whether a person belonging to a non-State armed group may be targeted as a fighter. This test assesses if the individual has a continuous combat role rather than sporadic participation. It is distinct from the criteria for Additional Protocol II applicability (intensity of violence and organization of the group) and does not apply to international armed conflicts where combatant privilege governs targetability. The test addresses contemporary challenges in asymmetrical warfare by providing a functional standard for distinction in NIACs.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: The three-step reservation compatibility test under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties requires verifying that a reservation:
questions.a: Is not prohibited by the treaty, is not excluded by the specified allowed reservations, and is compatible with the object and purpose of the treaty
opts: Is not prohibited by the treaty, is not excluded by the specified allowed reservations, and is compatible with the object and purpose of the treaty
Has been accepted by all other State parties, does not modify essential provisions, and can be withdrawn unilaterally
Is formulated in writing, communicated to the depositary, and ratified by the reserving State's legislature
Concerns neither a peremptory norm nor a human rights treaty nor a disarmament agreement
questions.solution: Article 19 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT) establishes a three-step test for the permissibility of reservations: (a) the reservation must not be prohibited by the treaty; (b) the treaty must not provide that only specified reservations are allowed (implying others are excluded); and (c) the reservation must be compatible with the object and purpose of the treaty. This test ensures that reservations do not undermine the treaty's essential bargain. The other options describe procedural formalities (Option C), consequences of acceptance (Option B), or categorical exclusions not found in Article 19 (Option D). The lesson explicitly references this three-step test as a key analytical tool for treaty law questions.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which statement accurately reflects the relationship between the doctrine of identification and strict liability statutes in corporate criminal liability?
questions.a: The doctrine of identification does not apply uniformly because strict liability statutes bypass the need for mens rea attribution
opts: The doctrine of identification attributes mens rea to a corporation only for offences requiring proof of negligence
Strict liability statutes require the prosecution to prove that a directing mind of the corporation possessed the requisite mens rea
The doctrine of identification does not apply uniformly because strict liability statutes bypass the need for mens rea attribution
Vicarious liability in corporate crime is limited to offences committed by employees acting outside the scope of their employment
questions.solution: The doctrine of identification (or 'directing mind' theory) attributes the mens rea of senior officers to the corporation for offences requiring a mental element. However, the lesson explicitly warns against assuming this doctrine applies uniformly to all corporate offences because strict liability statutes impose liability without proof of fault or mens rea. In such statutes, the prosecution need not identify a directing mind with guilty intent; the actus reus alone suffices. Option A incorrectly limits identification to negligence-based offences. Option B contradicts the definition of strict liability. Option D misstates vicarious liability, which typically applies to acts within the scope of employment.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: The distinction between the precautionary principle and the prevention principle in environmental law is that:
questions.a: The precautionary principle permits regulatory action despite scientific uncertainty, while the prevention principle requires a known risk to justify action
opts: The precautionary principle applies only when there is scientific certainty about environmental harm, whereas the prevention principle applies in cases of uncertainty
The precautionary principle permits regulatory action despite scientific uncertainty, while the prevention principle requires a known risk to justify action
The polluter pays principle operates solely as a cost-recovery mechanism and does not impose absolute liability for hazardous activities
The prevention principle imposes absolute liability irrespective of fault, while the polluter pays principle requires proof of negligence
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'Confusing the precautionary principle with the prevention principle; the former permits action despite scientific uncertainty, the latter requires known risk.' The precautionary principle (Rio Principle 15) allows authorities to take protective measures when scientific evidence is inconclusive but potential harm is serious. The prevention principle operates when risks are identified and known, requiring measures to prevent damage before it occurs. Option A reverses the roles. Option C misstates the polluter pays principle, which the lesson notes 'also imposes absolute liability for hazardous activities irrespective of fault.' Option D incorrectly assigns absolute liability to the prevention principle.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: In Bharat Aluminium Co v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services (2012), the Supreme Court of India held that:
questions.a: Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 applies only to arbitrations seated in India; for foreign-seated arbitrations, only Part II (enforcement) applies
opts: Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 applies only to arbitrations seated in India; for foreign-seated arbitrations, only Part II (enforcement) applies
The venue of arbitration determines the applicability of Part I, while the seat is relevant only for enforcement under Part II
Part I of the Arbitration Act applies to all international commercial arbitrations regardless of the seat
The seat and venue are legally synonymous under the Arbitration Act, and both determine the supervisory jurisdiction of courts
questions.solution: The Bharat Aluminium (BALCO) judgment overruled the earlier Bhatia International ruling. The Court held that Part I of the Arbitration Act (which provides for interim measures, setting aside awards, etc.) applies only to arbitrations seated in India. For foreign-seated arbitrations, only Part II (enforcement of foreign awards under the New York/Geneva Conventions) applies, thereby ending judicial intervention in foreign arbitrations. The seat determines the lex arbitri and supervisory jurisdiction, whereas venue is merely the physical location of hearings and does not affect the governing law. Option B reverses the roles of seat and venue. Option C states the overruled Bhatia position. Option D incorrectly equates seat and venue.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, as amended, what is the minimum default threshold for initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP)?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "The CIRP is initiated by a financial creditor, operational creditor or the corporate debtor itself upon a default of at least ₹1 crore (raised from ₹1 lakh by the 2020 amendment)." The 2020 amendment increased the threshold from ₹1 lakh to ₹1 crore. Options A, C, and D are incorrect thresholds.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970, as interpreted by the Supreme Court, operates as a bar on:
questions.a: Patents for new forms of known substances lacking enhanced therapeutic efficacy
opts: All pharmaceutical patents regardless of therapeutic value
Patents for new forms of known substances lacking enhanced therapeutic efficacy
Compulsory licensing applications for essential medicines
Parallel imports of patented pharmaceutical products
questions.solution: The lesson's 'common errors' section clarifies: "Treating Section 3(d) as a blanket bar on all pharmaceutical patents; it only blocks patents lacking enhanced therapeutic efficacy." This provision prevents 'evergreening' by denying patents for mere new forms (salts, esters, polymorphs) of known substances unless they demonstrate enhanced therapeutic efficacy. It does not bar all pharmaceutical patents, nor does it govern compulsory licensing or parallel imports.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, as amended, what is the mandatory requirement for admitting an electronic record as evidence?
questions.a: A certificate under Section 65B signed by a person occupying a responsible official position
opts: A certificate under Section 65B signed by a person occupying a responsible official position
Oral testimony of the person who created the electronic record
A forensic audit report certifying the integrity of the digital file
Notarised affidavit from the party producing the electronic record
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Overlooking the requirement of a Section 65B certificate for every electronic record; the 2020 Supreme Court ruling makes it mandatory." Section 65B(4) requires a certificate from a person occupying a responsible official position in relation to the operation of the relevant device, identifying the electronic record and describing the manner of its production. The Arjun Panditrao v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020) judgment clarified this is a condition precedent, not a mere formality. Oral testimony, forensic audit, or notarised affidavit cannot substitute this statutory certificate.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which Article provides Right to Constitutional Remedies?
questions.solution: Article 32 provides right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which Article deals with President's Rule?
questions.solution: Article 356 deals with President's Rule (failure of constitutional machinery in state).
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which case established the Basic Structure Doctrine?
questions.solution: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) established that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which writ is used to produce a detained person before court?
questions.solution: Habeas Corpus means 'produce the body' - used to produce a detained person before court to check legality of detention.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Under Article 226, High Courts possess a wider scope of power compared to the Supreme Court under Article 32. What specific type of right can a High Court enforce via writs that the Supreme Court generally restricts itself to Fundamental Rights?
questions.a: Any legal right or statutory duty violation, including errors of jurisdiction by lower courts
opts: Only Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Part III
Any legal right or statutory duty violation, including errors of jurisdiction by lower courts
Rights related exclusively to the enforcement of Directive Principles of State Policy
Fundamental Rights only when no remedy exists in ordinary law
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly distinguishes the scope of Article 226 from Article 32. While Article 32 is for Fundamental Rights, Article 226 grants High Courts wider powers. They can issue writs not just for Fundamental Rights but also for any 'legal right' or to correct errors of jurisdiction by lower courts or tribunals. The Supreme Court under Article 32 focuses on Fundamental Rights, whereas High Courts under Article 226 are not limited by this and can intervene in administrative actions violating natural justice or statutory duties.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Regarding the jurisdictional hierarchy between Article 32 and Article 226, what was the ruling in Raj Narain v. State of UP (1975) concerning the necessity of exhausting remedies?
questions.a: It is not necessary to exhaust remedies under Article 226 before approaching the Supreme Court under Article 32.
opts: Exhaustion of Article 226 remedies is mandatory before approaching the Supreme Court under Article 32.
It is not necessary to exhaust remedies under Article 226 before approaching the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Article 226 cannot be used if a National Emergency is declared under Article 352.
The Supreme Court can only intervene if the High Court has explicitly refused jurisdiction.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Raj Narain case clarified the relationship between the two articles. It held that it is not necessary to exhaust remedies under Article 226 before approaching the Supreme Court under Article 32. While High Courts are often approached first due to proximity and wider jurisdiction, the constitutional right to approach the Supreme Court directly for Fundamental Rights enforcement remains intact without prior exhaustion of High Court remedies.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: In judicial review of administrative action, the Wednesbury unreasonableness test requires the court to determine whether:
questions.a: The decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it.
opts: The decision is disproportionate to the legitimate aim pursued by the authority.
The decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it.
The decision violates a legitimate expectation of the affected person without adequate justification.
The decision was made in breach of procedural fairness or natural justice.
questions.solution: The Wednesbury test, adopted in State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam and Om Kumar v. Union of India, asks whether a decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have arrived at it. It does not involve proportionality analysis, legitimate expectation, or procedural fairness, which are separate grounds of review. The court does not substitute its own judgment but intervenes only where the decision is perverse, irrational, or beyond the range of reasonable responses.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Regarding the domestic implementation of treaties under Article 253 of the Constitution, which statement reflects the Indian judicial presumption?
questions.a: Treaties are presumed to be non‑self‑executing unless the treaty text expressly creates directly enforceable obligations.
opts: All treaties are self‑executing and directly enforceable in domestic courts without enabling legislation.
Treaties are presumed to be non‑self‑executing unless the treaty text expressly creates directly enforceable obligations.
Parliament must always enact legislation to implement any treaty, irrespective of its content.
The executive can implement treaties by executive order alone, bypassing Parliament.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that Indian courts presume non‑self‑execution unless the treaty text expressly creates directly enforceable obligations. Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing treaties, but the presumption is that treaties require domestic legislation to become enforceable in municipal law. This distinguishes the Indian approach from systems where treaties are automatically part of domestic law.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: In the context of diplomatic protection, the rule of exhaustion of local remedies means that:
questions.a: A State may espouse its national's claim only after the national has pursued and exhausted all available local remedies in the respondent State, unless they are demonstrably futile.
opts: A State may espouse its national's claim only after the national has pursued and exhausted all available local remedies in the respondent State, unless they are demonstrably futile.
The respondent State must exhaust its domestic judicial processes before an international claim can be brought against it.
The claimant State must exhaust diplomatic negotiations before resorting to international adjudication.
Local remedies refer only to administrative remedies, not judicial ones.
questions.solution: The lesson notes that diplomatic protection is inadmissible unless local remedies are exhausted or demonstrably futile. This is a well‑established rule of customary international law: the injured national must first seek redress through the respondent State's domestic legal system (both judicial and administrative) before the home State can exercise diplomatic protection. The rule ensures the respondent State has the opportunity to correct its own wrongs.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which of the following safeguards was NOT introduced by the 44th Amendment in relation to Emergency provisions?
questions.a: Requirement that the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is justiciable and cannot be used for political purposes.
opts: Mandatory parliamentary approval for a Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 within one month.
The non‑suspendability of Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty) during any Emergency.
Removal of the President's power to suspend the enforcement of Fundamental Rights during a Financial Emergency under Article 360.
Requirement that the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is justiciable and cannot be used for political purposes.
questions.solution: The 44th Amendment introduced mandatory parliamentary approval (special majority) for Article 352, made Article 21 non‑suspendable, and removed the President's power to suspend Fundamental Rights during a Financial Emergency (Article 360). However, the justiciability of the President's satisfaction under Article 356 and the prohibition on political misuse were established by the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), not by the 44th Amendment. The Amendment did not expressly make Article 356 satisfaction justiciable; that was a judicial development.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: In the doctrine of colourable legislation, the Supreme Court's two-step analysis requires first identifying the legislative field by applying which test, and then verifying constitutional competence?
questions.a: Pith and substance test; then checking the Seventh Schedule entry
opts: Pith and substance test; then checking the Seventh Schedule entry
Territorial nexus test; then checking Article 246
Repugnancy test under Article 254; then checking legislative history
Colourable exercise test; then checking the motive of the legislature
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states the Court applies a two-step analysis: first, identify the legislative field by the pith and substance; second, verify whether the legislature possesses the constitutional entry to legislate in that field. The pith and substance test determines the true nature and character of the legislation (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo). The territorial nexus test relates to extraterritorial legislation, not colourable legislation. Repugnancy under Article 254 applies when a valid State law conflicts with a Central law, not for determining competence. The doctrine does not permit questioning legislative motives (State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla).
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: According to Hamidullah v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1972), delegated legislation can be struck down on three grounds of ultra vires. Which of the following correctly lists these three grounds?
questions.a: Substantive ultra vires, procedural ultra vires, and violation of the Wednesbury principle (arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory)
opts: Substantive ultra vires, procedural ultra vires, and violation of the Wednesbury principle (arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory)
Excess of jurisdiction, error of law apparent on face of record, and violation of natural justice
Lack of legislative policy, absence of guidelines, and excessive delegation
Non-compliance with parent statute, violation of fundamental rights, and breach of international law
questions.solution: The lesson states Hamidullah established three conformity requirements: (i) must not exceed scope of delegated power (substantive ultra vires); (ii) must not be made in unauthorized manner (procedural ultra vires); (iii) must not be arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory (Wednesbury principle applied to rule-making). Option B describes grounds for judicial review of administrative decisions, not delegated legislation validity. Option C relates to the validity of the delegation itself (excessive delegation), not the exercise of delegated power. Option D mixes distinct grounds not specified in Hamidullah as the three ultra vires categories.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: The Supreme Court of India applies which standard for determining bias in administrative proceedings, distinguishing it from the English "real likelihood" test?
questions.a: Reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of a reasonable person
opts: Reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of a reasonable person
Real likelihood of bias as perceived by the court
Actual bias proven by direct evidence
Predetermined outcome based on prior statements
questions.solution: The lesson's 'confusing' section states: "Applying the 'real likelihood' bias test from English law without adapting it to the Indian 'reasonable apprehension' standard used by the Supreme Court." This confirms India uses the "reasonable apprehension" standard (whether a reasonable person would apprehend bias), not the English "real likelihood" test. The reasonable apprehension test focuses on the appearance of bias to a reasonable observer, while real likelihood requires the court to assess the probability of actual bias. Actual bias (Option C) is a higher threshold rarely proven. Predetermined outcome (Option D) relates to pre-judgment, a specific type of bias, not the general standard.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: In harmonious construction of Fundamental Rights, the Supreme Court follows a three-step technique. What is the correct sequence of these steps?
questions.a: (i) Identify literal meaning; (ii) Ascertain legislative intent and constitutional scheme; (iii) Adopt interpretation avoiding conflict and advancing constitutional purpose
opts: (i) Identify literal meaning; (ii) Ascertain legislative intent and constitutional scheme; (iii) Adopt interpretation avoiding conflict and advancing constitutional purpose
(i) Ascertain legislative intent; (ii) Identify literal meaning; (iii) Apply doctrine of implied repeal if conflict persists
(i) Apply basic structure test; (ii) Check for repugnancy under Article 254; (iii) Invoke federal supremacy
(i) Determine pith and substance; (ii) Check legislative competence; (iii) Apply colourable legislation doctrine
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly outlines the three-step technique: "(i) identify the literal meaning of each provision; (ii) ascertain the legislative intent and constitutional scheme; (iii) adopt an interpretation that avoids conflict and advances the constitutional purpose." Option B reverses the first two steps and incorrectly suggests implied repeal as a step within harmonious construction (it is a last resort when harmonious construction fails). Option C lists doctrines (basic structure, Article 254, federal supremacy) that are separate from the harmonious construction technique. Option D describes the two-step analysis for colourable legislation, not harmonious construction.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: In the doctrine of pith and substance, which of the following correctly describes the third stage of judicial analysis when a law appears to encroach on another legislature's domain?
questions.a: Assessing whether the incidental encroachment is merely ancillary or constitutes a colourable exercise of power
opts: Determining whether the law's preamble explicitly references the legislative entry
Classifying the law's true nature under the appropriate entry in the Seventh Schedule
Assessing whether the incidental encroachment is merely ancillary or constitutes a colourable exercise of power
Examining the statement of objects and reasons to ascertain legislative intent
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly outlines a three-stage analysis for the doctrine of pith and substance. The first stage involves extracting the "true nature" of the enactment by reading the preamble, statement of objects and reasons, and operative provisions. The second stage classifies that nature under the appropriate entry in the Seventh Schedule. The third stage, as stated in the text, "checks whether the incidental encroachment is merely ancillary or whether it constitutes a colourable exercise of power." This distinction is crucial because incidental encroachment is permissible while colourable legislation is not. Option A describes part of the first stage, Option B describes the second stage, and Option D describes a component of the first stage. Only Option C accurately captures the third stage.
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Under Article 254(2) of the Constitution, a state law on a Concurrent List subject that has received the President's assent will prevail over an earlier central law:
questions.a: Until Parliament enacts a subsequent law on the same subject overriding the state law
opts: Permanently, unless the state legislature itself repeals it
Until Parliament enacts a subsequent law on the same subject overriding the state law
Only if the central law was enacted before the Constitution came into force
Subject to judicial review by the Supreme Court under Article 136
questions.solution: The lesson text states: "Under clause (2), a state law that has been reserved for the President's assent and received it can prevail over an earlier central law, but only" (text truncated but the principle is clear from the 'Common Errors' section). The Common Errors section explicitly warns: "Assuming Article 254(2) gives permanent immunity to a state law; it only protects until Parliament enacts a subsequent overriding law." This confirms that the state law's precedence is temporary and lasts only until Parliament passes a new law on the same subject that overrides it. Option A is incorrect because immunity is not permanent. Option C is irrelevant to Article 254(2). Option D is incorrect because while judicial review exists, it is not the condition for the state law's prevalence under Article 254(2).
questions.subject: Law

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately reflects the Supreme Court's position on the technique of prospective overruling in constitutional adjudication?
questions.a: It is an exceptional judicial technique reserved for constitutional decisions with massive retroactive impact
