questions.q: In the Garbage Can Model of organisational choice, which of the following describes the outcome where a choice is made without solving the problem?
questions.solution: The Garbage Can Model (Cohen, March, Olsen, 1972) describes decision-making in organised anarchies. It identifies three distinct outcomes: (1) Resolution by oversight — the problem is solved without a specific decision focus; (2) Resolution by flight — participants leave the choice opportunity, taking the problem with them; (3) Decision by garbage can — a choice is made (e.g., a contract signed, a hire made) but the underlying problem remains unsolved because the solution attached to the choice opportunity randomly rather than through fit. Satisficing is a Simon concept, not a Garbage Can outcome.

questions.q: The 4-D cycle of Appreciative Inquiry consists of which sequence of phases?

Its rigorous 4-D cycle comprises: (1) Discovery — identifying “what gives life” (peak experiences/best practices); (2) Dream — envisioning “what might be” (ideal future); (3) Design — co-constructing “what should be” (provocative propositions/architecture); (4) Destiny — sustaining “what will be” (implementation/continuous learning). Option A is generic project management; C is DMAIC (Six Sigma); D is Lewin’s change model extended.

questions.q: According to Mintzberg's configurational archetypes, which organisational form relies on mutual adjustment as its primary coordinating mechanism and has the support staff as its dominant part?
questions.solution: Mintzberg identifies five archetypes, each pairing a coordinating mechanism with a dominant organisational part. Simple Structure uses direct supervision with the strategic apex dominant; Machine Bureaucracy uses standardisation of work processes with the technostructure dominant; Professional Bureaucracy uses standardisation of skills with the operating core dominant; Divisionalised Form uses standardisation of outputs with the middle line dominant. Adhocracy, the fifth archetype, is organic and project‑based, employing mutual adjustment as its coordinating mechanism and giving prominence to the support staff (e.g., experts, consultants). Therefore, the correct choice is Adhocracy.

questions.q: Herbert Simon's concept of bounded rationality replaces the classical rational model by asserting that decision‑makers:
questions.a: Select the first alternative that meets a predefined aspiration level
opts: Identify and evaluate all possible alternatives before choosing
Select the first alternative that meets a predefined aspiration level
Rely exclusively on slow, analytical System 2 thinking
Ignore cognitive limits and time constraints
questions.solution: Simon argued that human cognition, incomplete information, and limited time prevent exhaustive optimisation. Instead of maximising, managers "satisfice" — they search until they find an option that satisfies a minimum aspiration level, then stop. This three‑stage process (intelligence, design, choice) acknowledges constraints, unlike the classical model which assumes full information and utility maximisation. Option B captures the satisficing rule, while A describes the classical rational model, C misstates the dual‑process theory, and D contradicts the premise of bounded rationality.

questions.q: According to the Dynamic Capabilities framework evolved from RBV, why might a legacy bank with high capital reserves still fail in India's digital economy?

questions.solution: The text explains that while RBV focuses on static resources (VRIN), David Teece evolved this into the Dynamic Capabilities framework for fast-changing environments like India's digital economy. The lesson provides a specific example: a legacy bank with high capital reserves (a valuable resource) may still fail if it lacks the dynamic capability to pivot its IT infrastructure or integrate external competencies for fintech partnerships. Option B accurately reflects this nuance. Option A is incorrect because the text acknowledges the resource is valuable but insufficient without dynamics. Option C misinterprets the imitation aspect. Option D contradicts the text which implies static resources are insufficient in volatile environments.

questions.q: How does the introduction of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, alter the risk calculus for lenders compared to the previous regime?
questions.a: A. It shifts power from creditors to operational turnaround experts (Resolution Professionals) and encourages stricter credit assessment before lending.
opts: A. It shifts power from creditors to operational turnaround experts (Resolution Professionals) and encourages stricter credit assessment before lending.
B. It removes all bankruptcy costs, making debt financing infinitely cheaper for firms regardless of leverage.
C. It replaces the automatic route for Foreign Direct Investment with a restrictive licensing system for distressed companies.
D. It mandates that banks must lend 100% equity to distressed firms to avoid insolvency proceedings.
questions.solution: The text describes the IBC, 2016 as introducing a time-bound resolution process that shifts power from creditors to operational turnaround experts known as Resolution Professionals. This structural change alters the risk environment by encouraging lenders and investors to conduct stricter credit assessment before lending to avoid future insolvency proceedings. Option A accurately summarizes this shift in power dynamics and behavioral change for lenders. Option B is incorrect because the text mentions bankruptcy costs still exist (direct and indirect). questions.q: Regarding the Modigliani-Miller (MM) theorem, what happens to the value of a levered firm when corporate taxes are introduced into the model?
questions.a: B. The value of the levered firm equals the value of an unlevered firm plus the present value of the tax shield, as interest payments are tax-deductible.
opts: A. The value of the levered firm equals the value of an unlevered firm minus the present value of the tax shield.
B. The value of the levered firm equals the value of an unlevered firm plus the present value of the tax shield, as interest payments are tax-deductible.
C. The value of the firm becomes independent of capital structure regardless of whether taxes exist or not.
D. The cost of equity decreases with financial leverage because dividends on equity become tax-deductible.
questions.solution: The lesson outlines the evolution of MM propositions. Initially, without taxes, firm value is independent of capital structure. However, the introduction of corporate taxes changes the narrative because interest payments on debt are tax-deductible, creating a 'tax shield' while dividends on equity are not. Consequently, MM Proposition II with taxes states that the value of a levered firm equals the value of an unlevered firm plus the present value of this tax shield. Option B correctly states this relationship. Option A has the wrong sign (minus instead of plus). Option C ignores the impact of taxes mentioned in the text. Option D is incorrect because dividends are not tax-deductible, and the text says cost of equity increases with leverage due to higher risk.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes dynamic capabilities from ordinary operational capabilities according to the dynamic capabilities framework?
questions.a: Dynamic capabilities enable the firm to "do the right things" through strategic reorientation such as pioneering new technologies.
opts: Dynamic capabilities enable the firm to "do things right" through efficient execution of current processes.
Dynamic capabilities are static resources that confer advantage only while conditions remain stable.
Dynamic capabilities enable the firm to "do the right things" through strategic reorientation such as pioneering new technologies.
Dynamic capabilities are measured solely by the level of R&D expenditure.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that operational capabilities let a firm "do things right" (efficient execution), whereas dynamic capabilities let it "do the right things" (strategic reorientation). The example of Toyota’s production system as an operational capability and its shift to hybrid and hydrogen power‑trains as dynamic capabilities illustrates this distinction. Options A and B describe operational capabilities or static resources, not dynamic capabilities. Option D is incorrect because the lesson warns that high R&D spend alone does not guarantee dynamic capability; sensing, seizing, and transforming routines are required.

questions.q: In the integrated improvement hierarchy of Lean, Six Sigma, and Theory of Constraints, which performance dimension is primarily addressed by the Theory of Constraints?

Therefore, TOC’s primary focus is on maximising throughput by identifying and elevating system constraints. Option A describes Lean’s focus, Option B describes Six Sigma’s focus, and Option D is a subset of variation/defect reduction associated with Six Sigma rather than TOC’s core objective.

questions.q: According to the Gordon & Lintner bird‑in‑hand model, the valuation formula is P0 = D1 / (ke – g). If a firm raises its dividend payout ratio, what is the combined effect on the growth rate (g) and the required return on equity (ke)?
questions.solution: The bird‑in‑hand theory argues that investors prefer certain dividends over uncertain capital gains. A higher payout leaves less earnings to reinvest, so the sustainable growth rate g falls. At the same time, the certainty of cash dividends reduces perceived risk, lowering the discount rate ke. The lesson explicitly states that a higher payout "reduces the growth rate g but also lowers the discount rate ke because of reduced perceived risk." Therefore, both g and ke decrease.

questions.q: Under the Companies Act 2013, which of the following characteristics would disqualify a person from being appointed as an independent director of a listed company?
questions.a: Being a promoter of the company
opts: Holding a 1 % equity stake in the company
Being a promoter of the company
Serving as a non‑executive director in a subsidiary
Having a pecuniary relationship with the company exceeding Rs 10 lakh
questions.solution: The Act defines an independent director by a negative‑criteria test: the person must not be a promoter, must not have a material pecuniary relationship, and must not be a key managerial personnel of the company or its subsidiaries. Being a promoter is an absolute disqualification regardless of shareholding size. The lesson notes that "not a promoter" is part of the statutory definition, making option B the correct disqualifier.

questions.q: When lead‑time variability is stochastic, which adjustment is required in the safety‑stock calculation to avoid under‑estimation?
opts: Multiply demand standard deviation by the average lead time
Ignore lead‑time variability and use a single‑source formula
Use the maximum lead time observed in the past year
questions.solution: The lesson identifies a common trap: "Using a single‑source safety‑stock formula when lead‑time variability is stochastic; ignoring the square‑root‑of‑lead‑time adjustment." When lead time is not constant, the variability of demand over the lead period scales with the square root of the lead time. Applying this factor correctly inflates safety stock to cover the combined demand and lead‑time uncertainty, whereas ignoring it leads to systematic under‑estimation.

questions.q: In a football‑field valuation for a strategic acquisition, what is the typical weight assigned to the discounted‑cash‑flow (DCF) method?
questions.solution: The lesson states: "A typical weighting for a strategic acquisition is 40 % DCF, 35 % CCA, 25 % PTA." This weighting reflects the greater reliance on intrinsic cash‑flow analysis for strategic deals, while still incorporating market‑based multiples. Therefore, the DCF method normally receives a 40 % weight in the football‑field chart.

questions.q: A listed Indian firm has a levered equity beta (βl) of 1.20, a target debt‑to‑equity ratio (D/E) of 0.50 and the corporate tax rate (including surcharge and cess) is 25.17 %. Using the Hamada formula βu = βl / [1 + (1‑t)×(D/E)], what is the unlevered beta (βu) rounded to two decimal places?
questions.solution: The Hamada unlevering formula is βu = βl / [1 + (1‑t)(D/E)]. Here βl = 1.20, t = 0.2517, D/E = 0.50. Compute (1‑t) = 0.7483. Then (1‑t)(D/E) = 0.7483 × 0.50 = 0.37415. Denominator = 1 + 0.37415 = 1.37415. βu = 1.20 / 1.37415 ≈ 0.873. Rounded to two decimals, βu = 0.87. Option A matches this value.

questions.q: In the Blue Ocean Strategy’s Four Actions Framework, which of the following actions is NOT part of the framework?
questions.solution: The Four Actions Framework, introduced by Kim and Mauborgne, consists of four distinct moves: eliminate factors the industry takes for granted, reduce factors well below the industry standard, raise factors well above the industry standard, and create factors the industry has never offered. "Imitate" is not one of these prescribed actions; it contradicts the core idea of breaking away from existing competition. Therefore, the correct choice is Imitate.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a digital twin from a traditional SCADA system in the context of Industry 4.0 manufacturing?
questions.a: SCADA provides real‑time monitoring while a digital twin offers predictive simulation and a virtual replica of the physical asset.
opts: SCADA provides real‑time monitoring while a digital twin offers predictive simulation and a virtual replica of the physical asset.
A digital twin is limited to data collection, whereas SCADA performs control functions.
Both systems provide identical predictive capabilities.
SCADA includes physics‑based modelling equivalent to a digital twin.
questions.solution: SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems are designed for real‑time data acquisition, monitoring, and control of industrial processes. A digital twin, by contrast, creates a dynamic, physics‑based virtual replica of a physical asset or process, enabling predictive analytics, scenario simulation, and optimisation beyond mere monitoring. The other options misrepresent the capabilities: digital twins are not limited to data collection, they do not share identical predictive power with SCADA, and SCADA does not inherently include physics‑based modelling. Hence, option A is the accurate distinction.

questions.q: Which feature is unique to the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and not required under India’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework?
opts: Applies to all Indian listed companies
Uses nine principles aligned with the NGRBC
questions.solution: The CSRD introduces a double materiality perspective, obligating companies to report both how sustainability issues affect their financial performance (financial materiality) and how their operations impact society and the environment (impact materiality). India’s BRSR, while aligned with the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC) and its nine principles, follows a single materiality approach focused on stakeholder relevance. CSRD also extends to non‑EU firms with significant EU turnover and phases in assurance requirements, but the defining unique element is the double materiality assessment. Therefore, option B is correct.

questions.q: When valuing a real option using a binomial lattice, which discount rate should be applied to the expected payoff at each node under risk‑neutral valuation?
questions.solution: In risk‑neutral option pricing, the expected payoff at each node is discounted at the risk‑free rate because the probabilities are adjusted (risk‑neutral probabilities) to reflect a world where all assets earn the risk‑free rate. Using the project’s WACC, cost of equity, or cost of debt would double‑count risk adjustments and produce an incorrect option value. The binomial lattice parameters (up‑factor u, down‑factor d, risk‑neutral probability p) are derived using the risk‑free rate and the project’s volatility. Hence, the correct discount rate is the risk‑free rate.

questions.q: Under Section 47(vi) of the Income-Tax Act, 1961, a spin-off distribution of shares is tax-free for shareholders only if which two conditions are simultaneously satisfied?
questions.a: The subsidiary is an Indian company and the distribution is proportionate to existing shareholding
opts: The subsidiary is an Indian company and the distribution is proportionate to existing shareholding
The subsidiary is listed on a recognized stock exchange and the parent retains less than 20% equity
The transaction is approved by NCLT and a fairness opinion is obtained from a merchant banker
The parent company has held the subsidiary shares for more than 24 months and the spin-off ratio exceeds 1:10
questions.solution: Section 47(vi) explicitly states that the transfer of shares in a spin-off is not regarded as a transfer (hence tax-free) if the subsidiary is an Indian company and the distribution is made on a proportionate basis to the shareholders of the parent company. The lesson highlights this as a key trap: assuming tax-free status without verifying both the subsidiary's residency (Indian company) and the proportionality condition. Options B, C, and D describe procedural or valuation requirements (NCLT approval, fairness opinion, holding period) but are not the statutory conditions under Section 47(vi) for tax exemption.

questions.q: In International Capital Budgeting, why is it incorrect to discount foreign-currency cash flows converted at spot rates using the domestic WACC?
questions.a: It violates the Interest Rate Parity condition, which requires forward rates for conversion to maintain arbitrage-free valuation
opts: It violates the Interest Rate Parity condition, which requires forward rates for conversion to maintain arbitrage-free valuation
Spot rates are unavailable for emerging market currencies, making the conversion theoretically impossible
Domestic WACC already includes a country risk premium that double-counts exchange rate risk
The Adjusted Present Value (APV) method mandates the use of the foreign subsidiary's local WACC exclusively
questions.solution: The lesson identifies a key trap: "Using the domestic WACC to discount foreign-currency cash flows after converting at spot rates, ignoring the interest-rate-parity condition." Interest Rate Parity (IRP) dictates that the forward exchange rate, not the spot rate, must be used to convert future foreign cash flows to maintain consistency with the domestic cost of capital. Converting at spot rates and discounting at domestic WACC implicitly assumes zero interest rate differential, violating IRP and leading to valuation errors. The correct approach is either to forecast cash flows in foreign currency and discount at a foreign WACC, or convert using forward rates derived from IRP and discount at domestic WACC.
questions.subject: Management

questions.q: When applying the Erlang-C formula (M/M/c) to a service system where the squared coefficient of variation of service time (Cs²) exceeds 2, what adjustment is necessary?
questions.a: Apply the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula to incorporate general service time distributions
opts: Apply the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula to incorporate general service time distributions
Increase the number of servers (c) until the utilization factor falls below 70%
Replace the exponential service time assumption with a deterministic (M/D/c) model
Use the M/G/1 approximation with a modified arrival rate parameter
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly lists a key trap: "Applying the M/M/c Erlang-C formula directly to a service system with highly variable service times (Cs² > 2) without the Pollaczek-Khinchine adjustment." The standard Erlang-C (M/M/c) model assumes exponentially distributed service times (Cs² = 1). When service time variability is high (Cs² > 2), the exponential assumption is violated. The Pollaczek-Khinchine (P-K) formula provides the expected waiting time for an M/G/1 queue (general service times). For multi-server systems (M/G/c), approximations based on the P-K formula (e.g., the Allen-Cunneen approximation) are used to adjust the Erlang-C result for general service time distributions.

questions.q: Regarding the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, which statement accurately describes the nature of the "adequate jurisdiction" list for cross-border data transfers?
questions.a: It is a dynamic list that the Central Government may amend by notification, and the Data Protection Board can impose conditions on a case-by-case basis
opts: It is a dynamic list that the Central Government may amend by notification, and the Data Protection Board can impose conditions on a case-by-case basis
It is a static list of countries notified at the commencement of the Act and requires Parliamentary approval for any amendment
It mirrors the European Commission's adequacy decisions automatically, granting reciprocal status to all GDPR-adequate jurisdictions
It applies only to government-to-government data transfers and exempts private sector entities from localization requirements
questions.solution: The lesson identifies a key trap: "Treating the DPDP Act's 'adequate jurisdiction' list as static; the Central Government may amend it by notification, and the DPB can impose conditions on a case-by-case basis." This directly supports Option A. The DPDP Act empowers the Central Government to notify countries/jurisdictions as 'adequate' via notification (executive action), not requiring Parliamentary legislation. Furthermore, the Data Protection Board (DPB) has the authority to impose specific conditions for transfers even to adequate jurisdictions, making the framework dynamic and context-sensitive. Options B, C, and D contradict the statutory design described in the lesson.

questions.q: In a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) where "foreground IP is jointly owned" and "background IP remains with each party", what is the default legal position in India regarding a joint owner's right to sub-license the jointly owned foreground IP to a third party?
questions.a: Joint owners must account to each other for any exploitation (including sub-licensing) unless the agreement expressly states otherwise
opts: Joint owners must account to each other for any exploitation (including sub-licensing) unless the agreement expressly states otherwise
Each joint owner has an independent, unrestricted right to sub-license the joint IP without consent or accounting to the other owner
Sub-licensing requires unanimous consent of all joint owners, but no accounting for profits is required
The right to sub-license vests solely in the party that contributed the majority of the R&D expenditure for the foreground IP
questions.solution: The lesson highlights a key trap: "Confusing 'joint ownership of foreground IP' with an automatic right to sub-license; joint owners in India must account to each other for any exploitation unless the agreement states otherwise." Under Indian patent and copyright law (governed by the Patents Act, 1970 and Copyright Act, 1957), co-owners hold an undivided share. In the absence of a contrary agreement, a co-owner cannot grant a license (or sub-license) to a third party without the consent of the other co-owner(s), and if they exploit the IP commercially (including via licensing), they are liable to account for the profits to the other co-owners. The JDA clause on background IP is irrelevant to the default rules governing foreground IP exploitation.

questions.q: In a two‑sided ride‑hailing platform, which of the following best illustrates an indirect network effect?
questions.a: More riders joining the platform attracts additional drivers to sign up.
opts: More drivers joining the platform reduces waiting time for existing drivers.
More riders joining the platform attracts additional drivers to sign up.
A new messaging feature increases engagement among riders only.
The platform lowers its commission rate for all drivers uniformly.
questions.solution: Indirect network effects occur when growth on one side of a platform increases the value for the other side. In a ride‑hailing market, an increase in riders makes the platform more attractive for drivers because they can expect higher utilisation and earnings, thereby pulling more drivers onto the platform. Option A describes a direct effect (same‑side), C is a same‑side feature, and D is a pricing decision, not a network effect.

questions.q: According to the provided lesson on Advanced Comparative Analysis, why is literature written in Meitei Mayek (post-1992) not considered a 'new' literature but rather a revival of an ancient tradition?

Because it is a continuation of an ancient tradition interrupted by colonial policy, preserving specific vowel distinctions merged in Bengali script.
