questions.q: What is the canonical link function for the gamma family in a generalized linear model?
questions.solution: In a GLM the canonical link equates the linear predictor η to the natural parameter θ of the exponential family. For the gamma distribution the density can be written with natural parameter θ = −1/μ, so the canonical link is g(μ) = 1/μ, i.e. the reciprocal link. The log link is commonly used but is not canonical; identity and probit are not canonical for the gamma family.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For an orthogonal design matrix, the Lasso estimator simplifies to which thresholding rule?
questions.solution: When the columns of X are orthogonal, the Lasso objective separates across coefficients. The Karush‑Kuhn‑Tucker conditions give the closed‑form solution β̂_j = sign(β̂_j^OLS) (|β̂_j^OLS| − λ)_+, which is the soft‑thresholding operator. Hard thresholding would set coefficients to zero only when |β̂_j^OLS| < λ without shrinkage, ridge shrinkage never produces exact zeros, and no shrinkage would leave OLS estimates unchanged.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which of the following describes the back‑door criterion for identifying a causal effect?
questions.a: The set blocks all back‑door paths from treatment to outcome and contains no descendants of the treatment
opts: The set blocks all back‑door paths from treatment to outcome and contains no descendants of the treatment
The set blocks all front‑door paths from treatment to outcome
The set must include all mediators between treatment and outcome
The set must be empty to avoid conditioning on colliders
questions.solution: The back‑door criterion (Pearl) states that a set of variables Z is sufficient for identifying the causal effect of treatment T on outcome Y if (1) no variable in Z is a descendant of T, and (2) Z blocks every path between T and Y that contains an arrow into T (i.e., all back‑door paths). Blocking front‑door paths is irrelevant, including mediators would block part of the causal effect, and an empty set only works when there are no confounders.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: What is the expression for the variance of the ranked set sampling mean ȳ_RSS?
questions.solution: In ranked set sampling we draw m sets of size r, rank each set, and measure the unit with rank k from the k‑th set. The RSS mean is ȳ_RSS = (1/m) Σ_{k=1}^r ȳ_{(k)}. Because the measured units are independent across sets and ranks, its variance is Var(ȳ_RSS) = (1/m^2) Σ_{k=1}^r m Var(ȳ_{(k)}) = (1/m) Σ_{k=1}^r σ_{(k)}^2 / r = (1/mr) Σ_{k=1}^r σ_{(k)}^2, where σ_{(k)}^2 is the variance of the k‑th order statistic.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: How is overdispersion commonly addressed in a generalized linear model?
questions.a: By introducing a dispersion parameter estimated via Pearson χ²/df or quasi‑likelihood
opts: By fixing the dispersion parameter to one
By introducing a dispersion parameter estimated via Pearson χ²/df or quasi‑likelihood
By replacing the link function with the identity link
By using only canonical link functions
questions.solution: Overdispersion occurs when the observed variance exceeds the variance implied by the exponential family. The standard remedy is to introduce a dispersion parameter φ and estimate it, typically by the Pearson χ² statistic divided by the residual degrees of freedom, or by adopting a quasi‑likelihood approach that specifies only a variance function V(μ) and retains the same estimating equations. Fixing φ=1 ignores overdispersion, changing the link does not address extra‑variation, and canonical links alone do not solve overdispersion.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the second‑order delta method, the bias of a smooth transformation g(θ̂ₙ) is approximated by which term?
questions.solution: The second‑order Taylor expansion of g(θ̂ₙ) around θ includes the quadratic term ½(θ̂ₙ−θ)ᵀ H_g(θ)(θ̂ₙ−θ). Taking expectations and using Var(θ̂ₙ) ≈ Σ/n gives E[g(θ̂ₙ)] ≈ g(θ) + ½ tr[H_g(θ) Σ]/n. Hence the bias correction is of order n⁻¹ with coefficient ½ tr[H_g(θ) Σ].
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The first‑order Edgeworth correction for the distribution of a standardized sample mean involves which cumulant of the underlying distribution?
questions.solution: For a standardized sum Zₙ, the Edgeworth expansion is P(Zₙ ≤ z) = Φ(z) + n⁻¹ᐟ² p₁(z)φ(z) + … where p₁(z) = (κ₃/6)(z²−1). The polynomial p₁ depends on the third cumulant κ₃ (skewness). The fourth cumulant κ₄ appears only in the second‑order term p₂(z).
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In a normal hierarchical model with conjugate priors, the full conditional distribution for a variance component is:
questions.solution: With a normal likelihood and an inverse‑gamma prior on the variance, the posterior full conditional for the variance remains inverse‑gamma because the inverse‑gamma is conjugate to the normal variance. This closed form enables direct Gibbs sampling and improves mixing compared to Metropolis steps.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For a variable sampling interval (VSI) control chart with short interval h₁, long interval h₂, and in‑control ARL₀, the in‑control average time to signal (ATS) is:
questions.a: ARL₀ × (h₁·p + h₂·(1−p)) where p is the proportion of points in the warning region
opts: ARL₀ × (h₁·p + h₂·(1−p)) where p is the proportion of points in the warning region
questions.solution: ATS = E[∑ h_i] = ARL₀ × E[h] because the number of sampling intervals until a signal has mean ARL₀. The expected interval length is h₁·p + h₂·(1−p), where p = P(statistic falls in warning region) under in‑control conditions. This replaces the simple ARL when intervals vary.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the Edgeworth expansion of the distribution function of the standardized sum Z_n, the first-order correction term involves which of the following?
questions.solution: The Edgeworth expansion refines the CLT by adding terms involving standardized cumulants. For standardized sum Z_n, the distribution function F_n(z) = Φ(z) + n^{-1/2} (κ_3/(6σ^3)) (1 - z^2) φ(z) + O(n^{-1}). The first-order correction is proportional to n^{-1/2} and contains the third cumulant κ_3, the factor (1 - z^2), and the standard normal density φ(z). Option A matches this expression exactly. Options B and C correspond to higher-order terms involving κ_4 and κ_3^2, while D has the wrong sign inside the polynomial. Therefore A is correct.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Lugannani–Rice saddlepoint approximation for the tail probability P(X > x) is given by which expression?
questions.solution: The Lugannani–Rice formula provides a highly accurate saddlepoint approximation for tail probabilities. It states P(X > x) ≈ 1 - Φ(ŵ) + φ(ŵ)(1/ŵ - 1/ẑ), where ŵ = sign(ť)√{2(ťx - K(ť))} and ẑ = ť√{K''(ť)}. This expression combines the standard normal tail with a correction factor that involves the saddlepoint ť. Option A reproduces the formula exactly. Options B, C, and D either change the sign of the correction term or use Φ instead of 1-Φ, which would give the lower tail or an incorrect approximation. Hence A is the correct choice.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the normal–normal hierarchical model y_ij|θ_j ~ N(θ_j, σ^2), θ_j|μ,τ^2 ~ N(μ, τ^2), the posterior mean of θ_j shrinks the group sample mean toward the overall mean μ. The shrinkage weight depends on which ratio?
questions.solution: In the normal–normal hierarchical model, the posterior distribution of each group mean θ_j is normal with mean that is a weighted average of the group sample mean ȳ_j and the overall mean μ. The weight given to the overall mean (the shrinkage factor) is determined by the ratio of the within-group variance σ^2 to the between-group variance τ^2. Specifically, the posterior mean equals (n_j/σ^2 ȳ_j + 1/τ^2 μ) / (n_j/σ^2 + 1/τ^2), showing that the relative influence of μ increases as σ^2/τ^2 grows. The lesson explicitly states that the weights are determined by the ratio σ²/τ². Therefore option A is correct.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which of the following correctly defines the effective number of parameters p_D in the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC)?
questions.solution: The Deviance Information Criterion is defined as DIC = D̄ + p_D, where D̄ is the posterior mean deviance and p_D is the effective number of parameters. The lesson gives p_D = D̄ - D(θ̄), i.e., the difference between the posterior mean deviance and the deviance evaluated at the posterior mean of the parameters. This measures model complexity. Option A matches this definition. Option B reverses the subtraction, option C doubles the difference, and option D adds the two quantities, none of which correspond to the standard definition. Thus A is correct.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For a central composite design with a full 2^k factorial core, the axial distance α that ensures rotatability is:
questions.solution: Rotatability of a central composite design means that the prediction variance depends only on the distance from the design centre. For a design with a full 2^k factorial core, the axial distance α must satisfy α = (2^k)^{1/4}. This result follows from equating the moments of the design points on the factorial and axial portions. The lesson states this condition explicitly. Options B, C, and D give incorrect powers or bases. Therefore option A is the correct answer.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In kernel density estimation, the bandwidth h that minimises the mean integrated squared error (MISE) satisfies h ∝ n^α. What is the value of α?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the MISE is minimised by h ∝ n^{-1/5}. This rate arises from balancing the squared bias (order h^4) and variance (order 1/(nh)) terms in the MISE expansion for a second‑order kernel. Setting derivative to zero gives h ∝ n^{-1/5}. The other exponents correspond to different bias‑variance trade‑offs or to optimal rates for derivative estimation, not for density estimation itself.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For an irreducible, aperiodic, positive‑recurrent discrete‑time Markov chain with transition matrix P, which of the following characterises the unique stationary distribution π?
questions.a: π_i = lim_{n→∞} P^n_{ij} for all j
opts: π_i = lim_{n→∞} P^n_{ij} for all j
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that for such a chain a unique stationary distribution π exists solving πP = π, Σ π_i = 1, and π_i = lim_{n→∞} P^n_{ij} for all j. Option B reproduces this limit property. Option A holds only for doubly stochastic matrices, not in general. Option C contradicts positivity of π. Option D gives the row sums of P, which equal 1, not the stationary probabilities.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Principal Component Analysis performed on the correlation matrix versus the covariance matrix yields different component loadings unless a specific condition holds. What is that condition?
opts: The sample size exceeds the number of variables
questions.solution: The lesson warns that confusing eigenvalues of the correlation matrix with those of the covariance matrix gives different loadings unless variables are standardised. Standardising each variable to zero mean and unit variance makes the covariance matrix equal to the correlation matrix, so the two PCAs coincide. Uncorrelatedness or a diagonal covariance matrix does not guarantee equality of the two matrices; they would still differ by the variances on the diagonal.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Consider a three‑way I × J × K contingency table. The saturated log‑linear model includes all main effects, two‑factor interactions, and the three‑factor interaction. The model of no three‑factor interaction omits the three‑factor term. The likelihood‑ratio statistic G² for testing this reduced model against the saturated model has degrees of freedom equal to:
questions.solution: The saturated model contains a three‑factor interaction term with (I-1)(J-1)(K-1) free parameters (due to identifiability constraints). Removing this term reduces the parameter count by exactly that amount. Hence the difference in the number of free parameters between the saturated and the no‑three‑factor‑interaction model is (I-1)(J-1)(K-1), which is the degrees of freedom for the G² test. The other options correspond to total cells minus one, main‑effect parameters, or two‑factor interaction parameters.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which entropy condition characterises a Donsker class of functions in empirical process theory?
opts: Polynomial growth of uniform covering numbers
Pointwise convergence of the empirical process
questions.solution: A class ℱ is Donsker if the bracketing integral ∫₀¹ √log N[ ](ε,ℱ,L₂(P)) dε is finite. This condition ensures asymptotic equicontinuity and a Gaussian limit in ℓ∞(ℱ). Polynomial covering numbers give VC‑type classes, which are sufficient but not necessary. Pointwise convergence alone does not guarantee the uniform CLT. Zero VC dimension is unrelated to the Donsker property.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the de‑biased Lasso, the matrix Θ is constructed to approximate which quantity?
questions.solution: The de‑biased (desparsified) Lasso uses Θ ≈ (XᵀX/n)⁻¹, i.e. an estimator of the precision matrix. With this approximation, √n(β̂_db_j − β₀_j) converges to N(0,σ²Θ_jj). The covariance matrix is the inverse of the precision matrix, while the design matrix and penalty matrix play different roles in the original Lasso optimisation.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For a valid back‑door adjustment set in a directed acyclic graph, which condition must be satisfied?
questions.a: The set contains no descendants of the treatment
opts: The set contains all ancestors of the treatment
The set contains no descendants of the treatment
The set includes all mediators between treatment and outcome
questions.solution: The back‑door criterion requires that the adjustment set blocks every back‑door path from treatment to outcome and contains no descendant of the treatment. Including a descendant would open a collider path and bias the effect estimate. Ancestors, mediators, or confounders may be included or excluded depending on the graph structure, but the prohibition on descendants is mandatory.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which alpha‑spending function yields conservative early boundaries in a group sequential design?
questions.solution: The O’Brien‑Fleming alpha‑spending function allocates very little type‑I error at early looks, producing high critical boundaries early and lower ones later. This makes early stopping for efficacy difficult, hence conservative early. The Pocock function spends alpha uniformly across looks, giving constant boundaries. Constant and linear spending are not standard names for these classic designs.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Under a Dirichlet process prior with concentration parameter α, the prior expected number of clusters among n observations is approximately:
questions.solution: For a Dirichlet process DP(α,G₀), the Chinese restaurant process predictive rule gives E[K_n] = α ∑_{i=1}^{n} 1/(α+i−1) ≈ α log n for large n. The concentration parameter α controls the rate of new cluster creation; larger α yields more clusters, but growth is logarithmic, not linear or inverse.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the role of countable additivity in Kolmogorov's axiomatic framework?
questions.a: It enables the treatment of continuous sample spaces and limiting arguments essential for statistical inference.
opts: It ensures that the probability of the empty set is zero.
It enables the treatment of continuous sample spaces and limiting arguments essential for statistical inference.
It implies the complement rule P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A).
It guarantees that the probability of any event is non-negative.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'This last axiom, countable additivity, distinguishes the modern theory from earlier finite-additivity approaches and enables the treatment of continuous sample spaces and limiting arguments essential for statistical inference.' The other options are consequences of the axioms generally, but countable additivity specifically is credited with enabling continuous spaces and limiting arguments. The probability of the empty set being zero, the complement rule, and non-negativity are either axioms themselves or immediate consequences not uniquely tied to countable additivity.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the continuous analogue of Bayes' theorem, the posterior density π(θ|x) is proportional to which expression?
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The continuous analogue replaces sums with integrals and probability mass functions with densities, yielding the posterior density π(θ|x) ∝ f(x|θ)π(θ), which is the cornerstone of Bayesian statistics.' This shows the posterior density is proportional to the product of the likelihood f(x|θ) and the prior density π(θ). The denominator (marginal likelihood) acts as the normalizing constant, so the proportionality is to the product, not sum, ratio, or inverse ratio.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: If X and Y have a bivariate normal distribution, which of the following is a property of the conditional distribution of Y given X = x?
questions.a: It is normal with variance independent of x.
opts: It is normal with mean independent of x.
It is normal with variance independent of x.
It is normal with both mean and variance depending on x.
It is not necessarily normal unless ρ = 0.
questions.solution: The lesson states regarding the bivariate normal distribution: 'The conditional distribution of Y given X = x is normal with mean μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(x − μ_X) and variance σ_Y²(1 − ρ²).' The mean depends on x linearly, but the variance σ_Y²(1 − ρ²) is constant (independent of x). This is a defining property of the bivariate normal. The distribution is always normal regardless of ρ (unless degenerate), so option D is false. Option A is false because the mean depends on x. Option C is false because the variance does not depend on x.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Lindeberg–Feller Central Limit Theorem extends the classical Lindeberg–Lévy CLT by relaxing which assumption?
questions.a: Identical distribution of the random variables
opts: Identical distribution of the random variables
questions.solution: The lesson states: 'The Lindeberg–Lévy CLT is the classical version; the Lindeberg–Feller CLT extends it to independent but not identically distributed variables under a Lindeberg condition that prevents any single variable from dominating the sum.' The classical Lindeberg–Lévy CLT assumes i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) variables with finite variance. The Lindeberg–Feller version keeps independence but drops the identical distribution requirement, replacing it with the Lindeberg condition. It does not relax independence (A), does not drop finite variance (C) — the condition implies it — and the Lindeberg condition is the new requirement, not something relaxed (D).
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: According to the Cramér–Rao lower bound, the variance of any unbiased estimator θ̂ of a differentiable parameter θ satisfies:
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'The Cramér–Rao lower bound states that for any unbiased estimator of a differentiable parameter, Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ), where I(θ) = E[(∂/∂θ log f(X;θ))²] is the Fisher information.' This is the standard formulation: the variance is bounded below by the inverse of the Fisher information. Option A has the inequality direction correct but misses the reciprocal. Option C reverses the inequality. Option D states equality, which only holds for efficient estimators achieving the bound, not for all unbiased estimators.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the frequentist framework, a 95% confidence interval for a parameter θ is constructed using a pivot. Which statement correctly describes the interpretation of this interval?
questions.a: The interval is random and, in repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals will contain the true fixed parameter θ.
opts: The interval is random and, in repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals will contain the true fixed parameter θ.
There is a 95% probability that the true parameter θ lies inside the particular interval computed from the observed sample.
The parameter θ is considered random and the interval is fixed once the sample is observed.
The coverage probability of the interval always equals the nominal level 0.95 for any sample size.
questions.solution: The lesson states that a confidence interval (L, U) satisfies Pθ(L ≤ θ ≤ U) = 1−α for all θ. The interval is random because it depends on the sample; the parameter is fixed. The correct frequentist interpretation is that in repeated sampling a proportion 1−α of such intervals will cover the true parameter. The phrasing “there is a 95% probability that μ lies in this interval” is a common mistake. Coverage can differ from the nominal level for small samples or discrete parameters, so it is not guaranteed to equal 0.95 in every case.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: According to the Neyman–Pearson lemma, for testing a simple null hypothesis H₀: θ = θ₀ against a simple alternative H₁: θ = θ₁, the most powerful test of size α rejects H₀ when which quantity exceeds a constant k?
opts: The Wald statistic (θ̂ − θ₀)ᵀ I(θ̂)(θ̂ − θ₀)
The score statistic U(θ₀)ᵀ I(θ₀)⁻¹ U(θ₀)
The generalized likelihood ratio λ = 2[ℓ(θ̂) − ℓ(θ̂₀)]
questions.solution: The Neyman–Pearson lemma explicitly states that for simple hypotheses the most powerful test of size α rejects when the likelihood ratio L(θ₁)/L(θ₀) exceeds a constant k, with k chosen to achieve the desired size. The Wald statistic, score statistic, and generalized likelihood ratio are used for composite hypotheses or asymptotic testing, not for the simple‑vs‑simple setting of the lemma.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Basu’s theorem connects completeness, sufficiency, and ancillarity. Which of the following is a direct consequence of Basu’s theorem?
questions.a: A complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic.
opts: A complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic.
An ancillary statistic is always a function of a minimal sufficient statistic.
A sufficient statistic is always complete if the family is exponential.
The factorization theorem implies that any ancillary statistic is also sufficient.
questions.solution: Basu’s theorem states that if a statistic is both complete and sufficient, then it is independent of any ancillary statistic. This is a fundamental result linking the three concepts. The other options are false: ancillarity does not imply being a function of a minimal sufficient statistic; sufficiency does not guarantee completeness even in exponential families unless the family is full rank; and the factorization theorem characterizes sufficiency, not ancillarity.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In Bayesian decision theory with squared‑error loss L(θ, δ) = (θ − δ)², the Bayes rule δ*(x) that minimises the posterior expected loss is which posterior summary?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: “Under squared error loss, δ* is the posterior mean; under absolute error loss, the posterior median.” The Bayes rule minimises the posterior expected loss ∫ L(θ,δ) π(θ|x) dθ. For squared‑error loss this integral is minimised by the posterior mean. The posterior mode corresponds to the MAP estimator under a 0‑1 loss, and the posterior variance is a measure of dispersion, not a point estimator.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Horvitz–Thompson estimator Ŷ_HT = ∑_{i∈s} y_i/π_i is used for design‑based estimation of a population total. Which property holds for this estimator under any sampling design with positive first‑order inclusion probabilities?
opts: It is model‑unbiased under a superpopulation model.
Its variance is always zero for simple random sampling without replacement.
It requires known second‑order inclusion probabilities to be unbiased.
questions.solution: The lesson states: “The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) estimator of the population total Y = ∑_{i∈U} y_i is Ŷ_HT = ∑_{i∈s} y_i/π_i. It is design‑unbiased: E_p[Ŷ_HT] = Y for any design with π_i > 0.” Design‑unbiasedness means the expectation is taken with respect to the sampling design, not a superpopulation model. The variance is not zero for SRSWOR; it equals N²(1−f)S²/n. Second‑order inclusion probabilities are needed for variance estimation, not for unbiasedness.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Fisher z-transformation z = ½ log((1+r)/(1−r)) applied to the sample correlation coefficient r yields an asymptotic variance that is:
questions.solution: The delta method gives the asymptotic distribution of a smooth function g(T_n). For the sample correlation r, Fisher's z = ½ log((1+r)/(1−r)) is the variance‑stabilizing transformation. The derivative of z with respect to ρ is 1/(1−ρ²). Since √n(r−ρ) → N(0,(1−ρ²)²), the delta method yields √n(z−ζ) → N(0,1). Hence the asymptotic variance of z is 1/n. However, the exact finite‑sample variance of z is 1/(n−3), which is the standard approximation used in practice. The lesson explicitly states that Fisher's z has asymptotic variance 1/(n−3).
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which of the following regularity conditions is NOT required for the asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator?
opts: The true parameter lies in the interior of the parameter space.
The Fisher information matrix is finite and positive definite.
questions.solution: Asymptotic normality of the MLE relies on standard regularity conditions: identifiability, interior true parameter value, differentiability of the log‑likelihood (usually twice), finite and positive definite Fisher information, and dominance conditions for differentiation under the integral. Compactness of the parameter space is not a required condition; the parameter space can be open or unbounded as long as the true value is interior and the other conditions hold. The lesson lists interior true value, differentiable log‑likelihood, and finite Fisher information as key conditions, but does not mention compactness.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In decision-theoretic estimation, a generalized Bayes rule derived from an improper prior is:
questions.solution: A generalized Bayes rule is obtained by formal Bayes calculations with an improper prior. While proper priors yield admissible Bayes rules under mild conditions, impropriety can break admissibility. The lesson states: "Treating a Bayes rule with an improper prior as automatically admissible; impropriety can lead to inadmissible generalized Bayes rules." Therefore such a rule may be inadmissible. Minimaxity and consistency are separate properties not guaranteed by impropriety.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In calibration weighting for survey sampling, the calibrated weights w_i* = w_i (1 + q_i x_iᵀ λ) are chosen to satisfy Σ w_i* x_i = X. A potential problem that can arise is:
questions.a: The calibrated weights may become negative.
opts: The weights always sum to the population size.
The calibrated weights may become negative.
The Lagrange multipliers λ are always zero.
The auxiliary totals X must be estimated from the sample.
questions.solution: Calibration forces the weighted sample totals of auxiliary variables to match known population totals X. The calibrated weights are w_i* = w_i (1 + q_i x_iᵀ λ). If the Lagrange multiplier λ is large or the auxiliary variables have extreme values, the adjustment factor (1 + q_i x_iᵀ λ) can become negative, producing negative weights. The lesson warns: "Using calibration weights without checking the positivity of calibrated weights; negative weights can produce erratic estimates and variance underestimation." The other statements are false: weights need not sum to population size, λ is generally non‑zero, and X is known, not estimated.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For the Wilcoxon signed‑rank test of a symmetric location parameter with sample size n, the asymptotic variance of the test statistic under the null hypothesis is:
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Wilcoxon signed‑rank statistic has null mean 0 and variance n(n+1)(2n+1)/24. This exact variance formula is given for the signed‑rank test. The other options correspond to variances of other rank statistics (e.g., Mann‑Whitney U) or incorrect scalings.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Hotelling's T² test for equality of mean vectors across groups assumes which of the following?
questions.a: The covariance matrices are equal across groups
opts: The covariance matrices are equal across groups
The sample sizes are equal across groups
The data are normally distributed with known covariance
questions.solution: Hotelling's T² test for comparing mean vectors requires the assumption of a common covariance matrix (homoscedasticity) across the groups, in addition to multivariate normality. The lesson explicitly warns that interpreting a non‑significant T² as evidence of equal means when covariance matrices differ substantially is a mistake. Equality of covariance matrices is therefore a key assumption; diagonal covariance, equal sample sizes, or known covariance are not required.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In multiple linear regression, a variance inflation factor (VIF) exceeding 10 for a predictor indicates:
questions.solution: The variance inflation factor is defined as VIF = 1/(1−R_j²), where R_j² is the coefficient of determination from regressing predictor X_j on all other predictors. A VIF larger than 10 signals that the variance of the estimated coefficient is inflated by more than a factor of 10 due to severe collinearity among the predictors. The lesson lists this threshold as a diagnostic for severe collinearity. Heteroscedasticity, non‑linearity, and influential outliers are detected by other diagnostics (e.g., residual plots, leverage, Cook's distance).
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The naive nonparametric bootstrap fails to provide consistent confidence intervals for the sample median because:
questions.a: The median is not a smooth function of the empirical distribution
opts: The median is not a smooth function of the empirical distribution
The median requires a parametric model assumption
The bootstrap sample size must be smaller than the original sample size
questions.solution: Bootstrap consistency requires the statistic to be a smooth (Hadamard differentiable) function of the empirical distribution. The sample median is not Hadamard differentiable, so the ordinary bootstrap distribution does not converge to the correct limiting distribution; the m‑out‑of‑n bootstrap (resampling m < n observations) restores consistency. The lesson explicitly mentions this failure for the median and the need for the m‑out‑of‑n bootstrap. The median does not require a parametric model, its variance is finite for continuous distributions, and the bootstrap sample size is normally taken equal to n.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Factor Analysis (FA), which of the following statements correctly describes a key distinction?
questions.a: PCA components are uniquely defined up to sign; FA loadings are rotationally indeterminate.
opts: PCA assumes a latent variable model with unique variances; FA is a descriptive variance-maximizing rotation.
PCA components are uniquely defined up to sign; FA loadings are rotationally indeterminate.
In PCA, communalities are estimated and less than 1; in FA, communalities equal 1.
FA reproduces the covariance matrix exactly only when the number of factors equals the number of variables.
questions.solution: PCA components are eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix and are uniquely determined up to a sign change. In contrast, FA loadings are not unique because any orthogonal rotation of the loading matrix yields the same covariance structure; rotation (e.g., varimax) is used to achieve simple structure. Moreover, PCA communalities are fixed at 1, while FA communalities are estimated and typically less than 1. FA reproduces the covariance matrix exactly only when the number of factors equals the rank of the matrix, not merely the number of variables. Therefore, option B correctly captures the distinction.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: When identifying an ARIMA(p,d,q) model using the Box-Jenkins methodology, what is the correct sequence for examining the autocorrelation function (ACF) and partial autocorrelation function (PACF)?
questions.a: Difference the series to achieve stationarity first, then examine ACF and PACF of the differenced series.
opts: Examine ACF and PACF of the original series, then difference if needed.
Difference the series to achieve stationarity first, then examine ACF and PACF of the differenced series.
Fit an ARMA model to the original series, then check residuals for stationarity.
Use the raw ACF to determine p and q, and the raw PACF to determine d.
questions.solution: The Box-Jenkins methodology requires the series to be stationary before identification. The first step is to apply differencing of order d until the series appears stationary. Only after differencing should the sample ACF and PACF of the differenced series be examined to suggest appropriate AR (p) and MA (q) orders. Examining the raw ACF/PACF of a non-stationary series leads to misleading patterns. Thus, option B describes the correct sequence.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U test) assumes which of the following under the null hypothesis?
questions.a: The two samples come from identical continuous distributions.
opts: The two samples have equal variances but possibly different shapes.
The two samples come from identical continuous distributions.
The two samples have the same median but may differ in scale.
The two samples are normally distributed with equal means.
questions.solution: The Wilcoxon rank-sum test is a nonparametric test that assumes the two independent samples are drawn from identical continuous distributions under the null hypothesis. This assumption implies equality of location, scale, and shape. A significant result may indicate a difference in location, but it can also arise from differences in scale or shape. The test does not require normality or equal variances alone. Therefore, option B correctly states the null hypothesis assumption.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The delta method provides an asymptotic normal approximation for a function g(T_n) of an estimator T_n. For which of the following functions does the standard first-order delta method fail at the point where the derivative is zero or does not exist?
questions.solution: The first-order delta method requires g to be differentiable at the limit point θ. For g(x)=x^2, the derivative at 0 is 0, but the method still applies (though the asymptotic variance is zero, requiring a second-order expansion for a non-degenerate limit). For g(x)=√x at 0, the derivative is infinite, so the method fails; however, the function is not differentiable at 0. For g(x)=log(x) at 1, the derivative exists and is 1, so the method works. For g(x)=|x| at 0, the function is not differentiable (left and right derivatives differ), so the standard first-order delta method fails. Hence, option D is the correct choice.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which location estimator has the maximum possible breakdown point of 0.5?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly gives the breakdown points: the sample mean has ε* = 0, the median has ε* = 0.5, which is the maximum possible for a location estimator. Huber’s ψ-function yields gross‑error sensitivity γ* = c but its breakdown point is not 0.5; Tukey’s biweight has redescending influence but also does not achieve the maximal 0.5 breakdown point. Hence the sample median is the correct answer.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Lasso prediction error bound O_P(s log p / n) holds under which design condition?
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Under the restricted eigenvalue (RE) condition on X, the Lasso achieves prediction error ||X(β̂ − β)||₂²/n = O_P(s log p / n)." The irrepresentable and mutual incoherence conditions are related to variable selection consistency, not directly to the prediction error bound. Orthogonal design is a special case but not the general condition cited. Therefore the required condition is the restricted eigenvalue condition.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For the SCAD penalty to possess the oracle property, the tuning parameter λ must satisfy which rates?
questions.solution: The lesson lists a common mistake: "Believing that SCAD’s oracle property holds for any tuning parameter λ; it requires λ → 0 and √n λ → ∞ at appropriate rates, otherwise selection consistency fails." This directly states the necessary asymptotic rates for λ. The other options contradict this requirement: λ → ∞ would over‑penalize, a fixed λ would not vanish, and λ → 0 alone without √n λ → ∞ would not guarantee selection consistency.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For a random sample of size n from a continuous distribution with cdf F, the random variable F(X(k)) follows which distribution?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the marginal density of the k-th order statistic has a beta-binomial form which shows that F(X(k)) follows a Beta(k, n - k + 1) distribution. This is a standard result in order statistics: the probability integral transform of the k-th order statistic yields a Beta distribution with parameters k and n - k + 1. The other options are incorrect parameterizations or wrong distributions.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In a full-rank exponential family with natural parameter space having non-empty interior, the sufficient statistic T(X) is:
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: 'if the family is full rank and the natural parameter space has non-empty interior, T(X) is also complete.' For full-rank exponential families, the natural sufficient statistic T(X) is minimal sufficient by the factorization theorem and the structure of the canonical form. Therefore, T(X) is both complete and minimal sufficient. This property underpins the Lehmann-Scheffé theorem for UMVUE derivation.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: A decision rule δ is minimax if it:
questions.a: Minimizes the maximum risk over all possible parameter values
opts: Minimizes the maximum risk over all possible parameter values
Minimizes the Bayes risk for a given prior distribution
Has constant risk function for all parameter values
Is admissible and has the smallest risk at a specific parameter value
questions.solution: By definition in decision theory, a minimax rule minimizes the supremum (maximum) of the risk function over the parameter space. It guards against the worst-case scenario. Option B describes a Bayes rule. Option C describes an equalizer rule, which may be minimax if it achieves the minimax value, but constancy alone is not the definition. Option D confuses admissibility with minimaxity; a minimax rule need not be admissible, and admissibility does not imply minimaxity.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) for testing H0: θ = θ0 against H1: θ = θ1 stops sampling when the likelihood ratio falls outside the interval:
questions.solution: Wald's SPRT continues sampling while the likelihood ratio Λn = L(θ1)/L(θ0) lies between the boundaries A and B, where A ≈ (1 - β)/α and B ≈ β/(1 - α) for desired Type I error α and Type II error β. The test stops and rejects H0 if Λn ≥ A, and accepts H0 if Λn ≤ B. The interval is therefore (β/(1 - α), (1 - β)/α). Option C reverses the boundaries. Option A uses error probabilities directly, not the likelihood ratio boundaries.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Which principle of experimental design ensures that unknown confounding factors are evenly distributed across treatment groups?
questions.solution: Randomization is the principle that assigns each experimental unit an equal chance of receiving any treatment. By doing so, it distributes unknown or unmeasured confounding factors evenly across treatment groups, preventing systematic bias. Replication provides an estimate of experimental error and increases precision, while local control (blocking) reduces variability by grouping homogeneous units. Blocking is a technique to implement local control, not the principle that equalizes unknown confounders. Therefore, the correct answer is Randomization.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: How many blocking factors are incorporated in a Latin Square Design?
questions.solution: A Latin Square Design extends the randomized block idea to two blocking factors. It arranges treatments in a square grid so that each treatment appears exactly once in each row and each column, thereby controlling for two sources of heterogeneity (e.g., row and column effects). A completely randomized design has no blocking factors, a randomized block design has one blocking factor, and a Latin square has two. Hence, the correct choice is Two.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: What is the primary objective of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in multivariate analysis?
questions.a: It maximizes variance explained by linear combinations
opts: It maximizes variance explained by linear combinations
It tests equality of mean vectors
It estimates factor loadings for latent variables
questions.solution: Principal Component Analysis seeks to transform a set of correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated linear combinations called principal components. The first principal component captures the maximum possible variance in the data, the second captures the maximum remaining variance subject to orthogonality, and so on. This variance‑maximization property distinguishes PCA from discriminant analysis (classification), MANOVA (testing mean vectors), and factor analysis (estimating latent factor loadings). Thus, the correct description is that PCA maximizes variance explained by linear combinations.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: According to the national accounts definitions, Net National Product (NNP) is obtained by subtracting which component from Gross National Product (GNP)?
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Net national product (NNP) subtracts depreciation from GNP." Gross National Product equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad. Net Domestic Product subtracts depreciation from GDP, while Net National Product subtracts depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) from GNP. Indirect taxes and subsidies relate to the distinction between factor cost and market prices, not to the NNP calculation. Therefore, the component subtracted from GNP to obtain NNP is Depreciation.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In a two-factor split-plot design with a completely randomised whole-plot structure, the linear model contains two error terms: whole-plot error (variance σ²_W) and subplot error (variance σ²_S). If an analyst incorrectly pools these two error strata into a single error term for all F-tests, what is the primary consequence for the whole-plot factor test?
questions.a: The Type I error rate for the whole-plot factor is inflated above the nominal level.
opts: The test becomes conservative, reducing power but maintaining the nominal Type I error rate.
The test statistic follows a non-central F-distribution under the null hypothesis.
The Type I error rate for the whole-plot factor is inflated above the nominal level.
The denominator degrees of freedom increase, making the test more sensitive to subplot effects.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "Ignoring this hierarchy inflates Type I error for the whole-plot factor." In a split-plot design, the whole-plot factor must be tested against the whole-plot mean square (MS_W), which has fewer degrees of freedom and typically larger variance than the subplot mean square (MS_S). Pooling the errors replaces MS_W with the smaller MS_S (or a pooled MS), making the F-ratio larger than it should be. This leads to rejecting the null hypothesis too often, i.e., inflated Type I error. Option A is incorrect because the test becomes anti-conservative, not conservative. Option B describes the distribution under the alternative, not the consequence of pooling. Option D is incorrect because while denominator df may increase, the problem is the wrong error variance, not increased sensitivity.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Consider the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test for a unit root in a time series y_t. The test regression is Δy_t = α + β t + (ρ-1)y_{t-1} + Σ_{i=1}^p γ_i Δy_{t-i} + ε_t. Which of the following statements about the ADF test is correct?
questions.a: The lagged differences Δy_{t-1} … Δy_{t-p} are included to absorb serial correlation in ε_t.
opts: The null hypothesis is ρ = 0 (stationarity) and the alternative is ρ < 0.
Critical values for the t-statistic on (ρ-1) are taken from the standard t-distribution tables.
The lagged differences Δy_{t-1} … Δy_{t-p} are included to absorb serial correlation in ε_t.
The test is valid only when the series has no deterministic trend (β = 0).
questions.solution: The lesson states: "The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test regresses Δy_t on y_{t-1} and lagged differences Δy_{t-1} … Δy_{t-p} to absorb serial correlation." This is the precise purpose of the augmentation terms. Option A is incorrect: the null is ρ = 1 (unit root), not ρ = 0; the alternative is ρ < 1 (stationarity). Option B is incorrect: the test statistic has a non-standard distribution (Dickey-Fuller tables), not the standard t-distribution. Option D is incorrect: the ADF test can include a deterministic trend (β t) in the regression; the critical values differ for models with/without trend, but the test remains valid.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the Rao-Wu bootstrap for stratified multistage sampling, the replicate weight for unit i in replicate r is given by w_i^{(r)} = w_i × (m_h / (m_h - 1)) × I(i ∈ PSU_h^{(r)}), where m_h is the number of PSUs in stratum h. Why must the calibration step (e.g., post-stratification or raking) be repeated independently within each bootstrap replicate?
questions.a: To ensure the variability introduced by the calibration process itself is captured in the variance estimate.
opts: To reduce the computational burden by using the same calibrated weights across replicates.
To ensure the variability introduced by the calibration process itself is captured in the variance estimate.
To satisfy the finite population correction factor (1-f) required for large sampling fractions.
To maintain the original inclusion probabilities of the PSUs in each stratum.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "The bootstrap must replicate the calibration step in each replicate: recompute calibrated weights w_i^{(r)} using the same control totals. This ensures that the variability from calibration is captured." Calibration adjusts weights to match known population totals; this adjustment is a random process that depends on the specific sample. If calibration is done only once on the original sample and those weights are used for all replicates, the additional variability from re-calibrating each replicate sample is ignored, leading to underestimation of the true variance. Option A is opposite to the correct reasoning. Option C refers to a separate issue (finite population correction). Option D is about the bootstrap sampling design, not the calibration step.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In a Central Composite Design (CCD) with k factors, the axial distance α required for rotatability is given by which expression?
questions.solution: The lesson states that for a Central Composite Design (CCD), rotatability requires α = (2^k)^(1/4). This is the fourth root of 2 raised to the power k. Option A matches this exactly. Option B gives the square root, Option C omits the base 2, and Option D incorrectly places the exponent as k/4 on base 2 rather than the fourth root of 2^k.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For the Arellano–Bond first-difference GMM estimator, the moment conditions E[y_is · Δε_it] = 0 are valid for which range of s?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states: "The moment conditions are E[y_is · Δε_it] = 0 for s ≤ t-2." This is because lagged levels y_it-2, y_it-3, ... serve as instruments for Δy_it-1 under the assumption that ε_it is serially uncorrelated. Using s ≤ t-1 would include y_it-1 which is correlated with Δε_it = ε_it - ε_it-1. Options C and D are incorrect ranges.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The Prasad–Rao estimator of the Mean Squared Error (MSE) for the Fay–Herriot EBLUP includes an additional term compared to the naive MSE estimator. This term accounts for:
questions.a: the variability of the estimated variance component σ̂_v^2
opts: the variability of the estimated variance component σ̂_v^2
the bias in the sampling variances σ_e,i^2
the correlation between area-specific random effects
questions.solution: The lesson states: "Candidates must derive the EBLUP weight γ_i, write the REML log-likelihood for the area-level model, and explain why the Prasad–Rao estimator includes a term for the variability of σ̂_v^2." The Prasad-Rao MSE estimator adds a term that captures the uncertainty from estimating the variance component σ_v^2 (the between-area variance), which the naive MSE estimator ignores by treating σ_v^2 as known. Options B, C, and D are not mentioned as the specific reason for the additional term in the Prasad-Rao estimator.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: According to Rubin's rules for combining m imputed datasets, the total variance T for a scalar estimand is given by which formula?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly provides Rubin's rules: "the overall estimate θ̄ = (1/m) Σ θ̂^(k), total variance T = W + (1+1/m)B, where W = (1/m) Σ U^(k) is the within-imputation variance and B = (1/(m-1)) Σ (θ̂^(k) - θ̄)^2 is the between-imputation variance." Option A matches this formula exactly. The factor (1+1/m) inflates the between-imputation variance B to account for the finite number of imputations m. Options B, C, and D incorrectly specify the weighting of W and B.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In calibration estimation, which distance function guarantees positive calibrated weights?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the entropy distance G = Σ w_i* log(w_i*/w_i) guarantees positive weights, whereas the chi-square distance yields linear GREG weights but does not inherently guarantee positivity. The entropy formulation ensures w_i* > 0 because the log function is undefined for non-positive values, forcing the optimization to stay in the positive domain.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: What is a strict design requirement for applying Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) for variance estimation?
opts: At least three PSUs per stratum
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that BRR is applicable to stratified designs with two primary sampling units (PSUs) per stratum and requires a Hadamard matrix of appropriate order. It is a common error to assume BRR works for any stratified design; it strictly requires exactly two PSUs per stratum.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In propensity score weighting for nonresponse adjustment, what do extreme weights typically indicate?
questions.solution: The lesson highlights that using propensity score weights without checking overlap (common support) is a mistake. Extreme weights indicate violations of the positivity assumption (i.e., some units have near-zero probability of response), which inflates variance and destabilizes estimates.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: When applying the Laplace mechanism for differential privacy, the global sensitivity must be defined as:
questions.a: The maximum possible change over all neighboring datasets
opts: The sample standard deviation of the query
The maximum possible change over all neighboring datasets
The variance of the estimator in the sample
The range of the variable in the sample
questions.solution: The lesson warns against computing global sensitivity on the sample rather than the population. For differential privacy, sensitivity must be the maximum possible change in the query output over all pairs of neighboring datasets (differing by one record), ensuring the privacy guarantee holds universally, not just for the observed sample.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: What is the primary consequence of violating the Conditional Independence Assumption (CIA) in statistical matching (data fusion)?
questions.a: Biased joint distributions and invalid inference
opts: Biased joint distributions and invalid inference
questions.solution: The lesson states that under CIA (Y ⟂ Z | X), the joint distribution factorizes as f(y,z|x) = f(y|x)f(z|x). It explicitly warns that assuming CIA holds without testing leads to biased joint distributions and invalid inference when the assumption is violated, as the synthetic matching no longer reflects the true relationship between Y and Z given X.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Compared with the Fay–Herriot EBLUP, the Bayesian hierarchical modeling approach for small-area estimation:
questions.a: Avoids the need for analytic MSE approximations and handles non–Gaussian models without linearization.
opts: Requires analytic mean squared error approximations for each domain.
Cannot accommodate non–Gaussian sampling models such as binomial proportions.
Avoids the need for analytic MSE approximations and handles non–Gaussian models without linearization.
Provides only point estimates without a natural measure of uncertainty.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the Bayesian approach avoids the need for analytic MSE approximations, handles non–Gaussian sampling models (e.g., binomial for proportions) without linearization, and permits informative priors. Option C captures these advantages exactly, while A and B describe limitations of the EBLUP, and D is false because the posterior variance provides a natural uncertainty measure.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the Kalman filter, missing observations in the time series are handled by:
questions.a: Skipping the update step for that time point.
opts: Imputing the missing value with the one–step–ahead prediction.
Skipping the update step for that time point.
Setting the measurement error variance to zero.
Restarting the filter with a diffuse prior.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly notes that missing observations are handled naturally by skipping the update step. The prediction step still propagates the state forward, but no measurement update occurs. Options A, C, and D describe ad–hoc or incorrect procedures not mentioned in the text.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: After performing propensity score matching, a researcher must:
questions.a: Check covariate balance in the matched sample using standardized differences.
opts: Assume that the propensity score balancing property guarantees covariate balance.
Check covariate balance in the matched sample using standardized differences.
Use the estimated propensity scores as covariates in a regression model.
Discard the propensity scores and rely solely on the matching algorithm.
questions.solution: The lesson warns against confusing the propensity score balancing property with actual covariate balance in the matched sample and states that balance must be checked after matching. Option B reflects this required diagnostic step, whereas A repeats the misconception, and C and D describe unrelated or incorrect practices.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The de–biased (de–sparsified) Lasso obtains asymptotically normal estimates for valid confidence intervals by:
questions.a: Adding a correction term that involves an estimate of the precision matrix.
opts: Increasing the tuning parameter λ until the model is sparse.
Adding a correction term that involves an estimate of the precision matrix.
Using the Lasso coefficient estimates directly without further adjustment.
Applying the bootstrap to the selected model.
questions.solution: The lesson describes the de–biased Lasso as β̂_db = β̂_Lasso + Θ̂ X'(y − Xβ̂_Lasso)/n where Θ̂ approximates the precision matrix, yielding asymptotically normal estimates. This correction term is the key innovation; options A, C, and D do not represent the de–biasing mechanism.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: For a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model with precision matrix Q = τ(D − ρW), the model is proper (i.e., defines a valid probability distribution) if the spatial dependence parameter ρ satisfies:
questions.a: ρ ∈ (1/λ_min , 1/λ_max) where λ_min and λ_max are the extreme eigenvalues of D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}.
opts: ρ ∈ (1/λ_min , 1/λ_max) where λ_min and λ_max are the extreme eigenvalues of D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}.
questions.solution: The lesson states the propriety condition as ρ ∈ (1/λ_min , 1/λ_max). This interval ensures the precision matrix is positive definite. Options A, C, and D are either too restrictive or incorrect and do not match the eigenvalue–based condition given in the text.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In a generalized linear model with a Poisson response distribution, which link function is the canonical link?
questions.solution: The canonical link for a Poisson GLM is the log link because the Poisson distribution belongs to the exponential family with natural parameter θ = log(μ). The canonical link equates the linear predictor η to the natural parameter, giving η = log(μ). This simplifies the score equations since the sufficient statistic equals the linear predictor. The identity link is canonical for the normal distribution, logit for binomial, and probit is not a canonical link for any standard exponential family member.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: The variance of the Kaplan–Meier estimator of the survivor function at a given time t is commonly estimated using which formula?
questions.solution: Greenwood’s formula provides the standard non‑parametric variance estimator for the Kaplan–Meier survivor function. It is derived from the product‑limit representation and uses the observed numbers of events d_i and numbers at risk n_i at each event time: Var(Ŝ(t)) = Ŝ(t)² Σ_{t_i ≤ t} d_i / [n_i (n_i − d_i)]. The delta method, bootstrap, and jackknife are alternative approaches but Greenwood’s formula is the classic closed‑form estimator taught in survival analysis.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: When a symmetric kernel smoother is applied at the edges of the predictor range, what specific problem arises?
questions.solution: Kernel estimators suffer from boundary bias because the symmetric kernel assigns weight to observations outside the data range, effectively using fewer data points on one side of the target point. This asymmetry in the effective kernel leads to a biased estimate of the regression function at the boundaries. The bias does not vanish even as the bandwidth shrinks, unless a boundary correction (e.g., reflection, local linear fitting) is applied. Increased variance, overfitting, and multicollinearity are separate issues not specific to the boundary.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In the leapfrog integrator used by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, what is the correct sequence of updates for one step of size ε?
questions.a: Momentum half‑step, position full‑step, momentum half‑step
opts: Momentum half‑step, position full‑step, momentum half‑step
Position half‑step, momentum full‑step, position half‑step
questions.solution: The leapfrog (Verlet) integrator preserves volume and reversibility by alternating half‑step momentum updates with a full‑step position update. Starting from (θ_t, p_t), first update momentum by half step: p_{t+ε/2} = p_t + (ε/2) ∇ log π(θ_t). Then update position using the new momentum: θ_{t+ε} = θ_t + ε M⁻¹ p_{t+ε/2}. Finally complete the momentum update: p_{t+ε} = p_{t+ε/2} + (ε/2) ∇ log π(θ_{t+ε}). This symmetric scheme yields high acceptance probabilities.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Stacking combines predictions from multiple models by determining weights that solve which optimization problem?
questions.a: Minimize the cross‑validation prediction error of the combined predictor subject to non‑negative weights summing to one
opts: Minimize the Bayesian Information Criterion of the combined model
Minimize the cross‑validation prediction error of the combined predictor subject to non‑negative weights summing to one
Maximize the posterior model probabilities derived from BIC approximations
Minimize the Akaike Information Criterion of the combined model
questions.solution: Stacking directly targets predictive performance. The stacking weights w_m are obtained by solving a constrained quadratic programming problem: minimize ‖y − Σ_m w_m ŷ_m‖² subject to w_m ≥ 0 and Σ_m w_m = 1, where ŷ_m are the cross‑validated predictions from each candidate model. This minimizes the estimated out‑of‑sample prediction error of the combined predictor. BIC or AIC weighting uses information criteria approximations to posterior model probabilities, which is a different model‑averaging approach.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: In Functional Data Analysis, what is a key distinction between the Karhunen–Loève expansion and a standard PCA applied to discretized data?
questions.a: The Karhunen–Loève expansion uses the continuous covariance operator and yields orthogonal eigenfunctions, while standard PCA on discretized data depends on the grid.
opts: The Karhunen–Loève expansion uses the continuous covariance operator and yields orthogonal eigenfunctions, while standard PCA on discretized data depends on the grid.
The Karhunen–Loève expansion requires discrete observations, while standard PCA works with continuous functions.
Standard PCA yields eigenfunctions that are orthogonal in L2, while the Karhunen–Loève expansion does not guarantee orthogonality.
The Karhunen–Loève expansion is only applicable to Fourier bases, whereas standard PCA works with any basis.
questions.solution: The Karhunen–Loève expansion represents a random function in the Hilbert space L2(T) using the continuous covariance operator C(s,t). Its eigenfunctions φk are orthogonal functions derived from the integral equation ∫C(s,t)φk(s)ds = λkφk(t). In contrast, standard PCA on discretized data operates on a finite grid; the resulting eigenvectors depend on the specific discretization points and do not represent continuous orthogonal functions. The lesson explicitly warns against confusing these two approaches, noting that the former uses the continuous covariance operator and yields orthogonal eigenfunctions, while the latter depends on the grid. Therefore, option A correctly captures this distinction.
questions.subject: Statistics

questions.q: Tamil belongs to which language family?
questions.solution: Tamil is Dravidian.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: Which script is used for Tamil?
questions.solution: Tamil is written in Tamil script.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: When was Tamil included in the Eighth Schedule?
questions.solution: Tamil: It is one of the original Eighth Schedule languages (1950) and was declared a classical language in 2004.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: Who wrote Thirukkural?
questions.solution: Thirukkural is by Thiruvalluvar.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: Which of the following is a major period or movement in Tamil literature?
questions.solution: Sangam literature is a major movement/period in Tamil literature.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: According to the provided lesson, how should the term 'Sangam' be interpreted in the context of Tamil literary studies?
questions.a: A literary tradition or period of intense poetic activity spanning several centuries.
opts: A precise historical event where poets gathered at a specific location in Madurai.
A single moment in time when the eight anthologies were composed simultaneously.
A literary tradition or period of intense poetic activity spanning several centuries.
An archaeological site discovered during excavations in ancient Tamil Nadu.
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly states that treating 'Sangam' as a precise historical event or specific gathering place is a persistent misconception. Evidence suggests it refers to a literary tradition or period of intense activity spanning roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE, rather than a single moment. The texts display linguistic transitions from Old Tamil to Middle Tamil over this span, indicating a continuum of production. Therefore, interpreting it as a specific location or simultaneous event contradicts the textual and linguistic evidence presented in the lesson.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: Which of the following best explains the fragmentation of the Sangam corpus, where only four anthologies are substantially preserved?
questions.a: A deliberate thematic bias in transmission that favored political and heroic texts over nature poetry.
opts: The texts were deliberately destroyed by invading armies to erase Tamil history.
Natural decay of manuscripts over a period of 600 years without human intervention.
A deliberate thematic bias in transmission that favored political and heroic texts over nature poetry.
The original eight anthologies were written on perishable materials that could not survive the monsoons.
questions.solution: The lesson clarifies that the fragmentation is not merely an accident of preservation but reflects a deliberate thematic bias. The surviving Purananuru and Akananuru focus heavily on war, kingship, heroism (Viram), and political ethics (Aram-Porul). In contrast, the lost anthologies likely contained nature poetry, love lyrics, and pastoral scenes. This suggests later editors or patrons valued martial virtue over pastoral tranquility, leading to a survivorship bias where 'political' and 'heroic' texts were preserved while others were lost.
questions.subject: Tamil Literature

questions.q: In the context of Tolkappiyam, what does the distinction between 'Ettolkaappiyam' and 'Purattolkaappiyam' indicate about the text's composition?
questions.a: That the sections may not have been composed simultaneously or by a single author, reflecting different literary developments.
opts: That the entire text was composed by a single author named Tolkappiyar in one sitting.
That the sections were composed simultaneously to provide a unified rulebook for all Tamil speakers.
That the sections may not have been composed simultaneously or by a single author, reflecting different literary developments.
That 'Ettolkaappiyam' deals with poetics while 'Purattolkaappiyam' deals with phonology.
questions.solution: The lesson states that textual criticism suggests the three parts of Tolkappiyam (Ettolkaappiyam, Ettokai, Purattolkaappiyam) may not have been composed simultaneously or by a single author. 'Ettolkaappiyam' deals with phonology and syntax for Old Tamil, while 'Purattolkaappiyam' introduces concepts like Akal and Alankara reflective of later literary developments. This internal inconsistency indicates the text is a dynamic document that evolved, rather than a monolithic work composed at one time.

questions.q: The Tamil Lexicon (1924-1939) adopted a philological principle of 'chronological layering' for its entries. This methodology primarily implies that:

The Lexicon includes Sanskrit loanwords with Tamilised phonology (e.g., arakkam from arakṣa) and draws from over 1,200 source texts including both literary and inscriptional evidence, not just centamiḻ. The chronological layering principle is about dating senses historically, not about alphabetical arrangement.

Applying Sanskrit rasa theory uncritically to Tamil akam poetics without accounting for Tolkāppiyam's framework

Its main purpose was to promote Sanskritized vocabulary and diction among the educated middle class.
questions.solution: Gurajada Apparao's Kanyasulkam was not merely a story but a direct intervention in social structures. It served as a legal and moral indictment of the dowry system by exposing its evils through a tragic narrative. questions.q: Regarding the concept of 'Vrittam' (verse) versus 'Gadyam' (prose) in Telugu literature, which observation correctly identifies an exception to the general rule of genre evolution?
questions.a: Early prose was often poetic in nature (poetic prose), while later poetry adopted prose-like syntax for realism.
opts: Early prose was often poetic in nature (poetic prose), while later poetry adopted prose-like syntax for realism.
All early prose works strictly followed Sanskrit metrics and lacked any narrative flexibility or influence from English literature.
Later poetry completely abandoned Sanskrit loan words, resulting in a vocabulary that contained no Dravidian roots whatsoever.
The distinction between verse and prose remained rigid throughout history with no fluid boundaries or exceptions ever occurring.
questions.solution: An exception to the general rule is found in the fluid boundaries between genres. Early prose was often poetic in nature (poetic prose), while later poetry adopted prose-like syntax for realism. Additionally, poets switched from verse to prose due to the need for greater narrative flexibility and the influence of English literature.

questions.a: It should be interpreted metaphorically as 'illusion' or 'maya' to shift focus from escapism to spiritual detachment.
opts: It should be translated literally as 'earth' to ground the poem and avoid metaphysical elevation.
It should be interpreted metaphorically as 'illusion' or 'maya' to shift focus from escapism to spiritual detachment.
It must be analyzed only in its literal sense because any metaphorical interpretation constitutes an error in translation.
The word should be ignored entirely as it serves no structural purpose in the sher-e-oopar.
questions.solution: The lesson's solution strategy for analyzing semantic shift suggests discussing how a translator might render 'duniya' as 'illusion' (maya) rather than just 'earth'. This metaphorical interpretation shifts the focus from escapism to spiritual detachment. The conclusion in the text argues that Ghalib's genius lies in the tension between literal and metaphorical readings, but the specific technique for analysis involves exploring the metaphorical shift. Option 1 correctly identifies this analytical step described in the lesson, whereas Option 0 suggests a rigid literalism contrary to the 'advanced' approach of exploring ambiguity.

questions.q: In the context of classical Urdu ghazal structure, what is the primary structural function of the 'maqta' compared to the preceding sher s?
questions.a: It provides a thematic closure or meta-commentary, often shifting from emotional turbulence to equilibrium.
opts: It serves as the opening couplet that establishes the radif for the entire poem.
It acts merely as a signature containing the poet's pen-name without thematic weight.
It provides a thematic closure or meta-commentary, often shifting from emotional turbulence to equilibrium.
It is a mandatory section where the poet must switch from Urdu to Hindi script to signify Partition trauma.
questions.solution: The lesson states that the ghazal relies on a dual mechanism of radif and qaafiya. The maqta is specifically defined as the final couplet serving a unique structural function beyond just being an ending. It acts as a signature containing the takhallus (pen-name) and often provides a thematic summary or meta-commentary. Crucially, it signals a transition from the emotional turbulence of earlier sher s to a state of equilibrium. Option A is incorrect because the maqta is the final couplet, not the opening one. Option B is incorrect because the text explicitly attributes thematic weight (resignation, acceptance) to Mir's maqtas. Option D conflates the concept of hybridity in Partition narratives with the structural rules of classical ghazal.
questions.subject: Urdu Literature

questions.q: How does the 'Logic of Discontinuity' in a ghazal fundamentally differ from the narrative structure of a masnavi?
questions.a: In a ghazal, every couplet must stand alone as a complete unit with internal logic, unlike the masnavi's continuous thread.
opts: A ghazal requires a continuous narrative thread, whereas a masnavi consists of standalone couplets.
A masnavi relies on a recurring radif, while a ghazal does not use any repeating words.
In a ghazal, every couplet must stand alone as a complete unit with internal logic, unlike the masnavi's continuous thread.
The masnavi uses qaafiya-based rhyming, whereas the ghazal relies solely on Sufi metaphors.
questions.solution: The text explicitly contrasts the ghazal with the masnavi. It states that the ghazal is not merely a sequence of rhyming couplets but a construct governed by discontinuity. Every couplet in a ghazal must stand alone as a complete unit possessing its own internal logic; removing one does not destroy coherence. This stands in sharp contrast to the masnavi, which follows a continuous narrative thread. Option A reverses the definitions. Option B is incorrect because the text states the masnavi does not follow a qaafiya-based structure like the marsiya or ghazal. Option D incorrectly attributes Sufi metaphors as the sole reliance of the ghazal, ignoring the formal constraints of radif and qaafiya mentioned in the text.

questions.q: In Qurratulain Hyder's 'Aag Ka Darya', how does the concept of hybridity manifest in the characters' self-perception and language?
questions.a: Hybridity is experienced as traumatic loss and liminality, where characters are neither fully Indian nor fully Pakistani in their self-perception.
opts: Characters celebrate a creative fusion of Hindi and Urdu scripts as a positive cultural achievement.
The river serves as a metaphor for linguistic mixing, but characters feel fully Indian or fully Pakistani.
Hybridity is experienced as traumatic loss and liminality, where characters are neither fully Indian nor fully Pakistani in their self-perception.
The text depicts hybridity solely through code-switching between English and Persian idioms without affecting cultural identity.
questions.solution: The lesson defines hybridity in Partition narratives as extending beyond linguistic mixing to the fracturing of identity and memory. In 'Aag Ka Darya', the river metaphorically flows through changing territories carrying sediment from one culture to another. Crucially, the text states that this literary hybridity is distinct from Western theory because it is often traumatic, not a celebrated fusion. Characters embody a liminal space, being neither fully Indian nor fully Pakistani. Option A contradicts the text which says it is not celebrated as creative fusion. Option B contradicts the 'liminal space' description. Option D is incomplete as it ignores the profound cultural and identity trauma described.

questions.q: When analyzing Faiz Ahmed Faiz's modernist prose or poetry, how does the 'Architecture of Ambiguity' utilizing Sufi metaphor function?
questions.a: It blurs the boundary between literal and metaphorical meanings to allow political oppression to be discussed through spiritual imagery.
opts: It strictly adheres to linear narrative progression to ensure clarity for the reader.
It blurs the boundary between literal and metaphorical meanings to allow political oppression to be discussed through spiritual imagery.
It requires the reader to choose between a literal meaning of 'black night' and a symbolic meaning, never allowing both simultaneously.
It replaces Sufi metaphysics entirely with Western existentialist philosophy to avoid ambiguity.
questions.solution: The text explains that modernist Urdu literature borrows from Sufi metaphysics to create an architecture of ambiguity challenging linear narrative. In Faiz's work, the boundary between lover and beloved is blurred to represent the relationship between the human soul and the Divine or Nation. This allows discussing political oppression using spiritual imagery. The text explicitly states that in Faiz's work, literal and metaphorical layers are often simultaneous (e.g., 'black night' referring to both prison darkness and metaphysical despair). Option A contradicts the 'challenging linear narrative' aspect. Option C is incorrect because the text says layers are simultaneous, not mutually exclusive choices. Option D is incorrect as it claims Sufi metaphysics are replaced, whereas the text says they are borrowed from.

questions.q: The classical Urdu marsiya is composed in which metrical form, consisting of six‑foot lines arranged in six‑hemistich stanzas with a fixed radif‑qafiya scheme?
questions.solution: The lesson states that the marsiya’s classical structure follows a fixed stanzaic pattern of six hemistichs (misra) employing the musaddas metre (six‑foot line). Masnavi is a rhymed couplet form used for narrative poetry, ghazal is a lyric form with independent couplets, and rubai is a quatrain. Only musaddas matches the described six‑foot, six‑hemistich stanza with consistent radif and qafiya.

questions.q: Which scholar institutionalised Urdu literary historiography through the Anjuman Taraqqi‑e‑Urdu and the journal "Urdu", establishing the "four pillars" canon of Ghalib, Mir, Sauda and Zauq?
questions.solution: According to the lesson, Shibli Nomani initiated critical historiography, but his associate Abdul Haq institutionalised the discipline via the Anjuman Taraqqi‑e‑Urdu and the journal Urdu, fixing a canon that privileged the "four pillars" and marginalised regional and women writers. Sajjad Zaheer represents the Marxist Progressive Writers’ approach, while Gopi Chand Narang later applied New Criticism.

questions.q: In the comparative study of Sufi orders’ influence on Urdu poetic imagery, which order is associated with ecstatic motifs (such as sama‘ and wajd) as opposed to the Qadiri emphasis on annihilation (fana) symbols?
questions.solution: The lesson explicitly distinguishes Chishti ecstatic motifs from Qadiri annihilation symbols. Chishti practice emphasises auditory ecstasy (sama‘) and emotional states (wajd), which appear as ecstatic imagery in poetry, whereas Qadiri symbolism centres on fana (annihilation) and baqa (subsistence). Naqshbandi and Suhrawardi are not mentioned in this comparative framework.
